true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate downsize method definitions with different arities create ambiguity and potential breakage

The diff adds a new `downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` method (line 149) while retaining the existing `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` (line 145). Ruby will use the last defined method when arities match, but having two methods with the same name and overlapping arities (both accept 4-5 arguments) is confusing and fragile. The old 4-argument form `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height)` will now call the new method with `dimensions = max_width` and `opts = max_height` (an Integer), causing `"#{max_width}x#{max_height}"` to never be constructed — instead `dimensions` (an Integer) is passed to `optimize`, which passes it to `downsize_instructions` where it is interpolated as `#{dimensions}\>`, producing e.g. `100\>` instead of `100x100\>`. This silently breaks any existing caller using the old 4-argument form. The old method should be removed or renamed, and all callers updated to use the new dimensions-string form.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client-side upload size validation hardcoded to 10MB, ignoring site settings and diverging from server-side limit

The client-side validation in `validateUploadedFile` now hardcodes `maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024` (10MB), replacing the previous `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`. This means the client will allow uploads up to 10MB regardless of the site's configured `max_image_size_kb` or `max_attachment_size_kb`. If an admin sets `max_image_size_kb` to 500KB, the client will still permit a 9MB upload, which will then be processed by the server (downloaded, downsized up to 5 times) before being rejected or accepted. This wastes server resources and provides a poor user experience (upload appears to proceed, then fails or is unexpectedly downsized). The client-side check should use the site setting, or at minimum the server-side limit should be communicated to the client. The hardcoded value also affects attachments, which may have a different limit.

true_positives.golden_comment: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
In-place downsize of tempfile corrupts file and breaks subsequent Upload.create_for which reads tempfile.size

`OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", ...)` writes the converted image to the same path as the input. ImageMagick's `convert` with identical input and output paths is undefined/unsafe — it can truncate or corrupt the file because the output file is opened before the input is fully read. Even if it works in some ImageMagick versions, after the loop `tempfile.size` (line 72) is called on the original Tempfile object, which may have a stale cached size from before the in-place modification, causing `Upload.create_for` to record an incorrect filesize in the database. The downsized file should be written to a separate temp path, and the tempfile reference updated, or the size re-read from disk after downsizing.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.

false_positives.candidate:
413 error handler hardcodes 10MB instead of using site setting, showing wrong limit to user

In `displayErrorForUpload`, the 413 (Payload Too Large) handler now hardcodes `maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024` instead of `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb`. When the web server (nginx/Apache) rejects an upload with 413, the user sees an error message stating the limit is 10MB, even if the site's actual configured limit is different (e.g., 500KB). This is misleading and was previously using the correct site setting. The hardcoded value should be reverted to use the site setting, or the message should not display a specific limit when it cannot be determined accurately.

API URL download limit changed from max_image_size_kb to hardcoded 10MB, allowing downloads of files that will be rejected or cause processing issues

The API URL download limit was changed from `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` to a hardcoded `10.megabytes`. This means the server will now download up to 10MB from an arbitrary user-supplied URL (SSRF surface is pre-existing, but the size limit change matters), and then the downsizing loop attempts to reduce it. If `max_image_size_kb` is set to e.g. 500KB, the server downloads 10MB, then runs up to 5 ImageMagick conversions on a potentially huge image. The hardcoded 10MB also ignores the site's configured maximum image size entirely for the download step. The download limit should remain tied to `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb` (or a separate, explicit setting) to avoid downloading files that are far larger than what will be accepted.

Downsize condition checks FileHelper.is_image?(filename) but filename may be nil or misleading for URL-based uploads

For API URL uploads, `filename = File.basename(URI.parse(url).path)` (line 56). If the URL has no path (e.g., `http://example.com`), `URI.parse(url).path` returns `""`, and `File.basename("")` returns `""`. Then `FileHelper.is_image?("")` likely returns false, so downsizing is skipped — but the downloaded content might actually be an image. Conversely, if the URL path ends with `.png` but the content is not an image (or is a malicious file), `is_image?` returns true and ImageMagick will attempt to process it. The check should be based on the actual file content (magic bytes) or the downloaded file's detected type, not just the filename extension from the URL. Additionally, `FileHelper.is_image?` may not exist or may behave differently than expected — the code should verify the method exists and handles edge cases.

Downsize loop runs in deferred job without timeout, potentially blocking worker for extended period

When `synchronous` is false (the default for non-API requests), `create_upload` runs inside `Scheduler::Defer.later` (line 19). The downsizing loop can invoke ImageMagick up to 5 times on a large image. ImageMagick `convert` on a very large image (e.g., 10000x10000 pixels) can take tens of seconds or minutes per invocation. There is no timeout on the `convert_with` shell command (line 161 in optimized_image.rb: `` `#{instructions.join(" ")} &> /dev/null` ``), so a single malicious upload could tie up a background worker for an extended period, potentially causing job queue backup. The shell command should have a timeout (e.g., using `Timeout.timeout` around the backtick execution, or ImageMagick's own `-limit` options), and the overall downsizing operation should be bounded.

Downsize loop runs on any image upload regardless of user permissions, enabling CPU-exhaustion DoS

The downsizing loop executes for every image upload when `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb > 0`, with up to 5 ImageMagick `convert` invocations per upload. ImageMagick conversion is CPU-intensive. A malicious user (or bot) can upload many large images (up to the 10MB download limit for API URL fetches, or whatever the web server accepts for direct uploads) to trigger repeated expensive image processing, consuming server CPU and potentially causing denial of service. There is no rate limiting, no check on image dimensions before processing (a 10MB image could be 20000x20000 pixels, making each convert extremely expensive), and no queueing — this runs synchronously in the request (or deferred job) without bounds on pixel count. The loop should check image dimensions first and reject images that are absurdly large, and/or limit total processing time.

Downsize loop uses file size as proxy for image dimensions, causing infinite/ineffective resizing for already-small large files

The condition `while attempt > 0 && tempfile.size > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` downsizes based on file size, but `OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", ...)` reduces dimensions by 80%, not file size proportionally. A high-resolution but already-compressed image (e.g., a 9MB JPEG that is 2000x2000) will be resized to 1600x1600, which may still be > max_image_size_kb in bytes, causing repeated downsizing up to 5 attempts (down to ~33% of original dimensions) even though the image dimensions are already reasonable. Conversely, a small-dimension but poorly-compressed image may loop unnecessarily. More critically, the loop can exit with `tempfile.size` still > `max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` after 5 attempts, and the upload proceeds anyway via `Upload.create_for` — there is no check that the downsize actually succeeded in bringing the file under the limit, so the original intent (allow large images by auto-reducing them) is not enforced; the upload will then likely fail at the `Upload` model validation level with a confusing error, or worse, bypass the intended size restriction if validation is missing. The loop should verify the result and reject the upload if the file is still too large after downsizing attempts.

Shell command injection risk in convert_with via unsanitized file paths

The `convert_with` method executes a shell command via backticks: `` `#{instructions.join(" ")} &> /dev/null` ``. The `instructions` array includes `from` and `to` paths that originate from user-controlled data — in the new `uploads_controller.rb` code, `tempfile.path` is passed as both `from` and `to` to `OptimizedImage.downsize`. While Tempfile paths are generally safe (generated by Ruby), the `from` path in other callers (e.g., `OptimizedImage.create_for` line 31: `Discourse.store.path_for(upload)`) derives from upload filenames which are user-controlled. If a filename contains shell metacharacters (e.g., `;`, `` ` ``, `$()`), and the path is not properly escaped in the `convert`/`gifsicle` command construction, this could lead to command injection. The `resize_instructions` and `downsize_instructions` methods interpolate `#{from}` and `#{to}` directly into the command array without shell escaping. This is a pre-existing risk but is amplified by the new code path that passes tempfile paths directly. The instructions should use `Shellwords.escape` on all path arguments, or better, use `Open3`/`system` with array arguments to avoid shell interpretation entirely.

content_type is nil for API URL uploads, causing Upload.create_for to receive nil content_type

When the upload comes via API URL (`file.nil? && url.present? && is_api?`), `content_type` is never assigned (it is only set in the `else` branch at line 60). The downsizing block at line 64 does not set `content_type` either. Then at line 72, `Upload.create_for(..., content_type: content_type, ...)` passes `nil` for content_type. This may cause the Upload record to have a nil or incorrect content_type, affecting how the file is served (MIME type) and potentially breaking image detection or security checks downstream. The content_type should be inferred from the downloaded file (e.g., using `FileHelper` or Marcel/mime-types) when downloading from a URL.

true_positives.golden_comment: The EmbeddableHost model's before_validation callback calls self.host.sub! to strip http://, https://, and path segments, but if self.host is nil, this raises NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
before_validation mutates nil host, crashing validation when host is blank

The `before_validation` block calls `self.host.sub!(...)` unconditionally. When `host` is nil (e.g. a create/update request with a missing `embeddable_host[host]` param, which the controller does not guard against), `nil.sub!` raises `NoMethodError`, turning a simple validation failure into a 500 error. Guard with `self.host = host.to_s` or `if host.present?` before calling `sub!`, and add a presence validation on `host` (currently only a format validation exists, which is skipped for nil/blank values depending on configuration).

true_positives.golden_comment: The update and destroy methods in Admin::EmbeddableHostsController do not validate the existence of the EmbeddableHost record retrieved by ID. If EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first returns nil (i.e., the host does not exist), attempting to call methods on the nil object (e.g., save_host or destroy) will result in a NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
update/destroy crash with NoMethodError when the host id does not exist

`update` and `destroy` do `EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first` and then call `save_host(host)` / `host.destroy` without a nil check. If the id is missing or stale (e.g. the record was deleted in another tab, or a crafted request), `host` is nil and the request raises `NoMethodError` (500 error) instead of returning a 404. `save_host` also dereferences `host.host = ...` on a possibly-nil object. Add a `raise ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound` (or render 404) when the record is not found.

true_positives.golden_comment: record_for_host compares lower(host) = ? but does not normalize the parameter’s case, so mixed‑case referer hosts may fail to match even though comparison intends to be case‑insensitive.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Referer host matching is case-sensitive and does not downcase the incoming host

`record_for_host` does `where("lower(host) = ?", host)` where `host = uri.host`. The stored column is lowered by the DB comparison, but the incoming `uri.host` is NOT downcased. `URI.parse('http://EVILTROUT.COM/x').host` preserves case, so a referer from `http://EVILTROUT.COM` will not match a stored `eviltrout.com`, and conversely the check is inconsistent with the model's own normalization. Downcase the parsed host (`host = uri.host.to_s.downcase`) before the query so matching is deterministic regardless of referer casing.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Consider ensuring that migrated hosts are normalized to the same format as newly created EmbeddableHost records so existing embedding configurations keep working.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration lacks a unique index on host and does not downcase migrated values

The migration creates `embeddable_hosts` with `host` and `category_id` but no unique index. Since `record_for_host` matches case-insensitively (`lower(host) = ?`), duplicate rows (including case variants) will silently coexist and all match — there is no DB-level guard. Also, the migrated values from the old `embeddable_hosts` site setting are inserted verbatim (`'#{h}'`) without stripping `http://` prefixes or paths (the model's `before_validation` normalization is bypassed because raw SQL INSERT is used), so a legacy value like `http://example.com/path` becomes a stored host of `http://example.com/path`, which will never match a referer (referer matching compares only `uri.host`). The migration should normalize each host (strip scheme/path, downcase) before insert and add a unique index on `lower(host)`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The contents of `category_fabricator.rb` and `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` have been swapped, resulting in the loss of original category fabricators and potentially causing errors in fabricator usage.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Category fabricators were moved into the wrong file: category_fabricator.rb now defines the embeddable_host fabricator and embeddable_host_fabricator.rb defines categories

The diff shows `spec/fabricators/category_fabricator.rb` was overwritten to contain ONLY the `Fabricator(:embeddable_host)` block, deleting the `:category`, `:diff_category`, `:happy_category`, and `:private_category` fabricators. Meanwhile `spec/fabricators/embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` (new file) contains the category fabricators. The file names are swapped relative to their contents: every spec that does `Fabricate(:category)` relies on the category fabricators being loaded (Fabrication auto-loads all files under spec/fabricators, so loading may still work), but this is a serious maintainability/correctness defect — the file named `category_fabricator.rb` no longer defines a `:category` fabricator, and `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` does not define `:embeddable_host`. Any tooling, generator, or developer that expects fabricators to live in the file matching their name (and any `require` of a specific fabricator file) breaks. The contents of the two files must be swapped back so each file defines the fabricator matching its name.

true_positives.golden_comment: The SQL query in the `app/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller.rb` file uses string interpolation (`'#{h}'`) to insert values, which is vulnerable to SQL injection. It should use parameter binding or proper quoting to prevent this security vulnerability.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
SQL injection in data migration via string interpolation of site setting values

The migration builds an INSERT statement by interpolating the raw `embeddable_hosts` site setting value directly into SQL: `execute "INSERT INTO embeddable_hosts (host, category_id, created_at, updated_at) VALUES ('#{h}', #{category_id}, ...)"`. The value comes from the `site_settings` table (previously admin-editable free text, one host per line). Any quote or SQL metacharacter in that setting (e.g. a host line containing `'); DROP TABLE ...;--`) is executed verbatim against the database during `rake db:migrate`. This is a critical SQL injection / data-integrity risk on every deployment that has the old setting populated. Use parameterized queries (`execute` with bind params, or `sanitize_sql_array`, or ActiveRecord inserts) instead of string interpolation.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The migration accesses execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking if the query returned any rows, which causes a crash when no embed_category setting exists. This can lead to a broken feature when attempting to edit category/host relationships.

false_positives.candidate:
@on('didInsertElement') combined with @observes('editing') refocuses the input on every edit toggle and on insert, stealing focus unexpectedly

The `_focusOnInput` method is decorated with both `@on('didInsertElement')` and `@observes('editing')`. The observer fires whenever `editing` changes (becoming true when entering edit mode, and again when leaving), and `didInsertElement` fires on render. When `editing` becomes false after save/cancel, the observer still runs and schedules `this.$('.host-name').focus()` — but by then the input is gone (the `{{#if editing}}` block rendered the read-only view), so `this.$('.host-name')` is empty and focus is lost (or, in a race, focus may be applied to a removed element). This causes the page focus to jump to the body after saving. The `@observes('editing')` should be guarded to only focus when entering edit mode (`if (this.get('editing'))`), or the observer should be removed in favor of focusing only on `didInsertElement` when `isNew`.

Authorization relies on redundant before_filter in addition to route constraint; ensure_staff allows moderators, route allows only admins — verify intended privilege level

The routes declare `resources :embeddable_hosts, constraints: AdminConstraint.new` (admin-only), but the controller adds `before_filter :ensure_logged_in, :ensure_staff` (staff = admins + moderators). The effective access is the intersection (admin-only via route), so moderators get 404 rather than 403. This is not a vulnerability per se, but the controller's `ensure_staff` is misleading dead weight and inconsistent with sibling admin controllers that rely on the route constraint alone (e.g. `Admin::EmbeddingController` uses `ensure_staff` too but its routes also use `AdminConstraint`). More importantly, the `create`/`update`/`destroy` actions mutate which external sites can embed and iframe forum content (a security-sensitive setting affecting X-Frame-Options / referer allowlisting); confirm admin-only is intended and remove the redundant/misleading `ensure_staff` filter, or document why moderators are filtered at the controller level but blocked at the route level.

Blank category_id silently falls back to uncategorized, masking client errors

`host.category_id = SiteSetting.uncategorized_category_id if host.category_id.blank?` silently converts a missing/invalid category selection into the uncategorized category. If the admin UI sends `category_id` as an empty string (e.g. the category chooser not initialized — see the `edit()` finding where `categoryId` can be undefined), the host is saved pointing at uncategorized without any error, so embedded posts land in the wrong category with no feedback. This should either be a validation error when `category_id` is blank on create, or at minimum the fallback should only apply when the param is absent, not when it's an invalid/nonexistent id. Also, `uncategorized_category_id` is typically a negative sentinel (-1) that may not correspond to a real Category row, so `belongs_to :category` will be nil and the badge renders blank.

Controller specs only assert inheritance; no tests for create/update/destroy behavior, authorization, or validation errors

Both new controller specs (`Admin::EmbeddableHostsController` and `Admin::EmbeddingController`) contain a single test asserting the class is a subclass of `Admin::AdminController`. There are no tests covering: successful host creation/update/destroy, rejection of non-staff users, handling of missing/invalid host params (which currently 500 due to the nil-host bug in the model), the nil-record 404 path in update/destroy, or the embedding show/update serialization shape. Given these endpoints mutate security-sensitive embed allowlisting, the test coverage is inadequate — the existing bugs (nil host crash, missing record crash) would not be caught.

Embedded topic category now comes from EmbeddableHost, but when no host matches, category is nil and PostCreator may create an uncategorized topic or fail

`TopicEmbed.import` now does `eh = EmbeddableHost.record_for_host(url)` and passes `category: eh.try(:category_id)` to `PostCreator`. When the URL's host is not in the allowlist (which can happen because `TopicRetriever#invalid_host?` gates retrieval, but `TopicEmbed.import` is also called directly from feed polling `Jobs::PollFeed` and potentially other paths that may not check the allowlist first), `eh` is nil/false and `category` is nil. `PostCreator` with a nil category will create a topic in the uncategorized category (or fail validation if `allow_uncategorized_topics` is false and the user is not staff). Previously the category came from the global `SiteSetting.embed_category` which always had a value. The behavior change means feed-polled or directly-imported embeds without a matching host silently land in uncategorized (or error). The import path should either skip import when no host matches (return nil) or fall back to a configured default category, and this should be tested.

EmbeddingSerializer embeds only ids but the client expects hydrated host objects with category

`EmbeddingSerializer` declares `has_many :embeddable_hosts, serializer: EmbeddableHostSerializer, embed: :ids`, so the JSON payload contains `embeddable_hosts: [1,2,3]` plus a side-loaded `embeddable_hosts` array. The Ember admin route does `this.store.find('embedding')`, and the store's `_hydrateEmbedded` (store.js.es6) maps `embeddable_host_ids` → `embeddable_hosts` only when the payload uses the `_ids` suffix convention with `__rest_serializer: "1"`. The serializer emits `embeddable_hosts` (already plural, ids) rather than `embeddable_host_ids`, so the client-side hydration in `_hydrateEmbedded` (which matches `/(.+)\_id(s?)$/`) will NOT fire for this key, and `embedding.embeddable_hosts` in the controller will be a plain array of integers, not model objects — the `embeddable-host` component's `host.host`, `host.category`, `host.isNew` bindings will all break. Either emit `embeddable_host_ids` with side-loaded objects (matching the rest_serializer convention used elsewhere), or embed objects directly (`embed: :objects`).

Locale string 'Allowed Hosts' is used as a table column header for a single host value, and 'Post to Category' is ambiguous

The new `admin.embedding` locale block defines `host: "Allowed Hosts"` (plural) which is used in `embedding.hbs` as the column header for an individual host value (`{{i18n "admin.embedding.host"}}` above a column of single hostnames). A column listing individual hosts should be labeled "Host" or "Allowed Host", not "Allowed Hosts". Similarly `category: "Post to Category"` describes the category that embedded topics are posted into — it is used as a column header for the category badge, so "Category" would be clearer. These are user-facing admin strings; the plural/ambiguous wording will confuse admins managing the allowlist.

Mass-assignment of arbitrary params into EmbeddableHost attributes

`save_host` assigns `host.host = params[:embeddable_host][:host]` and `host.category_id = params[:embeddable_host][:category_id]` directly from params. While the model only has `host` and `category_id` columns, this pattern bypasses strong-parameter protection and will silently accept and persist any future attribute added to the model (e.g. if a column is later added), and it does not validate that `category_id` refers to an existing category — a bogus category_id is stored, violating referential expectations (the column is `null: false` but there is no FK/validation), leaving orphaned hosts whose category badge renders nothing. Use explicit permitted params and validate the category exists.

No test for blank/nil host (which crashes before_validation) and no test for case-insensitive referer matching

The spec covers trimming http/https/paths and `host_allowed?` for exact hosts, but does not test: (1) `EmbeddableHost.new(host: nil).valid?` — which currently raises `NoMethodError` on `nil.sub!` in `before_validation` (the bug noted in the model finding); (2) case-insensitive matching (`host_allowed?('http://EVILTROUT.COM')` vs stored `eviltrout.com`) — which the current `record_for_host` implementation gets wrong because it doesn't downcase `uri.host`; (3) uniqueness — two hosts differing only by case (`Example.com` vs `example.com`) can both be saved because there is no uniqueness validation, and `lower(host) = ?` matching means they are duplicates functionally. Add a uniqueness validation (scoped with `lower`) and tests for these cases.

No uniqueness validation on host — duplicate/case-variant hosts can be created

`EmbeddableHost` validates only the format of `host`. There is no `validates_uniqueness_of :host` (case-insensitive). Because `record_for_host` matches with `lower(host) = ?`, storing both `Example.com` and `example.com` creates functionally duplicate rows that both match the same referers; the admin UI will show two rows for the same site, and deleting one still leaves embedding enabled. Add `validates_uniqueness_of :host, case_sensitive: false` (and ideally a unique index in the migration) to prevent duplicate allowlist entries.

Removing the 'embeddable hosts not set' check changes behavior: embeds are now allowed with zero configured hosts in some paths

The old code raised `Discourse::InvalidAccess.new('embeddable hosts not set') if SiteSetting.embeddable_hosts.blank?` before checking the referer. The new code only calls `EmbeddableHost.host_allowed?(request.referer)`. `host_allowed?` returns `record_for_host(host).present?`, and `record_for_host` returns `false` when the referer is nil/unparseable — so with no hosts configured the behavior is equivalent (denied). However, the explicit 'not set' guard also protected against a nil/blank referer edge case and made the failure mode explicit; more importantly, `Topic#expandable_first_post?` (app/models/topic.rb line 869) had its `SiteSetting.embeddable_hosts.present?` condition removed, so the 'expand embed' UI is now shown whenever any `TopicEmbed` exists for the topic, even if no `EmbeddableHost` rows exist at all — meaning content can be expanded/retrieved for hosts that were never approved. The gating condition should be `EmbeddableHost.exists?` (or equivalent) rather than removed entirely.

Serializer defines trivial attribute methods that just delegate to the object; also missing category object for the client

The explicit `def id; object.id; end` etc. methods are redundant — `attributes :id, :host, :category_id` already generates them. More importantly, the admin UI (`embeddable-host.hbs`) renders `{{category-badge host.category}}`, which requires a `category` object on the client model, but the serializer only emits `category_id`. The client store can hydrate `category_id` → `category` via `Discourse.Category.findById` only when the payload is processed as a rest_serializer payload with the root containing categories; the `EmbeddingSerializer` side-loads hosts but does not include a `categories` array, so `Discourse.Category.findById` may return undefined if categories aren't already loaded in the client. The serializer should either embed the category (`has_one :category` / `embed: :objects`) or the embedding payload should side-load categories, otherwise the category badge column renders blank.

Table is only rendered when embeddable_hosts is non-empty, so a new host cannot be added when the list is empty

`{{#if embedding.embeddable_hosts}}` wraps the entire `<table>` including the `{{embeddable-host}}` rows. When there are zero hosts, the table (and its header row) is not rendered at all — only the 'Add Host' button shows. When the admin clicks 'Add Host', `addHost` pushes a new record into `embedding.embeddable_hosts`, which makes the `{{#if}}` become true and the table appears — so functionally it works. However, the `{{#each}}` over a possibly plain array (see controller finding) and the conditional table mean the header only appears after the first add; more importantly, if `embeddable_hosts` is a plain array of ids (not models), `{{#if}}` is truthy for `[1,2]` but `{{embeddable-host host=host}}` receives an integer, breaking rendering. The template should render the table header unconditionally and iterate safely.

X-Frame-Options ALLOWALL is set even when the referer check fails (header set before the raise propagates in some paths)

In `ensure_embeddable`, `response.headers['X-Frame-Options'] = "ALLOWALL"` is set AFTER the `raise Discourse::InvalidAccess` guard inside the `if` block, but the `rescue URI::InvalidURIError` re-raises a new `Discourse::InvalidAccess`. When the referer is invalid, `EmbeddableHost.host_allowed?` returns false and `raise` executes before the header line — so the header is not set on denial (good). However, the header is set unconditionally for ANY request that passes the referer check, including the `count` action which returns JSON counts for arbitrary embed_urls — this is fine. The actual concern: `ALLOWALL` is a non-standard value (browsers ignore invalid X-Frame-Options values, falling back to default framing protections, but some older/other implementations may treat it permissively). More importantly, setting `ALLOWALL` (rather than removing the header or using CSP frame-ancestors) means any site can frame the content IF the referer check passes — but the referer check is the only gate, and browsers can suppress referers (privacy settings, `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`), in which case `request.referer` is nil, `host_allowed?(nil)` returns false, and access is denied — which is safe but breaks legitimate embeds for users with strict referrer policies. This is a known tradeoff; the finding is that the code sets a non-standard header value `ALLOWALL` which is not a valid X-Frame-Options directive (valid values are `DENY` and `SAMEORIGIN`); modern browsers ignore it, so the protection relies entirely on the referer check, and the header provides no real defense. Consider using CSP `frame-ancestors` with the allowlisted hosts instead.

_hydrateEmbedded plural branch maps ids but does not handle missing/undefined entries and mutates obj while iterating

The new plural branch `obj[k].map(function(id) { return self._lookupSubType(subType, type, id, root); })` assumes `obj[k]` is always an array. If a serializer emits `color_ids: null` or omits entries, `obj[k].map` throws. Additionally, `_lookupSubType` can return `undefined` (when the id isn't found in the side-loaded collection), producing an array full of `undefined` holes assigned to `obj[self.pluralize(subType)]` — downstream code doing `colors[0].get('id')` (as the new store test does) will crash. The singular branch guards with `if (hydrated)`, but the plural branch does not filter out unresolved ids. Filter out falsy results: `obj[k].map(...).filter(function(x){ return !!x; })` or similar, and guard `if (!obj[k]) { return; }`.

addHost pushes a new record into embedding.embeddable_hosts but the array may be a plain JS array of ids, not an Ember array of models

Depending on whether the store hydrates the `embeddable_hosts` relationship (see the EmbeddingSerializer finding), `this.get('embedding.embeddable_hosts')` may be a plain array of integer ids rather than an Ember.Array of `embeddable-host` models. `pushObject` is an Ember.Array method; on a plain array it throws `pushObject is not a function`, breaking the 'Add Host' button. Even when it is an Ember array, pushing a `createRecord('embeddable-host')` with no attributes creates a record with `host: undefined`; the component's `cantSave` checks `Ember.isEmpty(host)` on the buffered host string, which is correct, but the new record is immediately rendered in `editing` mode (because `host.isNew` is true) with an empty host input — acceptable — yet if the user cancels, `deleteHost` removes it from the array but the record remains in the store's identity map as a new record; this is minor. The primary risk is the type mismatch of `embeddable_hosts`.

basePath type normalization only replaces the first underscore, breaking multi-word admin model types

`type.replace('_', '-')` (without a global flag) replaces only the FIRST underscore. The `ADMIN_MODELS` list contains `'embeddable-host'` (single word, fine), but any future admin model with two underscores (e.g. `site_customization_field` → expected `site-customization-field`) would only become `site-customization_field` and fail the `indexOf` check, silently routing an admin model's requests to the non-admin base path `/` instead of `/admin/`. Use `type.replace(/_/g, '-')` for correctness and robustness.

edit() reads host.category.id but the serializer only provides category_id, so category is undefined and categoryId becomes undefined

`edit()` does `this.set('categoryId', this.get('host.category.id'))`. The `EmbeddableHostSerializer` only emits `id, host, category_id` — there is no embedded `category` object on the client model unless the store hydrates `category_id` into a `category` property. The store's `_hydrateEmbedded` does map `category_id` → `category` via `Discourse.Category.findById(id)` (store.js.es6 `_lookupSubType` special-cases 'category'), but only when the payload is marked `__rest_serializer: "1"` AND the key matches `/(.+)\_id(s?)$/` — the host serializer emits `category_id`, which matches, so hydration may occur. However, the `EmbeddingSerializer` uses `embed: :ids` for hosts, so host objects are side-loaded under an `embeddable_hosts` key; whether each side-loaded host object gets `_hydrateEmbedded` applied depends on the root payload having `__rest_serializer: "1"` (the controller passes `rest_serializer: true`, which should set it). If hydration does not run (e.g. the side-loaded array isn't processed through `_hydrate` with the root), `host.category` is undefined and `this.get('host.category.id')` returns undefined, so `categoryId` is undefined and the category chooser starts blank on edit — the admin cannot see the current category and saving would send `category_id=undefined`, which the server treats as blank and resets to uncategorized. This needs verification/fix: prefer `this.get('host.category_id')` which is always present on the model.

expandable_first_post? no longer checks that any embeddable host is configured

`expandable_first_post?` was changed from `SiteSetting.embeddable_hosts.present? && SiteSetting.embed_truncate? && has_topic_embed?` to just `SiteSetting.embed_truncate? && has_topic_embed?`. The first condition existed to ensure embedding was enabled (at least one allowed host configured). With it removed, any topic that has a `TopicEmbed` row (e.g. created before hosts were reconfigured, or via feed polling) will show the 'expand embed' affordance even when the site has zero `EmbeddableHost` records, exposing embedded content to visitors on disallowed origins. The check should be replaced with `EmbeddableHost.exists?` (or a cached equivalent), not deleted.

invalid_host? now depends on EmbeddableHost.host_allowed? which returns false for nil referer, but the retriever is initialized with an embed_url, not a referer — semantics changed

`TopicRetriever#invalid_host?` calls `EmbeddableHost.host_allowed?(@embed_url)`. `host_allowed?` → `record_for_host(host)` does `URI(host)` and extracts `uri.host`. The `@embed_url` is the URL of the external page being embedded (e.g. `http://eviltrout.com/2013/02/10/why-discourse-uses-emberjs.html`), so `uri.host` is `eviltrout.com` — this is correct and matches the old `SiteSetting.allows_embeddable_host?` behavior. However, `record_for_host` returns `false` (not nil) when URI parsing fails, and `host_allowed?` returns `record_for_host(host).present?` → `false.present?` → `false`, so `invalid_host?` returns `!false` = `true` — correct. The semantics are preserved. The only concern is that `record_for_host` returns `false` or a record, and `.present?` on `false` is `false` — fine. No bug here; this finding is withdrawn as it is a restatement. (Not reporting.)

save() sends buffered 'host' property but the server expects the 'host' attribute inside embeddable_host params

In `save()`, `const props = this.get('buffered').getProperties('host')` fetches the buffered value of the `host` attribute (a string like 'example.com'), then `props.category_id = this.get('categoryId')` and `host.save(props)`. The REST adapter's `update`/`createRecord` wraps attrs as `data['embeddable_host'] = attrs`, so the request body becomes `embeddable_host[host]=example.com&embeddable_host[category_id]=...` — this part is actually correct. However, `getProperties('host')` returns `{host: <string>}` only if the buffered content mixin exposes it that way; if the buffer stores the whole record, `props` could be the record itself and `props.category_id = ...` would mutate the record. More concretely: after a successful save the code does `host.set('category', Discourse.Category.findById(this.get('categoryId')))` but never calls `this.rollbackBuffer()` / `this.set('buffered.host', ...)`, so the buffered (dirty) state persists and `cantSave` (which depends on `buffered.host`) keeps the old value; on the next edit the stale buffer is shown. The buffer must be committed/rolled back after a successful save.

update action is a no-op that just re-renders, giving a false sense that embedding settings can be saved

`Admin::EmbeddingController#update` simply re-renders the embedding serializer without reading or persisting any params. The route `put "customize/embedding" => "embedding#update"` and the admin controller's `saveChanges` action (`this.get('embedding').update({})`) both target it. Since hosts are created/updated/deleted through `Admin::EmbeddableHostsController`, the embedding `update` endpoint is misleading dead code: a client PUTing embedding-level settings (if any are ever added) would silently succeed without persisting anything. Either implement it to accept and persist embedding-level attributes, or remove the route/action to avoid a misleading API surface.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
unsubscribe action crashes with NoMethodError when no TopicUser record exists

In TopicsController#unsubscribe, `tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` can return nil (a user who has never interacted with the topic has no topic_users row). The code then unconditionally calls `tu.notification_level` and `tu.save!`, raising NoMethodError on nil and returning a 500. The unsubscribe link is sent in notification emails to any notified user, including users who never opened the topic, so this path is reachable in production. The code should use `TopicUser.change(current_user.id, params[:topic_id], notification_level: ...)` (which creates the row if missing, as done in #set_notifications) or guard for nil.

true_positives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Typo in property name stopNotificiationsText

The computed property is named `stopNotificiationsText` (missing 'i' in 'Notifications'), and the template references `{{{stopNotificiationsText}}}` so it works, but the misspelling will confuse future maintainers and any external references. Rename to `stopNotificationsText` in both the controller and the template.

false_positives.candidate:
List-Unsubscribe header still points only to user preferences, not the per-topic unsubscribe URL

header_args sets `result['List-Unsubscribe'] = "<#{template_args[:user_preferences_url]}>"` when add_unsubscribe_link is set. The PR adds a per-topic unsubscribe_url to template_args, but the List-Unsubscribe header (the machine-readable one-click unsubscribe used by Gmail etc.) still points to the generic preferences page. For one-click unsubscribe (RFC 8058 / Gmail's unsubscribe button) to actually stop topic notifications, the header should use the per-topic unsubscribe_url when present: `result['List-Unsubscribe'] = "<#{template_args[:unsubscribe_url] || template_args[:user_preferences_url]}>"`. As written, mail clients offering 'unsubscribe' will send users to preferences instead of stopping topic emails, and the feature is only half-wired.

No test verifies the per-topic unsubscribe_url appears in the email body or List-Unsubscribe header

The spec adds `unsubscribe_url: "/t/1234/unsubscribe"` to the message_with_unsubscribe builder, but the assertions only check that the List-Unsubscribe header is present and that the body contains the user_preferences_url. Nothing asserts that the body contains the per-topic unsubscribe URL (the new locale string interpolates %{unsubscribe_url}), nor that the header uses it. Given the mailer change and the locale change, a regression that drops unsubscribe_url from template_args (raising I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument) or renders the wrong link would not be caught. Add assertions that `message_with_unsubscribe.body` includes '/t/1234/unsubscribe' and that the rendered unsubscribe_link text contains it.

Triple-stache rendering of stopNotificiationsText injects the topic title as raw HTML The template renders `{{{stopNotificiationsText}}}` (unescaped). The controller builds this string via `I18n.t("topic.unsubscribe.stop_notifications", { title: this.get("model.fancyTitle") })`, and the locale string is "You will stop receiving notifications for {{title}}." — the tags require unescaped output, but so does the interpolated topic title. `fancyTitle` is HTML-escaped server-side (Topic#fancy_title calls ERB::Util.html_escape), but I18n interpolation in the JS client does not re-escape, and any markup that survives in fancyTitle (e.g. entities produced by SmartyPants rendering, or double-encoding edge cases) is injected raw into the DOM. This is an XSS risk if fancyTitle ever contains unescaped content (e.g. via plugins or serializer changes). Safer: keep the in the template and interpolate the title with escaped {{ }}, e.g. `You will stop receiving notifications for {{model.fancyTitle}}.` in the template itself.

Unsubscribe route fetches the full topic view instead of the lightweight unsubscribe endpoint

The route's model hook calls `PostStream.loadTopicView(params.id)`, which loads the entire topic (all posts) — the same heavy request as viewing the topic — even though the server-side unsubscribe action (TopicsController#unsubscribe) already performs the state change when the URL is hit. The Ember route is registered at /t/:slug/:id/unsubscribe, but the browser first hits the Rails route (GET topics#unsubscribe) which mutates state and renders the show template with preloaded data; the Ember app then re-fetches the full topic view client-side. This doubles the work and loads the whole post stream just to display a one-line confirmation page. The route should rely on the preloaded topic data from the server render (like topic-from-params does via modelFor) or fetch a minimal topic payload.

afterModel sets a nested property path that Ember.set may not observe correctly

`topic.set("details.notificationReasonText", null)` sets a nested path on the topic model. In this Ember version, setting a nested path via a single set() call works, but the topic's `details` object comes from updateFromJson and may be a plain object; also the intent (per the comment 'hide the notification reason text') is to suppress the notification banner on this page. If `details` is undefined at that point (updateFromJson may not have created it), set() will throw or silently fail. Safer to guard: `if (topic.get('details')) { topic.set('details.notificationReasonText', null); }` or set the whole details object. Without a test this is unverified behavior.

dropdown-button title is concatenated into HTML without escaping renderString now conditionally pushes `"

" + title + "

"` where title comes from `this.get('title')`. Previously the title was always rendered (same injection), so this is not a regression, but the value is interpolated raw into an HTML string buffer. If any caller passes a user-controlled title (e.g. a topic title), this is an XSS vector. The surrounding code also interpolates row.title, row.description, and id unescaped (lines 44-47), so the component generally assumes trusted input. Worth noting as a latent XSS risk, especially since the new unsubscribe page embeds this component via topic-notifications-button.

respond_instructions placeholder emitted inside the context-posts block The template renders `
%{respond_instructions}
` both inside the `if context_posts.present?` block (line 6) and again unconditionally at line 19. When context posts exist, the respond instructions appear twice in the HTML email. The first occurrence (inside the context block, before the 'previous discussion' posts) appears to be a leftover from the re-indentation; it should be removed so instructions appear only once at the bottom.

unsubscribe action does not verify the user can see the topic

TopicsController#unsubscribe builds `TopicView.new(params[:topic_id], current_user)` but never calls `guardian.ensure_can_see!` on the topic. TopicView.new may not raise for topics in restricted categories the user cannot access (unlike #show, which rescues Discourse::InvalidAccess). The action then mutates the user's TopicUser notification level and calls perform_show_response, which serializes the topic view — potentially leaking topic existence/content (title, excerpt via @description_meta) for topics in secure categories to unauthorized logged-in users. Compare with #toggle_mute and #clear_pin which call `guardian.ensure_can_see!(@topic)`.

unsubscribe added to skip_before_filter :check_xhr, allowing non-XHR state changes

The PR adds :unsubscribe to `skip_before_filter :check_xhr`. check_xhr exists to reject non-XHR requests to JSON API endpoints; skipping it for unsubscribe means the endpoint accepts plain browser GETs (which is required for email links, so this is intentional), but it also means the action must handle HTML and JSON formats itself — which it does via perform_show_response's respond_to. This is acceptable for an email-link endpoint, but note the action is also now reachable via direct navigation and will render the full topic page HTML; combined with the missing guardian check (separate finding) this widens exposure. No code change strictly required, but the security review of the HTML path should be deliberate.

unsubscribe renders the full topic show response, leaking topic content and tracking a visit

After mutating notification state, #unsubscribe calls perform_show_response, which renders the full topics/show template with the preloaded TopicViewSerializer (all posts the user can see, topic metadata) and sets @description_meta from the topic excerpt. The Ember route (topic-unsubscribe.js.es6) only needs the topic's id/title/notification state, not the entire topic payload. This both leaks more data than the unsubscribe page needs and is wasteful. It also means the unsubscribe URL behaves like a topic view (canonical URL, meta description), which is incorrect for a state-changing endpoint.

unsubscribe toggles notification level instead of unsubscribing, and mutates state on a GET request

The unsubscribe endpoint is a GET route (config/routes.rb lines 440-441) that permanently mutates the user's TopicUser notification_level (a side effect on GET, which breaks web semantics, makes the link prefetchable/crawlable, and means email scanners or browser prefetchers silently change user state). Worse, the toggle logic is wrong for an 'unsubscribe' action: if the user is watching/tracking (level > regular) it sets level to regular — i.e. clicking 'stop receiving notifications about this topic' leaves the user at 'regular', which still sends emails for this topic. The intent (per the email copy 'stop receiving notifications about this particular topic') is to set the level to muted. The else-branch muting only happens when the user is already at regular or muted, so a watching user who clicks unsubscribe keeps receiving notifications.

unsubscribe_link locale text says 'these emails' for the per-topic link

The first sentence of the expanded unsubscribe_link text reads 'To unsubscribe from these emails, visit your [user preferences](%{user_preferences_url}).' followed by 'To stop receiving notifications about this particular topic, [click here](%{unsubscribe_url}).' The first sentence is now inaccurate/misleading in notification emails: the preferences link unsubscribes from all notification emails, not 'these emails' (the topic-specific ones). Reword to e.g. 'To unsubscribe from all emails, visit your [user preferences](...).' so users don't think the preferences link only affects the current topic's emails.

unsubscribe_url passed to email template args is never defined for digest and other non-notification emails

send_notification_email now always passes `unsubscribe_url: post.topic.unsubscribe_url` into email_opts, and the locale string `unsubscribe_link` (server.en.yml) now interpolates `%{unsubscribe_url}`. Email::MessageBuilder#body and #html_part call `I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args)` whenever `add_unsubscribe_link` is true. Any email built with add_unsubscribe_link: true but without an unsubscribe_url opt (e.g. the digest mailer, which sets add_unsubscribe_link via build_email defaults — check digest path in user_notifications.rb which does not go through send_notification_email) will raise I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument when rendering the unsubscribe link. The digest email (UserNotifications#digest) does not pass unsubscribe_url, so digest emails with the unsubscribe footer will fail to build/send.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
should_block? performs a write during validation, and its return value is wrong when no record exists

BlockedEmail.should_block? is called from EmailValidator.validate_each (lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13), i.e. during User validation, yet it mutates the database (increments match_count, sets last_match_at, saves). This means a mere validation attempt — including failed validations, GET-triggered checks, or User.new(...).valid? in a console — permanently writes to blocked_emails. Also, when no record exists, `record` is nil and the method returns nil (falsy) — fine — but when a record exists with action_type :do_nothing, it still performs the write even though the email will not be blocked, inflating match_count for emails that are explicitly allowed. The statistics write should be moved out of the validation path (e.g. into the controller after a failed signup, or done atomically and only when actually blocking).

true_positives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Domain whitelist/blacklist regex is injectable and matches substrings

email_in_restriction_setting? builds a Regexp directly from the SiteSetting value: `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)` after only escaping dots. The setting is admin-controlled so the injection risk is limited to admins, but the bigger correctness/security bug is that the pattern is unanchored: '@(example\.com)' matches 'user@sub.example.com' AND 'user@notexample.com' (substring match, no boundary). A blacklist entry for 'example.com' will also block 'myexample.com', and a whitelist entry for 'example.com' will wrongly admit 'user@evilexample.com'. The domain list should be split on commas/whitespace and each domain anchored: Regexp.new("@#{Regexp.escape(domain)}$", true) per domain, matching any of them. This is a real bypass/false-positive issue for the email restriction feature that this PR relocates into the validator.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Email matching is case-sensitive; blocked emails can be bypassed with case variation

should_block? does `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` with no downcasing or normalization. The users table stores email as given (User validates uniqueness on the raw email string), and the signup form sends whatever the user typed. An attacker who adds a BlockedEmail entry for 'spam@example.com' can trivially bypass it by registering 'SPAM@example.com' or 'Spam@Example.com'. The lookup must normalize: `BlockedEmail.where(email: Email.downcase(email)).first` (the codebase already has Email.downcase used in users_controller.rb:269), and ideally the email column should be stored downcased on create (before_validation). Without this the entire blocklist feature is ineffective.

false_positives.candidate:
Blocked-email check is skipped when the email is blank or nil

validate_each receives `value` which is the raw attribute. If value is nil (email not yet assigned) or an empty string, `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` is still called with nil/'' — for nil, `where(email: nil).first` returns nil so it is harmless, but the guard `record.errors[attribute].blank?` means the blocked check only runs when no other error exists. More importantly, the validator never checks that value is a syntactically valid email before doing the domain regex match: `value =~ regexp` on line 21 will raise NoMethodError (undefined method =~ for nil) if value is nil when a whitelist/blacklist setting is present, crashing validation with a 500 instead of a validation error. Add `return if value.blank?` at the top of validate_each.

Blocked-email validation only runs when email_changed?, so existing users changing other attributes bypass the blocklist, and email changes are not checked against BlockedEmail

`validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` means the custom EmailValidator (which includes the BlockedEmail.should_block? check) only runs when the email attribute has changed. This is intentional for the signup path, but it means: (1) any code path that creates or saves a User with an email that matches a BlockedEmail entry but where email_changed? is false (e.g. an admin editing a user, or a user whose email was set before the blocklist entry was added and who re-saves) will not be blocked; (2) more critically, the change_email flow in UsersController (users_controller.rb:265-286) creates an EmailToken for a new email but never validates the new email against BlockedEmail — a blocked user can change their email to another blocked address via the preferences flow, because EmailToken creation does not run User email validation. The blocklist must also be enforced in the change_email path (and ideally in EmailToken creation), not only on User save with email_changed?.

Changing email validation from separate presence/uniqueness validators to combined `validates` alters error messages and hash shape returned to the client

The old code used `validates_presence_of :email` and `validates_uniqueness_of :email`, which add errors like 'Email can't be blank' and 'Email has already been taken'. The new `validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true` produces the same default messages, so that part is equivalent — but the PR also adds `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice(...)` to the create failure response in users_controller.rb. The client (create_account_controller.js:274) checks `result.errors && result.errors.email` — with to_hash, errors.email is an array of message strings, which works — but the change from the previous response shape (message only) is an API contract change for any other API consumer, and `user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")` echoes back the submitted email verbatim, including any HTML/script content, into a JSON response that the client pushes into rejectedEmails and re-renders; ensure the client treats it as text (it does, via Ember binding) but note the response now includes raw user input. The bigger issue: uniqueness validation on email is not case-insensitive — 'User@Example.com' and 'user@example.com' are treated as different by `validates :uniqueness_of`, yet the DB unique index on users.email is also case-sensitive, so this is consistent, but the BlockedEmail lookup (see separate finding) is what must be case-insensitive.

EmailValidator spec does not test the whitelist/blacklist domain logic that was moved into it

The spec only stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? and checks the blocked path. The validator also contains the relocated email_domains_whitelist / email_domains_blacklist logic (lines 4-12), which is security-relevant (it is the only thing preventing signups from blacklisted domains). There are no tests covering: whitelist present and email not in whitelist → error; whitelist present and email in whitelist → no error; blacklist present and email in blacklist → error; blacklist present and email not in blacklist → no error. Since this PR moves that logic from User into EmailValidator, the existing User model specs (if any) may no longer exercise it. Add specs for the domain restriction branches.

Error response now includes raw submitted attributes (name, username, email) without sanitization

The create failure path now returns `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")`. These are the raw, un-sanitized params the user submitted (set via User.new_from_params). The values are echoed back in the JSON response and the JS client pushes result.values.email into rejectedEmails and compares it against the email input. While Ember escapes on render, returning raw user input in an API response is an unnecessary reflection vector; at minimum the email should be the normalized/downcased form. Consider returning only what is needed (the email) and normalizing it.

Missing newline at end of file

The file ends without a trailing newline (the diff shows '\ No newline at end of file'). This is a minor style issue but can cause problems with some tools and diffs.

No test for case-insensitive matching of blocked emails

The spec suite for BlockedEmail covers default action_type, statistics updates, and both action types, but never tests that should_block? matches an email regardless of case (e.g. record 'block@spam.org' vs query 'BLOCK@SPAM.ORG'). Given that email case-insensitivity is a real-world requirement (and the current implementation is case-sensitive, which is a bug), this is exactly the scenario that needs a regression test. Add a test asserting BlockedEmail.should_block?('BLOCK@SPAMFROMHOME.ORG') returns true when the stored record is lowercase.

blocked_emails.email has no length limit and no normalization; unique index is case-sensitive

t.string :email with no limit defaults to 255 in most adapters, but there is no downcasing on store and the unique index on email is case-sensitive (default PostgreSQL behavior). Combined with the case-sensitive lookup in BlockedEmail.should_block?, entries 'Spam@x.com' and 'spam@x.com' are treated as distinct rows, defeating the blocklist. The migration should either add a functional unique index on lower(email) or enforce downcasing in the model's before_validation, and the model should normalize on lookup.

rejectedEmails comparison is case-sensitive, so a rejected email can be re-submitted with different casing

The client-side check `this.get('rejectedEmails').contains(email)` compares the exact string. If the server rejected 'Spam@Example.com', the user can immediately retype 'spam@example.com' (or any case variation) and the client-side check passes; the form will be re-submitted and only fail again server-side. The comparison should be case-insensitive (compare downcased values), matching the server-side normalization the BlockedEmail lookup should have (see related finding). Also note the server returns the email in result.values.email — if the server normalizes differently than the client, the client-side rejection will never trigger.

true_positives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Feed polling fetches an admin-configured URL with open-uri without scheme/SSRF restrictions

`SimpleRSS.parse open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` uses Kernel#open on a URL. While the setting is admin-controlled, `open` on a string starting with `|` executes a shell command (the classic open-uri/Kernel#open pipe vulnerability) — if the setting value ever begins with `|` (or is otherwise attacker-influenced via a compromised admin UI, import, or YAML injection), this is remote command execution. Even restricting to http(s), there is no protection against SSRF to internal addresses (169.254.169.254, localhost services). The code should use `URI.parse` + `Net::HTTP`/`open-uri`'s `URI.open` equivalent with an explicit scheme whitelist (http/https only) and ideally block private/link-local IP ranges.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage origin check uses indexOf, which is bypassable

The message handler validates the sender with `if (discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1) { return; }`. `String#indexOf` performs a substring match, so an origin like `http://evil.com/?x=http://discourse.example.com` (or `http://discourse.example.com.evil.com` if discourseUrl lacks a scheme/trailing slash) contains the discourse URL as a substring and passes the check. A malicious page could then send a `discourse-resize` message with an arbitrary height, resizing the iframe to hide or distort content (a clickjacking/UX-integrity issue; the data is only a height so impact is limited, but the check is still wrong). The origin must be compared exactly: `e.origin !== discourseUrl` (after normalizing both to origins).

true_positives.golden_comment: The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Referer host check compares against a single configured host, allowing bypass and enabling unauthorized embedding

ensure_embeddable validates only that `URI(request.referer).host == SiteSetting.embeddable_host`. Two problems: (1) the Referer header is fully client-controlled — an attacker can simply send a request with a forged `Referer: http://<embeddable_host>/` header (e.g. via curl) and pass the check, so this is not an authorization boundary at all; (2) the check is an exact string match against one host, so subdomains or any other legitimate embedding host are rejected, and conversely any page on the configured host (including attacker-controlled paths if the host serves user content) is accepted. Combined with the fact that the endpoint renders full topic content (TopicView with posts) for any `embed_url` whose host matches `embeddable_host` (see TopicRetriever#invalid_host?), this exposes forum content to scraping and enables the iframe to be embedded from arbitrary pages on that host. The referer check should be treated as defense-in-depth only; access control must not rely on it.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate: XSS via unescaped URL interpolation into raw HTML post content TopicEmbed.import builds the 'imported from' footer by interpolating the caller-supplied `url` directly into an HTML anchor: `"#{url}"`. The post is then created with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`, which (per Post#cook in app/models/post.rb line 133) returns `raw` verbatim with no sanitization. A URL containing a single quote (e.g. `http://x/' onmouseover='alert(1)`) or HTML like `http://x/'>

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
i.content can be nil, causing NoMethodError on .scrub

`content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` — SimpleRSS items do not guarantee a `content` element (it is optional in RSS 2.0; `content:encoded` may be absent, and Atom entries may only have `summary`). When absent, `i.content` is nil and `.scrub` raises NoMethodError, aborting the whole hourly poll (and since `sidekiq_options retry: false`, the failure is silent until someone notices missing imports). Guard with `i.content.to_s.scrub` or skip items without content.

true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage targetOrigin is the raw Referer header, enabling message leakage to attacker-controlled origins

The layout sends the resize message with `parent.postMessage({...}, '<%= request.referer %>')`. The targetOrigin is taken verbatim from the client-controlled Referer header. If the Referer is not a valid origin (e.g. a full URL with a path, or an attacker-supplied value), the browser behavior is undefined/lenient in older engines, and more importantly the referer is attacker-controlled, so the height data (and the fact that the embed loaded) can be posted to an origin the site operator never intended. targetOrigin should be a fixed, known origin — the configured `SiteSetting.embeddable_host` (normalized to scheme://host) — not the request's Referer. Also note `request.referer` is interpolated into a JS string literal without escaping; a Referer containing a quote would break out of the string (minor, since the value is also attacker-controlled, but it is a JS injection point).

false_negatives.golden_comment: postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

false_positives.candidate:
Content-hash comparison uses the mutated string but the update path can silently skip revisions

On update, `if content_sha1 != embed.content_sha1` triggers a PostRevisor revision. But `content_sha1` is computed from `contents` AFTER the 'imported from' footer was appended (line 13), while the stored hash was computed the same way on insert, so far so good. However, if the remote article's URL changes (e.g. trailing slash differences, http→https, redirects), a NEW TopicEmbed row is created for what is the same article, producing a duplicate topic — there is no canonicalization of `embed_url` (the unique index on embed_url then also silently allows near-duplicate URLs). Conversely, if only the footer link text changed, every row would be revised. The embed_url should be canonicalized (normalized URI: lowercase host, strip fragment, default ports, trailing slash) before lookup/insert.

Controller spec expects TopicRetriever to be used synchronously, but the controller enqueues a job

The test 'tells the topic retriever to work when no previous embed is found' stubs `TopicRetriever.expects(:new).returns(retriever)` and expects `retrieve` to be called during `get :best`. But the controller (app/controllers/embed_controller.rb line 15) calls `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...)` — it never instantiates TopicRetriever in the request. In test mode `queue_jobs` is false (config/site_settings.yml developer.queue_jobs test: false), which may execute the job inline, but the spec does not stub Jobs.enqueue and does not assert on the enqueued job; if the job runs inline the mock expectation may pass by accident, and if jobs are queued the expectation fails. The spec should assert `Jobs.expects(:enqueue).with(:retrieve_topic, ...)` instead of mocking TopicRetriever, otherwise it is testing an implementation the controller does not have and will break or silently mislead.

Disqus importer creates users with User.create! which can raise and abort the whole import

`post_user = User.create!(email: email, username: UserNameSuggester.suggest(email))` — the bang version raises on validation failure (duplicate email race, invalid username suggestion, etc.), and the exception is not rescued inside the `parser.threads.each` loop, so one bad author email aborts the entire import mid-way (the `ensure` restores settings but all remaining threads are lost, and already-created topics remain — a partial import with no idempotency). Use `User.create` and skip/fallback to the default user on failure, or rescue and log per-post.

Disqus importer now depends on TopicEmbed.import_remote fetching t[:link], but never passes created_at and loses the permalink post

The refactored import calls `TopicEmbed.import_remote(user, t[:link], title: t[:title])` and no longer creates the original permalink post (`raw: "[[Permalink](#{t[:link]})]"` with `created_at: Date.parse(t[:created_at])` was removed). Consequences: (1) the topic's created_at is now the import time, not the original thread creation date — topic ordering and 'new' lists are wrong for all imported threads; (2) the explicit permalink back to the Disqus thread is gone (import_remote's Readability extraction may or may not include it); (3) `import_remote` ignores any created_at option — TopicEmbed.import has no created_at parameter at all, so there is no way to preserve dates. The importer should pass `created_at` through TopicEmbed.import (add an opts parameter forwarded to PostCreator, which already supports `created_at`).

Embed route is defined before the /t/:id routes and lacks a format constraint

`get 'embed/best' => 'embed#best'` is placed in the middle of the routes (line 245), before the topic routes. It does not conflict with existing routes, but it also has no `format: false` / constraints, so `/embed/best.json` or `/embed/best.xml` would match and run the controller (params[:embed_url] required, so it would 400 — minor). More relevant: the route is not constrained to GET-only semantics beyond the verb, and there is no rate limiting at the routing layer; combined with the per-request job enqueue finding, this endpoint is an easy amplification target. Consider `get 'embed/best' => 'embed#best', format: false` and Rack::Attack throttling on /embed/.

Embed view renders post.cooked with raw, relying entirely on the cooking pipeline for safety `
<%= raw post.cooked %>
` renders cooked HTML unescaped. This is consistent with the main forum, but combined with the raw_html cook method (see the TopicEmbed findings) it means imported feed content is rendered with zero sanitization in this iframe, which is embedded on third-party sites. The embed surface should be treated as higher risk: at minimum, posts shown here should be re-sanitized on output, and raw_html posts should never be displayed without a Sanitize pass.

EmbedController renders a TopicView for any user (including anonymous) without checking topic access

`@topic_view = TopicView.new(topic_id, current_user, {best: 5})` — TopicView is constructed with `current_user`, which is nil for anonymous requests (the embed iframe is loaded cross-origin from the embedding site, so no Discourse session cookie is sent). Whether TopicView enforces access for nil users depends on its internals, but the embed endpoint then renders `post.cooked` raw for every post returned. If the embedded topic is in a restricted category, is a private message, or is otherwise not publicly visible, its content is exposed to anyone who knows/guesses the embed_url — and embed_urls are the external article URLs, which are often public. The controller must verify the topic is publicly visible (e.g. `Guardian.new(nil).can_see?(topic)` / topic.category.read_restricted check) before building the view, and return 404 otherwise.

PostRevisor revision of an imported post does not preserve cook_method, so the update is re-cooked as Markdown

On update, `PostRevisor.new(post).revise!(user, absolutize_urls(url, contents), skip_validations: true, bypass_rate_limiter: true)` sets a new `raw` (HTML). PostRevisor#update_post assigns `@post.raw = @new_raw` and saves; the Post `before_save` callback (app/models/post.rb line 321) recomputes `self.cooked = cook(raw, ...)` unless new_record?. `cook` checks `cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]` — the post retains cook_method raw_html from creation, so cooked == raw. OK in the current flow. BUT: PostRevisor never touches cook_method, and if the post's cook_method were ever reset (e.g. by an edit through the normal UI, which doesn't set cook_method but also doesn't clear it — actually it persists), the HTML raw would be run through the Markdown pipeline and mangled. More importantly, the revision path relies on the column persisting; there is no test pinning that an updated imported post still has cook_method raw_html and cooked == raw. The spec gap is noted in the topic_embed_spec finding; additionally, `update_column(:content_sha1, ...)` skips callbacks — acceptable here, but if the revise! fails (returns false because raw unchanged — impossible here since contents changed) the hash would still be updated, desyncing hash from content. Guard: only update the hash if the revision actually happened.

Raw HTML from remote feeds is stored and rendered without sanitization

TopicEmbed.import creates posts with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`, and Post#cook (app/models/post.rb line 133) returns `raw` unchanged for that method, bypassing the entire Markdown/sanitization pipeline. The `contents` come from an external RSS/Atom feed (Jobs::PollFeed passes `i.content.scrub` — `scrub` only replaces invalid byte sequences, it does not sanitize HTML) or from `Readability::Document` output in import_remote. Any script, event handler, or iframe in the feed content is stored verbatim in `cooked` and rendered unescaped via `<%= raw post.cooked %>` in app/views/embed/best.html.erb line 19 and in the regular topic view. A compromised or malicious feed source yields stored XSS against every viewer of the imported topic. The content must be passed through Sanitize (as the normal cooking pipeline does) before being stored.

RetrieveTopic job is enqueued on every cache-miss request with no deduplication

When no TopicEmbed exists for the URL, the controller enqueues `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...)` and renders 'loading'. The loading page reloads every 30 seconds (app/views/embed/loading.html.erb), and each reload enqueues ANOTHER RetrieveTopic job. TopicRetriever has a 60-second Redis throttle (`retrieved_recently?`) that mitigates duplicate work, but: (1) the throttle key is per-URL and setnx-based, so the first job sets it and subsequent jobs bail — OK — but the throttle only lasts 60s while the loading page reloads every 30s indefinitely, so after 60s a new job is enqueued and the cycle repeats for as long as the topic is missing (e.g. the remote page is down or the import keeps failing), hammering the remote site and the job queue; (2) many concurrent viewers of the same not-yet-imported URL each enqueue jobs. There should be a longer-lived 'import in progress / failed' marker (e.g. a Redis key with a TTL of minutes, or a DB flag) so the job is enqueued at most once per N minutes per URL.

RetrieveTopic triggers a full synchronous PollFeed run inside the request job

perform_retrieve calls `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` inline when `feed_polling_enabled?`. PollFeed downloads and parses the entire RSS feed and imports every item (each import creates/revises posts).
