Used backup codes are nulled instead of removed, breaking exhaustion detection and leaving null entries in stored JSON

`backupCodes[index] = null` replaces the used code with `null` rather than removing it from the array. Consequences: (1) the stored JSON array accumulates nulls, so `backupCodes.length` no longer reflects remaining codes; (2) when all 10 codes are used, the array is `[null × 10]`, `user.backupCodes` remains a non-null encrypted string, so the `!user.backupCodes` check that should produce `MissingBackupCodes` never triggers — users see 'incorrect backup code' forever instead of being told to generate new codes; (3) the null entries are indistinguishable from data corruption. The fix is to `backupCodes.splice(index, 1)` so the array shrinks and eventually becomes empty, at which point the encrypted empty array can be stored as null or the emptiness checked explicitly.

Zod schema makes password optional when `totpEmail` is set, but the backup code flow still requires password for CAL users — schema does not account for backup code submission

However, the schema does not validate the `backupCode` field at all — it's passed through via `.passthrough()`. `Array.from(Array(10), () => crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex"))` creates an intermediate array of 10 undefined values — minor inefficiency

This is a micro-optimization and not a real performance issue, but the pattern `Array(10)` creates a sparse array which can have surprising behavior. Low severity, style-adjacent but technically a minor bug pattern.

`backupCodes` is stored as encrypted TEXT containing a JSON array — no database-level constraint ensures it's valid JSON or limits size

requestReschedule evt.destinationCalendar drops the user's destination calendar fallback

true_positives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing refresh_token is silently replaced with the literal string "refresh_token"

When the parsed token response has no `refresh_token`, the code sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"` — the literal string. This placeholder is then merged into the stored credential (e.g. office365calendar `o365AuthCredentials = { ...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data }`, zoom `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token`). On the next refresh, the service will send `refresh_token=refresh_token` to the provider, which will fail with `invalid_grant`, permanently breaking the credential instead of preserving the previous refresh token. The correct behavior when a provider omits `refresh_token` (common — many providers only return it on the first consent) is to keep the existing refresh token from the stored credential, not to fabricate one.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
minimumTokenResponseSchema uses invalid zod index-signature syntax and will not validate as intended

The schema is written as `z.object({ access_token: z.string(), [z.string().toString()]: z.number(), [z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional() })`. Computed keys with zod schemas are not valid index signatures — zod index signatures must be created with `z.record(...)` or `.catchall(...)`. As written, zod will treat these computed properties as literal key names (the stringified schema objects) rather than catch-alls, so `minimumTokenResponseSchema.safeParse(response)` will strip/reject almost every real token response (any response containing `expires_in`, `refresh_token`, `token_type`, etc. will fail or be stripped), causing `parseRefreshTokenResponse` to throw "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned" for every synced refresh. The intent (require `access_token`, allow arbitrary extra fields) should be expressed as `z.object({ access_token: z.string() }).passthrough()` (or `.catchall(z.unknown())`).

true_positives.golden_comment: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Function returns a Zod SafeParseResult but callers treat it inconsistently (some read `.data`, some read `.success`)

`parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the whole `SafeParseResult` object. The function should either return the parsed data directly (throwing on failure, which it already does) or all callers must be audited; returning the raw SafeParseResult invites exactly this class of bug.

The jsforce connection is constructed with `accessToken: credentialKey.access_token` (the OLD token, line 106) rather than the freshly fetched `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`, so the very first API call after a refresh uses a stale access token and fails with 401. true_positives.golden_comment: The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

`appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws a `ZodError` on invalid input. Because the handler does not catch it, Next.js returns a 500 and the raw Zod error (including the received payload shape) leaks to the caller. The endpoint should use `safeParse` and return a 400 with a generic message. The same applies to the `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` on line 57, which throws on malformed/undecryptable payloads, producing an unhandled 500.

This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

false_positives.candidate:
APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is a string-or-undefined value, not a boolean, and is truthy for an empty-string secret

`export const APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED = process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY;` — this evaluates to `string | undefined`, not `boolean`. It is used in boolean contexts (`if (!APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED)`), which works, but the exported name and type imply a boolean and the value can be the empty string `""` (falsy, ok) or the secret string itself (truthy). More subtly, the flag does not include `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`, so `refreshOAuthTokens`/`parseRefreshTokenResponse` check `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` — meaning the webhook endpoint is enabled whenever the secret+key are set even if no sync endpoint is configured, which is presumably intended, but the flag should be an explicit boolean (`!!(...)`) and the webhook handler should additionally verify that the encryption key is non-empty before decrypting (see the app-credential.ts finding about the `|| ""` fallback).

Comment says to generate the webhook secret with `openssl rand -base64 32` but the encryption key comment says 24 bytes; the webhook secret has no length requirement and 32 is fine, but the two comments are inconsistent about which key is which

The `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` comment says `openssl rand -base64 32` (44 chars, ~256 bits — fine for a shared secret) while `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` says "must be 32 bytes for AES256" and `openssl rand -base64 24` (24 bytes = 192 bits, which is AES-192, not AES-256; 32 bytes needs `openssl rand -base64 32` or `openssl rand 32 | base64`). The encryption key comment is wrong: base64 of 24 random bytes is 24 bytes of key material = AES-192, not AES-256 as claimed. If `symmetricDecrypt` requires a 32-byte key, self-hosters following the comment will get a key of the wrong length. The comment should say `openssl rand -base64 32` for a 32-byte (AES-256) key, matching the existing `CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY` guidance at line 90.

Decryption uses an empty-string key fallback and stores attacker-controlled JSON verbatim as the credential key

`symmetricDecrypt(reqBody.keys, process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY || "")` silently falls back to an empty key. Depending on the implementation of `symmetricDecrypt` in `@calcom/lib/crypto`, an empty key may either throw or — worse — decrypt with a predictable key, letting an attacker who knows the code forge `keys` payloads. The handler must verify `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` is set (and of the expected length) before decrypting and return 500/403 otherwise. Additionally, the decrypted `keys` value is `JSON.parse`d with no schema validation and written directly into `prisma.credential.key` (lines 78 and 85). A valid webhook caller (or anyone if the secret check is bypassed) can store arbitrary JSON — including a `refresh_token`/`access_token` of their choosing for any user and any app — which is then used by the calendar/video services to act against third-party APIs. The decrypted payload should be validated against a per-app credential schema before persisting.

Endpoint does not restrict HTTP method or content type

The handler responds to any HTTP method (POST, GET, PUT, ...) and never checks `req.method`. A GET request with a query-string body would still be parsed by Next.js into `req.body` for some content types, and more importantly there is no method gate, so the endpoint's behavior is not constrained to the documented webhook POST. It should return 405 for non-POST methods. Relatedly, `req.body` may be a string if the content type is not JSON, which would make the Zod parse fail with a 500 (see the parse finding).

HubSpot refresh treats the refreshOAuthTokens return value as a HubspotToken, but in sync mode it is a fetch Response — expiryDate becomes NaN and the credential is corrupted

`const hubspotRefreshToken: HubspotToken = await refreshOAuthTokens(...)` then `hubspotRefreshToken.expiryDate = Math.round(Date.now() + hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn * 1000)`. In the normal path the inner function returns the HubSpot SDK token object (has `expiresIn`), but in the credential-sync path `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a `fetch` `Response` object, which has no `expiresIn` — so `expiryDate` is `NaN`, `hubspotRefreshToken.accessToken` is `undefined`, and the credential is updated with `key: { ...Response-ish garbage }` (line 198), destroying the stored HubSpot credential. `hubspotClient.setAccessToken(undefined)` then breaks all subsequent calls. The sync response must be parsed (`await response.json()`) and mapped to the HubspotToken shape before use.

Lark refresh passes the fetch Response to handleLarkError which expects a Response in normal mode but the sync path also returns a Response — however the normal path previously returned a Response too; the real issue is handleLarkError is not applied consistently and errors are not surfaced

`const resp = await refreshOAuthTokens(async () => await fetch(...), "lark-calendar", credential.userId)` then `const data = await handleLarkError<RefreshTokenResp>(resp, this.log)`. In the normal path `resp` is the `fetch` `Response` (same as before the change — ok). In the sync path `resp` is also a `Response` — ok by luck. But `handleLarkError` presumably throws on non-OK Lark responses; in sync mode a non-200 from the sync endpoint (e.g. 404 for unknown user) will be interpreted as a Lark API error and its body parsed as `RefreshTokenResp`, yielding `data.data.refresh_token === undefined`, which is then written into the credential (lines 91-96), wiping the user's Lark tokens. The sync response must be validated (ok status + expected shape) before its fields are persisted.

New credentials created by the webhook are not marked with any indication they are externally managed, and team credentials are not supported

The webhook always creates/updates a credential with `userId: reqBody.userId` and never sets `teamId`. Self-hosters syncing credentials for users who belong to teams will have the credential attached to the user rather than the team, so team event types that resolve credentials by `teamId` will not see the synced credential. Conversely, a webhook caller can attach a credential to any user id (the endpoint trusts `userId` after only checking the user exists), which is by design for this feature but means the endpoint is a full credential-write primitive for arbitrary users — combined with the weak secret check, this is a significant privilege. At minimum the created credential should be validated against the app's expected key schema (see earlier finding) and the behavior for team-owned apps should be documented/handled.

New env vars added to globalEnv include secrets that should not be listed as build-time env for all packages

`CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`, and `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME` were added to `globalEnv`. `globalEnv` in turbo affects cache hashing for every task in every package; listing server-only secrets there is not itself a leak (turbo does not print values), but it means builds of unrelated packages (website, ai, embed) will be invalidated when these secrets rotate and implies they are needed at build time for those packages, which they are not. More importantly, the web app's build env list (`@calcom/web#build` `env` array, lines 27-38) was NOT updated to include these variables, so production builds may not have them available at runtime in some deployment setups that rely on the turbo env allowlist. The web build env should include the four new variables (at least the ones read at runtime: `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME`, `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`).

Salesforce getClient now refreshes the token on every instantiation and overwrites the stored credential, and prisma is not imported

The diff adds a full token-refresh block inside `getClient` (lines 75-99) that runs on every service construction — i.e. on every calendar operation — POSTing to Salesforce with the stored `refresh_token` and then `prisma.credential.update(...)`. Two problems: (1) `prisma` is used at line 96 but is never imported in this file (no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"` in the shown content), which is a compile/runtime error (`ReferenceError: prisma is not defined`) the first time any Salesforce calendar operation runs; (2) unconditionally refreshing on every `getClient` call discards the access-token caching/expiry logic that previously lived in the jsforce connection, causing an extra token request per operation and — because Salesforce rotates refresh tokens — can invalidate the stored refresh token if the update races with another concurrent operation. The refresh should happen only when the stored access token is expired, and `prisma` must be imported.

Sync request sends credentials lookup parameters as URLSearchParams without a Content-Type header or any authentication

The POST body is `new URLSearchParams({ calcomUserId, appSlug })` but no `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded` header is set (fetch sets it automatically for URLSearchParams bodies in modern runtimes, so this is mostly fine), and — more importantly — no authentication or shared secret is sent, so the sync endpoint cannot verify the caller is really this Cal.com instance (see the security finding). Also `appSlug` values passed by callers are inconsistent: googlecalendar passes `"google-calendar"`, office365video passes `"msteams"`, zoom passes `"zoomvideo"` — the sync endpoint must know this exact mapping; the PR description does not document the canonical slug list, which will cause silent mismatches for self-hosters.

Synced refresh response is passed to handleErrorsJson which expects a Response; expiry_date becomes NaN when syncing

`const responseBody = await handleErrorsJson<ITokenResponse>(response);` — in the sync path `response` is a fetch `Response` (fine), but the code then computes `responseBody.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + (responseBody?.expires_in || 0) * 1000)`. The credential-sync contract (per `parseRefreshTokenResponse` and the PR description) is that the sync endpoint returns only the access token and an expiry timestamp, not `expires_in`. So `expires_in` is undefined, `expiry_date` becomes `Date.now()`, and `isExpired` (line 56, `expiryDate < Math.round(+new Date())`) immediately treats the fresh token as expired, causing an infinite refresh loop on every API call. The adapter must handle the sync response shape (absolute expiry) distinctly from the Microsoft token shape (relative `expires_in`).

Synced refresh response is read as `res?.data` but refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response, so `token` is undefined and the credential update throws

In `refreshAccessToken`, `const res = await refreshOAuthTokens(...)` then `const token = res?.data`. In the normal (non-sync) path `res` is `fetchTokens.res` (a GaxiosResponse, which has `.data`) — fine. But in the credential-sync path `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw `fetch` `Response` object, which has no `.data` property, so `token` is `undefined` and `token.access_token` throws a TypeError. The catch block then treats any error message other than "invalid_grant" by returning the stale `myGoogleAuth`, so the token is never refreshed and every subsequent API call fails with 401 until the credential is manually fixed. The response must be normalized (e.g. `await res.json()` when it is a `Response`) before reading `.data`.

Team-owned credentials (userId null) silently fall back to the provider refresh path even when syncing is enabled, causing inconsistent behavior

`if (APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT && userId)` — when `userId` is null (team credential), the function takes the `else` branch and calls `refreshFunction()`, i.e. it refreshes directly against the provider using the stored refresh token. But the entire premise of the feature (per the PR description) is that the self-hoster's app store is the source of truth and the Cal.com instance may not even have valid client secrets for the provider. For team credentials the refresh will fail (or worse, succeed against a provider the self-hoster has decommissioned), and the two code paths diverge. The function should either support team credentials in the sync call (e.g. pass `teamId`) or explicitly throw/log when syncing is enabled but the credential is team-owned, rather than silently falling back.

Token refresh result is used without checking HTTP status; axios errors and sync-mode Response objects are both mishandled

`const tokenInfo = await refreshOAuthTokens(async () => await axios.post(...), ...)` then `if (!tokenInfo.data.error)`. In the normal path `tokenInfo` is an axios response (`.data` is the body — ok), but axios throws on non-2xx by default so the `else` branch logging `tokenInfo.data` is only reachable for 2xx responses containing an `error` field. In the sync path `tokenInfo` is a `Response` and `tokenInfo.data` is `undefined`, so `!tokenInfo.data.error` throws a TypeError (`Cannot read properties of undefined`) which is uncaught in `refreshAccessToken` and propagates to `getToken`, failing the whole calendar operation. The response must be normalized and its HTTP status checked.

Unrelated hardcoded redirect URI change bundled into the rename commit

The diff changes `const redirectUri = WEBAPP_URL + `/api/integrations/${appConfig.slug}/callback`` to the literal ``WEBAPP_URL + `/api/integrations/zoho-bigin/callback` ``. If `appConfig.slug` is not exactly `"zoho-bigin"` this changes the OAuth redirect URI and breaks the Zoho Bigin install flow (the redirect URI must match the one registered in the Zoho console). This change is unrelated to the credential-sync feature and should be reverted or justified.

Webex refresh passes the refreshOAuthTokens result to handleWebexResponse, which clones/reads it as a Response; in sync mode the body shape differs and expiry_date is never set from the sync payload

`const responseBody = await handleWebexResponse(response, credential.id);` — `handleWebexResponse` (line 270) expects a fetch `Response` and returns `responseClone.json()`. In the normal path `response` is a `Response` (ok). In the sync path it is also a `Response` (ok), but the sync endpoint returns only `{ access_token, expiry_date }` (per the PR contract), which does not match `webexRefreshedTokenSchema` (requires `scope`, `token_type`, `refresh_token`, `refresh_token_expires_in`). `parsedToken.success` will therefore be false and the adapter rejects with "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned" — meaning Webex token refresh is permanently broken whenever credential syncing is enabled. The sync response must be mapped onto the webex token shape (preserving the existing refresh token and computing expiry) instead of being validated against the provider schema.

Webhook secret comparison is not timing-safe and fails open when env vars are unset

The webhook secret is compared with `!==` (non-constant-time, enabling timing attacks) and, more importantly, when `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` is unset the comparison becomes `header !== undefined`. If the attacker sends a request without the configured header, `req.headers[...]` is `undefined`, so `undefined !== undefined` is false and the check passes — the endpoint is then only protected by `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED`, which is truthy whenever both env vars are set... but note `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` is computed as `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, so if the secret is unset the feature flag is falsy and the endpoint returns 403. However, if `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` is set to an empty string (as in the shipped `.env.example`: `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET=""`), the flag is falsy too. The real risk: if an operator sets `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` and `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` but the header name env var (`CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME`) is misconfigured or the secret is an empty string while the flag logic changes, any request without that header passes authentication. Additionally, `req.headers[...]` is `string | string[] | undefined`; comparing an array to a string with `!==` always passes for array-valued headers, and the value is never validated to be a string. Use a constant-time comparison (e.g. `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on hashed buffers) and explicitly reject when either env var is missing or empty.

Zoho CRM refresh swallows all errors and leaves this.accessToken stale/undefined, then API calls proceed with an invalid token

`refreshAccessToken` wraps everything in try/catch and on error only does `this.log.error(e)` — it does not rethrow, does not invalidate the credential, and does not set `this.accessToken`. `getToken` resolves successfully regardless, so `createEvent`/`updateEvent`/`deleteEvent` proceed to call the Zoho API with an empty or stale `this.accessToken`, producing confusing 401/NO_AUTH errors instead of a clear "credential invalid" signal. Additionally, in sync mode `zohoCrmTokenInfo` is a `Response` and `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data` is `undefined`, so `!zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error` throws inside the try and is swallowed by the same catch. The refresh must surface failures (or mark the credential invalid) rather than silently continuing.

Zoom refresh validates the sync endpoint response against the Zoom provider schema, which the sync payload does not satisfy

`const parsedToken = parseRefreshTokenResponse(responseBody, zoomRefreshedTokenSchema);` — when credential syncing is enabled, `parseRefreshTokenResponse` uses `minimumTokenResponseSchema` (only requires `access_token`), so `parsedToken.data` will contain only the fields the sync endpoint returned (e.g. `access_token` and an expiry). But lines 119-122 then unconditionally read `newTokens.refresh_token` and `newTokens.expires_in` — both `undefined` for a sync response — so `key.refresh_token` is set to `undefined` (wiping the stored refresh token) and `key.expiry_date` becomes `NaN`, permanently breaking the Zoom credential. The code must preserve the existing `refresh_token` and derive `expiry_date` from the sync payload's absolute expiry when present.

appStoreMetadata lookup uses the DB app slug but the credential is written with appMetadata.slug — mismatch for apps whose metadata slug differs from the DB slug

`const appMetadata = appStoreMetadata[app.slug as keyof typeof appStoreMetadata];` then the credential is created/updated with `appId: appMetadata.slug`. If `appStoreMetadata`'s key differs from `appMetadata.slug` (the lookup key vs the inner slug), the credential's `appId` will not match the `app.slug` that was validated to exist, and downstream credential resolution (which filters by `appId`) will not find it. The code should assert `appMetadata.slug === app.slug` or use `app.slug` consistently for the credential write.

findFirst-then-update/create race allows duplicate credentials and lost updates

The handler does `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })` and then either `update` or `create` based on the result. Two concurrent webhook calls for the same user/app both see no credential and both `create`, producing duplicate credentials for the same user+app (the schema does not enforce uniqueness on `(userId, appId)` — other callbacks in this codebase, e.g. zoomvideo/webex/tandem, explicitly `deleteMany` existing credentials first, confirming duplicates are possible). Concurrent updates can also overwrite each other. The write should be atomic — e.g. a transaction, or `upsert` on a unique constraint, or `updateMany`/`create` guarded by a transaction with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` semantics.

handleErrorsJson is called on the value returned by refreshOAuthTokens, which may be a parsed body rather than a Response

`const responseJson = await handleErrorsJson(response);` assumes `response` is a fetch `Response`. In the sync path `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a `Response` (ok), but in the normal path it returns the result of the inner fetch — which here is also a `Response`, so this works — however the type contract of `refreshOAuthTokens` is `any` and other callers pass axios responses. If the contract is normalized to "parsed body" (as recommended in the refreshOAuthTokens finding), this call site breaks. The two paths must be reconciled so `handleErrorsJson` always receives a `Response`.

handleZoomResponse is called on the refreshOAuthTokens result, which in sync mode is a Response but in normal mode is also a Response; however the sync body lacks Zoom's error field so invalid_grant handling is bypassed

`const responseBody = await handleZoomResponse(response, credential.id);` — `handleZoomResponse` throws on non-OK responses and returns the parsed JSON. In sync mode, if the sync endpoint returns 200 with an error payload or a non-JSON body, `responseClone.json()` may throw or return an unexpected shape; the subsequent `if (responseBody.error)` check (line 98) assumes the Zoom error shape. A sync endpoint that returns `{ "error": "user_not_found" }` with 200 would be treated as a Zoom `invalid_grant` only if the string matches; otherwise it falls through to schema validation and rejects with a generic error, and the credential is never invalidated even though the user's tokens are gone. The sync path needs explicit status/shape validation.

parseRefreshTokenResponse accepts `any` response and an unused schema parameter in sync mode

The signature is `(response: any, schema: z.ZodTypeAny)`. In sync mode the `schema` argument is completely ignored (only `minimumTokenResponseSchema` is used), so callers pass provider-specific schemas that are silently discarded — meaning a sync endpoint returning extra/malformed fields is accepted as long as `access_token` is a string. The `any` type also disables type checking at every call site. The function should type the response as `unknown` and, in sync mode, still validate the minimal shape strictly (and ideally require an expiry field, since the whole point of the sync contract is to return token + expiry).

parseRefreshTokenResponse already throws on invalid responses; the subsequent `.success` check is dead code and the merge can still persist a placeholder refresh_token

`const tokenResponse = parseRefreshTokenResponse(responseJson, refreshTokenResponseSchema);` — the helper throws `"Invalid refreshed tokens were returned"` when parsing fails, so `tokenResponse.success` is always `true` here and the `tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data` guard is dead. More importantly, when the provider omits `refresh_token`, the helper injects the literal string `"refresh_token"` (see parseRefreshTokenResponse finding), and line 264 merges that into `o365AuthCredentials`, overwriting the real refresh token and permanently breaking future refreshes. The merge should preserve the existing `refresh_token` when the response doesn't include one.

refreshOAuthTokens is called with credential.userId which may be null for team credentials, silently disabling sync for team Google calendars

`refreshOAuthTokens(fn, "google-calendar", credential.userId)` — `credential.userId` is `number | null`. For team-owned Google Calendar credentials `userId` is null, so the sync branch is skipped and the code falls back to refreshing directly against Google with the stored refresh token. For self-hosters using this feature, team credentials will not be synced and will break once the self-hoster rotates/decommissions the Google OAuth client. This should be surfaced (log/throw) rather than silently falling back, consistent with the refreshOAuthTokens finding.

true_positives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blacklist comparison is case-sensitive while blacklist entries are lowercased

`blacklistedGuestEmails` entries are lowercased (line 71), but the guest emails from user input are compared without lowercasing (`blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)` on line 77). A blacklisted address such as `blocked@example.com` can be bypassed by submitting `Blocked@Example.com` (emails are case-insensitive in the local part per common practice and Prisma stores what is given). The guest filter should lowercase `guest` before comparing, e.g. `!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest.toLowerCase())`. The same case-sensitivity issue applies to the duplicate-attendee check on line 76 (`guest === attendee.email`), allowing the same person to be added twice with different casing.

true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Authorization check uses AND instead of OR for team admin/owner, and allows any attendee to add guests

The permission check computes `isTeamAdminOrOwner = (await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...))`, which is only true when the user is BOTH a team admin and a team owner — a condition that is essentially never true (a user has one role per team). Combined with the `isAttendee` check on line 52, this means the effective authorization is: the booking organizer OR ANY existing attendee of the booking. Any attendee (a guest invited to the meeting) can therefore call `viewer.bookings.addGuests` and add arbitrary email addresses to the booking, triggering calendar updates and emails to those addresses. This is a privilege-escalation/authorization flaw: guests should not be able to modify the attendee list. The `&&` should be `||` (matching the intended 'admin or owner' semantics), and the `isAttendee` branch should almost certainly be removed or restricted (e.g., only the organizer or team admin/owner may add guests).

true_positives.golden_comment: The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sendAddGuestsEmails ignores eventTypeMetadata email-disable settings and sends scheduled email to new guests without their context

Unlike every other send* function in this file (e.g., `sendScheduledEmails`, `sendRescheduledEmails`, `sendLocationChangeEmails`), `sendAddGuestsEmails` (line 525) accepts no `eventTypeMetadata` parameter and therefore never checks `eventTypeDisableHostEmail`/`eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail`. Event types configured with `disableStandardEmails` (metadata) will still receive organizer/attendee emails when guests are added, violating the organizer's email preferences. The handler has `booking.eventType` available and should pass `booking.eventType.metadata` through. Additionally, new guests receive `AttendeeScheduledEmail` (line 542) — a full 'booking confirmed' email — which may be misleading since no new booking was created for them; a dedicated 'you were added as a guest' template would be more accurate, but at minimum the metadata-based suppression must be honored.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.

uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.
Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.

false_positives.candidate:
'Add guests' action is offered for bookings where it cannot work (recurring series tab removes edit menu, but action also appears for past/cancelled/rejected bookings and non-organizers)

The `add_members` action is unconditionally added to `editBookingActions` (lines 194-200), which is only rendered under `bookedActions` → shown when `isConfirmed` (line 549) for upcoming bookings, or for past bookings (line 554). It is therefore offered for past bookings (where the server handler does not reject past bookings — see handler finding) and for cancelled bookings in some render paths. Additionally, the menu is shown to any viewer of the booking list; given the server-side authorization flaw (attendees can add guests), the UI gives no indication of who may use it. At minimum the action should be hidden for past bookings (`isBookingInPast`) and cancelled bookings, consistent with how `cancel` is filtered (lines 249-251).

Attendee creation is not atomic with the duplicate/blacklist filtering — race condition can create duplicate attendees

The handler first reads the booking's attendees (line 26), filters out emails already present (line 74-78), and then performs a separate `prisma.booking.update` with `createMany` (lines 92-106). There is no transaction and no unique constraint enforcement shown between the read and the write. Two concurrent `addGuests` calls (or a concurrent booking flow adding the same attendee) can both pass the duplicate check and both insert the same email, producing duplicate Attendee rows for one booking. This corrupts attendee lists, calendar events, and emails. The read-filter-write sequence should be wrapped in an interactive transaction (`prisma.$transaction`) with the duplicate check re-evaluated inside it, or rely on a DB unique constraint on (bookingId, email) with `skipDuplicates`/error handling.

Calendar update failure aborts the mutation after attendees were already persisted, leaving DB and calendar out of sync

`eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` (line 165) is awaited outside any try/catch and outside the DB transaction. If the calendar update throws (network error, invalid credentials, provider failure), the new Attendee rows created at line 92 remain committed in the database, but the mutation returns an error to the client. The booking now has guests in the DB who never received a calendar invite update, and a retry would hit the duplicate filter and report 'emails_must_be_unique_valid'. Either wrap the DB write and calendar update in a transaction with compensating logic, or catch the calendar error and report partial success; as written, failures leave inconsistent state with no rollback.

Calendar update uses the requesting user's credentials instead of the booking organizer's credentials

`getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` (line 158) loads the credentials of whoever is calling the mutation, and the `EventManager` is constructed with `...user` (the caller). If the caller is a team admin/owner or (per the flawed check) an attendee rather than the booking organizer, the calendar update for the organizer's event is attempted with the wrong user's credentials — the update may fail, be written to the wrong calendar, or be attributed to the wrong account. Calendar mutations for a booking should use the booking organizer's credentials (the booking already includes `user.credentials` and `user.destinationCalendar` in the query at lines 35-40, which are loaded but never used). The loaded organizer credentials should be passed to the EventManager instead of `ctx.user`'s.

Client-side validation accepts an array containing a single empty string as valid input path is blocked, but empty-string entries in multi-row input are not rejected before submit when combined with valid emails

The zod schema `z.array(z.string().email())` (line 26) rejects empty strings, so `handleAdd` correctly blocks submission when any row is empty — but only after the user clicks Add, and the error message shown ('emails_must_be_unique_valid') does not distinguish 'invalid/empty email' from 'duplicate email'. More importantly, `isInvalidEmail` is never reset to `false` when the user subsequently edits the emails to valid values (it is only reset on cancel or success), so after one failed attempt the red error banner stays visible even when the input becomes valid. The error state should be cleared on value change (e.g., in `setMultiEmailValue` wrapper) or recomputed on each submit attempt.

Email sending failure is silently swallowed with only a console.log

The `try { await sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests); } catch (err) { console.log("Error sending AddGuestsEmails"); }` block (lines 167-171) swallows all email errors and still returns `{ message: "Guests added" }` as success. New guests are added to the booking and the calendar is updated, but if the email dispatch fails (SMTP down, template render error), neither the new guests nor the organizer is notified, and the organizer sees a success toast. The error is only written to server logs with no structured logging (the codebase uses `logger` from `@calcom/lib/logger` elsewhere). At minimum this should use the structured logger and ideally surface a degraded-success indication to the caller.

ICS method REQUEST with status CONFIRMED is sent to existing attendees as if the event were (re)confirmed, without indicating what changed

The ICS attachment uses `method: "REQUEST"` and `status: "CONFIRMED"` (lines 15-17) with title 'new_guests_added'. For existing attendees this is a calendar update that will re-render the event in their calendar client; because the ICS contains the full updated attendee list, most clients will handle it, but the ICS `title`/`subtitle` ('Added - New guests added to your event' / 'emailed_you_and_any_other_attendees') is used as the event summary in some clients, potentially overwriting the real event title in the attendee's calendar view. The ICS should carry the actual event title (as `AttendeeScheduledEmail` does) rather than the notification title, so calendar clients do not display 'Added - New guests added to your event' as the meeting name.

MultiEmail mutates/reassigns the `value` prop and uses array index as React key, and removal of the last email hides the input entirely

Line 14 reassigns the `value` prop (`value = value || []`), which is a React anti-pattern (props should not be reassigned) though functionally harmless here. More concretely: (1) `key={index}` on line 26 for a list of editable text inputs causes React to reuse DOM/component state incorrectly when a middle row is removed — typing in row 2 after deleting row 1 can show stale values; a stable key (or the field content) should be used. (2) When the user removes the last remaining email via the remove button (lines 39-43), `value` becomes `[]`, and the component renders only the 'add emails' button (lines 77-91) — the label disappears and the UI affordance changes shape, which is disorienting inside the AddGuestsDialog where the dialog starts with `[""]` (one empty row) and the label 'Add Emails' is shown above the input.

Newly added guests are created with an empty name and the organizer's locale/timezone, and no Attendee-scheduling metadata (no bookingFields responses, no seats handling)

New attendees are created with `name: ""` (line 85), so they appear as blank names in the UI attendee list (BookingListItem renders `name || email`, so this is partially mitigated) and in emails. They also inherit the organizer's `timeZone` and `locale` (lines 87-88), which is a reasonable default but means per-attendee translations in `sendAddGuestsEmails` use the organizer's locale for guests. Furthermore, the handler does not consider `seatsPerTimeSlot` (group bookings): adding guests to a seated booking does not create `SeatReference` rows or decrement/increment seat counts, so a booking with seats can exceed its capacity silently. If seats bookings are in scope, seat references must be created and capacity validated; if not, the handler should reject bookings whose eventType has `seatsPerTimeSlot` set.

No validation that the booking is in a state that permits adding guests (cancelled/past bookings can be modified)

The handler fetches the booking by id and only checks existence and caller permission. It never checks `booking.status` (e.g., CANCELLED or REJECTED) or whether the booking is in the past. Adding guests to a cancelled booking resurrects attendee rows, sends 'guests added' emails and calendar REQUEST updates for an event that was cancelled, and mutates historical/past bookings. Other handlers in this router (e.g., editLocation) enforce status constraints. A guard such as rejecting when `booking.status === BookingStatus.CANCELLED` (and arguably when the booking end time is in the past) is needed.

Organizer email subject uses attendees[0].name which may be a newly added guest with an empty name

The subject interpolates `name: this.calEvent.attendees[0].name` (line 28). In the handler, newly created guests are inserted with `name: ""` (addGuests.handler.ts line 85), and attendee ordering after `createMany` is not guaranteed to put the original booker first. If a newly added guest (empty name) ends up at index 0, the organizer email subject renders as 'Guests Added: <eventType> with  at <date>' with a blank name. The subject should use the original booker (the attendee that existed before the addition) or fall back to the organizer/team name as the attendee template does (`this.calEvent.team?.name || this.calEvent.organizer.name`).

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Read-modify-write of retryCount is not atomic; concurrent cron runs can lose increments

The handler reads `retryCount` in the findMany (line 58) and later writes `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` (lines 184 and 195) based on that stale read. If the cron job runs concurrently (overlapping invocations, or the same reminder processed twice), both runs read the same value and write the same incremented value, so failures are undercounted and a reminder that failed twice may never reach retryCount > 1, defeating the retry limit. Use an atomic increment (`retryCount: { increment: 1 }`) instead of computing from the fetched value.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
deleteMany with retryCount > 1 deletes ALL workflow reminders (including EMAIL and WHATSAPP), not just SMS

The cleanup query at the top of the handler uses `OR: [{ method: SMS, scheduledDate <= now }, { retryCount: { gt: 1 } }]`. The second OR branch has no `method` filter, so every WorkflowReminder row in the database with retryCount > 1 is deleted — including EMAIL and WHATSAPP reminders that may be legitimately scheduled and pending. This causes silent loss of email/WhatsApp reminders for all users. The retryCount branch must be scoped to `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` (and arguably also `scheduled: false`), e.g. `{ method: WorkflowMethods.SMS, retryCount: { gt: 1 } }`.

false_positives.candidate:
Cleanup deletes SMS reminders whose scheduledDate has passed even if they were successfully scheduled and are still pending delivery

The first OR branch deletes all SMS reminders with `scheduledDate <= now` regardless of the `scheduled` flag. A reminder that was successfully scheduled with Twilio (scheduled: true, referenceId set) but whose scheduledDate has just passed is deleted from the DB before we can confirm delivery/cancellation status. This was pre-existing behavior, but combined with the new retry logic it also means a successfully scheduled reminder is removed at its fire time, so any downstream logic that relies on the WorkflowReminder row (e.g. cancellation when a booking is cancelled/rescheduled) loses the referenceId needed to cancel the Twilio message. The delete should be scoped to `scheduled: false` (or the deletion of past-due rows should only apply to unscheduled/failed reminders).

Failed retryCount update in catch block is not awaited error-handled; a DB failure here throws out of the loop iteration silently

Inside the catch block, the `prisma.workflowReminder.update` call can itself throw (e.g. transient DB error). If it does, the exception propagates out of the for-loop and aborts processing of all remaining reminders in this run, and the outer handler never sends its 200 response (the request hangs until timeout). The update should be wrapped or the loop should be resilient so one bad row doesn't abort the whole batch.

Reminders with no message or no sendTo are silently skipped and never retried or cleaned up

The retry increment only happens inside `if (message?.length && message?.length > 0 && sendTo)` (the else branch) or in the catch block. If `message` is empty/null (e.g. workflowStep has neither reminderBody nor template REMINDER) or `sendTo` is missing (e.g. SMS_NUMBER action with no sendTo configured, or booking without smsReminderNumber), the code falls through without scheduling, without incrementing retryCount, and without any error. The reminder stays `scheduled: false` forever and is re-fetched and re-processed by the cron on every run indefinitely — an infinite no-op loop and unbounded DB growth. These cases should either increment retryCount (so the cleanup deletes them) or be logged/handled explicitly.

Unscheduled reminders query does not exclude reminders that already exhausted retries

The findMany fetches all unscheduled SMS reminders within 7 days without filtering on retryCount. Reminders with retryCount >= 2 are only removed by the deleteMany at the start of the same run; between runs (or if the deleteMany fails/partially fails), they are re-fetched and re-processed, incrementing retryCount further and generating repeated Twilio attempts/log noise. Adding `retryCount: { lte: 1 }` to the where clause makes the retry cap robust and avoids wasted work.

true_positives.golden_comment: Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Org scope authorization misses org-level members when org has no child teams

In buildOrgAuthorizationCondition, userIdsFromOrg is only populated when teamsFromOrg.length > 0. If the organization has no child teams, userIdsFromOrg is set to [] and the second OR branch ('userId = ANY(...) AND isTeamBooking = false') is omitted entirely. This means direct members of the organization (users with a membership on the org team itself, not on a child team) are excluded from the org-scope query when the org has no sub-teams. The previous Prisma object implementation had the same structural issue only if the query was built the same way, but here the SQL makes the omission explicit and silently drops all non-team bookings for org members. The user ID list should include members of the org team itself (teamIds already includes options.orgId, so MembershipRepository.findAllByTeamIds should be called with the full teamIds array unconditionally, not only when child teams exist).

false_negatives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

false_positives.candidate:
Authorization check queries membership without verifying the org exists or belongs to the expected context

isOrgOwnerOrAdmin checks MembershipRepository.findUniqueByUserIdAndTeamId({ userId, teamId: orgId }) and verifies role is OWNER or ADMIN. However, it does not verify that the team with id=orgId is actually an organization (isOrganization=true). If a caller passes a regular team's ID as orgId, and the user is an OWNER/ADMIN of that regular team, the authorization check passes and the user gets access to insights scoped to that 'org'. The zod schema only validates that orgId is a number, not that it corresponds to an organization. This could allow privilege escalation if the API layer doesn't separately validate that orgId is an organization. The service should verify that the orgId refers to an actual organization (e.g., by checking team.isOrganization) before granting access.

Event type filter SQL has unparenthesized OR, causing incorrect precedence when combined with other conditions

The eventTypeId filter is built as Prisma.sql`("eventTypeId" = ${id}) OR ("eventParentId" = ${id})` without wrapping parentheses. When this is combined with other filters via buildFilterConditions' reduce (which wraps as `(${acc}) AND (${condition})`), the OR is actually parenthesized correctly in the multi-filter case. However, when eventTypeId is the ONLY filter, getFilterConditions returns the bare OR expression. If a caller then combines this with authorization conditions via getBaseConditions, it wraps as `(${authConditions}) AND (${filterConditions})`, which is correct. But the test at line 384-386 of the test file expects the bare unparenthesized OR, and any future caller that embeds the filter condition without wrapping (e.g., `WHERE ${filterConditions} AND something_else`) would get wrong precedence: `eventTypeId = X OR eventParentId = X AND something_else` evaluates as `eventTypeId = X OR (eventParentId = X AND something_else)`. The filter builder should wrap multi-clause OR conditions in parentheses for safety, matching defensive SQL construction practices.

Integration test queries wrong table and lacks assertions on authorization enforcement

The getBaseConditions integration test runs `SELECT id FROM "BookingTimeStatusDenormalized" WHERE ${baseConditions}` but the test setup creates bookings via prisma.booking.create — it never creates any BookingTimeStatusDenormalized rows. The test expects results to equal [{ id: userBooking.id }], which would only pass if BookingTimeStatusDenormalized is populated by a database trigger or if the test database has some sync mechanism. If the denormalized table is populated asynchronously or by a separate process, this test is flaky and depends on timing. Additionally, the test only verifies the positive case (authorized user sees their booking). It does not verify that the NOTHING_CONDITION actually blocks unauthorized access at the SQL level, nor that the org/team scope conditions correctly exclude bookings from other teams. The removed 'Caching' describe block also means caching behavior (cachedAuthConditions/cachedFilterConditions) is no longer tested at all, despite the service still implementing it.

NOTHING_CONDITION SQL lacks spaces around equals sign, inconsistent with other SQL fragments

The constant is defined as Prisma.sql`1=0` while all other SQL fragments in the file use spaced operators (e.g., '"userId" = ${id}'). This is purely cosmetic but makes the codebase inconsistent. More importantly, the test file defines its own NOTHING_CONDITION = Prisma.sql`1=0` at line 10 rather than importing it from the service, which means if the service's definition changes, the test won't catch it. The constant should be exported from the service and imported in tests.

Org scope includes the org team ID in teamId ANY() list, matching org-level team bookings incorrectly

teamIds is built as [options.orgId, ...teamsFromOrg.map(t => t.id)] and used in the condition '("teamId" = ANY(${teamIds})) AND ("isTeamBooking" = true)'. Including the organization's own ID in the teamId list means any booking whose teamId equals the org ID is treated as an authorized team booking. Whether this is intended depends on the data model (whether bookings can have teamId pointing at an organization), but the previous object-based implementation used the same list, so this is a pre-existing semantic question — however, the raw SQL makes it harder to audit. More importantly, the asymmetry with buildTeamAuthorizationCondition (which only uses the specific team ID) suggests the org ID inclusion may be unintentional. This should be verified against the BookingTimeStatusDenormalized schema and the intended authorization semantics.

Prisma.Sql equality comparison via toEqual may not reliably compare SQL fragments

The tests use expect(conditions).toEqual(Prisma.sql`...`) to compare Prisma.Sql objects. Prisma.Sql instances are objects with .strings and .values properties (and internal symbols). toEqual does a deep structural comparison, which may pass or fail depending on Prisma's internal representation, symbol properties, and whether the values arrays contain the same references. Two Prisma.sql fragments with identical SQL text and parameters may not be deep-equal if Prisma attaches non-enumerable properties or if the values contain different object identities. This makes the tests brittle: they test Prisma's internal object structure rather than the actual SQL semantics. A more robust approach would compare conditions.strings and conditions.values explicitly, or execute the SQL against the database and compare results. The PR description even notes 'All test expectations now use direct Prisma.sql comparisons instead of inspecting .strings and .values properties' — this is a regression in test quality, not an improvement.

Removal of findMany method is a breaking API change for all callers of InsightsBookingService

The PR removes the public findMany(findManyArgs) method entirely and replaces it with getBaseConditions() which returns a raw Prisma.Sql fragment. Any existing caller that used service.findMany({ select, where, orderBy, ... }) to query BookingTimeStatusDenormalized will now fail to compile or at runtime. The PR description frames this as a test-only change ('updates the InsightsBookingService integration tests'), but the service file diff shows a substantial API removal. Callers must now construct their own $queryRaw queries with the returned SQL fragment, which changes the contract significantly: they lose Prisma's type-safe select/where/orderBy/pagination handling and must hand-write SQL for everything beyond the WHERE clause. This is a breaking change that should be called out explicitly, and all call sites in the codebase must be updated in the same PR (or the old method kept as a wrapper). The PR provides no evidence that callers were migrated.

Test cleanup function has inconsistent delete vs deleteMany usage and potential foreign key failures

The cleanup function mixes deleteMany and delete for the same models: it uses prisma.booking.deleteMany({ where: { id: booking.id } }) and prisma.eventType.deleteMany({ where: { id: eventType.id } }) but prisma.membership.delete({ where: { id: orgMembership.id } }) and prisma.team.deleteMany for teams. More critically, the cleanup order deletes the booking before the event type (correct), but deletes memberships before teams and users — however, it deletes the main membership via deleteMany({ where: { id: membership.id } }) which is fine, but then deletes orgMembership via delete. The additional memberships are deleted first, then additional users, then additional teams, then booking, eventType, main membership, orgMembership, team, org, user. If any foreign key constraint exists (e.g., Booking references EventType, EventType references User/Team, Membership references User/Team), the order matters. Deleting the user at the end after deleting teams should be fine, but if the booking still references the event type when eventType.deleteMany runs, it could fail. The test creates a booking with eventTypeId and userId, so deleting the event type while the booking exists would violate FK constraints unless cascade is configured. The cleanup deletes booking first (line 176-178), so this is OK, but the pattern is fragile and the deleteMany-with-single-id pattern is misleading — delete would be clearer.

Test for non-owner/admin user only tests MEMBER role, not other non-privileged states

The test 'should return NOTHING for non-owner/admin user' creates a user with MembershipRole.MEMBER. It does not test edge cases such as: a user with no membership at all (should also return NOTHING), a user with a membership that is not accepted (accepted: false), or a user who is a member of a child team but not the org. The isOrgOwnerOrAdmin function checks membership.accepted and membership.role, so unaccepted memberships should return NOTHING, but this path is not tested. Missing test coverage for the accepted=false case is notable because the code explicitly checks it.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
updateManyByCredentialId called with empty data object relies on @updatedAt side effect

`SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` is called with an empty `data` object purely so Prisma's `@updatedAt` bumps `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt`. This is implicit and fragile: `updateMany` with empty data still issues an UPDATE touching every SelectedCalendar row for the credential (a write lock and WAL churn on potentially many rows) just to refresh a timestamp, and if the schema ever drops `@updatedAt` the call silently becomes a no-op while still scanning/updating rows. The repository method should accept an explicit intent (e.g. a dedicated `touchUpdatedAtByCredentialId` that sets `updatedAt: new Date()` explicitly) so the write is self-documenting and doesn't depend on a schema side effect.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
macOS-only sed syntax breaks the script on Linux

Line 68 uses `sed -i '' -E ...`, where the empty string argument is the macOS/BSD `sed` syntax for in-place editing without backup. On GNU sed (Linux, CI runners), `sed -i ''` treats `''` as a file name and fails with an error, so the script cannot update `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` on Linux. The script should use a portable form such as `sed -i.bak -E ... && rm -f "$ENV_FILE.bak"` or detect the platform, especially since this is a developer helper that may be run in containers/CI.

true_positives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Authorization failure throws a generic Error instead of a TRPCError, producing a 500

When the credential is not found or not owned by the user, the handler throws `new Error("Credential not found or access denied")`. In tRPC, a plain `Error` is surfaced to the client as an INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR (500) with the message potentially masked in production, whereas authorization failures should be `TRPCError({ code: "FORBIDDEN" })` (or `NOT_FOUND`) so the client gets a correct 403/404 and the UI can distinguish 'access denied' from a real server error. The current code conflates a client-input/authorization problem with a server failure.

true_positives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hardcoded 'en-US' locale for cache timestamp formatting

The cache timestamp is formatted with `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { dateStyle: "short", timeStyle: "short" })`, ignoring the user's locale from `useLocale()`. Every other user-facing string in the component is localized via `t(...)`, but the date is always rendered in US format, which is inconsistent for international users. The formatter should use the current locale (e.g. from `useLocale()`'s `i18n.language`) instead of the hardcoded 'en-US'. Additionally, `new Date(cacheUpdatedAt)` assumes the tRPC payload deserializes the timestamp to a Date/string; if superjson/date serialization changes, this could render 'Invalid Date'. A safer approach is to format the raw value defensively.

false_positives.candidate:
Authorization check only covers direct user credentials, not delegation credentials

The handler verifies ownership with `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { id: credentialId, userId: user.id } })`. However, the connectedCalendars UI passes `connectedCalendar.credentialId` for delegation-credential calendars too (the wrapper renders CredentialActionsDropdown for every connected calendar, including those with `delegationCredentialId` set). For a delegation credential, the `Credential` row's `userId` is the organization/service-account owner, not the logged-in user, so `findFirst` returns null and the mutation throws — meaning the feature silently fails for delegated calendars. Conversely, if any code path ever passes a credentialId belonging to a delegation credential owned by the same user id, the subsequent `prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany({ where: { credentialId } })` deletes cache rows for that credential without scoping to the requesting user. The delete should additionally verify the credential is a non-delegation credential owned by the user (e.g. also check `delegationCredentialId: null` or resolve the credential through the user's enriched credential list) before deleting cache rows.

Cache deletion does not invalidate the connectedCalendars query, so cache status stays visible after deletion

The `deleteCache` mutation's `onSuccess` only shows a toast and calls the optional `onSuccess` prop; it never invalidates `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`. The parent wrapper passes `onSuccess={onChanged}`, but `onChanged` is an optional callback prop of `SelectedCalendarsSettingsWebWrapper` and is not wired to refetch the `connectedCalendars` query inside this component (the query is owned by `SelectedCalendarsSettingsWebWrapper` with `suspense: true`). After a successful delete, the cached `cacheUpdatedAt` remains in the query cache, so the dropdown continues to show 'Cache Status / Last updated: ...' and the 'Delete cached data' action for a credential whose cache was just deleted. The mutation should invalidate `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` in `onSettled`/`onSuccess`, mirroring what the disconnect mutation already does.

Cache status is shown for any Google Calendar credential with a cacheUpdatedAt, including delegation credentials that cannot be deleted

`hasCache = isGoogleCalendar && cacheUpdatedAt` does not consider `delegationCredentialId`. For a delegation-credential Google Calendar connection, the dropdown renders the cache status and the 'Delete cached data' action, but `canDisconnect` is false. Clicking delete will call the `deleteCache` mutation with the delegation credential's id, which (per the handler's `userId: user.id` ownership check) will fail with 'Credential not found or access denied' and show a generic error toast. Either the delete action should be hidden for delegation credentials, or the handler should support deleting cache for credentials the user is authorized to manage.

ConnectedCalendarList receives disableConnectionModification prop but the wrapper computes shouldDisableConnectionModification and never passes it

The wrapper computes `shouldDisableConnectionModification = isDisabled || disableConnectionModification` (line 166) and passes it to `SelectedCalendarsSettingsHeading`, but when rendering `ConnectedCalendarList` (line 179-187) it passes the raw `disableConnectionModification` prop and omits the scope-based `isDisabled` component. As a result, when a scope is disabled (`disabledScope === scope`), the heading hides the 'add calendar' control but each `CredentialActionsDropdown` still receives `disableConnectionModification={false}` and remains fully enabled, letting users delete cache / disconnect integrations while the rest of the scope is locked. The wrapper should pass `shouldDisableConnectionModification` (or `isDisabled || disableConnectionModification`) into `ConnectedCalendarList`.

Delete-cache confirmation dialog closes immediately and fires mutation without awaiting it

In the delete-cache `ConfirmationDialogContent`, `onConfirm` calls `deleteCacheMutation.mutate({ credentialId })` and then synchronously `setDeleteModalOpen(false)`. The dialog therefore closes instantly regardless of whether the mutation succeeds or fails, and there is no pending/loading state on the confirm button. If the mutation fails (e.g. the authorization issue for delegation credentials), the user already saw the dialog close and only gets an error toast, with no way to retry from the dialog. The dialog should stay open while `deleteCacheMutation.isPending` and close only in `onSuccess` (the same pattern should be applied to the disconnect dialog at line 148).

Developer-only webhook test script committed to the repository root scripts directory

This script is a local developer convenience for exposing a webhook URL via Tunnelmole and mutating a `.env` file. Committing it to the shared `scripts/` directory implies it is a supported repo tool, but it hardcodes paths (`../.env`), a fixed port, and a third-party tunneling service, and it writes to a real environment file. It should either be moved out of the repo (e.g. documented in a README/CONTRIBUTING note) or clearly marked as a local-only helper, otherwise it invites accidental execution in shared environments.

Interface and mock declare getCacheStatusByCredentialIds but mock class also has undeclared deleteManyByCredential

The mock class `CalendarCacheRepositoryMock` implements `deleteManyByCredential()` (line 23 of the mock) which is not part of `ICalendarCacheRepository`, while the real `CalendarCacheRepository` has no `deleteManyByCredential` method — the deletion paths use `prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany` directly (e.g. `CalendarService.unwatchCalendar` line 955 and `deleteCache.handler.ts` line 28). This asymmetry means the mock does not actually mirror the real repository's surface: code that calls `repository.deleteManyByCredential(...)` would work against the mock but crash against the real implementation. Either add `deleteManyByCredential` to the interface and implement it in the real repository (and use it in the handler/service), or remove it from the mock so the mismatch is caught at compile time.

Migration comment contradicts the actual SQL (default value is provided)

The migration's warning comment says 'Added the required column `updatedAt` ... without a default value. This is not possible if the table is not empty.', but the SQL below it adds the column with `NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()`, which is exactly the safe pattern for non-empty tables. The stale Prisma-generated warning is misleading to reviewers and suggests the migration is unsafe when it is not. The comment block should be removed or corrected to reflect that a default is provided.

No tests cover getCacheStatusByCredentialIds, deleteCacheHandler, or the CredentialActionsDropdown flow

The PR adds a new repository method (`getCacheStatusByCredentialIds`), a new tRPC mutation (`deleteCache`) with an authorization check, and a new UI component with destructive actions, but none of the changed files include or reference tests. In particular there is no test verifying that (a) `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` returns the max updatedAt per credential and handles credentials with no cache rows, (b) `deleteCacheHandler` rejects credentialIds not owned by the session user, and (c) the dropdown hides the delete action for delegation credentials. Given the authorization-sensitive nature of `deleteCache`, at minimum a handler-level test for the ownership check is warranted before merge.

cacheUpdatedAt enrichment changes the connectedCalendars output shape without a schema/type guard

The handler spreads `...calendar` and adds `cacheUpdatedAt`, changing the tRPC output type of `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`. The UI consumes it via `RouterOutputs` inference, so this is type-safe end-to-end, but there is no explicit output schema (`output()` parser) on the procedure and no test pinning the new field. If the enrichment is later removed or renamed, downstream consumers (including platform atoms that are published as a library) will break at runtime rather than at compile time in external consumers. Adding an output schema or at least a handler-level test asserting `cacheUpdatedAt` presence would make the contract explicit.

connectedCalendars now always instantiates the real CalendarCacheRepository, bypassing the disabled-cache mock

The handler unconditionally does `new CalendarCacheRepository()` and calls `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds`. The codebase has a `CalendarCacheRepositoryMock` used when the calendar-cache feature is disabled (its methods log 'Skipping ... due to calendar-cache being disabled'), and `CalendarCache.init(null)` elsewhere selects mock vs real based on configuration. By hard-instantiating the real repository, every `connectedCalendars` query now performs an extra `calendarCache.groupBy` database round-trip even on deployments/teams where calendar cache is disabled, adding latency to a query that is rendered on the installed-apps page and in onboarding. The handler should resolve the repository through the same factory/feature-flag mechanism used by `CalendarCache.init` so the extra query is skipped when the feature is off.

getCacheStatusByCredentialIds includes cache rows keyed only by userId (in-memory delegation credentials)

The repository's own `getCachedAvailability` documents that for in-memory delegation credentials the cache is queried solely by `userId` + `key` (no `credentialId`), because those credentials have no DB row. `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` groups strictly by `credentialId`, so cache entries created under the userId-only path (negative/in-memory credential ids) will never be attributed to any credential, and the UI will show no cache status even though cache data exists and is being served. The status query should also aggregate rows where `credentialId` is an in-memory delegation credential id and map them to the user's real credential, or the handler should fall back to a userId-based lookup.

getCacheStatusByCredentialIds returns stale cache timestamps for expired entries

`getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` groups `CalendarCache` rows by `credentialId` and takes `_max.updatedAt` without filtering on `expiresAt`. The cache read path (`getCachedAvailability`) only serves rows where `expiresAt >= now`, so a credential whose cache rows have all expired will still report a non-null `updatedAt` in the UI ('Last updated: ...'), even though no usable cache exists and the next availability lookup will be a cache miss. The `where` clause should include `expiresAt: { gte: new Date() }` (or the UI should treat expired timestamps as no cache) so the displayed status reflects actually-serveable cache.

updateManyByCredentialId does not scope by userId, allowing cross-user updates if misused

The new `updateManyByCredentialId(credentialId, data)` filters only on `credentialId`. Credential ids are globally unique so this is safe for the current single caller, but unlike sibling methods (`findManyUserLevel`, `updateUserLevel`, `deleteUserLevel`) it has no user-level guard, and the caller in `CalendarService.fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache` passes `this.credential.id` without re-verifying the credential belongs to the current user context. Any future caller that passes an unvalidated credentialId (e.g. from request input) would mass-update another user's SelectedCalendar rows. The method should either also require/verify `userId` in the where clause or be documented/enforced as internal-only.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reminder cancellation calls are not awaited, so failures are silent and ordering is not guaranteed

In the `updatedBookings.forEach(...)` loop, `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId)` and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId)` are invoked without `await` (and the enclosing `forEach` callback is not async). These functions are async and internally catch errors, so the promises float. Consequences: (1) the handler can return before the `cancelled: true` DB update (or the Twilio cancel / row delete for SMS) has completed, so a crash or early response can leave reminders un-cancelled; (2) unhandled promise rejections are possible if the internal try/catch is bypassed; (3) for SMS reminders, `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` now deletes the DB row immediately, so a non-awaited call racing with the later `prismaPromises`/`apiDeletes` `Promise.all` creates unclear ordering. The loop should be `for...of` with `await`, or the promises should be collected and awaited.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
immediateDelete path uses the wrong SendGrid endpoint and never deletes the DB row

`deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminderId, referenceId, immediateDelete = true)` sends `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends` with `{ batch_id: referenceId, status: "cancel" }` in the body. As noted in the PR description, the correct SendGrid cancellation API is `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends/{batch_id}` with `{ status: "cancel" }` — the batch id belongs in the URL path. With the batch_id in the body, SendGrid will not cancel the scheduled send. Furthermore, when `immediateDelete` is true the function `return`s immediately after the API call and never deletes or marks the `workflowReminder` row, so the row stays in the DB with `scheduled: true` and the stale `referenceId`; the CRON cleanup at the top of `scheduleEmailReminders.ts` will eventually delete it only when `scheduledDate` passes, but the SendGrid send itself was never cancelled. This path is used when a workflow or a workflow step is deleted (workflows.tsx lines 214 and 521), meaning deleting a workflow can leave its scheduled emails active. Fix the URL to `/v3/user/scheduled_sends/${referenceId}` and delete/mark the DB row after a successful cancellation.

true_positives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New cancelled column is nullable with no default, so existing and new rows have NULL instead of false

The migration adds `"cancelled" BOOLEAN` (nullable, no default) and the Prisma schema declares `cancelled Boolean?`. Every existing row gets NULL, and new reminders created in `scheduleEmailReminder`/`scheduleSMSReminder` (emailReminderManager.ts lines 169-193, smsReminderManager.ts lines 148-172) do not set `cancelled`, so they are also NULL. The CRON query uses `cancelled: true`, which correctly excludes NULL rows in Prisma, but any code doing truthiness checks or `cancelled === false` comparisons will misbehave, and the column wastes storage on NULLs. Prefer `BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT false` in the migration and `cancelled Boolean @default(false)` in the schema so the flag has a well-defined value for all rows.

false_positives.candidate:
CRON cancellation uses wrong SendGrid endpoint and can cancel the wrong batch

The new cancellation loop calls `client.request({ url: "/v3/user/scheduled_sends", method: "POST", body: { batch_id: reminder.referenceId, status: "cancel" } })`.
