For the common case of an allowed request, this adds an extra cache Get (permDenialCache) on every Check call, even though the denial cache only ever contains entries for denied requests. Since denials are expected to be rarer than allows, the ordering could be reversed (check permCache first, and only consult permDenialCache on a permCache miss or a negative checkPermission result) to avoid the extra lookup on the hot allowed path. This is a minor performance concern given the local in-memory cache, but it is a real extra allocation and map lookup on every authorization check.

Denial cache is keyed on the request's userUID string, not the resolved internal user identifier, allowing UID-reuse confusion

The denial cache key uses checkReq.UserUID, which is the raw UID portion parsed from the subject (e.g. 'user:test-uid' -> 'test-uid'). However, GetUserIdentifiers (line 452-479) explicitly supports looking up users by numeric internal ID when the UID parses as an integer (line 465-468: 'Assume that numeric UID is user ID'). This means the same subject UID string can resolve to different internal users depending on whether it is treated as a UID or an internal ID, and across namespaces the same UID string may map to different internal IDs. The positive permission cache (userPermCacheKey) is keyed on the resolved userIdentifiers.UID (line 360, 379), but the denial cache is keyed on the unresolved request UID. If a user's UID is changed, or if a numeric subject is interpreted as an internal ID in one request and a UID in another, denial entries will be applied to the wrong resolved identity. The denial cache should be keyed on the resolved UserIdentifiers (both UID and internal ID) exactly like permCache, not on the raw request subject.

Denial cache is populated even when the permission check failed due to a transient error path, and denials are never invalidated on permission grants

At line 153-155, whenever the freshly-fetched permissions from the DB produce allowed==false, the denial is written to permDenialCache with a 30s TTL (shortCacheTTL). There is no invalidation when permissions are granted, revoked, or when a dashboard/folder is created. Combined with the client-side change in rbac.go that disables the authlib client cache (NoopCache) for in-proc mode, the server-side denial cache becomes the only cache in the path, so a user who is denied once (e.g. before a dashboard is created, or before a permission is assigned) will continue to receive Allowed:false for up to 30 seconds even after the grant/create succeeds. This directly undermines the PR's stated goal ('allow users to fetch newly created dashboards and folders'): a creator who first hits a Check that is denied (e.g. a pre-creation existence probe, or a check for a parent folder they don't yet have) will have that denial cached and subsequent checks for the newly created resource will be short-circuited at line 117-121. The denial cache must either be keyed to avoid caching denials for resources that may not exist yet, be invalidated on resource creation/permission changes, or only cache denials when the resource is confirmed to exist.

Denial cache key omits identity type, allowing cross-identity authorization bypass

The denial cache key is built as userPermDenialCacheKey(namespace, userUID, action, name, parent) using only the raw userUID string from the request subject (checkReq.UserUID), without including checkReq.IdentityType. The same UID string can be used with different identity types (e.g. 'user:123', 'service-account:123', 'anonymous:123' all yield UserUID '123' after ParseTypeID). A denial cached for one identity type (say an anonymous user or a service account with UID '123') will be returned for a real user with the same numeric UID, causing Check() to return Allowed:false at line 117-121 without ever consulting permissions. Conversely, and more dangerously, the key does not distinguish identities, so a denial entry created for identity type A is treated as authoritative for identity type B. The consequence is incorrect authorization decisions (denials for legitimate users, or stale denials applied to different identities sharing a UID string). The key must include the identity type (and ideally the resolved internal user ID from UserIdentifiers rather than the raw subject UID).

Denial-cache test does not cover the core security property: denial entries must not leak across identity types or resources

The new test 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' (line 973-995) only verifies that a denial entry causes a denial. It does not test the critical negative cases that this PR's key design makes possible: (1) a denial cached for identity type 'anonymous' with UID '0' must not deny a 'user:0' or 'service-account:0' subject (same UID string, different identity type — see the key-construction issue); (2) a denial for (name='a_b', parent='c') must not deny (name='a', parent='b_c') given the ambiguous underscore-joined key; (3) a denial cached before a permission grant must stop applying after the grant (invalidation). Without these tests, the cross-identity and collision bugs in the denial cache key would pass CI. Tests should be added that assert a denial entry for one identity type / one resource does not affect a different identity type / resource.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
GrafanaRuleListItem in FilterView is missing the React key prop

In FilterViewResults, the 'grafana' case renders <GrafanaRuleListItem rule={rule} groupIdentifier={groupIdentifier} namespaceName={...} showLocation={true} /> without a key prop, while the 'datasource' and default cases correctly use key={key}. React will warn about missing keys in lists and may cause incorrect reconciliation when the filtered rule list changes (e.g., rules reordering or being removed while loading more pages), potentially leading to stale UI state being attached to the wrong rule rows.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silence drawer only opens for ruler rules; silencing is broken for Grafana rules in the list view

The silence drawer is rendered only when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) && showSilenceDrawer` (line 104), where `rule` is the RulerRuleDTO. In the list view, RuleActionsButtons is rendered with only promRule (GrafanaRuleListItem passes `promRule={rule}` and no `rule` prop), so `rule` is undefined, rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(undefined) is false, and clicking 'Silence notifications' in the AlertRuleMenu sets showSilenceDrawer=true but no drawer ever opens — the click appears to do nothing. Meanwhile the menu item itself is shown because canSilence is computed from grafanaSilenceAbility (prom-rule based). This is a broken user flow: the Silence action is advertised but non-functional in the list view. The GrafanaGroupLoader test asserts the silence menu item is present, but no test verifies the drawer actually opens from the list view.

false_positives.candidate:
Delete menu item requires rulerRule, so Delete is never available in the list view where ruler rules are no longer fetched

The Delete menu item is gated on `canDelete && rulerRule` (line 165) and calls handleDelete(rulerRule, groupIdentifier). In the new list view (GrafanaRuleListItem → RuleActionsButtons.V2 → AlertRuleMenu), only promRule is passed; rulerRule is undefined. Therefore the Delete menu item never renders in the alert list, even for users with delete permission — canDelete may be true (via grafanaDeleteAbility from useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities) but the `&& rulerRule` condition suppresses the item. Conversely, in RuleActionsButtons.V2 the delete flow is wired via handleDelete={() => showDeleteModal(identifier, groupIdentifier)} which uses the identifier, not the rulerRule object — so the menu's handleDelete signature (rule: RulerRuleDTO, groupIdentifier) is incompatible with the list view. This is a functional regression: users cannot delete Grafana-managed rules from the list view. The GrafanaGroupLoader.test.tsx test 'should render correct menu actions' expects exactly 4 menu items and notably does NOT include delete in its assertions (silence, copyLink, duplicate, export) — consistent with delete being broken/hidden, and the test enshrines the broken behavior.

Error handling only covers missing promResponse; a failed Prometheus query with error but no data shows the generic error Alert, but a failed query that returns data=undefined with isLoading=false is conflated with 'no data'

The component checks `if (!promResponse)` to show an error Alert, but RTK Query returns `data: undefined` both when the query failed AND potentially during refetching/polling edge cases. The old code checked `!rulerResponse && !promResponse`. More importantly, the query error object (promResponse error from useGetGrafanaGroupsQuery) is never inspected — the component destructures only { data, isLoading }, so an HTTP error (e.g., 403, 500) results in data=undefined and the generic 'Failed to load rules' Alert without the actual error message. The old GrafanaRuleLoader surfaced rulerRuleGroupError/promRuleGroupError via RulerRuleLoadingError. Error detail is lost in the new implementation.

Extra closing brace in getGrafanaRuleKey produces malformed key

getGrafanaRuleKey returns `grafana-${namespace.uid}-${groupName}-${rule.uid}}` — there is a trailing `}` with no matching opening brace. This produces keys like 'grafana-uid-group-ruleuid}' which are still unique so functionally mostly harmless, but it is clearly a typo that makes keys inconsistent with the datasource key format and could confuse debugging; it should be `grafana-${namespace.uid}-${groupName}-${rule.uid}`.

Federated rule group check silently disabled in useAllRulerRuleAbilities, allowing edit/delete of federated rules

The old useAllAlertRuleAbilities computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)` from the CombinedRuleGroup, and federated rules were treated as immutable (no edit/delete/duplicate). The refactored useAllRulerRuleAbilities (lines 242-245) hardcodes `const isFederated = false;` with a TODO comment, and its signature only receives the RulerRuleDTO and groupIdentifier — it has no access to the group's source_tenants. As a result, for cloud (Mimir/Cortex) federated rule groups, Update/Delete/Duplicate/Pause abilities are no longer suppressed by immutability, and the UI will offer edit/delete actions on federated rules that the backend ruler will reject (or worse, the permission checks that previously gated these actions are bypassed at the UI level). This is a real authorization/UX regression for multi-tenant federated setups.

Menu test asserts exactly 4 items but Delete is silently missing — test enshrines broken delete flow

The test 'should render correct menu actions when More button is clicked' grants AlertingRuleDelete permission and folder delete permission in beforeEach, then asserts the menu contains silence, copyLink, duplicate, export and `expect(menuItems.length).toBe(4)`. Given the delete permission is granted, a correct implementation would show 5 items (including Delete). The assertion of exactly 4 items passes only because AlertRuleMenu gates Delete on `canDelete && rulerRule` and rulerRule is undefined in the list view (see AlertRuleMenu.tsx line 165). The test therefore locks in the regression where Delete is unavailable from the list view despite the user having delete permissions. The test should either assert Delete is present (and the component fixed) or explicitly document/verify the intended behavior.

Pause menu item requires rulerRule, but the list view no longer fetches ruler rules, so Pause is never available for Grafana rules in the list

The Pause menu item is gated on `canPause && rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) && groupIdentifier.groupOrigin === 'grafana'` (line 123) and renders <MenuItemPauseRule rule={rulerRule} .../>. In the new list view, GrafanaRuleListItem renders RuleActionsButtons with only promRule (no rulerRule), so rulerRule is undefined in AlertRuleMenu. rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(undefined) returns false (isGrafanaRulerRule checks typeof rule === 'object'), so the Pause menu item never renders in the list view even when canPause is true (computed via the grafana prom-rule abilities). Additionally, MenuItemPauseRule requires a RulerGrafanaRuleDTO to pause the rule via the ruler API — with ruler data removed from the list view, pausing from the list is broken for Grafana-managed rules. Either the pause action needs a prom-rule-based implementation (e.g., PATCH via prometheusApi) or the menu item must be hidden consistently; as written, the ability check says 'can pause' but the UI silently omits the action, and the OR-ed canPause logic gives a false signal.

Removing the ruler fetch eliminates 'Creating' and 'Deleting' transient states from the group list

The old GrafanaGroupLoader fetched both the Prometheus groups and the ruler group, matched them by UID, and rendered: (a) ruler rules without a prom counterpart as 'Creating' (RuleOperation.Creating), and (b) prom rules without a ruler counterpart as 'Deleting' (RuleOperationListItem with RuleOperation.Deleting). The new implementation only fetches promResponse and renders only prom rules. Consequences: (1) A rule that was just created (ruler has it, Prometheus hasn't evaluated/propagated it yet) will not appear in the list at all until Prometheus picks it up — the user gets no feedback that creation is in progress. (2) A rule being deleted may linger as a normal-looking row (or disappear abruptly) instead of showing a 'Deleting' state. (3) The RulesTable.test.tsx still contains tests for 'Creating'/'Deleting' states (lines 151-200) but those test RulesTable with CombinedRule objects, not this loader — the GrafanaGroupLoader.test.tsx had its 'creating state' and 'deleting state' tests removed (see diff: 'should render rule with url and creating state when only ruler rule exists' and 'should render delete rule operation list item when only prom rule exists' were deleted). This is a deliberate product decision perhaps, but it removes user-facing state feedback and the PR description does not mention it; at minimum the removed tests indicate lost coverage of previously supported behavior.

Stale comment about preloading ruler rules remains after ruler prefetch was removed

The comment at lines 81-82 says 'This is not mandatory to preload ruler rules, but it improves the UX / Because the user waits a bit longer for the initial load but doesn't need to wait for each group to be loaded'. The ruler prefetch (alertRuleApi.util.prefetch('getGrafanaRulerGroup', ...)) was removed in this PR (see diff), so the comment now describes behavior that no longer exists. The comment should be updated to describe the Prometheus group cache population only.

Test names say 'Should not render' but mocks grant the permission — assertions are inverted relative to test intent

The tests are named 'Should not render Edit button for users with the update permission' and mock useIsRuleEditable to return isEditable: true (i.e., the user HAS update permission), then assert the Edit button is NOT in the document. The test names and the mocked state contradict each other: either the name should be 'without the update permission' (matching RulesTable.test.tsx naming) or the mock should return isEditable: false. As written, the test passes but its name misleads future maintainers about what is being verified. Same issue for the Delete test (line 74) and the cloud rule tests (lines 89, 100).

getIsProvisioned prefers ruler rule provenance over prom rule provenance, inconsistent with the ruler-less list view

getIsProvisioned(rule, promRule) returns isProvisionedRule(rule) if a ruler rule exists, otherwise isProvisionedPromRule(promRule). In the list view only promRule exists, so provisioning status comes from promRule.provenance. The new GrafanaPromRuleDTOBase type adds `provenance?: string` (unified-alerting-dto.ts line 135), so this works, but the two sources can disagree (ruler provenance vs prom provenance), and the duplicate flow (RedirectToCloneRule with isProvisioned) will behave differently between the list view and the rule details view for the same rule. More importantly, isProvisionedPromRule checks `prometheusRuleType.grafana.rule(promRule) && Boolean(promRule.provenance)` — for cloud prom rules provenance is undefined so it returns false, which is correct. The risk is divergence between the two code paths; a single source of truth should be used.

isProvisioned derived from promRule.provenance, but GrafanaRuleListItem also accepts an operation prop that is never passed by callers

GrafanaRuleListItem accepts an optional `operation?: RuleOperation` prop and passes it to AlertRuleListItem, but neither caller (GrafanaGroupLoader line 70-77 nor FilterView line 157-162) passes `operation`. Since the ruler-based matching that produced Creating/Deleting operations was removed, the prop is dead code. Additionally, isProvisioned is computed as Boolean(provenance) from the prom rule — the newly added provenance field on GrafanaPromRuleDTOBase. If the Prometheus API does not actually populate provenance on rule DTOs (it's an optional field added in this PR), provisioned rules will incorrectly appear editable/deletable in the list. This needs verification against the backend API contract.

skipToken sentinel is a module-level Symbol shared across hook instances, enabling cross-component cache confusion

skipToken is a single module-level Symbol used as a sentinel to mean 'do not compute abilities for this rule'. useGrafanaPromRuleAbility/useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities map skipToken to `undefined` and then call useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined), which returns abilities computed for an undefined rule: isEditable=false, isRemovable=false, but Duplicate = toAbility(AlwaysSupported, rulesPermissions.create) and View = toAbility(AlwaysSupported, rulesPermissions.read) — i.e., [true, <global-permission>]. In AlertRuleMenu, canDuplicate/canExport etc. are OR-ed between ruler and grafana abilities, so for cloud rules (where rulerRule is undefined and useRulerRuleAbilities returns [false,false]... actually useAllRulerRuleAbilities(undefined,...) returns MaybeSupported=false) the grafana side with skipToken yields Duplicate=[true, create-permission] even though promRule is a cloud rule, not a Grafana rule. Wait — AlertRuleMenu only passes promRule to useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities when prometheusRuleType.grafana.rule(promRule) is true, so skipToken is used for cloud rules and abilities are computed for undefined. For undefined rule: Duplicate supported=true, allowed=rulesPermissions.create (global AlertingRuleCreate). So canDuplicate = (ruler: false) || (grafana-undefined: true && create) = true for cloud rules if the user has global create permission — but duplicating a cloud rule via the grafana identifier path would be wrong. Actually handleDuplicateRule uses `identifier` which for cloud rules comes from getEditableIdentifier → ruleId.fromRulerRuleAndGroupIdentifierV2 — but rule (rulerRule) is undefined in the list view for cloud rules... This needs verification, but the core design smell is real: passing skipToken still computes and returns 'supported' abilities for a non-existent rule, and consumers OR them with ruler abilities, which can incorrectly enable actions. The sentinel should short-circuit to [false, false] instead of computing abilities for undefined.

useAllAlertRuleAbilities marked @deprecated but still exported and used; deprecation direction contradicts new hooks

useAllAlertRuleAbilities is marked `@deprecated Use {@link useAllRulerRuleAbilities} instead`, but useAllRulerRuleAbilities takes (rule: RulerRuleDTO | undefined, groupIdentifier) while useAllAlertRuleAbilities takes a CombinedRule and internally derives the groupIdentifier via groupIdentifier.fromCombinedRule. The deprecation message points to a hook with a different, lower-level signature, which is not a drop-in replacement. Meanwhile useAlertRuleAbility (singular, line 179) still uses useAllAlertRuleAbilities and is NOT deprecated, and RuleActionsButtons.V2 still calls useRulerRuleAbility directly. The deprecation is misleading and the migration path is unclear; either provide a proper replacement wrapper or remove the @deprecated tag.

useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities treats Grafana rules as always supported, hiding actions while folder permissions load

In useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities, `MaybeSupported = loading ? NotSupported : AlwaysSupported` (line 309). Unlike the ruler-based hook, there is no isRulerAvailable concept, so once loading is false every action is 'supported'. However, `loading` here comes from useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable, which returns `loading: false` when `!rule || !folderUID` (line 355) — i.e., when the rule is undefined (skipToken case) or folderUid is missing, loading is false and abilities are computed with isEditable=false/isRemovable=false. That part is fine, but the deeper issue is that `useFolder` loading state only covers the folder fetch; if the folder fetch fails or returns no folder, `isEditable`/`isRemovable` are false while `MaybeSupported` is true, so e.g. Duplicate (which only checks rulesPermissions.create, not folder metadata) is shown even when folder-scoped permissions are unknown. More importantly, the asymmetry with the ruler hook (which gates on isRulerAvailable) means Grafana rules in the list view will show action buttons based purely on global permissions, ignoring folder-scoped RBAC for Duplicate — a permission-UI inconsistency.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
New interpolation test does not cover the shard-splitting double-interpolation path or non-idempotent variables

The added test 'Interpolates queries before execution' (lines 75-88) only verifies that runSplitQuery interpolates `$__auto` and `$step` once when called directly. It does not cover the composition with runShardSplitQuery, where targets are interpolated by runShardSplitQuery and then interpolated again by runSplitQuery. There is no test asserting that a query executed through the shard-splitting path is interpolated exactly once, nor a test with a variable whose interpolated value contains `$`-syntax or LogQL special characters (which would expose re-interpolation corruption). The shard test at shardQuerySplitting.test.ts:84-101 uses a mock datasource whose applyTemplateVariables is the real implementation backed by a `replace` stub, but its assertions only check the final expr/step, and the mock's replace is idempotent, so double interpolation would not be detected. A regression test that runs a query with a non-idempotent variable through runShardSplitQuery and asserts the executed expression is interpolated exactly once is missing.

Shard-split sub-requests re-interpolate already-interpolated targets inside runSplitQuery, and the shard selector can be corrupted by the second interpolation pass

runShardSplitQuery interpolates targets once (line 49-52) and groups them by their interpolated stream selector (getSelectorForShardValues on the interpolated expr). It then builds subRequest = { ...request, targets: interpolateShardingSelector(targets, shardsToQuery) } (line 154) and calls runSplitQuery(datasource, subRequest, ...) (line 163). runSplitQuery now unconditionally re-applies datasource.applyTemplateVariables to those targets (querySplitting.ts:296-299). Since interpolateShardingSelector injects a matcher like `__stream_shard__=~"20|10"` into the expression, a second interpolation pass runs template expansion over an expression that already contains interpolated content. If any template variable's value contains characters that look like LogQL or variable syntax, or if applyTemplateVariables is non-idempotent (e.g. it appends/replaces based on current content), the shard matcher or the user's query can be corrupted, causing queries to hit the wrong shards or fail to parse. Additionally, the shard grouping was computed from the once-interpolated selector, but execution uses a twice-interpolated expression, so grouping and execution can diverge. The two splitting layers must agree on a single interpolation point; as written, the shard path interpolates twice.

Test expectation changed from 1 to 5 applyTemplateVariables calls without verifying per-shard-group interpolation correctness

The test 'Interpolates queries before running' (line 110-112) now asserts `expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)`. This reflects that interpolation moved from once-per-request (the old interpolateVariablesInQueries call) to once-per-target inside runShardSplitQuery plus additional calls inside runSplitQuery for each shard sub-request. The count of 5 is incidental (depends on shard grouping internals) and the test does not assert that each executed sub-request's expression was interpolated exactly once and not re-interpolated. If runSplitQuery's new interpolation causes double interpolation on this path, this test would still pass because the mock's replacement is idempotent. The test should assert on the executed expressions (which it partially does) with a non-idempotent mock, or explicitly verify single interpolation per executed query.

runSplitQuery mutates the caller's request object (request.queryGroupId) and, via shared target references, the caller's targets

Line 303 does `request.queryGroupId = uuidv4()`, mutating the DataQueryRequest passed in by the caller. When runSplitQuery is invoked from runShardSplitQuery (shardQuerySplitting.ts:163), the subRequest is a shallow copy `{ ...request, targets }`, so this assignment writes queryGroupId onto the shard-splitting request object as well. Combined with the in-place mutation performed by applyTemplateVariables on the shared target objects (see related finding), the caller's request and targets are modified as a side effect of running a split query. This is a data-integrity hazard: the same request object may be reused by the datasource for subsequent queries (e.g. streaming/refresh), and mutated targets (interpolated expr, step) would then be re-interpolated or sent with stale values. The function should clone the request (`{ ...request, queryGroupId: uuidv4() }`) and ensure targets are not mutated in place.

runSplitQuery mutates the caller's request.targets via applyTemplateVariables, causing double interpolation and corrupted queries when called from shard splitting

runSplitQuery now maps request.targets through datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, ...). In the Loki datasource, applyTemplateVariables performs template variable interpolation in-place on the query object (it mutates query.expr and other fields, as evidenced by the shardQuerySplitting test mocks which do `query.expr = query.expr.replace(...)` and return the same object). runShardSplitQuery (shardQuerySplitting.ts:48-54) already interpolates the targets with applyTemplateVariables and then passes a subRequest built from the original `request` object into runSplitQuery (shardQuerySplitting.ts:163). Because the subRequest spreads `...request` but shares the same target object references, runSplitQuery interpolates the already-interpolated queries a second time. Consequences: (1) variables that expand to text containing `$`-like patterns or already-interpolated values can be re-interpolated, corrupting the LogQL expression; (2) `$__interval`/`$__range`-style variables are computed against the split sub-range on the second pass, producing wrong step/range values; (3) any variable whose interpolated output resembles a variable name gets expanded again. The shard-splitting path therefore executes queries with doubly-interpolated expressions. Fix: either make applyTemplateVariables return a copy (non-mutating), or have runSplitQuery/runShardSplitQuery operate on cloned targets so interpolation happens exactly once per query execution path.

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
LoggerMiddleware now depends on middleware ordering to include plugin context, and silently loses traceID

The PR moves contextual attributes (pluginId, endpoint, dsName, dsUID, uname) out of LoggerMiddleware into ContextualLoggerMiddleware, and LoggerMiddleware now calls `m.logger.FromContext(ctx)` to pick them up. This only works if ContextualLoggerMiddleware runs before LoggerMiddleware in the chain — which it does in pluginsintegration.go (line 160 before 161), but the coupling is implicit and fragile: any reordering, or any other caller of NewLoggerMiddleware that doesn't include NewContextualLoggerMiddleware first, silently drops pluginId/endpoint/dsName/dsUID/uname from the 'Plugin Request Completed' log line. Additionally, the old code appended `traceID` from `tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)` to the log params; that field was removed entirely and is not provided by instrumentContext, so trace IDs are no longer present in plugin request logs — a regression in log/telemetry correlation. Either restore the traceID param in LoggerMiddleware or document the loss.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext returns a brand-new logger, discarding the passed context and any recorded state

TestLogger.FromContext ignores its ctx argument and returns `NewTestLogger()`, a completely fresh logger. Any test that uses FromContext to verify that contextual attributes (e.g., those added by ContextualLoggerMiddleware) propagate into log output will silently pass or fail incorrectly because the returned logger has none of the context's attributes and none of the recorded logs of the original. The fake should either record the received context (e.g., store it in a field) or return a logger that captures FromContext calls, so tests can assert on context propagation. As written, it makes the new FromContext-based logging path effectively untestable with this fake.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

false_positives.candidate:
CallResource dereferences req without a nil check

MetricsMiddleware.CallResource reads `req.PluginContext` and `req.Body` without checking `req == nil`, unlike LoggerMiddleware.CallResource which guards with `if req == nil`. A nil *backend.CallResourceRequest will panic with a nil pointer dereference. Add the same nil guard before accessing req fields.

CheckHealth dereferences req without a nil check

MetricsMiddleware.CheckHealth reads `req.PluginContext` without checking `req == nil`, unlike LoggerMiddleware.CheckHealth which guards with `if req == nil`. A nil *backend.CheckHealthRequest will panic with a nil pointer dereference. Add the same nil guard before accessing req fields.

CollectMetrics dereferences req without a nil check

MetricsMiddleware.CollectMetrics reads `req.PluginContext` without checking `req == nil`, unlike LoggerMiddleware.CollectMetrics which guards with `if req == nil`. A nil *backend.CollectMetricsRequest will panic with a nil pointer dereference. Add the same nil guard before accessing req fields.

ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not instrument SubscribeStream, PublishStream, or RunStream contexts

The new ContextualLoggerMiddleware only enriches the context for QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, and CollectMetrics. SubscribeStream, PublishStream, and RunStream pass the context through unchanged, so any logging performed downstream for streaming requests loses the pluginId/endpoint/dsName/dsUID/uname contextual attributes that the old InstrumentationMiddleware provided (it had the same gap, but the PR's stated goal is to move that behavior, and the LoggerMiddleware now relies on `FromContext(ctx)` to pick up these attributes). If streaming requests are expected to log with the same context, instrumentContext should be applied there too; otherwise the behavior change should be called out.

FromContext silently discards the context's logger when the type assertion fails

grafanaInfraLogWrapper.FromContext calls `d.l.FromContext(ctx)` and type-asserts the result to `*log.ConcreteLogger`. If the assertion fails (e.g., the context carries a different logger implementation, or infra log's FromContext returns a different type in some code path), the method falls back to `d.New()`, which returns a logger with only the wrapper's existing context — completely discarding whatever logger/attributes were stored in the provided ctx. This means the contextual attributes added by ContextualLoggerMiddleware (via log.WithContextualAttributes) can be silently dropped, producing log lines missing pluginId/endpoint/etc. with no error or indication. At minimum this fallback should be more defensive (e.g., preserve the infra logger from context without the ConcreteLogger assertion, or log a warning).

Logger name 'plugin.instrumentation' is now misleading after the rename to MetricsMiddleware

The logger passed to NewLoggerMiddleware is still named `log.New("plugin.instrumentation")`. Since the PR renames InstrumentationMiddleware to MetricsMiddleware and moves contextual logging out of it, the logger name should be updated (e.g. `plugin.requests` or `plugin.metrics`) to avoid confusion in log aggregation and dashboards that filter on the `plugin.instrumentation` logger name. Existing alerting/queries referencing the old logger name will also silently stop matching if the name is changed, so this should be coordinated, but leaving the stale name contradicts the PR's stated goal of 'better naming and consistency'.

MetricsMiddleware shares a single mutable instance across all clients, causing a data race on the `next` field

NewMetricsMiddleware creates one MetricsMiddleware instance (imw) and then, inside the ClientMiddlewareFunc closure, assigns `imw.next = next` every time the middleware is applied. In Grafana, the middleware chain is applied per plugin client (potentially many times, concurrently during plugin initialization and request handling). Multiple goroutines can therefore write to the same `imw.next` field simultaneously, and a request being served by one client can observe another client's `next` (or a partially written pointer), causing requests to be routed to the wrong plugin client or a fatal concurrent map/pointer race. The previous InstrumentationMiddleware had the same pattern, but the rename is a good opportunity to fix it. The middleware should return a new MetricsMiddleware per invocation (e.g., `return &MetricsMiddleware{pluginMetrics: imw.pluginMetrics, pluginRegistry: pluginRegistry, next: next}`) so each decorated client has its own immutable `next`.

MetricsMiddleware swallows the downstream response when request-size instrumentation fails

In QueryData (and CallResource), if `instrumentPluginRequestSize` returns an error (which happens whenever the plugin is not found in the registry, i.e. `plugins.ErrPluginNotRegistered`), the middleware returns `nil, err` immediately without ever calling `m.next.QueryData`. This means a plugin that is temporarily missing from the registry causes all its requests to fail outright, instead of just skipping the size metric. The request should still be forwarded to the next client; only the metric observation should be skipped (or logged). The same issue exists in CallResource at line 161. This is a behavior regression risk: previously the instrumentation middleware did not gate the request on registry lookup success for the size metric path in the same way, and more importantly, failing the actual plugin request because a metric could not be recorded is incorrect — metrics must never break the request path.

QueryData dereferences req without a nil check, unlike the LoggerMiddleware

MetricsMiddleware.QueryData iterates `req.Queries` and reads `req.PluginContext` without first checking `req == nil`. The sibling LoggerMiddleware explicitly guards every method with `if req == nil { return m.next... }`, and the SDK's plugins.Client contract allows nil requests in some paths/tests. A nil *backend.QueryDataRequest will cause a nil pointer dereference panic inside the middleware, crashing the request goroutine. Add the same nil guard used in logger_middleware.go (lines 63-65, 77-79, 90-92, 104-106) before accessing req fields.

Test function still named TestInstrumentationMiddleware after rename

The test function is still named `TestInstrumentationMiddleware` even though the file was renamed to metrics_middleware_test.go and the type under test is now MetricsMiddleware. Rename to `TestMetricsMiddleware` for consistency with the rename. More importantly, the test suite has no coverage for: (1) nil request handling (the middleware lacks nil guards — see related findings), (2) behavior when the plugin is not registered in the registry (the middleware currently fails the request — see related findings), and (3) the shared-instance race in NewMetricsMiddleware. These gaps hide real bugs introduced/preserved by this refactor.

instrumentPluginRequest returns early on registry lookup failure, skipping the request entirely

instrumentPluginRequest calls `m.pluginTarget(ctx, pluginCtx.PluginID)` and returns the error immediately if the plugin is not registered, without invoking `fn(ctx)`. This means the actual plugin request (`m.next.QueryData/CallResource/CheckHealth/CollectMetrics`) is never executed when the plugin is missing from the registry — the middleware turns a metrics-labeling problem into a hard request failure. Metrics collection must not prevent the underlying request from running. The correct behavior is to still execute `fn(ctx)` and return its result, only skipping (or defaulting) the metric observation when the target cannot be resolved.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit enforcement is racy: check-then-act allows exceeding the configured limit

CreateOrUpdateDevice first calls CountDevices and only falls back to updateDevice when count >= deviceLimit, otherwise it performs an INSERT ... ON CONFLICT. This is a classic TOCTOU race: under concurrent anonymous requests (the normal case for a public Grafana instance), many goroutines can observe count < limit simultaneously and all insert new devices, exceeding AnonymousDeviceLimit. The limit is a security/abuse-control feature (bounding anonymous device rows), so silently exceeding it defeats its purpose. The count and insert are not performed in a single transaction or with any locking, so there is no atomicity. A correct implementation would enforce the limit atomically (e.g., conditional INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) ...) < limit, or a transaction with locking/serializable isolation), or at minimum treat the limit as best-effort and document it.

true_positives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Anonymous authentication is now performed synchronously on the request path with no timeout, and device-limit errors abort authentication entirely

The previous implementation ran TagDevice in a goroutine with a 2-minute timeout (context.WithTimeout) precisely so that slow or failing device tagging would not block or break request authentication. This PR removes the goroutine and the timeout and calls a.anonDeviceService.TagDevice(ctx, ...) synchronously with the request context. Two consequences: (1) every anonymous request now pays the latency of a COUNT(*) query plus an INSERT/UPDATE against the database on the critical auth path, adding DB load and latency to all anonymous traffic; (2) when TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached (which, per the updateDevice issue, can happen for brand-new devices), Authenticate returns nil, err and the anonymous user is completely denied access — turning a telemetry/abuse-control limit into a full authentication outage for new visitors. The limit should degrade gracefully (log and continue serving the anonymous identity) rather than rejecting the request, and the DB work should not be on the synchronous auth path without a timeout.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
updateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached for any device that does not exist or is outside the time window, not only when the limit is reached

updateDevice runs an UPDATE ... WHERE device_id = ? AND updated_at BETWEEN ? AND ? and returns ErrDeviceLimitReached whenever RowsAffected == 0. RowsAffected is 0 both when the device does not exist (a brand-new device hitting a full table) and when the device exists but its updated_at is outside the [now-30d, now+1m] window (e.g., an expired device that the periodic cleanup has not yet removed, or clock skew). In both cases the caller (client.go Authenticate) treats ErrDeviceLimitReached as a hard failure and rejects the anonymous request, so legitimate first-time visitors can be denied access even though the device table is not actually full. The error conflates 'device not found / stale' with 'limit reached'; the update path should distinguish these (e.g., fall back to insert when the row is missing, or return a distinct error) instead of failing authentication.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TagDevice now propagates store errors that were previously only logged, changing error semantics for all callers

TagDevice previously logged tagDeviceUI failures at Debug level and returned nil; the PR adds `return err` after the debug log. Combined with the synchronous call in client.go, any transient DB error (connection pool exhaustion, timeout, deadlock) now propagates up through Authenticate. In client.go only ErrDeviceLimitReached is treated as fatal, but other callers of TagDevice (and any future callers) now receive errors they did not before, and the local-cache set in tagDeviceUI (line 87) happens before the DB write, so a failed write still marks the device as cached for ~29 minutes, suppressing retries. The change silently alters the contract of a public-ish method (marked FIXME: Unexport) without updating its other call sites or tests to cover the new error propagation.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Device-limit test only covers the 'new device rejected' case, not the 'existing device still updated when limit reached' case

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit creates one device with limit=1, then tries to create a second, different device and asserts ErrDeviceLimitReached. It never verifies the intended behavior that motivated updateDevice: when the limit is reached, an already-known device should still be updated (its updated_at refreshed) rather than rejected. Without that case, the updateDevice path (including its WHERE updated_at BETWEEN ? AND ? window and its RowsAffected==0 -> ErrDeviceLimitReached mapping) is untested, and a regression that rejects known devices when the table is full would pass CI. A test should create device A, fill the limit, then re-tag device A and assert success and a refreshed updated_at.

Every anonymous request now runs an unconditional COUNT(*) over the anon_device table before insert

When deviceLimit > 0, CreateOrUpdateDevice executes `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM anon_device WHERE updated_at BETWEEN ? AND ?` on every single call, before deciding whether to insert or update. On a busy instance with anonymous access enabled this turns each request into a full-table range scan (there is no index on updated_at shown in the changed files), adding per-request DB load that scales with the number of devices. The count is also only needed to decide the insert-vs-update branch; a cheaper design would attempt the upsert and only consult the count when a conflict/limit condition is actually hit, or maintain the count incrementally. As written this is a per-request O(n) query on the hot path of every anonymous request.

New device_limit setting has no default documentation, no validation, and no sample config entry

cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit is read via anonSection.Key("device_limit").MustInt64(0). There is no validation that the value is non-negative (a negative value silently disables the limit because database.go checks `s.deviceLimit > 0`, which may be intended but is undocumented), no entry in conf/sample.ini or docs describing the setting, and no default.ini documentation of its meaning (max number of anonymous devices tracked in the last 30 days). Since this is a user-facing configuration knob that changes authentication behavior (rejecting anonymous users when reached), it needs documentation and a sane guard (e.g., reject or clamp negative values with a warning) so operators do not misconfigure it.

anonymousDeviceLimit typed as `number | undefined` but backend always serializes an int64 (0 when unset)

The Go DTO declares `AnonymousDeviceLimit int64 `json:"anonymousDeviceLimit"`` with no omitempty, so the backend always sends a JSON number (0 when the setting is unset/default). The TypeScript type `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined` and the runtime default `anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined` imply the field may be absent, but it never is; consumers checking `config.anonymousDeviceLimit === undefined` to detect 'not configured' will never see undefined, they will see 0. The frontend type should be `number` (matching the always-present JSON), or the Go field should be a pointer with omitempty if absence is meaningful. As written the `| undefined` is misleading and any frontend logic branching on undefined is dead code.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup progress is logged at Error level instead of Info/Debug

In CleanAnnotations (and the equivalent MaxCount and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags loops), every batch logs 'Annotations to clean by time' / 'cleaned annotations by time' / 'Tags to clean' / 'cleaned tags' via r.log.Error(...). These are routine progress messages for a normal background cleanup operation, not errors. Logging them at Error level will spam error-level logs and alerting/observability pipelines on every cleanup cycle, and makes it impossible to distinguish real failures from normal operation. They should be logged at Info or Debug level (the surrounding cleanup service already logs a Debug summary of affected rows).

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup job interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute

The diff changes `ticker := time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 10)` to `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1)` in CleanUpService.Run. This is unrelated to the stated PR goal (splitting annotation cleanup queries to avoid MySQL deadlocks) and has major operational impact: every cleanup job — temp file cleanup, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, user invites, short URLs, query history (including two EnforceRowLimitInQueryHistory passes over 200k/150k row limits) — now runs every minute instead of every 10 minutes. On large instances this multiplies background DB load tenfold, increases lock contention with user traffic (the very problem this PR tries to reduce for annotations), and shortens the effective cleanup cadence assumptions elsewhere. If this change is intentional it must be called out in the PR description and justified; as an unexplained side change it should be reverted.

false_positives.candidate:
Log statement includes a stale 'err' value that is always nil at that point

The log call `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, "cond", cond, "err", err)` is placed after `if err != nil { return 0, err }`, so `err` is always nil when the log line executes. The same pattern appears in the MaxCount branch (line 554) and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags (line 576). The 'err' key is dead/misleading log output; it should be removed or the log moved before the error check.

MaxAge cleanup condition interpolates annotationType and cutoffDate directly into SQL

The batch condition is built with fmt.Sprintf(`%s AND created < %v ORDER BY id DESC %s`, annotationType, cutoffDate, ...) and passed to fetchIDs, which concatenates it into `SELECT id FROM annotation WHERE <cond>`. annotationType is a caller-supplied string (alertAnnotationType/dashboardAnnotationType/apiAnnotationType constants today, but the function signature accepts any string) and is interpolated unquoted and unvalidated into the WHERE clause. If annotationType ever contains SQL syntax (e.g. via a future caller or config), this is a SQL injection vector; at minimum it is fragile string-built SQL. The value should be validated against a whitelist of known type expressions or passed as a bound parameter.

MaxCount cleanup can loop forever or over-delete when rows are concurrently inserted

The MaxCount branch selects IDs with `ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT/OFFSET MaxCount, BatchSize` and deletes them, repeating until a batch affects 0 rows. The termination condition is `affected == 0` from the DELETE. Two issues: (1) If annotations are being inserted concurrently with higher IDs, each iteration selects a fresh window past MaxCount and deletes it, so the loop keeps deleting newly inserted annotations indefinitely — the loop only stops when a full batch window contains no rows, which under sustained insert load may never happen within the 9-minute cleanup timeout, and it will delete annotations that were just created and should be kept (the newest MaxCount are preserved only relative to the snapshot at each iteration, but new inserts above the cutoff keep getting deleted). The old single-statement version had the same windowing semantics per execution but was bounded to one statement per run; the new untilDoneOrCancelled loop makes it unbounded. (2) If a concurrent transaction deletes some of the selected IDs between fetchIDs and deleteByIDs, RowsAffected < len(ids) but > 0, so the loop continues — that part is fine — but if ALL selected IDs vanish concurrently, affected == 0 and the loop exits early even though more excess annotations remain. The loop should be bounded (e.g. a max iteration count or a deadline check) and the select should be re-evaluated consistently.

New large-batch test only runs on SQLite and does not exercise the parameterized path for other dialects

The new test case 'should not fail if batch size is larger than SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER' creates 40003 annotations with batch size 32767. The SQLite-specific interpolation path in deleteByIDs is only taken when `r.db.GetDBType() == migrator.SQLite`; CI integration tests run against SQLite by default, so the test exercises the interpolation branch. However, there is no test covering the parameterized branch with a batch size above 999 on MySQL/Postgres (where SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER does not apply but MySQL has its own max_allowed_packet / placeholder considerations), and no unit test for deleteByIDs chunking behavior. Given the change is motivated by MySQL deadlocks, the deadlock-avoidance behavior itself (separate SELECT and DELETE statements, no shared transaction) is not covered by any concurrency test.

Non-atomic select-then-delete can orphan annotation_tag rows when annotations are deleted between the two statements

The new cleanup deletes annotations by ID in one statement (deleteByIDs on 'annotation') but never deletes the corresponding annotation_tag rows in the same operation. The old code had the same gap for CleanAnnotations (tags were handled by CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags), so this is pre-existing, but the PR's stated goal is data integrity during cleanup and the test now asserts tag counts. Between the annotation DELETE and the next CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags run, annotation_tag rows reference deleted annotations (orphans), and any concurrent reader joining annotation_tag to annotation simply won't see them — acceptable — but if the process crashes between the two, orphans persist until the next cycle. More importantly, within a single Run() the annotation cleanup and orphan-tag cleanup are separate jobs, so tags for annotations deleted by MaxAge/MaxCount cleanup are only removed later. This should be documented or the tag deletion should be batched alongside (e.g. delete tags by annotation_id IN (...) before deleting the annotations).

Orphaned-tag cleanup matches annotation_tag.id, but the orphan condition references annotation_id

CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags builds the condition `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM annotation a WHERE annotation_id = a.id)` and fetches `SELECT id FROM annotation_tag WHERE <cond>`. The subquery correlates `annotation_id` (a column of annotation_tag) with `a.id`, which works because the outer query's annotation_tag columns are in scope. However, the fetched `id` is annotation_tag's own primary key, and deleteByIDs deletes `WHERE id IN (...)` on annotation_tag — that is consistent. The subtle issue is that the condition relies on implicit column scoping (`annotation_id` unqualified resolves to the outer annotation_tag), which is correct but fragile; it should be qualified as `at.annotation_id` with an alias for clarity and to avoid ambiguity if the schema changes. Not a functional bug today, but worth fixing while touching this code.

SQLite workaround interpolates IDs into SQL and keys off configured batch size rather than actual ID count

In deleteByIDs, when the database is SQLite and `r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999`, the IDs are string-interpolated directly into the DELETE statement (`DELETE FROM %s WHERE id IN (%s)`). Two problems: (1) the decision is based on the configured batch size, not on len(ids) — if the config is >999 but a batch returns fewer IDs (e.g. the final partial batch, or the MaxCount offset path), the code still takes the interpolation path unnecessarily; conversely the guard is correct only because fetchIDs is bounded by the same config. (2) Although the values are int64s produced by the database itself (so not attacker-controlled), building SQL by string concatenation is a fragile pattern that defeats the purpose of parameterized queries and will break if IDs ever become non-numeric. The condition should be `len(ids) > sqliteParameterLimit`, and the IDs should be chunked into multiple parameterized DELETEs of ≤999 parameters each rather than interpolated.

Test helper now assigns explicit IDs to annotations, which may mask auto-increment behavior differences across databases

createTestAnnotations was changed to set `ID: int64(i + 1)` explicitly on each annotation and to batch-insert with InsertMulti. Explicit primary keys bypass the database auto-increment sequence. On MySQL/Postgres, inserting explicit IDs does not advance the auto-increment counter, so subsequent inserts by the application (which rely on auto-increment) could collide with these test IDs or behave differently than production. More relevant to this PR: the cleanup orders by `id DESC`, and with explicit IDs the test data's ID ordering exactly matches insertion ordering, which is also what auto-increment would produce — so the tests don't catch any divergence. This is acceptable for a test fixture, but the helper should reset the auto-increment sequence after inserting explicit IDs (or use auto-generated IDs) so the fixture doesn't leave the table in a state that breaks later tests in the same database.

fetchIDs builds SQL by concatenation and rejects empty condition only at runtime

fetchIDs constructs `SELECT id FROM <table> WHERE <condition>` via fmt.Sprintf with caller-provided table and condition strings. The empty-condition guard is a runtime error return rather than a compile-time constraint. All current callers pass constant strings, so this is safe today, but the function is a generic SQL-string builder; a future caller passing user-influenced input would have an injection point. Consider making the condition a structured type or at minimum documenting that callers must pass only static SQL fragments.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete builds a log context from d.Log instead of the enriched per-request logger

In DualWriterMode3.Delete, line 96 creates log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method), but line 97 then does ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log), discarding the enriched logger. All subsequent log.Error calls in this method (and the klog logger in the async goroutine, which inherits ctx) lack the name/kind/method fields, unlike every other method in the file. It should be klog.NewContext(ctx, log).

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
DeleteCollection goroutine records storage metric instead of legacy metric

In DualWriterMode3.DeleteCollection, the asynchronous legacy write goroutine calls d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy) (line 166) instead of d.recordLegacyDuration(...). Legacy delete-collection latency and error rates are therefore recorded into the storage metric, making it impossible to monitor legacy write health for delete-collection, and double-counting storage durations.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete records storage duration with 'name' instead of 'kind' as the resource label

In DualWriterMode3.Delete, the success path calls d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage), passing the object name (e.g. a UID) as the resource/kind label, while every other method passes options.Kind. This produces a high-cardinality, inconsistent metric label (one time series per object name) and breaks aggregation by kind. The failure path on line 103 correctly uses options.Kind, so the two paths are also inconsistent with each other.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy Delete may run after the object was already deleted, and NotFound is not handled

In DualWriterMode3.Delete, the legacy delete runs asynchronously with no handling of NotFound. Because the unified delete already succeeded and returned to the client, a subsequent immediate re-create of the same name (a common pattern: delete then create) can race with the in-flight legacy delete, causing the legacy delete to remove the newly created legacy object — the two stores diverge and the legacy copy of the re-created resource is silently lost. Additionally, if the legacy delete returns NotFound (e.g. the object never existed in legacy), the error is recorded as a legacy failure metric even though it is an expected condition. The previous implementation explicitly tolerated apierrors.IsNotFound for both stores; that handling was dropped.

Async legacy writes capture and reuse the request context after the handler returns

Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection all spawn goroutines that use the incoming request ctx (via context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)) after the request handler has returned. The parent context is typically cancelled as soon as the HTTP request completes, so the derived 10-second timeout context is cancelled almost immediately, meaning the 'asynchronous safe-measure' legacy write will usually be aborted right away and effectively never run (or run with an already-cancelled context). This defeats the stated purpose of mode 3 ('write to unified storage and then asynchronously write to legacy as a safe measure') and silently drops the legacy write. A detached context (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx) or context.Background() with values preserved) should be used for the background legacy write.

Create passes the caller's mutable object to the async legacy write, allowing data races with the caller

In DualWriterMode3.Create, the same obj runtime.Object is passed both to d.Storage.Create (synchronously) and captured by the goroutine for d.Legacy.Create. The unified storage layer typically mutates the object in place (setting ResourceVersion, UID, defaults, managedFields). After Create returns, the caller (and the API machinery that serializes the response) may read or further mutate obj while the background goroutine is concurrently passing it to Legacy.Create. This is a data race on a shared object and can also cause the legacy store to receive an object whose ResourceVersion/UID was set by the unified store, which legacy create may reject or mishandle. A deep copy of the object should be made before handing it to the goroutine.

Create records legacy duration metric on storage failure path

In DualWriterMode3.Create, when d.Storage.Create fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) instead of d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...). This records a storage failure as a legacy-storage duration metric, corrupting the legacy/storage latency metrics dashboards. The same wrong-metric bug exists in Update (line 129), which calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) when d.Storage.Update fails.

Create returns the storage-created object but the async legacy create may fail, leaving stores permanently divergent with no reconciliation

In mode 3, Create returns success to the client as soon as the unified store write succeeds; the legacy write is best-effort and its failure is only counted in a metric. There is no retry, no dead-letter, and no reconciliation mechanism, so any legacy failure (including the systematic cancellation of the request context described above) permanently leaves the object missing from the legacy store. Since legacy APIs (e.g. /api/playlists) still read from the legacy store during migration, the object will be invisible to legacy consumers with no error surfaced to the user or operator beyond a metric. This is a data-integrity risk inherent to the design; at minimum the PR should document the divergence window/risk and provide an operational runbook, and ideally the async write should be retried or queued durably rather than fire-and-forget.

Legacy write failures are silently swallowed (only a metric, no log)

In all four async write paths (Create line 55-56, Delete line 112-113, Update line 139-140, DeleteCollection line 165-166), a failure of the legacy write is only recorded via d.recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, ...); there is no log.Error call. Since the whole point of the legacy write in mode 3 is to be a 'safe measure' keeping the legacy store in sync, silent failures mean operators have no log trail when the legacy store diverges from unified storage — divergence that will become user-visible the moment reads switch to unified-only or the legacy store is still being read by legacy APIs. Each async path should log the error (with kind/name) in addition to recording the metric.

Mode 3 integration test is inherently racy: it asserts legacy API state immediately after k8s writes that are only asynchronously propagated

doPlaylistTests (shared by the new 'mode 3' subtests at lines 132-144 and 191-204) performs k8s CRUD and then immediately reads through the legacy API expecting the data to be there — e.g. 'Do CRUD via k8s (and check that legacy api still works)' creates playlists via client.Resource.Create (line 496) and immediately checks /api/playlists (line 523-531); it updates via k8s (line 539) and immediately calls getFromBothAPIs (line 547) which GETs /api/playlists/<uid> (line 623-627); it deletes via k8s (line 572) and the subsequent legacy reads must reflect the deletion. In mode 3 the legacy write happens in a background goroutine after the k8s response returns, so these assertions race with the async legacy write and will flake (and, given the request-context cancellation issue, may fail deterministically). The mode 3 test runs need to poll/wait (require.Eventually) for legacy convergence instead of asserting immediately, otherwise the new mode 3 subtests are a source of CI flakiness.

Mode 3 unit tests never assert that the async legacy write actually happens

All Mode 3 tests (TestMode3_Create, TestMode3_Delete, TestMode3_Update, TestMode3_DeleteCollection) call the dual writer and immediately assert on the returned object/error. Because the legacy write now runs in a fire-and-forget goroutine, the tests return before (or regardless of whether) the legacy mock is invoked, so they cannot detect a regression where the legacy write is never executed, is cancelled immediately (the request-context cancellation issue), or races. The tests also never call m.AssertExpectations, so the setupLegacyFn expectations (e.g. line 30-32, 313-315) are not even verified. The tests should synchronize with the goroutine (e.g. a WaitGroup/channel in the mock, or assert with Eventually/AssertNumberOfCalls after a wait) and assert the legacy store was called exactly once.

TestMode3_Get shadows the package-level registry p with a local one, inconsistent with sibling tests

TestMode3_Get declares a local p := prometheus.NewRegistry() (line 119) while all other Mode 3 tests use the shared package-level var p (declared in dualwriter_mode1_test.go line 27). This is inconsistent and, more importantly, the shared package-level registry p is registered/used across many tests in the package; if NewDualWriter registers metrics on it, running tests in the same package can panic with 'duplicate metrics collector registration' depending on test order. The mode1 test file was changed in this PR to remove a shadowing local registry (dualwriter_mode1_test.go diff removes p := prometheus.NewRegistry()), suggesting the intent is to use the shared p everywhere — TestMode3_Get should be aligned.

Unbounded goroutine creation with no backpressure or panic recovery for async legacy writes

Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection each spawn an unbounded goroutine per request to perform the legacy write, with no worker pool, queue, or rate limiting. Under load (especially DeleteCollection, which is a single request fanning out to a legacy delete-collection), this can spawn a large number of concurrent goroutines hammering the legacy store, and a panic inside any of these goroutines (e.g. in legacy storage code or the mock in tests) crashes the whole Grafana process since there is no recover(). At minimum, panics in the async path should be recovered and logged; ideally the async writes should go through a bounded worker queue.

Update passes the shared UpdatedObjectInfo to the async legacy write, causing a data race and double evaluation

In DualWriterMode3.Update, the same objInfo rest.UpdatedObjectInfo is passed to d.Storage.Update and then captured by the goroutine for d.Legacy.Update. UpdatedObjectInfo.UpdatedObject is typically invoked lazily by each store; calling it twice (once per store) re-runs user-supplied transformation/validation logic concurrently with the request goroutine, and any state inside objInfo (or the underlying object it closes over) is shared unsynchronized between the two calls — a data race. The previous (pre-PR) implementation explicitly solved this by resolving objInfo.UpdatedObject once against the storage object and wrapping it in an updateWrapper with the already-computed object for the legacy call. That pattern was removed; the async legacy Update should receive a pre-resolved, immutable object (e.g. via an updateWrapper holding the object returned by Storage.Update) rather than the live objInfo.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache check-then-act race allows concurrent manifest reloads and duplicate work

GetWebAssets performs a read-lock check of entryPointAssetsCache (lines 41-43), releases the lock, and then re-acquires a write lock (line 48) to recompute the cache. Between the RUnlock and Lock, another goroutine can also pass the nil check and enter the write-lock section, so multiple goroutines can concurrently execute readWebAssetsFromFile/readWebAssetsFromCDN and overwrite entryPointAssetsCache. This is not a data race on the pointer itself (the mutex does protect the read/write of the variable), but it is a check-then-act race: in non-dev environments the cache is supposed to be computed once, yet N concurrent first-callers will all perform file I/O (or an HTTP request to the CDN) and each will assign the global. Consequences: wasted work, potential thundering-herd file/HTTP load on startup, and last-writer-wins assignment of the cache. The fix is a double-checked locking pattern: after acquiring the write lock, re-check `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` before doing the expensive work.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error from asset loading is discarded when cache is assigned and returned

At line 69-70, `entryPointAssetsCache = result` is assigned unconditionally and then `return entryPointAssetsCache, err` returns both the (possibly nil) result and the error. If readWebAssetsFromFile fails (e.g., assets-manifest.json missing or malformed), result is nil and err is non-nil, but the nil result is still stored into the package-level cache. On the next call in a non-dev environment, the fast path at line 45 (`cfg.Env != setting.Dev && ret != nil`) will see ret == nil and retry — which is arguably intended — but in dev mode the cache is overwritten with nil on every failed call, and more importantly the function returns a nil *dtos.EntryPointAssets together with a non-nil error while having mutated global state. Callers that ignore the error (or that only check the returned pointer) could dereference nil. Additionally, if a previous successful result existed and a later reload fails, the good cached value is clobbered with nil. The assignment should be conditional on err == nil (or result != nil), e.g. `if err == nil { entryPointAssetsCache = result }`.

false_positives.candidate:
CDN read error is silently overwritten by file read, losing the original error

Lines 55-67: when `cdn != ""`, `result, err = readWebAssetsFromCDN(ctx, cdn)` is called. If that fails, err is set and result is nil, then line 59 `if result == nil` falls through to readWebAssetsFromFile, which overwrites err. If the file read succeeds, the CDN error is completely lost and the function returns success — fine for fallback semantics, but if the file read also fails, the returned error describes only the file failure, not the CDN failure, making it impossible to diagnose why CDN loading was attempted and failed. More subtly, the CDN path is currently dead code (cdn is hardcoded to "" at line 54), so this error-masking behavior is latent. If/when the CDN is enabled, the error handling should preserve or wrap both errors (e.g., using errors.Join or logging the CDN error) rather than silently discarding it.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions always returns false regardless of feature flag state

The function `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then unconditionally returns `false` in both branches. This means SQL expressions are permanently disabled even when the `sqlExpressions` feature flag is explicitly enabled by an administrator. The intent (per the PR description and the CVE-2024-9264 fix) is to disable SQL expressions by default for security, but the implementation makes the feature flag non-functional: there is no configuration under which SQL expressions can be turned on. If the goal is a hard kill-switch, the feature-flag check should be removed entirely and the function deleted; if the goal is a default-off flag, the function should return the value of `h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` (or its negation, depending on flag semantics). As written, the dead conditional is misleading and the flag documented in the linked docs has no effect.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Stub DB methods return "not implemented" errors that are reachable and mishandled

The new `pkg/expr/sql/db.go` replaces the real DuckDB-backed implementation with a stub whose `TablesList`, `RunCommands`, and `QueryFramesInto` all return `errors.New("not implemented")`. These stubs are still wired into live code paths: `pkg/expr/sql/parser.go:TablesList` calls `duckDB.RunCommands(...)` (line 26) and `pkg/expr/sql_command.go:NewSQLCommand` calls `sql.TablesList(rawSQL)` (line 30), and `SQLCommand.Execute` calls `db.QueryFramesInto(...)` (line 100). Although `pkg/expr/reader.go` currently blocks the `QueryTypeSQL` path, the older/unmarshal path via `UnmarshalSQLCommand` (pkg/expr/sql_command.go:51) still constructs `SQLCommand` through `NewSQLCommand`, which will now always fail with a generic "error reading SQL command" wrapping the "not implemented" error from the stub. If any code path reaches `SQLCommand.Execute` (e.g., the legacy expression pipeline that does not go through `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery`), it will hit `db.QueryFramesInto` and return the "not implemented" error to the user as a query failure. The stub should either be removed along with the dead SQL command code, or the SQL command construction/execution paths should be fully removed rather than left as landmines that produce confusing errors.

false_positives.candidate:
Dead code: rsp.Values is overwritten when frame has zero rows

In `SQLCommand.Execute`, when `frame.Rows() == 0` the code sets `rsp.Values` to a `mathexp.NoData` value (lines 110-114), but then unconditionally overwrites `rsp.Values` with `mathexp.TableData{Frame: frame}` at lines 116-118. The `NoData` branch is therefore dead code and has no effect. This is a pre-existing bug (not introduced by this diff), but it is in a file touched by this security fix and affects the behavior of the SQL expression path: empty results are returned as an empty table rather than as NoData, which may affect how the frontend renders empty SQL expression results. The `if frame.Rows() == 0` block should either be removed or the unconditional assignment should be made conditional (e.g., `else`).

Malformed comment on indirect dependency line

Line 463 reads `github.com/fxamacker/cbor/v2 v2.7.0 // indirect; indirect0.0.0-20240809095826-8eb5495c0b2a`. The comment contains a corrupted version string (`indirect0.0.0-20240809095826-8eb5495c0b2a`) that appears to be a merge/rebase artifact where a version string was accidentally concatenated with the `// indirect` marker. This is a malformed `go.mod` comment. While Go tooling ignores trailing comments on require lines, this is clearly unintended text that should be cleaned up to just `// indirect` (the version is already specified in the require directive itself).

Misleading error message when SQL expressions are rejected

When SQL expressions are disabled, `ReadQuery` returns `fmt.Errorf("sqlExpressions is not implemented")`. This message is factually wrong: SQL expressions are implemented (see `pkg/expr/sql_command.go` and `pkg/expr/sql/`), they are deliberately disabled as a security measure for CVE-2024-9264. Returning "not implemented" to API consumers will cause confusion and may lead users to believe the feature is simply unavailable rather than intentionally disabled for security.
