The error should state that SQL expressions are disabled (e.g., "sqlExpressions are disabled" or reference the feature flag), so users and support staff understand the actual reason and know how to look for the relevant configuration.

SQL string is interpolated into a DuckDB command without parameterization, relying on a naive quote-escaping heuristic

`TablesList` builds a DuckDB command via `fmt.Sprintf("SELECT json_serialize_sql('%s')", rawSQL)` after only replacing single quotes with doubled single quotes (`strings.Replace(rawSQL, "'", "''", -1)`). This is a hand-rolled escaping scheme that is applied to user-supplied SQL before it is sent to the database engine. While the SQL expression path is currently disabled by the reader, this function remains reachable via `NewSQLCommand`/`UnmarshalSQLCommand` (see pkg/expr/sql_command.go:30), which does not check the feature flag. The escaping only handles single quotes and does not account for other SQL injection vectors (e.g., backslash escapes depending on DuckDB string literal semantics, or the fact that the input is itself SQL being embedded inside another SQL statement). This is exactly the class of vulnerability that CVE-2024-9264 addressed. Since the DuckDB dependency is being removed and the stub returns "not implemented", the cleanest fix is to delete this function and the entire SQL expression execution path rather than leave an unsafe string-interpolation helper in the codebase. If the code is kept, the raw SQL must never be embedded into another SQL statement via string formatting.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the coarse lock from BuildIndex introduces a race: two concurrent builds for the same key can both create indexes and leak one, and GetIndex can return a partially-constructed index

The PR removes the function-wide b.cacheMu.Lock() from BuildIndex (previously lines 88-89) and replaces it with a short lock only around the cache insertion at lines 137-139. This means two concurrent callers of BuildIndex for the same NamespacedResource key (which happens: searchSupport.init spawns concurrent builds via errgroup, and getOrCreateIndex can also trigger builds from concurrent Search/handleEvent calls) will both execute bleve.New/bleve.NewMemOnly, both run the builder writing documents, and both insert into b.cache — the second insertion silently overwrites the first. The overwritten bleve.Index is never closed, leaking file handles/disk state (for file-based indexes, the on-disk directory is left behind and will be reopened by a subsequent build, potentially corrupting or duplicating data). Additionally, between the builder writing documents (line 126) and the cache insertion (line 138), another goroutine calling GetIndex will not find the index and will start its own duplicate build. The original coarse lock prevented duplicate builds for the same key; the fix requires per-key locking (e.g., a sync.Map of in-flight builds keyed by NamespacedResource, or a keyed mutex) so that concurrent builds for the same key are deduplicated, while builds for different keys proceed in parallel.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates b.cache without holding cacheMu — data race with concurrent BuildIndex insertions

TotalDocs (line 144) ranges over b.cache with no lock. BuildIndex now writes to b.cache under b.cacheMu.Lock() at lines 137-139, and GetIndex reads under RLock. Since BuildIndex can run concurrently (the whole point of the PR's finer-grained locking), TotalDocs racing with a cache insertion is a concurrent map read/write — a fatal runtime error in Go (concurrent map iteration and map write). TotalDocs is called from searchSupport.init at line 216 (s.search.TotalDocs()) after group.Wait(), but also potentially from metrics or other paths concurrently with getOrCreateIndex-triggered builds. Fix: acquire b.cacheMu.RLock() around the iteration.

false_positives.candidate:
Event watcher goroutine does not check channel closure — blocks forever on closed channel and never exits

The goroutine at line 207 does `for { v := <-events; s.handleEvent(watchctx, v) }`. The events channel returned by WatchWriteEvents is closed by the SQL backend's poller when it exits (backend.go line 572: defer close(stream)). Receiving from a closed channel returns nil immediately and forever, so once the channel is closed this goroutine will spin in a tight infinite loop calling s.handleEvent(watchctx, nil) — which will panic on nil pointer dereference at line 226 (evt.Type) or at minimum burn CPU. The loop should be `for v := range events` or check `v, ok := <-events; if !ok { return }`.

IndexMetrics.IndexedKinds is incremented/decremented without nil check in handleEvent, unlike other IndexMetrics usages in the same file

In handleEvent, IndexMetrics.IndexedKinds.WithLabelValues(evt.Key.Resource).Inc() (line 263) and .Dec() (line 271) are called without checking if IndexMetrics is nil. Every other use of IndexMetrics in this file (lines 217, 282, 367) guards with `if IndexMetrics != nil`. If IndexMetrics is nil (which can happen if metrics registration failed or in tests), handleEvent will panic with a nil pointer dereference when processing ADDED or DELETED watch events. This is inconsistent and a latent crash. Fix: add the same nil guard, or better, initialize IndexMetrics to a no-op default so nil checks are unnecessary.

Init is now only called from the constructor, but remains exported and uses sync.Once with a shared initErr that Stop() overwrites, creating a data race and broken re-init semantics

The PR removes all lazy s.Init(ctx) calls from the gRPC handlers (Create, Update, Delete, Read, List, Watch, Search, History, Origin, IsHealthy, PutBlob, GetBlob) and instead calls s.Init(ctx) once in NewResourceServer. However, Init (line 293) is still an exported method on the server type, still guarded by s.once, and still writes to the shared s.initErr field. Meanwhile Stop() (line 320) unconditionally writes s.initErr = fmt.Errorf("service is stopping") without any synchronization. If any external caller (or future code) invokes Init concurrently with Stop, or calls Init after Stop, there is an unsynchronized read/write race on s.initErr. More importantly, the once.Do means that if Init is called again after Stop (e.g., a caller retries Init on the same server instance), it will return the stale initErr from the first run — but Stop has since overwritten initErr with "service is stopping"/"service is stopped", so the semantics are now muddled: a second Init returns whatever Stop last wrote. Since Init is now effectively an internal startup step, it should be unexported (init) or the initErr handling should be made race-free and Stop should not clobber the field that Init's once.Do closure reads.

Moving Init from lazy per-request to constructor changes the failure contract: NewResourceServer now blocks on full index build and can fail startup, but callers may not expect constructor to do heavy I/O

Previously, Init was called lazily on the first gRPC request (Create/Update/Read/List/Watch/Search/etc.), so NewResourceServer returned quickly and the server could start serving requests (returning init errors per-request) even if index building was slow or failed. Now NewResourceServer calls s.Init(ctx) synchronously at line 258, which calls searchSupport.init — this builds the entire search index (potentially minutes for large datasets) and starts watchers before the constructor returns. Consequences: (1) The gRPC server registration/startup path now blocks on index build; if the caller has a startup timeout, the process may be killed before the server is ready. (2) If index build fails, NewResourceServer returns an error and the entire ResourceServer fails to construct — previously the server would start and only Search requests would fail. (3) The ctx passed to Init is the server's internal background-derived context (line 229), not a startup timeout context — so a hung index build hangs the constructor forever with no cancellation. Callers of NewResourceServer need to be audited to ensure they can tolerate a long-blocking, failure-prone constructor; ideally Init should be called with a startup deadline context, or the constructor should return the server immediately and Init be called separately by the module lifecycle with proper timeout handling.

NewResourceServer calls s.Init(ctx) with a context that is never cancelled on construction failure, leaking the watcher goroutine and resources

NewResourceServer creates a cancelable context (ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(...)) at line 229 and stores it on the server struct (s.ctx, s.cancel). It then calls s.Init(ctx) at line 258, which starts the watcher (initWatcher) and, via searchSupport.init, spawns a goroutine reading from the storage event channel. If Init fails (e.g., search index build error or WatchWriteEvents error), NewResourceServer returns nil, err at line 261 — but it never calls s.cancel(). The server object is discarded, so the cancel function is unreachable, and the background goroutines started by initWatcher (the broadcaster goroutine piping events from s.backend.WatchWriteEvents(s.ctx)) keep running forever with a context that will never be cancelled. This is a goroutine/resource leak on every failed startup, and in HA or repeated-restart scenarios it will accumulate pollers holding DB connections. Fix: call s.cancel() (or defer it) before returning the error when Init fails.

Stop() overwrites initErr with a generic error, losing the original initialization error and breaking error reporting for callers that check Init after Stop

Stop() unconditionally sets s.initErr = fmt.Errorf("service is stopping") at line 321 and later s.initErr = fmt.Errorf("service is stopped") at line 339, overwriting whatever initErr was set during Init. Since Init uses sync.Once and returns s.initErr, any caller that calls Init after Stop (or concurrently) will get "service is stopped" instead of the real initialization error. More importantly, the lifecycle is now: NewResourceServer calls Init synchronously; if it fails, the constructor returns an error and the server is never used — so Stop is never called on a failed-init server. But for a successfully initialized server that is later stopped, if any code path still calls Init (it's exported), it gets the once-cached value... which Stop has clobbered. The initErr field is being used for two purposes (init result and stop status) without synchronization. Separate the concerns: keep initErr immutable after once.Do, and use a separate atomic/bool for stopped state.

bleveIndex.Write/Delete/Flush mutate shared batch state with no synchronization — unsafe for concurrent watch-event handling

bleveIndex.Write (line 172) checks b.batch != nil, calls b.batch.Index(...), and may call b.index.Batch(b.batch) and b.batch.Reset(). Delete (line 190) errors if batch != nil. Flush (line 198) calls b.index.Batch(b.batch), b.batch.Reset(), and sets b.batch = nil. These fields are documented as "only valid in single thread" (line 166) but after the PR's change, handleEvent in search.go can be invoked concurrently: the searchSupport.init goroutine (line 207) calls handleEvent in a single goroutine, but getOrCreateIndex (line 287) can trigger build() concurrently with handleEvent for the same key, and once the index is in the cache, multiple watch events for the same namespace could be processed... actually the searchSupport event loop is single-goroutine, but the index returned by BuildIndex is placed in the cache before Flush is called by searchSupport.build (line 372: index.Flush() after BuildIndex returns). Between BuildIndex returning (line 140) and searchSupport.build calling Flush (search.go line 372), the index is in the cache with b.batch still non-nil; a concurrent Search on that index is fine, but a concurrent handleEvent Write would see batch != nil and try to batch.Index into a batch that build() is about to Flush and nil out — a race on b.batch. More critically, after Flush sets b.batch = nil, concurrent Write calls go directly to b.index.Index which is safe, but the transition itself (Flush setting batch=nil while Write reads batch) is unsynchronized. The bleveIndex needs a mutex protecting batch, or the batch must be fully flushed and nilled inside BuildIndex before the index is published to the cache.

searchSupport.init starts a second, unbounded event-watching goroutine that duplicates the server's broadcaster watcher and never terminates

searchSupport.init (line 172) calls s.storage.WatchWriteEvents(watchctx) at line 203 with watchctx := context.Background() (line 202) and spawns a goroutine at line 207 that loops forever reading from the events channel and calling s.handleEvent. This is separate from the server's own initWatcher (server.go line 752) which also calls s.backend.WatchWriteEvents(s.ctx) and feeds a broadcaster. The searchSupport goroutine uses context.Background(), which is never cancelled — not by server.Stop() (which only calls s.cancel() on the server's own ctx), and not by any lifecycle hook. When the server shuts down, this goroutine keeps running, keeps consuming events from the storage backend's poller, and keeps mutating the search index. Additionally, both the server's broadcaster and this searchSupport goroutine independently call WatchWriteEvents on the same SQL backend, which spawns two poller goroutines (backend.go line 566) polling the same resource_history table — doubling DB load and potentially racing on index writes. The searchSupport watcher should use the server's cancellable context (s.ctx) and be tied to the server lifecycle, or the event handling should be unified with the existing broadcaster.

totalBatchesIndexed is incremented inside concurrent errgroup goroutines without synchronization — data race and incorrect metric

In searchSupport.init, totalBatchesIndexed is declared as a plain int at line 177 and incremented at line 189 inside group.Go(func() error { ... totalBatchesIndexed++ ... }) for each namespace. The errgroup runs up to s.initWorkers concurrent goroutines (group.SetLimit(s.initWorkers) at line 179), so multiple goroutines increment the same variable concurrently with no mutex or atomic. This is a data race (undefined behavior under the Go memory model) and will also produce an incorrect count in the span event at line 199 (attribute.Int("namespaced_indexed", totalBatchesIndexed)). Fix: use atomic.Int64, or compute the count as len(stats) after group.Wait() since every stat entry spawns exactly one goroutine.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Test cleanup uses wrong alias 'alias' instead of the actual created alias

In testCacheIDPByOrg (line 303) and testCacheIDPForLogin (line 381, 425), the cleanup is registered as getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove) — the literal string "alias" is used instead of the loop variable alias (e.g., "org-idp-" + i or "idp-alias-" + i). This means the cleanup attempts to remove an IDP with alias "alias" which doesn't exist, and the actual created IDPs are never cleaned up. This leaks test data across test runs, potentially causing interference with other tests that count IDPs or check login page contents. The same bug exists in the pre-existing testCacheIDPByOrg (line 303), suggesting it was copied. The cleanup should use the actual alias variable: getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get(alias)::remove) or better, capture the created IDP's alias from the response.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Login cache invalidation on IDP update misses changes to BROKER_PUBLIC config and other login-relevant fields

registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate(original, updated) only compares getLoginPredicate() results and getOrganizationId() between the original and updated models. The login predicate (IdentityProviderStorageProvider.LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate, line 252-256 of IdentityProviderStorageProvider.java) tests isEnabled(), !isLinkOnly(), !isHideOnLogin(), and the BROKER_PUBLIC config flag for org-linked IDPs. However, the update path only skips invalidation when both models pass the predicate AND organizationId is unchanged. If an update changes BROKER_PUBLIC from 'true' to 'false' (or vice versa) on an org-linked IDP, or changes enabled/linkOnly/hideOnLogin in a way that keeps the predicate result the same for the specific FetchMode combination, the cached getForLogin results become stale. Concretely: an org-linked IDP with BROKER_PUBLIC=true passes the predicate; updating it to BROKER_PUBLIC=false makes getLoginPredicate().test(updated) return false, so the first guard (!test(original) && !test(updated)) is false and the second guard (test(original) && test(updated)) is also false — invalidation does occur in that direction. But the reverse direction and, more importantly, updates that change BROKER_PUBLIC while the IDP remains org-linked and the predicate outcome is unchanged for one mode but the cached per-organization searchKey results differ are not handled: the cache key cacheKeyForLogin(realm, mode) is shared across ALL organizationIds (searchKey is stored inside IdentityProviderListQuery, not in the cache key), so invalidating only when organizationId changes is insufficient — a BROKER_PUBLIC change on an org-linked IDP alters which org-specific searchKey buckets are valid, yet if test(original) && test(updated) && Objects.equals(organizationId) the method returns without invalidating, leaving stale per-org cached IDP id sets. Additionally, the predicate's BROKER_PUBLIC check reads idp.getConfig().get(OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC) — for a realm-level IDP (organizationId == null) the predicate short-circuits true on the org check, but the cached getForLogin(ORG_ONLY, orgId) buckets for org-linked IDPs depend on BROKER_PUBLIC; an update that flips BROKER_PUBLIC while keeping the IDP org-linked and otherwise login-eligible will not invalidate when the predicate outcome is unchanged, serving stale IDP lists for that organization's login page.

ORG_ONLY branch with null organization re-checks isEnabled but not linkOnly/hideOnLogin/BROKER_PUBLIC, inconsistent with sibling branch

In searchForIdentityProviders, the onlyOrganizationBrokers branch when organization != null (lines 65-72) filters with idp.isEnabled() && !idp.isLinkOnly() && !idp.isHideOnLogin() && Boolean.parseBoolean(idp.getConfig().get(OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC)). But when organization == null (lines 74-77), it calls getForLogin(ORG_ONLY, null) and only re-checks idp.isEnabled() (line 75), not the other login criteria. The comment says 're-check isEnabled as idp might have been wrapped' — the wrapping (createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel) only overrides isEnabled(), so the other criteria (linkOnly, hideOnLogin, BROKER_PUBLIC) are already enforced by the underlying getForLogin query and don't need re-checking. However, the inconsistency is that the organization != null branch re-checks ALL criteria while the null branch re-checks only isEnabled. This is actually correct because the wrapped model only affects isEnabled(), but the asymmetry is confusing and fragile: if the wrapping logic changes to override more methods, the null-organization branch would silently miss them. More importantly, the ALL branch (line 79-82) also only re-checks isEnabled(), which is consistent with the null-org ORG_ONLY branch. The real issue is that the organization != null branch bypasses getForLogin entirely (using organization.getIdentityProviders()) and thus must re-check all criteria, while the other branches rely on getForLogin's filtering — this is a design inconsistency but not a bug per se. The added isEnabled() re-check in the ORG_ONLY-null and ALL branches is correct and necessary; no change needed, but the asymmetry in the organization != null branch (which doesn't use getForLogin) means it doesn't benefit from the new cache, potentially causing a performance regression for that specific path.

getForLogin cache key ignores organizationId, causing cross-organization cache pollution and incorrect results

cacheKeyForLogin(realm, mode) produces a key of the form realmId + ".idp.login." + mode — it does NOT include organizationId. The organizationId is only used as searchKey inside the IdentityProviderListQuery (line 223: searchKey = organizationId != null ? organizationId : ""). This means all organization-specific queries for a given FetchMode share a single cache entry. While IdentityProviderListQuery supports multiple searchKeys (as seen in getByOrganization with first/max pagination keys), the getForLogin implementation has a critical flaw: when a new searchKey is not found (cached == null, line 234), it calls cache.invalidateObject(cacheKey) (line 236) — which invalidates the ENTIRE cache entry for that mode, discarding all previously cached organizationId buckets. This is a correctness/performance issue: in a multi-org deployment, alternating requests for orgA and orgB login pages will constantly invalidate each other's cached results, defeating the cache entirely and causing repeated DB queries. Worse, there is a race: two concurrent requests for different orgs can interleave such that one thread invalidates the entry while another is reading stale data, and the IdentityProviderListQuery merge constructor (line 239) attempts to preserve old searchKeys but the invalidateObject already removed the entry from the cache, making the merge ineffective. The consequence is severe cache thrashing in multi-organization realms and potential for serving incorrect IDP lists if the invalidation/merge logic doesn't properly synchronize. The cache key should incorporate organizationId (e.g., realmId + ".idp.login." + mode + "." + (organizationId != null ? organizationId : "")) to properly partition per-organization results, matching the pattern used by cacheKeyOrgId.

getForLogin returns results in non-deterministic order due to HashSet, breaking login page IDP ordering

getForLogin (and similarly getByOrganization at line 200) collects IDP internal IDs into a Set<String> via Collectors.toSet() (line 229/238), then iterates over the set to build a HashSet<IdentityProviderModel> (line 244), and returns identityProviders.stream() (line 254). HashSet does not preserve insertion order, so the resulting stream has non-deterministic ordering. The callers (e.g., OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean.searchForIdentityProviders) apply .sorted(IDP_COMPARATOR_INSTANCE) after mapping, which may restore a deterministic order for the login page. However, the IdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin contract (server-spi line 165-184) does not specify ordering, and other callers may rely on stable ordering. More importantly, the default interface implementation (lines 165-184) uses Stream.concat of getAllStream results, which preserves database/insertion order. The cached implementation breaks this implicit ordering guarantee, potentially causing IDP display order to change between cache hits and misses, leading to inconsistent UI behavior and flaky tests. The cached IDs should be stored and returned in a deterministic order (e.g., LinkedHashSet or List) to match the uncached behavior.

getLoginPredicate BROKER_PUBLIC check can NPE if getConfig() returns null

The newly added predicate line 254: .and(idp -> idp.getOrganizationId() == null || Boolean.parseBoolean(idp.getConfig().get(OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC))) — if idp.getOrganizationId() is non-null but idp.getConfig() returns null (which is possible for IdentityProviderModel instances where config was not initialized), this will throw a NullPointerException. While IdentityProviderModel typically initializes config to an empty map, defensive coding is warranted in a predicate that is applied broadly (e.g., in cache invalidation paths where models may come from various sources). The consequence is a potential NPE during IDP create/update/remove operations in the InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider, breaking those operations. The code should use idp.getConfig() != null && Boolean.parseBoolean(...) or Objects.requireNonNullElse(idp.getConfig(), Map.of()).get(...).

remove(alias) calls registerIDPLoginInvalidation(storedIdp) with a possibly-null model, causing NPE via getLoginPredicate

In remove(String alias), storedIdp is obtained via idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias) and can be null if no IDP with that alias exists. registerIDPLoginInvalidation(storedIdp) (line 382-389) calls getLoginPredicate().test(idp), and the predicate chain starts with Objects::nonNull — actually the predicate is null-safe (Objects::nonNull returns false for null), so test(null) returns false and no invalidation occurs. However, this means removing a non-existent IDP silently skips login-cache invalidation, which is harmless. The real issue: when the IDP DOES exist, registerIDPLoginInvalidation only invalidates if the stored IDP currently qualifies as a login IDP. But consider an IDP that was previously a login IDP, was updated to hideOnLogin=true (which invalidates caches at update time), then removed — fine. The problematic case is when the cached getForLogin entries were populated, then the IDP is updated to hideOnLogin=true via a path that does NOT go through this storage provider's update (e.g., direct JPA delegate or another node in a cluster where invalidation hasn't propagated), then remove() is called: storedIdp reflects hideOnLogin=true, predicate returns false, login caches are NOT invalidated, yet the IDP is deleted — stale internal IDs remain in the cached IdentityProviderListQuery. The getForLogin method does handle null getById results by invalidating (lines 246-250), so this self-heals on next access, but the remove path should unconditionally invalidate login caches (or at least when the IDP existed) rather than relying on the current predicate state, because the cached query may contain the IDP from before it was disabled. The consequence is a window of stale data and reliance on the lazy null-check fallback.

testCacheIDPForLogin does not test invalidation when BROKER_PUBLIC config changes on an org-linked IDP

The test testCacheIDPForLogin covers: creating non-login IDPs, removing non-login IDPs, updating IDPs without changing login status, updating to change hideOnLogin, and linking a realm IDP to an org. However, it does NOT test the critical scenario where an org-linked IDP's BROKER_PUBLIC config is toggled (e.g., from 'true' to 'false'), which should invalidate the login caches because the IDP should no longer appear in ORG_ONLY/ALL results for that org. Given that registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate's logic (lines 403-418) specifically handles the BROKER_PUBLIC dimension via the login predicate, and the cache key issue (shared across orgs) makes per-org invalidation subtle, a test that: (1) caches getForLogin(ORG_ONLY, orgaId), (2) updates an org-linked IDP to set BROKER_PUBLIC=false, (3) verifies the cache is invalidated and the IDP no longer appears — is essential to validate correctness. Without this test, a regression where BROKER_PUBLIC changes don't trigger invalidation (or trigger incorrect invalidation) would go undetected.

update() calls getById(model.getInternalId()) which may return an organization-wrapped model, breaking alias-based invalidation

In update(IdentityProviderModel model), line 91 calls getById(model.getInternalId()) to obtain the original IDP for invalidation purposes. However, getById (lines 123-142) wraps the result via createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel when the ORGANIZATION feature is enabled, returning an anonymous subclass of IdentityProviderModel that overrides isEnabled(). This wrapped model is then passed to registerIDPInvalidation(idpById) (line 92) and registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate(idpById, model) (line 93). registerIDPInvalidation uses idp.getInternalId() and idp.getAlias() — these are not overridden so they work. But registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate calls getLoginPredicate().test(original) where original is the wrapped model; the predicate calls idp.isEnabled() which for the wrapped model performs an additional organization lookup (lines 432-446). If the organization is disabled or the provider is unavailable, isEnabled() returns false even if the underlying IDP is enabled, causing the predicate to incorrectly classify the original as not-a-login-IDP. This can lead to incorrect invalidation decisions: e.g., an IDP that is actually login-eligible but whose wrapped isEnabled() returns false due to a disabled org would be treated as !test(original), and if the update also results in !test(updated), the method returns early without invalidating login caches — leaving stale cached login IDP lists. The wrapped model should not be used for invalidation logic; the raw delegate model should be fetched (e.g., via idpDelegate.getById) for comparison purposes.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default KeyStore provider, not a BouncyCastle provider

getBouncyCastleProvider() is implemented as KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which returns whatever JCA provider supplies the default keystore type (typically SunJCE/SunJSSE on a stock JDK), not a BouncyCastle provider. The CryptoProvider contract (see the interface javadoc: 'BouncyCastle security provider. Can be either non-FIPS or FIPS based provider') and callers such as code that registers or queries CryptoIntegration.getProvider().getBouncyCastleProvider() expect an actual BouncyCastle provider instance. The WildFlyElytronProvider precedent returns null when no BC provider exists; this implementation should either return null (documenting that the authz client has no BC provider) or return a real BouncyCastleProvider, not an unrelated JCA provider. Returning the keystore provider can cause callers to register/query the wrong security provider.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
concatenatedRSToASN1DER produces invalid DER for r or s with high bit set

In concatenatedRSToASN1DER, the raw r and s halves of the signature are copied into a byte array of size len+1 with a leading zero byte (System.arraycopy(signature, 0, r, 1, len)) and then converted via new BigInteger(r). This always yields a positive BigInteger whose toByteArray() includes the leading zero byte, so the encoded INTEGER is always len+1 bytes long. That is correct only when the original value had its high bit set (requiring a sign-padding zero). When the high bit is clear, DER requires the minimal encoding without the leading zero; the extra 0x00 makes the INTEGER non-minimal and therefore invalid DER. Strict verifiers (and RFC 6979/JWS interop with other implementations) will reject signatures produced by this method whenever r or s has a clear high bit, which happens with probability ~1/2 per component. The correct approach is new BigInteger(1, Arrays.copyOfRange(signature, 0, len)) (signum 1, magnitude only), letting BigInteger.toByteArray() add the sign byte only when needed. Note the two throwaway ASN1Encoder.create().write(...) calls on lines 114-115 are dead code and should be removed.

true_positives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
readSequence mishandles indefinite-length encoding and can loop forever / mis-parse

readLength() returns -1 for the indefinite-length form (0x80, line 133-135), but readSequence() (line 49) treats the returned length as a plain int and loops while (length > 0), decrementing by the size of each element. With length == -1 the loop condition is true and length only grows more negative as elements are consumed, so the loop never terminates on well-formed input and will keep calling readNext() until it throws EOFException from an exhausted stream — i.e. indefinite-length SEQUENCE encodings (valid BER, produced by some libraries) are rejected with a confusing EOF error rather than parsed or cleanly rejected. Additionally, readSequence never checks that the declared length matches the bytes actually consumed, and readNext() computes element size as content length plus the bytes consumed for tag+length via mark/reset, which double-counts nothing but also does not validate against the remaining sequence length, so a sequence whose declared length disagrees with its contents is silently accepted. For a signature-verification path, accepting structurally inconsistent DER is undesirable; at minimum the indefinite-length case must be rejected explicitly with a clear IOException.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Adding abstract method order() to CryptoProvider breaks all external implementors (API break)

order() is added to the CryptoProvider interface as a plain abstract method with no default implementation. CryptoProvider is a public SPI in keycloak-common that third parties can implement (it is loaded via ServiceLoader from META-INF/services). Any existing external implementation of CryptoProvider will fail to compile/load against this change with AbstractMethodError at runtime when order() is called (CryptoIntegration.detectProvider now calls CryptoProvider::order on every loaded provider). This is a breaking API change to a published interface. It should be a default method (e.g. `default int order() { return 0; }`) to preserve backward compatibility, matching how getSupportedRsaKeySizes() and getSupportedKeyStoreTypes() are already defined as defaults in the same interface.

false_positives.candidate:
CryptoIntegration.init is only called from one create() overload; other factory methods leave crypto uninitialized

CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()) is added only to create(Configuration). The other public factory methods create() (line 60) and create(InputStream) (line 72) delegate to create(Configuration) so they are covered, but any code path that constructs AuthzClient without going through these factories, or any other entry point in the authz-client that uses CryptoIntegration.getProvider() (e.g. ECDSA signature verification of tokens via the crypto provider), will hit 'Illegal state. Please init first before obtaining provider' if init was never called. More importantly, init() is a global static one-shot: once any other component in the same JVM (e.g. the Keycloak server in the testsuite) has initialized CryptoIntegration with a different classloader, the authz client's later init() call is a no-op and the AuthzClientCryptoProvider service file is never loaded for the client's classloader, so the client silently uses whatever provider was detected first. The initialization should be tied to the classloader actually used by the authz-client classes and be robust to prior initialization, or the provider should be resolved per-classloader rather than globally.

Module artifactId/name/description say 'tests' but the module now contains production code and a service provider

The pom declares artifactId keycloak-authz-client-tests and the description states 'This module is supposed to be used just in the Keycloak repository for the testsuite. It is NOT supposed to be used by the 3rd party applications.' This PR adds production classes (AuthzClientCryptoProvider, ASN1Encoder/Decoder) and a META-INF/services/org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider service registration to this module, and AuthzClient.create() now calls CryptoIntegration.init, meaning the service file will be picked up by ServiceLoader whenever this jar is on the classpath. Shipping a CryptoProvider service registration in a module explicitly documented as testsuite-only is contradictory: if the jar leaks onto a 3rd-party or server classpath, the AuthzClientCryptoProvider (which throws UnsupportedOperationException for most operations) can be selected and break crypto operations. Either the provider classes should move to the real keycloak-authz-client artifact (as the PR description says the changes will later be synced to keycloak-client), or the pom description must be updated; as written the module's stated purpose and its new contents conflict.

Out-of-bounds length check uses the total input size instead of the remaining bytes

In readLength(), the sanity check for long-form lengths is `if (length >= limit)` where limit is the total length of the whole input byte array (set in the constructor), not the number of bytes remaining at the current read position. A nested element deep inside a larger structure can therefore declare a length up to the full input size even though far fewer bytes remain, and the check passes; the subsequent read(length) then fails only later with a generic EOF IOException. This weakens the early corruption detection the check is meant to provide (the comment says 'out of bounds length found'). The check should compare against the bytes remaining (limit minus bytes already consumed), e.g. track position and compare length > remaining.

Provider selection semantics inverted relative to the documented order() contract

CryptoProvider.order() is documented as 'The higher number has preference over the lower number', and the PR description says the Keycloak testsuite keeps using DefaultCryptoProvider via ordering. But detectProvider() sorts with Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order).reversed() and then picks foundProviders.get(0). Comparator.reversed() sorts descending, so get(0) is the provider with the LOWEST order value — the opposite of the documented contract. Concretely: AuthzClientCryptoProvider.order() == 100 and DefaultCryptoProvider.order() == 200, so when both are on the classpath (exactly the scenario this PR creates for the authz-client module, which depends on keycloak-core and is used in the testsuite where DefaultCryptoProvider is present), the authz client provider (100) wins over DefaultCryptoProvider (200), contradicting both the javadoc and the stated intent that the testsuite keeps using DefaultCryptoProvider. Either remove .reversed() or fix the javadoc; as written the code and documentation disagree and the wrong provider is selected.

Round-trip test never verifies the converted signature cryptographically and misses the high-bit-set case

The test only asserts that asn1derToConcatenatedRS(concatenatedRSToASN1DER(x)) == x. It never checks that the DER produced by concatenatedRSToASN1DER is accepted by Signature.verify (the actual consumer of this conversion in JWT verification), nor that the concatenated form verifies via a JCA Signature using the raw r||s (e.g. SHA256withECDSAinP1363Format). Because of the leading-zero bug in concatenatedRSToASN1DER (see separate finding), the produced DER is non-minimal whenever r or s has a clear high bit; a round-trip through the same buggy code hides this, but a real verifier would reject it. The test should include Signature.verify over the re-encoded DER and should force coverage of both high-bit-set and high-bit-clear r/s values (e.g. by looping over multiple signatures until both cases occur, since each occurs with ~50% probability).

Test uses a default 256-bit EC key for ES384/ES512, so the ES384/ES512 paths are not actually exercised

The test constructor generates the key pair with KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair(), which on a standard JDK produces a 256-bit (secp256r1) key. It then signs with Signature.getInstance(JavaAlgorithm.getJavaAlgorithm(algorithm.name())) — for ES384 that is SHA384withECDSA and for ES512 SHA512withECDSA — but the signature length is still determined by the 256-bit curve, so algorithm.getSignatureLength() (96/132 bytes for ES384/ES512) does not match the actual r||s size (64 bytes). asn1derToConcatenatedRS then splits the DER into halves of signLength/2 = 48/66 bytes, which does not correspond to the real r and s, and concatenatedRSToASN1DER re-encodes with the wrong lengths. The round-trip assertion may still pass because both directions use the same wrong length, masking the mismatch, but the test never validates behavior with a real P-384/P-521 key and never verifies the produced DER against Signature.verify, so it does not prove correctness for ES384/ES512. The test should generate a key on the matching curve (e.g. secp384r1/secp521r1 via ECGenParameterSpec) per algorithm, and ideally assert that the converted signature verifies with the public key.

integerToBytes truncates the most significant bytes when the value is larger than the target length

integerToBytes(BigInteger s, int qLength) handles the case qLength < bytes.length by copying the LAST qLength bytes (System.arraycopy(bytes, bytes.length - tmp.length, tmp, 0, tmp.length)). For an ECDSA r or s value, the magnitude can legitimately be up to qLength+1 bytes because BigInteger.toByteArray() prepends a 0x00 sign byte when the high bit is set; in that case dropping the leading zero is correct. But if the value is genuinely larger than qLength (e.g. a malformed/forged DER signature where r or s >= curve order, which is exactly the input an attacker controls when verifying a JWT), this silently truncates the most significant bytes and returns a wrong-length, wrong-value r/s instead of rejecting the signature. asn1derToConcatenatedRS is used on the verification path, so a crafted DER signature with oversized integers would be silently mangled rather than rejected, and the resulting concatenated value fed to the JCA verifier. The method should throw (e.g. IOException) when bytes.length > qLength + 1, or when the value does not fit in qLength bytes, instead of truncating.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
registerListener now gates V1 cleanup behavior behind ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ, breaking permission cleanup when only V2 is enabled

The diff wraps the entire event-handling body in 'if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ))'. Previously the listener unconditionally disabled permissions on role/client/group removal. ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is a separate feature flag from ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (the V2 evaluator is selected when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, see AdminPermissions.evaluator). With V2 enabled but V1 disabled, RoleRemovedEvent, ClientRemovedEvent, and GroupRemovedEvent will no longer trigger setPermissionsEnabled(..., false), leaving stale fine-grained permissions referencing deleted roles/clients/groups. This is a data-integrity regression: orphaned permissions remain active and may grant access based on policies referencing non-existent entities. The guard should either be removed (the cleanup is harmless when permissions are disabled) or check for either feature flag.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Null resource passed to policyStore.findByResource when the Clients type resource does not exist

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), when the per-client resource is not found, the code calls AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and immediately passes the result to authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource) without a null check. getResourceTypeResource returns null when the resource type resource has not been created (e.g., admin permissions were enabled but init() was not run, or the resource was deleted). Passing null to findByResource will cause a NullPointerException (or store-specific failure) instead of the intended graceful 'return false'. The sibling method hasPermission(String scope) at line 244-247 correctly checks 'if (resource == null) return false;', showing the per-client variant is missing the same guard.

true_positives.golden_comment: Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getEvaluationContext is dead code and mutates a possibly-immutable map

The private method getEvaluationContext(ClientModel authorizedClient, AccessToken token) is never called anywhere in the class (all token-exchange related methods throw UnsupportedOperationException). Additionally, it calls super.getBaseAttributes() and then attributes.put(...) — if DefaultEvaluationContext.getBaseAttributes() returns an immutable map, this would throw UnsupportedOperationException at runtime. Since the method is unused, it should be removed; leaving unused, broken code in a security-sensitive permission evaluator is a maintenance hazard and may confuse future maintainers into wiring it up incorrectly.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.

false_positives.candidate:
Unused static import TOKEN_EXCHANGE and unused logger/scope imports

The class has 'import static org.keycloak.services.resources.admin.permissions.AdminPermissionManagement.TOKEN_EXCHANGE;' (line 46) which is never referenced, an unused 'logger' field (line 51), and unused imports including org.keycloak.authorization.model.Scope (line 27). These are harmless but indicate the class was scaffolded from a template and not cleaned up; the unused TOKEN_EXCHANGE import in particular suggests token-exchange support was planned but is explicitly unsupported (canExchangeTo throws).

canView() delegates to canViewClientDefault() which is a V1 method with different semantics, potentially bypassing V2 permission checks

canView() is implemented as 'return canViewClientDefault() || hasPermission(AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW);'. canViewClientDefault() is inherited from ClientPermissions (V1) and checks the caller's realm-management roles (view-clients / manage-clients) via root.hasOneAdminRole. This is intentional for backward compatibility (admins with realm-management roles retain access). However, canViewClientDefault() in the V1 implementation may also consult the client's own permission settings or other V1 state that is explicitly unsupported in V2 (isPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException). If canViewClientDefault() internally calls isPermissionsEnabled or resource() on the client, it would throw UnsupportedOperationException at runtime for V2. The method should be verified to only use role checks; otherwise V2 evaluation could crash. This is a speculative but concrete risk given that multiple other inherited methods throw UnsupportedOperationException.

getClientsWithPermission returns resource names (internal client IDs) rather than client IDs, producing unusable identifiers

getClientsWithPermission(String scope) iterates resources of type CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE and adds resource.getName() to the granted set. Per AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource and resolveClient, the resource name for a client is the client's internal model ID (client.getId()), not the clientId. Callers of getClientsWithPermission (e.g., admin endpoints that filter or search clients by permission) expect to receive identifiers they can use to look up clients — typically the client ID used in admin APIs. Returning internal model IDs (UUIDs) instead of clientIds makes the result unusable for API consumers and inconsistent with the rest of the admin API where clients are addressed by their model ID in URLs but by clientId in search. The Users V2 equivalent (UserPermissionsV2.getUsersWithPermission) has the same pattern with user IDs, which is consistent there because users are addressed by ID; for clients, the resource name is the internal ID, so the method should either return the internal IDs consistently (and document it) or map them back to clientIds. At minimum, the semantics should be verified against actual callers.

getResourceName only handles the Users resource type; Clients resources fall through to displayName which may be null

getResourceName(KeycloakSession session, Policy policy, Resource resource) resolves a human-readable name only for USERS resource type policies (returning 'All users' or the username). For a policy with resourceType 'Clients', the method skips the if-block and returns resource.getDisplayName(). Resources created by getOrCreateResource are created via resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, resourceServer.getClientId()) without setting a display name, so getDisplayName() returns null for client resources. Any admin UI or API listing permissions for Clients resource-type policies will show a null/empty resource name instead of the client ID or clientId, degrading the admin experience and potentially breaking UI rendering that assumes a non-null name.

getScope throws NullPointerException when resourceType is not in the schema

In getScope(KeycloakSession session, ResourceServer resourceServer, String resourceType, String id), when supportsAuthorizationSchema is true, the code calls SCHEMA.getResourceTypes().get(resourceType).getScopes() without checking whether getResourceTypes().get(resourceType) returns null. If a caller passes a resourceType that is not 'Users' or 'Clients' (e.g., a custom type, or null), this throws a NullPointerException instead of a meaningful ModelValidationException. The sibling method throwExceptionIfResourceTypeOrScopesNotProvided (line 196) explicitly validates 'SCHEMA.getResourceTypes().get(rep.getResourceType()) == null', showing the intended contract; getScope violates it. This NPE would surface as a 500 error rather than a 400 validation error when creating a scope permission with an invalid resource type through a path that reaches getScope before the other validation.

onAfter cleanup only removes scope permissions, leaving created user policies and clients behind

The @AfterEach onAfter method removes all scope permissions via permissions.findAll(...).forEach(p -> permissions.findById(p.getId()).remove()), but the tests create UserPolicyRepresentations via createUserPolicy (which registers realm cleanup callbacks) and, in testManageAllClients, create and delete a 'newClient'. The createUserPolicy helper does register a realm.cleanup() callback to remove the policy, so policies are cleaned up at realm teardown. However, testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient creates client roles ('myclient-role', 'myclient-subRole') via realm.admin() without registering cleanup, and these persist in the managed realm across tests within the same class if the realm is reused. If the test framework reuses the realm across test methods (ManagedRealm lifecycle), the second run of testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient would fail because the roles already exist. The test should register cleanup for the created roles, e.g., realm.cleanup().add(r -> ...remove roles...).

testManageOnlyOneClient assumes at least 2 default client scopes and indexes get(1) without verifying size

In testManageOnlyOneClient, the pre-permission negative check does 'ClientScopeRepresentation clientScopeRep = clientResource.getDefaultClientScopes().get(1);' — but this call is expected to FAIL with ForbiddenException before the permission is granted (the admin has no permission yet), so getDefaultClientScopes() throws and get(1) is never reached; the variable clientScopeRep is then unused in that block. Later, after granting MANAGE, the test does 'List<ClientScopeRepresentation> defaultClientScopes = clientResource.getDefaultClientScopes(); ... ClientScopeRepresentation clientScopeRep = defaultClientScopes.get(1);' — this assumes the client has at least 2 default client scopes. If the test realm's client has fewer than 2 default scopes (depends on realm config), this throws IndexOutOfBoundsException and the test fails for an unrelated reason. The test should assert the list size before indexing, or use get(0). The same pattern appears in testConfigureOnlyOneClient at line 234/242 using get(0), which is safer but still assumes a non-empty list.

testViewAllClients creates a client with null representation and only asserts FORBIDDEN, not validating the actual rejection reason

In testViewAllClients, the final negative check does 'realmAdminClient.realm(realm.getName()).clients().create(null)' and asserts the response is 403 FORBIDDEN. Passing a null ClientRepresentation is an unusual API call; the server may reject it with 400 Bad Request before even reaching the authorization check, depending on JAX-RS/RESTEasy null-body handling. If the server returns 400 instead of 403, the test fails for a reason unrelated to the permission logic being tested. The intent is clearly to verify that a view-only admin cannot create clients; a valid minimal ClientRepresentation (like the one used in testManageAllClients) should be passed instead so the 403 is attributable to the authorization layer.

true_positives.golden_comment: Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Exit code change from 4 to 3 for recreate upgrade breaks documented contract and existing automation

The constant RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE is changed from 4 to 3 in this PR. The accompanying documentation in docs/guides/server/update-compatibility.adoc (lines 128-130) is updated to say exit code 3 means 'Rolling Upgrade is not possible. The deployment must be shut down before applying the new configuration.' and exit code 4 means the feature is disabled. However, this is a breaking change to the exit-code contract of the `update-compatibility check` command: any existing CI/CD pipeline or script written against the previous release (where 4 meant 'recreate upgrade required') will now misinterpret exit code 3 as an unexpected error (picocli software error is 1, usage error is 2, and scripts commonly treat any non-0/3/4 code as failure) and, worse, will treat exit code 4 as a distinct 'feature disabled' case only if they were updated. Since the tool is explicitly documented as 'fully scriptable' and 'GitOps friendly' with consumers relying on exit codes, silently renumbering an existing exit code (rather than only adding the new code 4) breaks backward compatibility for anyone already using the command. The renumbering should be avoided (keep RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE = 4 and use a new code such as 5 for FEATURE_DISABLED), or at minimum the change must be called out as a breaking change in release notes; as written, the docs present the new numbering as if it were always the contract.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:

false_positives.candidate:
Exit code table formatting is broken: rows 0-3 are missing the leading pipe, producing a malformed AsciiDoc table

In the exit-code table (lines 116-135), the first four rows begin with `m|0`, `m|1`, `m|2`, `m|3` while the newly added row begins with `m|4` — all are missing the leading `|` cell delimiter that AsciiDoc tables require (a cell must start with `|`). Only the header row `|===` / `|Exit Code |Description` and the final row use the correct `|` prefix. As a result the rendered table will be malformed: the `m|N` rows will not be parsed as table rows at all (the `m` is an unintended literal prefix), so exit codes 0 through 3 will render as plain paragraph text outside the table, and only the header and the new exit-code-4 row will appear as a table. The rows should be `m|0` corrected to `|0` (i.e., `|m|0` style consistent with the last row: a leading `|` followed by the `m` cell marker). This makes the documented exit-code contract — which scripts depend on — visually broken in the published guide.

Feature check runs before configuration validation, so --features=rolling-updates is never actually parsed for the check itself

In UpdateCompatibilityCheck.run() (and identically in UpdateCompatibilityMetadata.run()), the guard `if (!Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ROLLING_UPDATES))` is evaluated at the very start of run(), before `validateConfig()` is called. Profile.isFeatureEnabled reads the statically initialized Profile (Profile.getInstance()), which is only configured from CLI options/environment during the normal Keycloak configuration/validation phase. The `--features` option is a standard Keycloak CLI option processed by the configuration machinery; whether it has been applied to the Profile singleton at the point run() executes depends on command initialization order in the Quarkus CLI framework. The distribution test UpdateCommandDistTest passes `--features=rolling-updates` as a CLI argument and expects the command to proceed, which suggests the option is honored, but the ordering is fragile: if Profile is initialized lazily or the feature option is applied after run() begins (e.g., when running via `kc.sh update-compatibility ... --features=rolling-updates` in a non-optimized or build-affected mode), the check would incorrectly report the feature as disabled and exit 4 even though the user explicitly enabled it. The feature check should be performed after validateConfig() (which triggers full option processing) or the enabled-features state should be read from the parsed command options rather than the global Profile singleton, to make the gating deterministic.

No test asserts the exit code for the feature-disabled path (exit code 4)

The new testFeatureNotEnabled test only asserts that the error message 'Unable to use this command. The preview feature 'rolling-updates' is not enabled.' appears in the CLI output; it never asserts the process exit code. The whole point of introducing CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED = 4 (and documenting it in docs/guides/server/update-compatibility.adoc lines 132-134 as the contract for scripts) is that automation can branch on exit code 4. Without an assertion such as `assertEquals(4, cliResult.exitCode())` (or the equivalent CLIResult API), a regression that exits with 0, 1, or 2 instead of 4 would not be caught, and the documented scripting contract would silently break. The test should assert the exit code equals CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED.

Test parameterization silently skips enabling the rolling-updates feature when updateStrategy is null

In createInitialDeployment(UpdateStrategy updateStrategy), when updateStrategy is null the method returns early at line 105-107 (`if (updateStrategy == null) { return kc; }`) before the code at lines 112-115 that sets the FeatureSpec with Profile.Feature.ROLLING_UPDATES.getKey(). The parameterized test upgradeStrategy() supplies both null and UpdateStrategy.RECREATE, so the null case (testImageChange-null and testCacheMaxCount-null) runs without the rolling-updates feature enabled in the Keycloak CR. Given that the operator documentation added in this PR (docs/guides/operator/advanced-configuration.adoc lines 446-450) states that 'the feature rolling-updates must be enabled. Otherwise, the Keycloak Operator will fail', the null-strategy test case is exercising a deployment configuration that the operator is documented to reject, and the test's expectations (e.g., eventuallyRollingUpgradeStatus for testCacheMaxCount-null) may be passing for the wrong reason or masking a validation failure. Either the null case should also enable the feature (so both parameters test the strategy behavior with the feature on), or the test should explicitly assert the operator's behavior when the feature is missing. As written, the test coverage for the default (no update strategy) path does not match the documented requirement.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
canManage() grants manage permission when only VIEW is granted

In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() (line 70), the fallback permission check is `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)`, i.e. it accepts the VIEW scope as sufficient for the global manage check. Every other manage check in the same class (canManage(GroupModel) at line 79, canManageMembers at line 93, canManageMembership at line 102) correctly requires only MANAGE/MANAGE_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP. As a result, an admin who has been granted only the 'view' scope on the Groups resource type (the 'Groups' all-resource) is treated as having global manage rights over groups: GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup (which calls auth.groups().requireManage()) and GroupResource operations that call requireManage() without a group argument would succeed for a view-only admin. This is a privilege escalation relative to the intended schema semantics where MANAGE is required for management operations. The check should be `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)`.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns resource ids, not group ids

In GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (lines 106-128), the code iterates resources of type GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE and adds `groupResource.getId()` to the returned set. In the V2 schema, per-group resources are created by AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource with the group id used as the resource *name* (resolveGroup returns group.getId(), and resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, ...) uses that as the name). The resource's own `getId()` is an internally generated UUID, not the group id. The method's contract (documented in GroupPermissionEvaluator: 'Stream of IDs of groups with view permission') and its consumers — UsersResource.searchForUser and BruteForceUsersResource.searchForUser, which do `session.setAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS, groupIds)` and rely on the user provider filtering users by group membership using those ids — expect actual group ids. Returning resource UUIDs means the group-membership filter for user search will never match any real group, so admins restricted to viewing members of specific groups will see an empty user list even though they have view-members permission. The code should resolve the group id from the resource name (the name is the group id per resolveGroup) rather than using the resource id.

false_positives.candidate:
Double semicolon in field declaration

Line 68: `private final GroupRepresentation topGroup = new GroupRepresentation();;` — there is an extra semicolon after the field declaration. This is a minor style issue (empty statement) and does not affect functionality, but it is a code smell that should be cleaned up.

Group-based user filtering applied unconditionally, changing behavior for admins with global view

Same pattern as UsersResource.searchForUser: BruteForceUsersResource.searchForUser (lines 144-153) now unconditionally calls `auth.groups().getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` and sets `session.setAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS, groupIds)` when non-empty, whereas the old code only did so when `!auth.users().canView()`. Combined with `toRepresentation` calling `usersEvaluator.grantIfNoPermission(session.getAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS) != null)` (line 159), this changes the grantIfNoPermission flag for admins who have global view-users permission but for whom getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns a non-empty set. In V2, GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns resource ids (not group ids — see separate finding), so the set can be non-empty with bogus ids, causing (a) the user search to be filtered by non-existent groups (returning no users), and (b) grantIfNoPermission to be set to true, which in UserPermissions.hasPermission (line 501) grants manage+view when the Users resource is absent. For an admin with the view-users role this is a functional regression (no users returned) and a potential security issue (grantIfNoPermission flipped). The `!auth.users().canView()` guard should be restored, or getGroupIdsWithViewPermission must reliably return an empty set for admins with global view.

Group-based user filtering is now applied even when the admin has global view-users permission

In UsersResource.searchForUser (lines 445-454), the previous code only set the `UserModel.GROUPS` session attribute (which restricts the user search to members of groups the admin can view) when `!auth.users().canView()`. The new code unconditionally calls `auth.groups().getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` and sets the session attribute whenever the returned set is non-empty. In GroupPermissions.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (V1, line 298-320) the method returns an empty set when `root.users().canView()` is true, so V1 behavior is preserved. However, in GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (line 106-107) the guard is also `if (root.users().canView()) return Collections.emptySet();` — so for admins with the view-users role the set is empty and no restriction is applied. But for admins who have *only* fine-grained permissions (no view-users role) and have been granted view on the all-users resource (Users resource type with VIEW scope), `root.users().canView()` in V2 (UserPermissionsV2 inherits UserPermissions.canView, which checks admin roles then hasPermission(VIEW_SCOPE, MANAGE_SCOPE) on the Users resource) returns true, so getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns empty — OK. The problem case: an admin with view-users role in V1 — canView() true, empty set, fine. The actual regression: the condition `if (!groupIds.isEmpty())` sets the session attribute, and later `toRepresentation` calls `usersEvaluator.grantIfNoPermission(session.getAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS) != null)`. Previously, when the admin had global canView(), the GROUPS attribute was never set, so grantIfNoPermission(false) was called and per-user canView filtering was applied normally. Now, if getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns a non-empty set for an admin who actually has global view (which should not happen given the guards, but the V2 override at GroupPermissionsV2 line 107 checks `root.users().canView()` — and UserPermissionsV2 does not override canView(), so it uses UserPermissions.canView which checks admin roles and the V1-style Users resource permission; in V2 the Users resource-type resource is different from the V1 'Users' resource, so hasPermission(MgmtPermissions.VIEW_SCOPE...) looks up resourceStore.findByName(server, "Users") — in V2 the resource-type resource is named "Users" as well (USERS_RESOURCE_TYPE = "Users"), so it may actually find the V2 resource-type resource and evaluate V2 permissions against it using V1 scope names 'view'/'manage' which do exist in the V2 schema. This cross-wiring means canView() may return true in V2 via the V1 code path, and then getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns empty — consistent. The real issue is subtler: the removal of the `!auth.users().canView()` guard means that for an admin with global view-users role, if getGroupIdsWithViewPermission erroneously returns a non-empty set (e.g. due to the resource-id vs group-id bug in GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, which adds resource ids that are not group ids), the user search would be restricted by a bogus group filter, hiding users the admin should see. Combined with the grantIfNoPermission(session.getAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS) != null) call, setting the attribute also flips grantIfNoPermission to true, which changes the semantics of UserPermissions.hasPermission: when the Users resource does not exist, `grantIfNoPermission && expectedScopes.contains(MANAGE_SCOPE) && expectedScopes.contains(VIEW_SCOPE)` grants permission. This is a behavior change for admins with global view: previously grantIfNoPermission stayed false; now it can become true if the group-ids set is non-empty, potentially granting manage+view when no Users resource exists. This is a security-relevant behavior change that depends on the group-ids set being correct.

GroupPermissionsV2 extends GroupPermissions but overrides almost all behavior, inheriting only unused V1 helpers

GroupPermissionsV2 extends GroupPermissions (line 37) but overrides canView(), canView(GroupModel), canManage(), canManage(GroupModel), canViewMembers, canManageMembers, canManageMembership, getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, and throws UnsupportedOperationException for all management methods. Null resource from getResourceTypeResource is dereferenced without a null check

In GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission (line 144), `resource = AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, AdminPermissionsSchema.GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE)` can return null (the method returns null when the resource type is unknown or the resource does not exist in the store, see AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceTypeResource lines 133-151). Per-object resources are created without a type, breaking findByType queries used by getGroupIdsWithViewPermission

In AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource (lines 118-128), when a new per-object resource is created (line 121: `resource = resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, resourceServer.getClientId())`), the resource type is never set. Only the resource-type resources created in init() have their type set (line 274). GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (line 121) uses `resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...)` to find all group resources with view permission. This means getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns at most one id (the all-groups resource id), and never the ids of individual groups that have view-members permissions. This completely breaks the feature where an admin with view-members permission on specific groups can see users in those groups via the user search. The fix: in getOrCreateResource, after creating the resource, call `resource.setType(resourceType)` so that per-object resources are typed and can be found by findByType.

Removal of AdminRoles.ADMIN from canView/canManage checks

In UserPermissionsV2.canView(UserModel) (line 47-53) and canManage(UserModel) (line 56-62), the admin role checks were changed from `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.ADMIN, AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS, AdminRoles.VIEW_USERS)` to `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS, AdminRoles.VIEW_USERS)` (and MANAGE_USERS only for canManage). The realm-admin role (AdminRoles.ADMIN, i.e. 'admin' role of the realm) is no longer explicitly checked. In Keycloak, the 'admin' role (realm admin) typically has all realm-management client roles including manage-users and view-users, so hasOneAdminRole(MANAGE_USERS, VIEW_USERS) would still return true for a realm admin because the admin role has those composite roles. However, hasOneAdminRole checks direct or composite role membership; the 'admin' role is a composite that includes manage-users and view-users, so it should still pass. But if a custom setup grants the 'admin' role without the composite including manage-users (unusual), the check would fail. More importantly, the V1 UserPermissions.canView() (line 297-307) also only checks MANAGE_USERS and VIEW_USERS, not ADMIN. So V2 now matches V1. In GroupsResource.getGroups (lines 109-115), when populateHierarchy is false, the filter changed from `g -> canViewGlobal || groupsEvaluator.canView(g)` to `groupsEvaluator::canView`. Custom implementations of GroupPermissionEvaluator that return false from canView(GroupModel) for groups without explicit per-group permission but true from canView() would now filter out all groups in the non-hierarchy path. This is an API contract change for the GroupPermissionEvaluator interface: the interface documentation for canView(GroupModel) says 'Or if it has a permission to VIEW or MANAGE the group', which implies per-group, while canView() is global. The old code explicitly OR-ed the two; the new code relies on implementations to do the fallback internally. Since GroupPermissionsV2.canView(GroupModel) does fall back to the all-groups resource, the built-in behavior is correct, but the contract is now implicit. Low severity.

The old code allowed an admin with global view (view-users/manage-users role) to list all subgroups regardless of per-group permissions; the new code requires per-group canView(g) for every subgroup. In V1, GroupPermissions.canView(GroupModel) (line 254-264) returns true if canView() (global) is true, so V1 behavior is preserved. In V2, GroupPermissionsV2.canView(GroupModel) (line 56-62) also returns true if the admin has MANAGE_USERS/VIEW_USERS roles. So for admins with global roles, behavior is unchanged. However, for admins with only fine-grained permissions, the old code's `canViewGlobal` was `auth.groups().canView()` — the same global check — so the old code was effectively `canView() || canView(g)`, and the new code is just `canView(g)`. So an admin with VIEW on the Groups resource type can view all subgroups — same as before. The change is effectively a no-op for V2 and V1 given the implementations, but it removes a redundant check. Not a bug per se; the real concern is that `requireView(group)` on line 176 already ensures the parent group is viewable, and the per-subgroup filter now relies entirely on canView(g) which in V2 falls back to all-groups — consistent. Low severity, likely no functional change; reporting because the removal of the global bypass could affect custom GroupPermissionEvaluator implementations that do not implement the fallback in canView(GroupModel).

canMapRoles and canManageGroupMembership now accept MANAGE scope in addition to the specific scope

In UserPermissionsV2, canMapRoles(UserModel) (line 77-83) was changed from `hasPermission(user, null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MAP_ROLES)` to `hasPermission(user, null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE, AdminPermissionsSchema.MAP_ROLES) || canManageByGroup(user)`. canViewMembers accepts MANAGE_MEMBERS scope — manage-members implies view-members

In GroupPermissionsV2.canViewMembers (lines 82-87), the check is `hasPermission(group.getId(), AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW_MEMBERS, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE_MEMBERS)`. canViewMembers now accepts MANAGE_MEMBERS scope, expanding view-members permission

In GroupPermissions.canViewMembers (line 330-341), the V1 implementation was changed from `hasPermission(group, VIEW_MEMBERS_SCOPE)` to `hasPermission(group, VIEW_MEMBERS_SCOPE, MANAGE_MEMBERS_SCOPE)`.
