getGroupIdsWithViewPermission does not check root.users().canManage() — manage-only admins get restricted

In GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (line 106-107), the guard is `if (root.users().canView()) return Collections.emptySet();`. UserPermissions.canView() (inherited by UserPermissionsV2) returns true if the admin has MANAGE_USERS or VIEW_USERS role, or has VIEW/MANAGE permission on the Users resource. An admin with only the manage-users role has canView() true (since canView checks MANAGE_USERS), so they get an empty set — correct. But an admin with fine-grained MANAGE permission on the Users resource type (but not VIEW) — UserPermissions.canView() checks `hasPermission(MgmtPermissions.VIEW_SCOPE, MgmtPermissions.MANAGE_SCOPE)` which accepts MANAGE as sufficient for view, so canView() returns true. So manage-only fine-grained admins also get empty set. The V1 removed method getGroupsWithViewPermission() had `if (root.users().canView() || root.users().canManage()) return Collections.emptySet();` — the canManage() check was redundant since canView() includes manage. So no functional difference. However, the V2 override does not check `root.users().canManage()` separately; if a future change makes canView() not include manage, this would break. Not a current bug. Retracting.

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission guard checks root.users().canView() but should also check canManage() for admins with manage-only fine-grained permission

In GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (line 107), the guard is `if (root.users().canView()) return Collections.emptySet();`. UserPermissions.canView() (inherited by UserPermissionsV2) returns true if the admin has MANAGE_USERS or VIEW_USERS role, OR has VIEW/MANAGE permission on the Users resource (V1-style check using MgmtPermissions.VIEW_SCOPE/MANAGE_SCOPE on the 'Users' resource). In V2, an admin with fine-grained MANAGE permission on the Users resource type would have canView() return true (since canView accepts MANAGE scope). So manage-only fine-grained admins get an empty set — correct. But what about an admin with fine-grained MANAGE on the Users resource type but the V1 'Users' resource doesn't exist (V2 uses a different resource)? UserPermissions.canView() calls hasPermission(MgmtPermissions.VIEW_SCOPE, MgmtPermissions.MANAGE_SCOPE) which looks up `resourceStore.findByName(server, USERS_RESOURCE)` where USERS_RESOURCE = "Users". In V2, the resource-type resource is also named "Users" (USERS_RESOURCE_TYPE = "Users"), so findByName would find the V2 resource-type resource. The scopes 'view' and 'manage' exist in the V2 schema. So canView() would evaluate V2 permissions using V1 code — this cross-wiring works by accident because the resource name and scope names match. But it's fragile. The guard should ideally use the V2-aware canView() (which UserPermissionsV2 inherits from UserPermissions, not overridden). Actually UserPermissionsV2 does NOT override canView() (the no-arg version) — it only overrides canView(UserModel). So root.users().canView() in V2 uses the V1 implementation, which checks admin roles and then V1-style hasPermission on the 'Users' resource. This works by accident as described. Not a bug per se, but fragile.

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns empty set for admins with global view, but the method is also used to set grantIfNoPermission — coupling creates fragile security logic

The getGroupIdsWithViewPermission method serves two purposes: (1) filtering users by group membership in user search, and (2) indirectly controlling the grantIfNoPermission flag in UsersResource.toRepresentation (line 459: `usersEvaluator.grantIfNoPermission(session.getAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS) != null)`). When the method returns an empty set (admin has global view), the GROUPS attribute is not set, and grantIfNoPermission remains false. When it returns a non-empty set (admin has group-restricted view), the attribute is set, and grantIfNoPermission becomes true. This coupling means that any bug in getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (e.g. returning resource ids instead of group ids, or returning non-empty for admins with global view) directly affects the grantIfNoPermission security flag. The method's contract should be clearly documented, and the coupling should be made explicit or refactored to avoid fragile security logic.

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission uses findByType but per-group resources have no type set — method returns wrong results

GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (line 121) calls `resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...)`. As established in the AdminPermissionsSchema finding, per-group resources created by getOrCreateResource do NOT have their type set (only resource-type resources have type set in init()). Therefore findByType(server, "Groups") will only match the 'Groups' resource-type resource (the all-groups resource), not individual group resources. The method will return the resource id of the all-groups resource (if it has view-members permission) instead of the ids of individual groups. This breaks the user search filtering for group-restricted admins. The fix requires both: (1) getOrCreateResource must set the resource type on per-object resources, and (2) getGroupIdsWithViewPermission must extract the group id from the resource name (not the resource id).

getOrCreateResource does not set resource type on per-object resources, preventing type-based lookups

In AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource (lines 92-131), when a new resource is created for a specific object (group, user, client), the code does `resource = resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, resourceServer.getClientId())` (line 121) and then `resource.updateScopes(...)` (line 123), but never calls `resource.setType(resourceType)`. The resource-type resources created in init() do set the type (line 274: `resource.setType(type)`). Per-object resources have no type set. This means that `resourceStore.findByType(server, "Groups", ...)` (used in GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission line 121) will NOT find per-group resources, because they have no type. Wait — GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission uses `resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...)` which searches for resources of type "Groups". But per-group resources created by getOrCreateResource do NOT have type "Groups" set — they have no type at all. So findByType would only find the resource-type resource (the 'Groups' all-groups resource), not individual group resources. This means getGroupIdsWithViewPermission would only ever return the resource id of the all-groups resource (if it has view-members permission), not individual group ids. This is a critical bug: the method is supposed to return ids of groups with view permission, but it will only find the all-groups resource (if it has the right type) and return its id. Actually, looking at init() line 271-276, the resource-type resources are created with `resource.setType(type)` where type is the resource type name (e.g. "Groups"). So findByType(server, "Groups") finds the all-groups resource. Per-group resources have no type, so they are not found. Therefore getGroupIdsWithViewPermission only returns the all-groups resource id (if it has view-members permission), which is wrong — it should return individual group ids. The fix: getOrCreateResource should set the resource type on per-object resources (e.g. `resource.setType(resourceType)` after creation), so that findByType can find them.

getOrCreateResource throws IllegalStateException for unknown resource types instead of returning null

In AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource (lines 92-131), the switch on resourceType now throws IllegalStateException for unknown types (line 111: `default -> throw new IllegalStateException("Resource type [" + resourceType + "] not found.")`). The old code set name = null for unknown types and then threw IllegalStateException at line 115 with a more descriptive message including the id. The new behavior throws earlier with a less informative message and, more importantly, changes the exception path: callers that previously received an IllegalStateException with the id context now receive one without it. Also, if resourceType is null, the switch will throw a NullPointerException (switch on null). The old code handled null resourceType by falling through to name = null and then the IllegalStateException. A null check on resourceType should be added before the switch.

getResourceName only handles USERS resource type, not GROUPS or CLIENTS

In AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceName (lines 328-350), when supportsAuthorizationSchema is true, the method only handles the USERS resource type (line 334: `if (USERS.getType().equals(resourceType))`). For GROUPS and CLIENTS resource types, it falls through to `return resource.getDisplayName();` (line 349). For group resources, the resource name is the group id (per resolveGroup), and getDisplayName() would return null or the name depending on the resource implementation. This means that in the admin UI or any consumer of getResourceName, group resources would display as null or empty instead of the group name. The method should be extended to resolve group names (similar to resolveUser which looks up the user and returns the username) and client names. This is a functional gap for the new Groups resource type: the display name resolution is incomplete. Low severity because it affects display only, but it is a missing feature for the newly added Groups resource type.

getScope throws NullPointerException when resourceType is not in the schema

In AdminPermissionsSchema.getScope (lines 229-244), when supportsAuthorizationSchema is true, the code does `SCHEMA.getResourceTypes().get(resourceType).getScopes()` without checking that `getResourceTypes().get(resourceType)` is non-null. If a caller passes a resourceType that is not one of 'Clients', 'Groups', 'Users' (e.g. a legacy resource type or a typo), getResourceTypes().get(resourceType) returns null and .getScopes() throws NullPointerException. The method is called during policy/scope validation; a null resourceType or an unsupported type would cause a 500 error instead of a ModelValidationException. A null check with a proper ModelValidationException should be added, similar to throwExceptionIfResourceTypeOrScopesNotProvided which does validate the resource type.

grantIfNoPermission is set based on session attribute that may be set by group filtering, changing permission semantics

In UsersResource.toRepresentation (line 456-468), `usersEvaluator.grantIfNoPermission(session.getAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS) != null)` sets the grantIfNoPermission flag on the UserPermissionEvaluator based on whether the GROUPS session attribute was set. The GROUPS attribute is set in searchForUser (line 448-451) whenever `auth.groups().getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` returns a non-empty set. Previously, this attribute was only set when `!auth.users().canView()` — i.e., when the admin did NOT have global view permission. Now it is set unconditionally (whenever the group-ids set is non-empty). In UserPermissions.hasPermission (line 490-521), when the Users resource does not exist (`resource == null`), the method returns `grantIfNoPermission && expectedScopes.contains(MANAGE_SCOPE) && expectedScopes.contains(VIEW_SCOPE)`. This means: if the admin has no global view (so the group filter was applied) AND the Users resource doesn't exist, the admin is granted both manage and view on all users returned by the filtered search. This is the intended behavior for group-restricted admins. But now, with the unconditional setting, an admin who HAS global view (canView() true) but for whom getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns a non-empty set (which should not happen given the guards, but could happen if the V2 implementation returns resource ids instead of group ids — see separate finding — or if there's a logic error) would have grantIfNoPermission set to true. Then, if the Users resource doesn't exist, hasPermission would grant manage+view even though the admin already has global view — no escalation. The real risk: an admin with NO global view and NO group permissions — getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns empty set, attribute not set, grantIfNoPermission false — correct. An admin with group view permissions — attribute set, grantIfNoPermission true — if Users resource doesn't exist, they get manage+view on users in their groups — this is the intended design (group-restricted admins can manage users in their groups). The change from conditional to unconditional setting only matters if getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns non-empty for an admin with global view, which the guards prevent. So the practical impact is limited to the V2 resource-id bug. Medium severity because it's a fragile coupling: the grantIfNoPermission flag is a security-sensitive toggle that depends on a session attribute set by a different subsystem.

groups() method returns GroupPermissionsV2 but the field type and superclass method signature use GroupPermissions

In MgmtPermissionsV2.groups() (lines 58-62), the method returns `GroupPermissions` (the superclass method signature in MgmtPermissions presumably returns GroupPermissions). The field `groupPermissions` is typed as `GroupPermissionsV2` (line 27). The method creates `new GroupPermissionsV2(session, authz, this)` and returns it as GroupPermissions. This is fine for polymorphism. However, the superclass MgmtPermissions.groups() likely returns a GroupPermissions instance (V1). The override correctly returns a V2 instance. No bug. The constructor of GroupPermissionsV2 takes (KeycloakSession, AuthorizationProvider, MgmtPermissions) — the `authz` field in MgmtPermissions must be accessible (protected). No issue.

handleCreatedResponse now closes the response, which is a contract change for callers that manage the response themselves

ApiUtil.handleCreatedResponse was changed to use try-with-resources on the Response (line 9: `try (response)`), which closes the response before returning. Previously, the method called `response.close()` explicitly at the end (old code line 12: `response.close();`), so the behavior is the same — the response was always closed. The change is purely a refactoring to use try-with-resources. However, callers that pass a response they intend to use after calling handleCreatedResponse (e.g. reading the status again or using the response object) would now get an already-closed response. Looking at the test usages, some callers wrap the response in try-with-resources and then call handleCreatedResponse (double close, harmless), and some call handleCreatedResponse directly (correct). The contract is unchanged (response was always closed), but the method name 'handleCreatedResponse' does not imply it closes the response; a caller might not expect the side effect. This is a minor API design concern, not a bug.

hasPermission does not verify that the resource found by name is actually a user resource (type check missing)

Same issue as GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission: UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission (line 105) uses `resourceStore.findByName(server, user.getId())` without type verification. If a group or client resource has the same name as a user id, the wrong resource would be used. Defense-in-depth gap; the fix is to set resource types on per-object resources and use type-aware lookups.

hasPermission fallback to all-groups resource applies even when a specific group resource exists but has no policies

In GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission (lines 130-165), the logic is: look up resource by groupId; if not found, fall back to all-groups resource. But if the resource IS found (a per-group resource exists), the code proceeds directly to evaluate permissions on that resource (line 152). It does NOT fall back to the all-groups resource if the per-group resource has no policies granting the requested scopes. This means: if an admin has a permission on the all-groups resource (e.g. VIEW on Groups resource type) AND a per-group resource exists for a specific group (created when a permission was defined for that group), the per-group resource is evaluated. If the per-group resource has no policies granting VIEW, the evaluation returns no permissions, and hasPermission returns false — even though the all-groups permission should grant view. This is a semantic question: in V2, should a per-group resource's existence override the all-groups permission? The current implementation says yes (per-group resource takes precedence, no fallback). This could be intended (per-group permissions override resource-type permissions) or a bug (resource-type permissions should apply unless explicitly overridden). The interface documentation and V2 design suggest that resource-type permissions apply to all objects of that type, and per-object permissions are additional. The current implementation makes per-object resources act as a complete override — if a per-group resource exists, the all-groups permission is ignored for that group. This could lead to unexpected denials: an admin with VIEW on all groups creates a per-group permission for a specific group (e.g. MANAGE for a different admin), and suddenly the first admin loses VIEW on that group because the per-group resource exists but doesn't grant VIEW. This is a design decision that should be documented; if unintended, the fallback should also apply when the per-group resource evaluation yields no matching scopes.

hasPermission fallback to all-users resource applies even when a specific user resource exists but has no matching policies

Same pattern as GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission: in UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission (lines 94-133), if a per-user resource exists (found by findByName), the code evaluates permissions on that resource only (line 116-118). It does NOT fall back to the all-users resource if the per-user resource evaluation yields no matching scopes. This means a per-user resource acts as a complete override of the all-users permission. If an admin has VIEW on all users (Users resource type) and a per-user resource exists for a specific user (created when a permission was defined for that user), the admin's VIEW permission on all users is ignored for that user — the evaluation only considers the per-user resource. If the per-user resource has no VIEW-granting policy, the admin cannot view that user, despite having VIEW on all users. This is likely unintended: resource-type permissions should apply to all objects unless explicitly overridden by a deny. The current implementation makes any per-object resource a complete override. This could cause unexpected permission denials.

hasPermission falls back to all-users resource for any user id without verifying the resource belongs to a user

In UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission(UserModel user, ...) (lines 94-133), when `resourceStore.findByName(server, user.getId())` returns null, the code falls back to the 'Users' resource-type resource and evaluates it. The guard `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource).isEmpty()` only checks that some policy exists on the all-users resource. This is the intended fallback for users without a dedicated resource, and user.getId() is used as the resource name consistently with AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveUser. However, the same pattern as in GroupPermissionsV2 applies: the fallback is applied unconditionally for any user whose resource is missing, which is correct, but the method also accepts `user == null` to explicitly query the all-users resource. The risk is that `canView(UserModel)`/`canManage(UserModel)` etc. are called with a user whose id happens to collide with a resource name of a different type (e.g. a group id or client id, since resource names are not namespaced per type in the store lookup — findByName searches by name only). If a group resource was created with name equal to some user's id (unlikely but possible since group ids and user ids are both UUIDs from the same id space in some stores), findByName would return the group resource and permissions would be evaluated against the wrong resource type. The V2 schema does set resource.setType(type) for resource-type resources but per-object resources created via getOrCreateResource do not set a type, so findByName cannot disambiguate. This is a defense-in-depth concern; the practical impact is low because ids are UUIDs. Reporting as medium because the fallback logic in both UserPermissionsV2 and GroupPermissionsV2 relies solely on name equality without type verification.

hasPermission resource lookup by user id uses findByName without type verification, and fallback to all-users resource may grant unintended access

In UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission (lines 94-133), `resourceStore.findByName(server, user.getId())` looks up a resource by name (the user id). Per-user resources in V2 are created with the user id as the name (AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveUser returns user.getId()). The lookup does not verify the resource type. If a resource with the same name exists for a different type (group or client), the wrong resource would be used. Additionally, the fallback to the all-users resource (line 109) is applied whenever the specific user resource is not found. This means an admin with a permission on the Users resource type (all users) is granted that permission for ANY user, even users for which a more restrictive per-user permission might be intended. This is the intended V2 design (resource-type permissions apply to all objects of that type unless overridden by per-object permissions). However, the fallback only checks `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource).isEmpty()` — if there is ANY policy on the all-users resource, the evaluation proceeds. If that policy grants, say, VIEW, then the admin can view any user. This is correct. The issue is that the fallback does not consider per-user deny policies when falling back: if a user has a per-user resource with a deny policy, findByName would find it and the fallback would not be used — correct. registerListener feature check moved outside the listener registration, changing behavior when feature is disabled at runtime

In AdminPermissions.registerListener (lines 73-99), the `Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ)` check was moved from inside the listener's onEvent method to wrap the manager.register call. Previously, the listener was always registered but only acted when the feature was enabled (checked per-event). Now, the listener is only registered if the feature is enabled at registration time. Since Profile features are static at server startup, this is functionally equivalent in practice. However, if registerListener is called before the profile is fully initialized (unlikely), the check could evaluate incorrectly. More importantly, the V2 feature ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 also needs this listener (for cleaning up permissions when groups/users/roles are removed). The check only tests ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1). If V2 is enabled but V1 is disabled (possible if V2 is a separate feature flag), the listener would not be registered, and group/role/client removal events would not clean up V2 permissions, leaving orphaned resources and policies. The check should be `Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ) || Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2)` or simply check for V2 as well.

The listener cleans up permissions when roles, clients, or groups are removed (lines 78-95). When V2 (ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2) is enabled, permissions are stored in the admin permissions client's resource server using the V2 schema. If V2 is enabled but V1 is disabled (possible if V2 is a standalone feature flag), the listener would not be registered, and removing a group would leave orphaned resources and policies in the V2 admin permissions client. Even if V2 typically implies V1, the check should explicitly include V2: `Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ) || Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2)`. The listener's onEvent calls `management(cast.getKeycloakSession(), realm).groups().setPermissionsEnabled(cast.getGroup(), false)` — in V2, GroupPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException (line 173-175), so even if the listener is registered, it would throw when a group is removed in V2. The listener should either be updated to handle V2 (e.g. delete the group's resource and associated policies directly) or the V2 setPermissionsEnabled should be implemented.

setPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException, breaking group removal cleanup listener in V2

GroupPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled (lines 172-175) throws UnsupportedOperationException. This method is called by AdminPermissions.registerListener's onEvent when a GroupModel.GroupRemovedEvent occurs (AdminPermissions.java line 94: `management(cast.getKeycloakSession(), cast.getRealm()).groups().setPermissionsEnabled(cast.getGroup(), false)`). When V2 is enabled and a group is deleted, the listener fires and calls setPermissionsEnabled(false), which throws UnsupportedOperationException. This exception would propagate up through the event listener, potentially causing the group deletion to fail or leaving the transaction in an inconsistent state. In V2, group permissions are stored as resources and policies in the admin permissions client; when a group is deleted, the corresponding resource and its associated policies should be cleaned up. The V2 implementation should either implement setPermissionsEnabled to delete the group's resource and policies, or the listener should be updated to handle V2 cleanup differently (e.g. by directly deleting the resource via the resource store). This is a data integrity issue: orphaned resources and policies accumulate in the admin permissions client when groups are deleted in V2.

setPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException, but no user-removal listener exists — orphaned user resources in V2

UserPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled (lines 156-159) throws UnsupportedOperationException. Unlike groups and roles, there is no UserRemovedEvent listener in AdminPermissions.registerListener that calls users().setPermissionsEnabled. However, when a user is deleted in V2, the per-user resource (created lazily by getOrCreateResource when a permission is defined for that user) remains in the admin permissions client as an orphan. The V1 implementation had a listener for roles and clients but not users (users permissions were realm-wide in V1, not per-user). In V2, per-user resources exist, so user deletion should clean them up. The absence of a user-removal listener combined with the UnsupportedOperationException in V2 means orphaned user resources accumulate. This is a data integrity issue. A UserRemovedEvent listener should be added (similar to GroupRemovedEvent) that deletes the user's resource and associated policies from the admin permissions client.

If the same anchor tag (e.g., `<a href="https://example.com">`) appears multiple times in the translation, only the first occurrence is removed, but the loop continues with the next translation anchor. Additionally, `replaceFirst` removes the first occurrence in the entire value, which may not correspond to the anchor found by `matcher.find()` if there are earlier identical strings. English reference file path is computed with a fragile regex that breaks for locale suffixes containing digits or hyphens

The English bundle is located via `file.getAbsolutePath().replaceAll("resources-community", "resources").replaceAll("_[a-zA-Z-_]*\\.properties", "_en.properties")`. The character class `[a-zA-Z-_]` does not include digits, so locale suffixes such as `messages_zh_CN.properties` (contains digits) or `messages_pt_BR.properties` (underscore is fine, but `zh_CN` is not matched by `[a-zA-Z-_]*` because of the digits) will not be replaced correctly. For `messages_zh_CN.properties` the regex `_[a-zA-Z-_]*\.properties` will match only `_CN.properties` (since `zh` is followed by `_`, which is in the class, but the digits `3`... actually `zh_CN` contains no digits; however locales like `messages_zh_CN.properties` are fine, but `messages_es_419.properties` or any locale with digits such as `messages_ca_ES_VALENCIA` or future `messages_zh_Hans_CN` would fail). More concretely, any locale code containing a digit (e.g. `messages_zh_CN` is fine, but `messages_hi_IN` is fine; the real problem is locales like `messages_pt_BR` are fine, but `messages_zh_TW` is fine — the actual breakage is for locales with digits like `messages_es_419` or `messages_en_US_POSIX`). When the replacement fails, the code tries to open a non-existent `_en.properties` path (e.g. `messages_zh_CN_en.properties` or a partially replaced name), causing a `RuntimeException("unable to read file ...")` that aborts verification of the entire file. This means the HTML sanitizer check silently fails (throws) for any translation file whose locale suffix contains a digit, instead of reporting illegal HTML. The path computation should use a robust method such as `file.getName().replaceFirst("_[^_]+(\\.[^_]+)*\\.properties$", "_en.properties")` or better, derive the English file from the parent directory and a fixed base name.

Error message substring extraction can produce confusing output when start/end indices overlap or exceed string lengths

In the error reporting code (lines 101-111), the start and end indices are computed to strip common prefix/suffix, then `value.substring(start, value.length() - end)` and `sanitized.substring(start, sanitized.length() - end)` are used. If `start + end > value.length()` (which can happen if the strings are very different), `value.length() - end` could be less than `start`, causing a `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException`. For example, if `value = "abc"` and `sanitized = "xyz"`, start would be 0 (no common prefix), end would be 0 (no common suffix), so `value.substring(0, 3)` is fine. But if `value = "a"` and `sanitized = "b"`, start=0, end=0, fine. The dangerous case is when the strings share a long common prefix and suffix that overlap: e.g., `value = "aaa"` and `sanitized = "aa"`, start would advance to 2 (common prefix "aa"), end would advance to 1 (common suffix "a"), then `value.substring(2, 3-1=2)` → `substring(2,2)` → empty string, and `sanitized.substring(2, 2-1=1)` → `substring(2,1)` → `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException` because start > end. This would crash the verifier with an unhelpful exception instead of reporting the illegal HTML. The code should guard against `start + end > length` by clamping or using `Math.min`.

This means anchor tags are stripped from the value before the sanitizer runs, so the sanitizer never sees them and cannot validate their attributes (e.g., `href` values). However, the design intent seems to be that anchors should be allowed if they match the English source. As written, the verifier will report false positives for any translation that contains an anchor tag matching the English source, because the anchor is removed before sanitization but the sanitizer would have stripped it anyway — actually the anchor is removed, so the sanitized value won't contain it, and the comparison `!Objects.equals(sanitized, value)` will detect the removal as a difference, reporting "Illegal HTML" for a perfectly valid translation. Unconditional unescapeHtml4 on sanitized value can reintroduce HTML entities that were intentionally escaped in the source, causing false mismatches

After sanitization, the code does `sanitized = org.apache.commons.text.StringEscapeUtils.unescapeHtml4(sanitized)` (line 95) to reverse the sanitizer's HTML entity escaping. However, the original value is also unescaped in `normalizeValue` (line 130). If the original message intentionally contains an HTML entity like `&` that should remain escaped in the output (e.g., to display a literal `&`), the sanitizer will escape it to `&amp;`, then `unescapeHtml4` will convert it back to `&`, which matches the normalized original. But if the original contains a literal `&` (i.e., the text "&" as displayed), the sanitizer escapes the `&` to `&amp;`, and unescapeHtml4 converts it to `&`, which matches. The issue is that `unescapeHtml4` is applied unconditionally, which can mask actual differences: if the sanitizer escapes a `<` to `<`, unescapeHtml4 converts it back to `<`, making the sanitized value appear unchanged even though the sanitizer altered it. This defeats the purpose of detecting illegal HTML: a translation containing `<script>` would be sanitized to `<script>`, then unescaped back to `<script>`, and the comparison `!Objects.equals(sanitized, value)` would see no difference, so the illegal HTML would NOT be reported. This is a critical flaw: the unescape step completely undermines the sanitizer's detection of disallowed tags. The comment says "Sanitizer will escape HTML entities for quotes and also for numeric tags like '<1>'", but the unescape reverses ALL entity escaping, including for `<` and `>`, making the check ineffective for detecting stripped tags.

normalizeValue choice-format replacement regex does not handle nested braces in choice patterns

The regex `[^}]*` stops at the first `}`, but choice formats can contain nested braces (e.g., `{0,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}` has no nested braces, but more complex patterns like `{0,choice,0#{1,choice,1#one|1<many}}` would break). For the current messages, this works, but it is fragile. A more robust approach would be to use a proper MessageFormat parser or a balanced-brace matcher.

normalizeValue special-case for templateHelp uses regex that only matches uppercase letters, missing lowercase claim names

In `normalizeValue`, for the key `templateHelp`, the code does `value.replaceAll("CLAIM\\.<[A-Z]*>", "")`. This regex only matches `CLAIM.<NAME>` where NAME consists solely of uppercase letters. If the actual message contains a claim name with lowercase letters (e.g., `CLAIM.<sub>` or `CLAIM.<email>`), the regex will not match, and the `<sub>` will be treated as an HTML tag by the sanitizer, causing a false "Illegal HTML" report. The regex should be `CLAIM\\.<[A-Za-z0-9_]*>` or similar to match typical claim names.

verify() method catches IOException from Files.readString but verifySafeHtml throws RuntimeException for IO errors, which is not caught and propagates as unchecked exception

The `verify()` method (line 46) wraps `Files.readString` and `verifyNoDuplicateKeys` in a try-catch for `IOException`, throwing `MojoExecutionException`. However, `verifySafeHtml()` (called at line 51) catches `IOException` internally and throws `RuntimeException` (lines 70, 79). This `RuntimeException` is not caught by the `verify()` method's catch block (which only catches `IOException`), so it propagates as an unchecked exception. In a Maven plugin context, an uncaught `RuntimeException` will cause the build to fail with a stack trace rather than a clean `MojoExecutionException` message. The `verifySafeHtml` method should either declare `throws MojoExecutionException` and throw that, or the `verify()` method should catch `RuntimeException` as well. This inconsistency in error handling makes the plugin's error reporting inconsistent.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Wrong null-check argument in constructor

In the AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth null check is `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")` — it checks `grantType` again instead of `rawTokenId`. As a result, a null `rawTokenId` is not rejected and is stored in the field, while the error message is misleading. A null rawTokenId would later produce a malformed encoded token id (e.g. `onrtac:null`) or an NPE during encoding/concatenation.

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isAccessTokenId matcher has inverted grant-shortcut comparison, making the new assertions always fail

In the new isAccessTokenId(String expectedGrantShortcut) matcher, the check is `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` — it returns false (no match) precisely when the grant shortcut DOES equal the expected value, and falls through to the UUID check otherwise. The condition is inverted; it should be `if (!items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`. Additionally, the substring indices are wrong: the prefix is 6 characters (2 session + 2 token + 2 grant), so the grant shortcut occupies characters at index 4–5, i.e. `substring(4, 6)`, not `substring(3, 5)` (the comment even says 'starts at character 4th char' — off-by-one in the code). As written, every expectCodeToToken/expectRefresh/expectDeviceCodeToToken/expectAuthReqIdToToken event assertion using this matcher will fail (or pass only accidentally), breaking the integration tests that were updated to use it.

Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.

false_positives.candidate:
Decoding a token id containing a colon in the raw id mis-parses the context

getTokenContextFromTokenId() uses `encodedTokenId.indexOf(':')` to split prefix from raw id. If the raw id itself contains a ':' (KeycloakModelUtils.generateId() produces UUIDs today, but the SPI contract allows custom encoders/providers and the raw id is opaque), the first colon is found correctly only if the prefix contains no colon — which holds for the default encoder. However, the bigger issue: any legacy or foreign token id that happens to contain a colon (e.g. `foo:bar`) is treated as an encoded id; `encodedContext.length() != 6` then throws IllegalArgumentException. Throwing on arbitrary token ids means any code path that decodes a token id (introspection, userInfo, admin API) will throw an unhandled exception for malformed/legacy ids that contain a colon but are not 6-char-prefixed, instead of degrading to UNKNOWN as the no-colon branch does. This is an inconsistent and fragile contract: ids without ':' are tolerated, ids with ':' but wrong prefix length crash the request.

Duplicate-shortcut validation compares map sizes, which does not detect collisions

postInit() validates uniqueness of grant shortcuts by checking `grantsByShortcuts.size() != grantsToShortcuts.size()`. This is incorrect: if two different grant types share the same shortcut, `grantsByShortcuts.put(shortcut, grantName)` overwrites one entry (size stays smaller) while `grantsToShortcuts` gains two entries — sizes differ, so it is caught. But if two different grant types share the same ID (impossible via getId contract) or, more realistically, if a shortcut collides AND a grant name collides in a compensating way, sizes can be equal while mappings are wrong. More importantly, the check cannot detect the case where one grant's shortcut equals another grant's shortcut AND the overwritten entry coincidentally keeps sizes equal (e.g. duplicate shortcut plus duplicate id). The robust check is to detect size shrinkage during insertion (compare size before/after each put) or explicitly check `grantsByShortcuts.containsKey(shortcut)` before putting. As written, the safety net the comment claims ('Validation if there are not duplicated shortcuts') is unreliable.

Encoded token id is generated in initToken but other token-creation paths may bypass it

The encoding is applied only in TokenManager.initToken(). Any other code path that creates an AccessToken and sets its id directly (e.g. `token.id(KeycloakModelUtils.generateId())` elsewhere in TokenManager or in other services such as TokenExchangeProvider variants, service-account flows, admin impersonation, or the OIDC 'token' endpoint response building for ID-token-as-access-token in StandardTokenExchangeProvider where an IDToken is reused) will produce access tokens whose jti has no context prefix. Consumers relying on the prefix (the stated purpose: introspection/userInfo optimization, session-type lookup) will see a mix of prefixed and unprefixed ids and must handle both — the PR description claims the encoding is 'used only for access-tokens', but in practice only for access tokens created through initToken. If full coverage is intended, all AccessToken.id() assignments for access tokens must go through the encoder; if not, the fallback behavior for unprefixed ids must be documented and handled by consumers.

GRANT_TYPE attribute set on a DefaultClientSessionContext wrapper may not propagate to the persisted client session

In PreAuthorizedCodeGrantType.process(), the grant type is set via `sessionContext.setAttribute(Constants.GRANT_TYPE, ...)` where sessionContext is a `DefaultClientSessionContext` created by `DefaultClientSessionContext.fromClientSessionAndScopeParameter(...)`. Whether this attribute is visible later when TokenManager.initToken() reads it via the ClientSessionContext passed to createClientAccessToken depends on DefaultClientSessionContext.setAttribute delegating to the underlying AuthenticatedClientSessionModel notes. If DefaultClientSessionContext.setAttribute only writes to an in-memory map that is not the same instance passed to createClientAccessToken (a different wrapper is created inside TokenManager), the grant type will be lost and the token encoded with 'na'. This path should be verified with an integration test; the unit test does not cover it.

Grant maps are package-private mutable fields, exposing internal state

grantsByShortcuts and grantsToShortcuts are declared without an access modifier (package-private) and are non-final mutable fields on the factory. The unit test relies on this to inject state directly. Exposing mutable internal maps package-wide invites accidental external mutation and makes the class harder to reason about; they should be private with the test using the real postInit() path (or a package-private test hook that is clearly intended for tests).

Grant type read from client session context is not the grant type that created the token

getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext() reads the grant type from `clientSessionContext.getAttribute(Constants.GRANT_TYPE)`. However, this attribute is set on the client session context at token-creation time (e.g. in OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse, ResourceOwnerPasswordCredentialsGrantType, StandardTokenExchangeProvider) and, critically, in TokenManager.refreshToken() the attribute is overwritten with `OAuth2Constants.REFRESH_TOKEN` before creating the new access token. More importantly, the attribute persists on the client session across multiple token issuances: a client session created by an authorization-code grant keeps GRANT_TYPE=authorization_code, so a later access token issued via the refresh-token grant on the same client session would be encoded with the stale original grant type unless every issuance path overwrites it. Any token-creation path that does not set this attribute (e.g. service-account/client-credentials flows that build the ClientSessionContext differently, admin-initiated impersonation, or token creation via TokenManager.createClientAccessToken from other callers) will silently encode the wrong grant type or 'na'. The encoded grant type therefore cannot be trusted as 'the grant type used to create this token' without auditing every caller of createClientAccessToken/initToken.

Lazy refresh of grant maps is not atomic and can permanently cache a wrong mapping

getShortcutByGrantType() and getGrantTypeByShortcut() lazily populate the ConcurrentHashMaps when a grant type deployed after startup is encountered. The check-then-act sequence (`get` returning null, then lookup in sessionFactory, then `put`) is not atomic: two threads can both miss and both put, which is benign for identical values. However, if a custom OAuth2GrantTypeFactory is deployed whose shortcut collides with an existing one, the lazy path silently overwrites the existing mapping (grantsByShortcuts.put(shortcut, grantType)), permanently corrupting the shortcut→grant resolution for previously valid tokens — a token id encoded with the old mapping will now decode to the wrong grant type. The startup validation in postInit() is bypassed entirely by this lazy path.

New abstract method getShortcut() on OAuth2GrantTypeFactory breaks all existing third-party grant type factories

The PR adds `String getShortcut();` as a non-default method to the public SPI interface OAuth2GrantTypeFactory. Every existing custom implementation of this SPI (external extensions, downstream products) will fail to compile and, if already compiled, will throw AbstractMethodError at runtime when DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit() iterates all OAuth2GrantType factories and calls getShortcut(). This is a hard backward-incompatibility in a public SPI. The method should be declared `default` (e.g. returning null or a derived value) with a documented requirement to override, so existing factories keep working and unknown shortcuts degrade to the 'na'/UNKNOWN path.

Refresh grant overwrites the client session GRANT_TYPE attribute, mutating session state visible to other flows

In refreshToken(), `clientSessionCtx.setAttribute(Constants.GRANT_TYPE, OAuth2Constants.REFRESH_TOKEN)` overwrites the grant type stored on the (persistent) client session context. The original grant type that created the session (e.g. authorization_code) is lost from the session context. Any other consumer reading this attribute later (current or future) will see 'refresh_token' as the session's grant type, which misrepresents the session's origin. If the attribute is meant to record 'the grant type of the most recent token issuance', that should be documented; if it is meant to record the session's originating grant, overwriting it is a data-integrity bug.

Removal of the Context copy constructor is a breaking API change for custom OAuth2GrantType implementations

The PR deletes the public copy constructor `Context(Context context)` from OAuth2GrantType.Context. This is a public class in server-spi-private, and third-party/custom grant type providers (the SPI is designed for extension — the PR itself advertises 'provider adds ability for someone to introduce his own provider') may use this copy constructor to wrap/delegate contexts (a common pattern for decorating grant processing). Removing a public constructor without deprecation is a binary- and source-incompatible break for any external implementation. If the copy constructor is no longer needed internally, it should be deprecated first, not removed in the same change.

Session type detection calls getUserSession() which can be null for client-credentials/service-account sessions

getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext() unconditionally calls `clientSessionContext.getClientSession().getUserSession()` and then dereferences the result (`userSession.getPersistenceState()`). For client-credentials grants and service-account flows there is no user session (the client session is not attached to a user session), so getUserSession() can return null, causing an NPE during access-token creation for client-credentials — one of the most common grant types. The PR's own example (`trltcc:...` for a transient lightweight client-credentials token) implies client-credentials tokens are expected to be encoded, so this path must handle a null user session (e.g. defaulting to TRANSIENT).

Token type (lightweight vs regular) is derived from the current session/client state, not from the token being created

getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext() determines TokenType via `AbstractOIDCProtocolMapper.getShouldUseLightweightToken(session)`, which reads `session.getAttribute(Constants.USE_LIGHTWEIGHT_ACCESS_TOKEN_ENABLED)` and the client attribute. The session attribute is set by token-exchange code paths (e.g. lightweight token exchange) and may be set or cleared at arbitrary points during request processing. If the session attribute is set after initToken() runs, or if a token is created in a context where the session attribute reflects a different decision than the one actually applied to the token (TokenManager decides lightweight-ness in formatTokenType/applyMapper based on the same helper, but the two calls are not atomic), the encoded token-type shortcut can disagree with the actual token type. The PR's stated goal — 'recognize more reliably if access-token is lightweight or not' — is undermined if the encoded value can be wrong; consumers using the prefix to decide whether to trust in-token roles would make incorrect authorization decisions.

UNKNOWN constant value 'na' collides conceptually with the 'unknown' session/token shortcuts 'un' but is a grant-only sentinel mixed into the same namespace

The grant-type sentinel UNKNOWN = "na" is registered in the same shortcut maps as real grant shortcuts (grantsByShortcuts/grantsToShortcuts in the factory). A custom grant type factory could legitimately choose the shortcut "na", which would then be indistinguishable from 'unknown grant type' when decoding. The factory's duplicate-detection would not catch this because "na" is pre-registered after the loop, silently overwriting (or being overwritten by) a real grant. Reserving the sentinel namespace (e.g. validating that no grant shortcut equals "na" at startup) would prevent this ambiguity.

Unit test bypasses factory.postInit and hand-builds internal maps, so it does not test the real wiring

The test's @Before constructs DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory, calls init(null), then directly assigns the package-private fields grantsByShortcuts/grantsToShortcuts with a hand-built HashMap, bypassing postInit() entirely. This means the test never exercises the real population logic (iteration over OAuth2GrantType factories, duplicate-shortcut validation, UNKNOWN registration) and would not catch regressions in postInit(). It also means the test depends on package-private field access, making it brittle. A test that drives the factory through postInit with a real/mock KeycloakSessionFactory would cover the actual production path.

grantType captured in constructor can be stale when formParams are replaced via setFormParams

The constructor now eagerly captures `this.grantType = formParams.getFirst(OAuth2Constants.GRANT_TYPE)`, but the class still exposes `setFormParams(MultivaluedHashMap)` which replaces the formParams reference. Any caller that constructs the Context and then calls setFormParams() with different parameters (e.g. a wrapper that normalizes or replaces form params) will leave `grantType` holding the old value while `getFormParams()` returns the new ones — an inconsistent state. Either derive grantType lazily in getGrantType() from the current formParams, or update grantType inside setFormParams().

true_positives.golden_comment: Unsafe raw List deserialization without type safety. Calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent() can lead to a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Optional.get() without isPresent() check will throw NoSuchElementException when no recovery credential exists

The constructor calls RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) and immediately invokes credentialModelOpt.get() without checking isPresent(). Previously the code used getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream(...).findFirst().get() which had the same latent issue, but now that getCredential() explicitly returns an Optional that can legitimately be empty (federated lookup first, then local), any code path that renders the recovery-code input page for a user without a recovery credential (e.g., a race where the credential was removed, a misconfigured flow, or a user whose credential exists only in a storage provider that doesn't implement getCredentials) will throw NoSuchElementException and produce a 500 error instead of a graceful challenge. The bean should handle the empty case (e.g., throw a meaningful error, disable the input, or fall back), and ideally the template should not render the code-number prompt when no credential exists.

false_negatives.golden_comment: After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.

false_positives.candidate:
Recovery codes credential stored in user storage loses userLabel and used-code state

In updateCredential(), the recovery-codes branch builds a CredentialModel with only id, type, credentialData (the raw JSON list), and createdDate. It never sets userLabel, and it stores the list of codes as-is, so there is no per-code 'used' flag persisted. getCredentials() later reconstructs the model via RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(codes, createdDate, userLabel), which marks all codes as unused. This means a code that was already consumed during login remains valid in user storage: the federated isValid() will keep accepting a used recovery code, allowing unlimited reuse of a single recovery code. The provider must persist and honor the used/unused state (e.g., store the full RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel JSON including per-code used flags, and update it when a code is consumed), otherwise the one-time-use guarantee of recovery codes is broken for federated users.

Recovery codes stored in user storage are saved as raw (unhashed) codes

In createRecoveryCodesCredential, the generatedCodes list is serialized directly into a UserCredentialModel and passed to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(recoveryCodesCredential). Unlike the local-storage path, where recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(realm, user, credentialModel) hashes each code (RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues hashes the raw codes), the user-storage path stores the raw codes verbatim in the federated credential's challengeResponse/credentialData. Any user-storage provider that persists this value (LDAP attribute, external database, etc.) will hold plaintext recovery codes, which are equivalent to passwords for account recovery. The consequence is that a compromise of the user-storage backend (or its backups/logs) directly yields usable recovery codes, defeating the purpose of hashing them in the local Keycloak DB. The fix is to hash the codes (e.g., via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode) before building the UserCredentialModel, matching what the local credential provider does.

Recovery-codes federation test does not verify one-time use of codes or removal/invalidation after all codes are consumed

testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only logs in once with recovery code index 0 and asserts success. It never attempts to reuse the same code (which must fail), never consumes all 12 codes to verify the credential is invalidated/removed and the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action is re-triggered, and never verifies that the used-code state is persisted in the user storage. Given that the production change is specifically about creating and validating recovery codes in user storage, the absence of these assertions leaves the core security property (codes are single-use and the credential lifecycle works for federated users) untested. The test should reuse a consumed code and assert failure, and ideally drive the flow until all codes are used.

Test user-storage provider validates recovery codes by comparing raw input against stored values without hashing

In isValid(), the recovery-codes branch deserializes the stored credential data and checks generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse())). Because CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential now sends the raw (unhashed) codes to user storage (see the related finding), this comparison only works because both sides are raw. If the production code is fixed to hash codes before storing them in user storage, this test provider will break; conversely, as written, this provider demonstrates and endorses storing plaintext recovery codes in federated storage. The validation should hash the input (RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode / verifyRecoveryCodeInput) and compare against the stored hashed values, consistent with the local Keycloak credential provider.

Used recovery code is removed by credential ID even when the credential lives in federated user storage

After a successful recovery-code login, the code calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId()) when all codes are used. RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential() now returns the federated credential first, and for a federated credential the ID is the one assigned by the user-storage provider (or a dummy id). removeStoredCredentialById only removes credentials from the local Keycloak DB; for a federated credential this either throws, silently no-ops, or removes nothing, so the consumed-codes state in user storage is never updated. The consequence is that once all codes are used, the federated credential is never invalidated/removed and the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action logic (which keys off allCodesUsed() on the federated model) may repeatedly trigger or, worse, the storage-side credential keeps accepting codes. The removal path must go through the credential manager's federated-aware removal (e.g., updateCredential with the consumed state, or removeStoredCredentialById only for local credentials), not blindly call removeStoredCredentialById with a federated ID.

disableCredentialType does not support removing recovery codes from user storage

disableCredentialType() only handles OTP types (setting myUser.otp = null) and logs 'Unsupported to disable credential of type' for everything else, including RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE. Since supportsCredentialType() now advertises recovery-codes support and isConfiguredFor() reports it, the account console/admin REST will list recovery codes as a disableable credential for federated users, but attempting to disable/remove it will silently do nothing (the credential remains in storage and the user can still log in with it). The method should handle RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE by setting myUser.recoveryCodes = null, and getDisableableCredentialTypesStream() should include the recovery-codes type when present.

getCredential prefers federated credential but ignores local credential when both exist

getCredential() returns the first federated recovery-codes credential if present, and only falls back to the local stored credential when no federated one exists. If a user has recovery codes in both the local Keycloak DB (e.g., created before the user was federated, or created by a code path that bypassed the storage check) and in user storage, the local credential is silently ignored: login validation via credentialManager().isValid() may still check both, but the post-login bookkeeping in RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator (allCodesUsed check and removal) and the code-number display in RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean operate only on the federated one. This can lead to inconsistent state where a stale local credential remains valid forever and is never cleaned up, or where the displayed 'next code number' does not match the credential actually being validated. The method should either return all matching credentials or document/enforce a single source of truth, and callers should handle the both-exist case (e.g., prefer local, or remove the stale one).

true_positives.golden_comment: Returning null from getSubGroupsCount() violates the GroupModel contract (Javadoc says it never returns null) and may lead to NPEs in callers that expect a non-null count.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getSubGroupsCount() silently returns null when the group has been deleted, changing the API contract

The fix for the NPE changes `getSubGroupsCount()` to return `null` when the underlying group no longer exists in the database (`model == null ? null : model.getSubGroupsCount()`). Previously it would throw an NPE (or IllegalStateException via other paths). `GroupModel.getSubGroupsCount()` is declared to return `Long` and callers such as `GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount()` (services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/utils/GroupUtils.java:90) pass the result directly to `GroupRepresentation.setSubGroupCount(Long)`, and admin REST representations expose this as a numeric subgroup count. Returning null here means a concurrently-deleted group now yields a representation with a null subGroupCount instead of a consistent value or an explicit error, which can produce NPEs in downstream consumers that unbox the Long (e.g. JSON serialization paths or UI code doing arithmetic/comparison on the count) and silently masks the fact that the group was deleted mid-request. The correct behavior for a group that disappeared concurrently is to treat it as invalidated/not-found (consistent with `isUpdated()` and `getDelegateForUpdate()` which throw `IllegalStateException("Not found in database")`), not to return null.

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Concurrency test has a race that can make it pass without ever exercising the concurrent read path

In `createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti`, the reader thread loops `while (!deletedAll.get())` calling `groups(null, 0, Integer.MAX_VALUE, true)`, but the main thread deletes all 100 groups and then sets `deletedAll.set(true)` (line 155) without joining the reader thread. If the deletes complete before the reader thread is scheduled (common on fast machines or under CI load), the reader thread may execute zero iterations, so the test asserts `caughtExceptions` is empty without ever having performed a concurrent read during deletion — a false pass that does not reproduce issue #40368. Additionally, the reader thread is never joined, so the assertion on line 157 can run while the reader is still mid-request, and any exception thrown after the assertion is silently lost (the thread dies with an uncaught exception). The test should `join()` the reader thread before asserting, and ideally ensure the reader has performed at least one iteration before starting deletes (e.g. a CountDownLatch or AtomicBoolean confirming first read completed) so the concurrent window is actually exercised.

false_positives.candidate:
Concurrency test only exercises brief group listing, not the getSubGroupsCount path that was actually fixed

The PR fixes an NPE in `GroupAdapter.getSubGroupsCount()` (model/infinispan/.../GroupAdapter.java:272-276), which is invoked when `subGroupsCount=true` is requested on group hierarchy population (see `GroupUtils.populateGroupHierarchyFromSubGroups` with `subGroupsCount` flag, services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/utils/GroupUtils.java:40-42). However, the new test `createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti` only calls `managedRealm.admin().groups().groups(null, 0, Integer.MAX_VALUE, true)` — the `true` here is `briefRepresentation`, not `subGroupsCount`. The admin client `groups()` overload with a `briefRepresentation` boolean does not request subgroup counts, so the fixed code path (`getSubGroupsCount()` on a cached group whose DB row was concurrently deleted) is never executed by this test. The test would not have caught the original NPE. It should either call the endpoint that populates subGroupCount (e.g. the groups search with `subGroupsCount` parameter used by the admin console hierarchy endpoint) or directly fetch a group representation with subGroupCount while deletes are in flight.

Removal of groupMatchesSearchOrIsPathElement leaves an unused import and a dangling comment

The diff deletes the private method `groupMatchesSearchOrIsPathElement` but the file still contains the comment `//From org.keycloak.admin.ui.rest.GroupsResource` on line 94 directly above `toRepresentation`, which referenced the removed code's origin, and the removal was not part of the NPE fix described in the PR. More importantly, the removed method referenced `org.keycloak.utils.StringUtil` (via `StringUtil.isBlank`); if that import existed it is now unused, and if any other code in the codebase called this private helper it would fail to compile — but since it was private, the real issue is that this unrelated deletion is bundled into a concurrency bugfix PR, making the change harder to review and revert. The deletion should either be moved to its own PR or, if kept, the dead comment on line 94 should be removed and the unused import (if present in the base version) cleaned up.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Inconsistent metrics tag key: 'shard' vs 'shards'

The `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` timer at line 199 uses `tags={"shards": shard_tag}` while the `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` timer at line 185 and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` at line 192 use `tags={"shard": shard_tag}`. This inconsistency breaks dashboards/alerts that group by a single tag key, and makes it impossible to join produce-time and wait-produce-time series per shard. One of the two keys is wrong; they should be unified (likely `shard`, matching the singular form used elsewhere and the per-shard `spans.buffer.flusher_unhealthy` metric at line 243).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same inconsistency between the 'shard' and 'shards' metric tag keys across the same specific metrics (`spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce`, `spans.buffer.flusher.produce`, and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes`) and notes the same impact on dashboards and alerts.

false_positives.candidate:
max_processes=0 silently disables all flusher processes

`self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` treats a falsy `max_processes` (0) the same as `None`, falling back to one process per shard. More importantly, the CLI option `--flusher-processes` in `src/sentry/consumers/__init__.py` (line 433) has `default=1` and no validation that it is >= 1, so an operator passing `--flusher-processes 0` (or a negative value) gets `num_processes = min(0, len(shards)) = 0`, an empty `process_to_shards_map`, zero spawned processes, and a flusher that never flushes anything — segments accumulate in Redis until the hard backpressure path rejects all messages. There is no guard rejecting non-positive values, and no test covers this case.

Shard-to-process assignment is not stable across rebalances, causing duplicate/missing flush ownership

`process_index = i % self.num_processes` assigns shards to processes by their position in `buffer.assigned_shards` (the iteration order of the `partitions` mapping passed to `create_with_partitions`). When the consumer rebalances and the set/order of assigned partitions changes, the same Redis shard can be mapped to a different process index, and — critically — the *old* SpanFlusher instance's processes are never terminated on rebalance: `close()` (line 322) explicitly does not shut down the flusher, and `create_with_partitions` creates a brand-new SpanFlusher with new processes while the old ones keep running (they are daemon processes, so they survive until the whole consumer exits). Two processes can then flush the same shard concurrently, racing on `flush_segments`/`done_flush_segments` in Redis and potentially producing duplicate segments to the buffered-segments topic or corrupting segment state. The old code had a single process per SpanFlusher instance with the same close() behavior, but with one process per shard the blast radius of a leaked flusher is much larger (N leaked processes per rebalance, each holding a Kafka producer).

Per-shard SpansBuffer instances in the parent process are never used for flushing and create a second set of Redis connections

In `_create_process_for_shards`, a new `SpansBuffer(shards)` is created in the parent process and stored in `self.buffers[process_index]` (line 125). This parent-side buffer is only used in `submit()` for `record_stored_segments()` (line 270) and `get_memory_info()` (line 301). However, the actual flushing is done by a *separately pickled* `shard_buffer` inside the child process (line 97-104), which maintains its own Redis client pool and its own internal segment bookkeeping. This means: (1) the parent's `record_stored_segments()` updates statistics on a buffer whose Redis state is not the one being flushed, so backpressure decisions based on `any_shard_at_limit` in the child (line 172) and memory info from the parent (line 301) may be inconsistent; (2) the parent now holds N extra SpansBuffer objects each with Redis connection pools, doubling Redis connection usage; (3) `record_stored_segments` on the parent buffer tracks segments that the child buffer flushes, so the parent's view of stored segments drifts from reality. The original design had a single shared buffer; the multiprocessed version needs the bookkeeping to live in exactly one place.

Thread-based test processes are never killable, and kill() is skipped for them in production restart path

In `_ensure_processes_alive`, the restart path calls `process.kill()` only `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` (line 254). When `produce_to_pipe` is set, processes are `threading.Thread` instances (line 108), which have no `kill()` — so a hung thread-based flusher is never stopped before `_create_process_for_shards` spawns a replacement (line 259), leaking the old thread. In production this branch is not hit (real processes are used), but the asymmetry means the health-check/restart logic is only half-implemented for the thread mode that tests rely on, and any future use of thread mode in production would leak hung threads indefinitely. Additionally, `threading.Thread` has no `exitcode` attribute, so `getattr(process, "exitcode", "unknown")` at line 229 always yields "unknown" for threads, degrading the `no_process_unknown` metric cause.

Dead code: _create_process_for_shard is never called

`_create_process_for_shard(self, shard: int)` (lines 127-132) is defined but never referenced anywhere in the file — `_ensure_processes_alive` restarts via `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` directly. It appears to be leftover from an earlier per-shard restart design. Dead code in a concurrency-critical class invites confusion about which restart path is authoritative.

Shard assignment uses modulo on list position, not on shard id — shard ownership changes when partition set changes

The mapping `process_index = i % self.num_processes` where `i` is the enumeration index of `buffer.assigned_shards` means shard ownership is a function of *which other shards are assigned*, not of the shard id itself. If the consumer is assigned partitions {0,1,2,3} with num_processes=2, shard 0→proc0, 1→proc1, 2→proc0, 3→proc1. After a rebalance to {1,2,3}, shard 1→proc0, 2→proc1, 3→proc0 — shard 1 moved from proc1 to proc0. Since each process has its own SpansBuffer with its own Redis segment state and its own Kafka producer, a shard changing owner means the new owner starts with an empty in-memory view of that shard's segments while the old owner may still hold unflushed state. Combined with the fact that old processes are not stopped on rebalance (see close() finding), this can cause the same shard's segments to be flushed by two different buffers concurrently, producing duplicate or interleaved segments in the buffered-segments topic. A stable hash of the shard id (e.g., `shard % num_processes`) would keep ownership stable across rebalances as long as num_processes is unchanged.

join() terminates processes without joining them, risking lost in-flight Kafka produces

In `join()` (lines 328-348), after waiting for each process to exit (or the deadline to expire), the code calls `process.terminate()` (line 347) if it is still alive. `terminate()` sends SIGTERM, which kills the child immediately — any spans already produced to the Kafka producer's internal buffer but not yet acked (the `producer_futures` at line 200 are only awaited inside the main loop) are lost, and any segments already popped from Redis by `flush_segments` but not yet `done_flush_segments`-ed (line 205) are lost from Redis without being written to Kafka. The original single-process code had the same terminate() call, but with N processes the window for losing in-flight data is N times larger. A graceful shutdown would close the producer (flushing pending futures) before terminating, or at least join with a short grace period before SIGTERM.

New multiprocessed flusher test only checks process count, not that shards are actually flushed by the right process

`test_flusher_processes_limit` asserts `len(flusher.processes) == 2` and that 4 shards are distributed across the map, but never submits any spans, never advances the drift, and never asserts that any message is produced. It would pass even if the flusher processes crashed immediately on startup (they are daemon threads in test mode). There is no test that verifies: (1) each shard's segments are flushed exactly once when multiple shards share a process; (2) the per-process backpressure/health values are independent; (3) restart logic works per-process; (4) the `max_processes` default (None → one process per shard) behaves correctly. The existing `test_basic` only covers a single shard, so the multi-shard sharing path — the core new behavior of this PR — is effectively untested for correctness.

Flaky synchronization in test_basic: fixed 0.1s sleep instead of polling for the expected message

The new lines 60-62 add `step.poll()` followed by a hardcoded `time.sleep(0.1)` to 'give flusher threads time to process after drift change'. The flusher thread loop sleeps 1 second between iterations when there is nothing to flush (line 182 of flusher.py, though monkeypatched to no-op in the test), but the thread scheduling is still non-deterministic — under CI load, 0.1s may not be enough for the thread to wake, flush, and append to `messages` before `step.join()` and the `(msg,) = messages` unpacking at line 66. A polling loop (e.g., wait up to N seconds for `len(messages) == 1`) would be robust. This is a classic source of flaky tests in multiprocessed/threaded code.

Main consumer buffer and flusher shard buffers can diverge: process_spans writes to one buffer, flusher reads from another

`create_with_partitions` creates `buffer = SpansBuffer(assigned_shards=[p.index for p in partitions])` (line 67) which is passed to `process_batch` (line 79/90) — this is the buffer that `process_spans` writes segments into. Separately, `SpanFlusher.__init__` creates its own per-process `SpansBuffer(shards)` instances (flusher.py line 93) that the child processes use to call `flush_segments`. These are different Python objects with different Redis client pools, but they point at the same Redis keys. The critical question is whether `SpansBuffer` keeps any in-memory state that must be shared between the writer (process_batch) and the flusher (child process). Looking at the original single-process design, the same `buffer` object was shared between `process_batch` and the flusher thread, so any in-memory segment index maintained by SpansBuffer was consistent. Now the flusher uses a fresh SpansBuffer that never saw the `process_spans` calls — if SpansBuffer maintains an in-memory registry of stored segments (e.g., for `record_stored_segments` or segment size tracking), the flusher's buffer will have no knowledge of segments written by the main buffer, potentially causing segments to never be flushed or to be flushed with incorrect metadata. This needs verification against SpansBuffer's implementation; if SpansBuffer is purely Redis-backed this is fine, but the parent-side `self.buffers` used for `record_stored_segments` (flusher.py line 270) suggests there is in-memory state that is now split across three sets of objects.

--flusher-processes CLI option lacks validation for non-positive values

The `--flusher-processes` click option (lines 432-437) accepts any integer with no `click.IntRange(min=1)` or callback validation. Passing 0 results in `num_processes = 0` (see flusher.py line 60: `min(0, len(shards))`), which creates zero flusher processes and silently stops all flushing — segments accumulate in Redis until backpressure rejects all incoming messages, effectively halting span ingestion with no error surfaced until the Redis memory limit is hit. A `click.IntRange(min=1)` would fail fast at startup with a clear error message.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.

Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

true_positives.golden_comment: In BaseDetectorTypeValidator.update(), the validator incorrectly updates instance.type using validated_data.get('detector_type') instead of validated_data.get('type').

update() reads validated_data["detector_type"] but the serializer field is named "type"
