false_positives.candidate:
integerToBytes truncates the most significant bytes when the value is larger than the target length

integerToBytes(BigInteger s, int qLength) handles the case qLength < bytes.length by copying the LAST qLength bytes (System.arraycopy(bytes, bytes.length - tmp.length, tmp, 0, tmp.length)). For an ECDSA r or s value, the magnitude can legitimately be up to qLength+1 bytes because BigInteger.toByteArray() prepends a 0x00 sign byte when the high bit is set; in that case dropping the leading zero is correct. But if the value is genuinely larger than qLength (e.g. a malformed/forged DER signature where r or s >= curve order, which is exactly the input an attacker controls when verifying a JWT), this silently truncates the most significant bytes and returns a wrong-length, wrong-value r/s instead of rejecting the signature. asn1derToConcatenatedRS is used on the verification path, so a crafted DER signature with oversized integers would be silently mangled rather than rejected, and the resulting concatenated value fed to the JCA verifier. The method should throw (e.g. IOException) when bytes.length > qLength + 1, or when the value does not fit in qLength bytes, instead of truncating.

Out-of-bounds length check uses the total input size instead of the remaining bytes

In readLength(), the sanity check for long-form lengths is `if (length >= limit)` where limit is the total length of the whole input byte array (set in the constructor), not the number of bytes remaining at the current read position. A nested element deep inside a larger structure can therefore declare a length up to the full input size even though far fewer bytes remain, and the check passes; the subsequent read(length) then fails only later with a generic EOF IOException. This weakens the early corruption detection the check is meant to provide (the comment says 'out of bounds length found'). The check should compare against the bytes remaining (limit minus bytes already consumed), e.g. track position and compare length > remaining.

Provider selection semantics inverted relative to the documented order() contract

CryptoProvider.order() is documented as 'The higher number has preference over the lower number', and the PR description says the Keycloak testsuite keeps using DefaultCryptoProvider via ordering. But detectProvider() sorts with Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order).reversed() and then picks foundProviders.get(0). Comparator.reversed() sorts descending, so get(0) is the provider with the LOWEST order value — the opposite of the documented contract. Concretely: AuthzClientCryptoProvider.order() == 100 and DefaultCryptoProvider.order() == 200, so when both are on the classpath (exactly the scenario this PR creates for the authz-client module, which depends on keycloak-core and is used in the testsuite where DefaultCryptoProvider is present), the authz client provider (100) wins over DefaultCryptoProvider (200), contradicting both the javadoc and the stated intent that the testsuite keeps using DefaultCryptoProvider. Either remove .reversed() or fix the javadoc; as written the code and documentation disagree and the wrong provider is selected.

CryptoIntegration.init is only called from one create() overload; other factory methods leave crypto uninitialized

CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()) is added only to create(Configuration). The other public factory methods create() (line 60) and create(InputStream) (line 72) delegate to create(Configuration) so they are covered, but any code path that constructs AuthzClient without going through these factories, or any other entry point in the authz-client that uses CryptoIntegration.getProvider() (e.g. ECDSA signature verification of tokens via the crypto provider), will hit 'Illegal state. Please init first before obtaining provider' if init was never called. More importantly, init() is a global static one-shot: once any other component in the same JVM (e.g. the Keycloak server in the testsuite) has initialized CryptoIntegration with a different classloader, the authz client's later init() call is a no-op and the AuthzClientCryptoProvider service file is never loaded for the client's classloader, so the client silently uses whatever provider was detected first. The initialization should be tied to the classloader actually used by the authz-client classes and be robust to prior initialization, or the provider should be resolved per-classloader rather than globally.

Test uses a default 256-bit EC key for ES384/ES512, so the ES384/ES512 paths are not actually exercised

The test constructor generates the key pair with KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair(), which on a standard JDK produces a 256-bit (secp256r1) key. It then signs with Signature.getInstance(JavaAlgorithm.getJavaAlgorithm(algorithm.name())) — for ES384 that is SHA384withECDSA and for ES512 SHA512withECDSA — but the signature length is still determined by the 256-bit curve, so algorithm.getSignatureLength() (96/132 bytes for ES384/ES512) does not match the actual r||s size (64 bytes). asn1derToConcatenatedRS then splits the DER into halves of signLength/2 = 48/66 bytes, which does not correspond to the real r and s, and concatenatedRSToASN1DER re-encodes with the wrong lengths. The round-trip assertion may still pass because both directions use the same wrong length, masking the mismatch, but the test never validates behavior with a real P-384/P-521 key and never verifies the produced DER against Signature.verify, so it does not prove correctness for ES384/ES512. The test should generate a key on the matching curve (e.g. secp384r1/secp521r1 via ECGenParameterSpec) per algorithm, and ideally assert that the converted signature verifies with the public key.

Round-trip test never verifies the converted signature cryptographically and misses the high-bit-set case

The test only asserts that asn1derToConcatenatedRS(concatenatedRSToASN1DER(x)) == x. It never checks that the DER produced by concatenatedRSToASN1DER is accepted by Signature.verify (the actual consumer of this conversion in JWT verification), nor that the concatenated form verifies via a JCA Signature using the raw r||s (e.g. SHA256withECDSAinP1363Format). Because of the leading-zero bug in concatenatedRSToASN1DER (see separate finding), the produced DER is non-minimal whenever r or s has a clear high bit; a round-trip through the same buggy code hides this, but a real verifier would reject it. The test should include Signature.verify over the re-encoded DER and should force coverage of both high-bit-set and high-bit-clear r/s values (e.g. by looping over multiple signatures until both cases occur, since each occurs with ~50% probability).

Module artifactId/name/description say 'tests' but the module now contains production code and a service provider

The pom declares artifactId keycloak-authz-client-tests and the description states 'This module is supposed to be used just in the Keycloak repository for the testsuite. It is NOT supposed to be used by the 3rd party applications.' This PR adds production classes (AuthzClientCryptoProvider, ASN1Encoder/Decoder) and a META-INF/services/org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider service registration to this module, and AuthzClient.create() now calls CryptoIntegration.init, meaning the service file will be picked up by ServiceLoader whenever this jar is on the classpath. Shipping a CryptoProvider service registration in a module explicitly documented as testsuite-only is contradictory: if the jar leaks onto a 3rd-party or server classpath, the AuthzClientCryptoProvider (which throws UnsupportedOperationException for most operations) can be selected and break crypto operations. Either the provider classes should move to the real keycloak-authz-client artifact (as the PR description says the changes will later be synced to keycloak-client), or the pom description must be updated; as written the module's stated purpose and its new contents conflict.

The correct behavior for a group that disappeared concurrently is to treat it as invalidated/not-found (consistent with `isUpdated()` and `getDelegateForUpdate()` which throw `IllegalStateException("Not found in database")`), not to return null.

Additionally, the reader thread is never joined, so the assertion on line 157 can run while the reader is still mid-request, and any exception thrown after the assertion is silently lost (the thread dies with an uncaught exception). The test should `join()` the reader thread before asserting, and ideally ensure the reader has performed at least one iteration before starting deletes (e.g. a CountDownLatch or AtomicBoolean confirming first read completed) so the concurrent window is actually exercised.

Conditional passkeys UI is now enabled during re-authentication with a known user, breaking the re-authentication contract

In `authenticate()`, the WebAuthn conditional-UI form data is now set up whenever `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())` is true, which includes the case where `context.getUser() != null` (re-authentication, e.g. prompt=login). Previously the code only called `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)` in the `else` branch, i.e. only when no user was set. Enabling conditional UI (autofill passkeys on the username field) during re-authentication changes the login page into an autofill/conditional-UI page for a user who is already identified; the username is hidden and the page is expected to be a password-only re-authentication form. This is a behavioral regression for re-authentication flows and contradicts the intent of the surrounding code, which explicitly sets `USERNAME_HIDDEN` and `REGISTRATION_DISABLED` and the `USER_SET_BEFORE_USERNAME_PASSWORD_AUTH` note for the re-authentication case. The same change in `challenge(context, error, field)` (line 137) enables conditional UI on error pages during re-authentication. The condition should remain restricted to the non-re-authentication branch (user == null), as before.

Refactored `shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators` changes behavior for subclasses that override it to return false

`fillContextForm()` previously checked `if (user != null)` before building the `WebAuthnAuthenticatorsBean` and setting `ALLOWED_AUTHENTICATORS`; it now calls `shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators(context)` (line 101), whose base implementation returns `context.getUser() != null` (line 129). `WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator` overrides this to return `false` (line 65-67) so that authenticators are not listed during conditional UI. However, the base `WebAuthnAuthenticator.fillContextForm()` still sets `IS_USER_IDENTIFIED` based on a local `isUserIdentified` variable that is only set to `true` inside the `shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators` branch (line 108). For `WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator` during re-authentication (user != null), `shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators` returns false, so `isUserIdentified` stays false and `IS_USER_IDENTIFIED` is set to "false" even though a user is identified — the template may then render the page as an ID-less/passwordless page rather than a re-authentication page. The refactor conflates "user is identified" with "authenticators should be listed"; these are separate concerns and the `IS_USER_IDENTIFIED` flag should still be derived from `user != null`.

Error response during conditional-UI passkey failure sets re-authentication form attributes unconditionally

`createErrorResponse()` now calls `AuthenticatorUtils.setupReauthenticationInUsernamePasswordFormError(context)` (line 53). That helper only sets `USERNAME_HIDDEN` and `REGISTRATION_DISABLED` when the `USER_SET_BEFORE_USERNAME_PASSWORD_AUTH` auth note is "true", so in the normal (non re-authentication) conditional UI case it is a no-op. However, when a passkey conditional-UI authentication fails during re-authentication (user already set, note = "true"), this marks the form as re-authentication — which is correct — but the method is invoked on every error response, including errors that occur in the plain username/password flow where the user was NOT previously set (e.g. `WEBAUTHN_ERROR_API_GET` from the browser). In that case the note is absent and the call is harmless, but the placement suggests it is meant to run only for re-authentication errors; if the note is ever set by another path (e.g. a previous execution in the same auth session), a non re-authentication error page would incorrectly hide the username field and disable registration. The call should be guarded by an explicit check that this error occurred during a re-authentication flow, not placed unconditionally in the shared error-response path.

Static import from `browser` package into `util` package creates a package cycle and widens visibility of an internal constant

`AuthenticatorUtils` (in `org.keycloak.authentication.authenticators.util`) now statically imports `AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator.USER_SET_BEFORE_USERNAME_PASSWORD_AUTH` (line 35), and the constant was changed from `protected` to `public` (AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator.java line 58) solely to make this import possible. This introduces a dependency from the generic `util` package back into the `browser` package (a package cycle: browser → util → browser), and exposes an internal flow-state constant as part of the public API surface of `AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator`. The constant is an implementation detail of the username/password form flow; making it `public` invites external use and makes future refactoring harder. The constant should remain `protected`/package-private and the note name should either be defined in `AuthenticatorUtils` itself or in a neutral location, with `AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator` referencing it from there.

In `reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey`, the check for absence of the WebAuthn button is written as: `MatcherAssert.assertThat(driver.findElement(By.xpath("//form[@id='webauth']")), nullValue()); fail("Not expected to have webauthn button");` inside a `try` block, with `catch (Exception nsee) { // expected }`. `driver.findElement` throws `NoSuchElementException` when the element is absent, so the `assertThat(..., nullValue())` line is never reached in the expected (passing) case — the test passes via the catch block. If the element IS present, `findElement` returns a non-null element, `assertThat(element, nullValue())` fails with an `AssertionError`, which is also caught by the broad `catch (Exception)` and silently treated as expected. The test therefore cannot fail when the WebAuthn button is incorrectly shown; the assertion is dead code. The correct pattern (used elsewhere in the codebase) is `Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, () -> driver.findElement(...))`, as done in `PasskeysOrganizationAuthenticationTest` before this PR. Both occurrences (lines 291-296 and 312-317) have the same defect, so the test does not actually verify that passkeys are hidden for a user without a passkey during re-authentication.

If the template changes (e.g. the hidden field is rendered empty, or the form posts to a different action), the test would submit an empty username and fail with "Invalid username or password" rather than "Invalid password", or authenticate the wrong user. The test should explicitly assert the hidden username value (e.g. `loginPage.getAttemptedUsername()` equals the expected user) before submitting, as done in `PasskeysOrganizationAuthenticationTest.passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey`, to make the precondition explicit and the failure mode diagnosable.

Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ explicitly asserts that slice indices are non-negative ('Negative indexing is not supported.'), so any request with a negative cursor offset will raise an unhandled AssertionError and produce a 500 error. The comment claiming 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is factually wrong. This code path is reachable from the audit logs endpoint whenever an admin passes a cursor with a negative offset (cursors are client-supplied strings parsed in Cursor.from_string, which accepts negative integers).

false_positives.candidate:
BasePaginator.get_result change breaks prev-cursor pagination by clamping negative offsets to 0

The modification to BasePaginator.get_result changed `results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` to `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset; results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])`. For a prev cursor (is_prev=True) with a negative offset — which OffsetPaginator-style prev cursors legitimately produce (e.g. `Cursor(limit, page - 1, True, page > 0)` yields offset -1 on the first page) — the old code sliced with the negative offset, while the new code passes the raw negative offset only when is_prev is True... actually the new code preserves the negative offset for is_prev, but for non-prev cursors it clamps negative offsets to 0, silently returning the first page instead of erroring or handling the value. More importantly, the change alters behavior for all existing paginator subclasses (Paginator, DateTimePaginator) that share BasePaginator.get_result: previously a negative offset would hit Django's 'Negative indexing is not supported' assertion; now non-prev negative offsets silently clamp to 0, returning incorrect data (the first page) instead of failing. This is a silent data-correctness change to a shared, widely-used code path with no test coverage shown.

OptimizedCursorPaginator prev-cursor trimming logic uses unclamped offset, producing wrong page sizes

In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, the prev-cursor trimming branch checks `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra:` (line 891) using the raw `offset = cursor.offset`, but the actual slice was performed with `start_offset` which may differ from `offset` (when offset is negative and advanced features are enabled, or when offset is negative and is_prev is False where start_offset = max(0, offset)). When start_offset != offset, the length comparison `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` is computed against the wrong expected length, so the extra fetched row is not trimmed (or a legitimate row is trimmed), corrupting page contents and cursor boundaries. The same mismatch exists in the inherited BasePaginator code at line 192, where the slice now uses start_offset but the trim check still uses `offset`.

paginate() called with unknown keyword argument enable_advanced_features

The endpoint calls self.paginate(..., paginator_cls=OptimizedCursorPaginator, ..., enable_advanced_features=True). The paginate helper on the API endpoint base class does not accept an `enable_advanced_features` parameter — it forwards only known kwargs (queryset, paginator_cls, order_by, on_results, etc.) to the paginator constructor. Passing an unrecognized keyword will raise a TypeError at runtime ('unexpected keyword argument'), making the optimized path completely broken — every admin request with optimized_pagination=true will 500. Even if paginate forwarded **kwargs, the OptimizedCursorPaginator constructor signature is `__init__(self, *args, enable_advanced_features=False, **kwargs)`, so it would work only if forwarding exists, which it does not in the standard endpoint paginate implementation.

OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates BasePaginator.get_result almost line-for-line; the only behavioral differences are the negative-offset branch (which is broken, see other findings) and accepting an enable_advanced_features flag. There is no query optimization (no keyset/seek pagination, no deferred fields, no index hints, no count_hits avoidance). The claimed 'optimized query path for large datasets' in the docstring is false — the class performs the same OFFSET-based slicing as the base paginator, which is precisely the slow pattern for high-volume tables. Shipping this as a 'performance enhancement' is misleading and adds a maintenance burden and a dangerous code path for zero measured benefit.

It is not introduced by this diff, but it means the branch that un-reverses an explicitly descending order_by silently does nothing, which interacts with the new paginator subclass that relies on build_queryset. Worth fixing while touching this file, but not caused by this PR.

The endpoint's publish_status is EXPERIMENTAL and it is a public API surface. The PR adds an undocumented, admin-only query parameter (`optimized_pagination`) that switches paginator implementations and changes response cursor semantics. API consumers cannot discover this parameter, and because cursor formats differ between DateTimePaginator and OptimizedCursorPaginator (datetime-millis vs raw value), a client that flips the flag mid-pagination will receive cursors it cannot use with the other paginator, causing incorrect/empty pages. The parameter should be documented, or the feature should be server-side only.

The added comment in Cursor.__init__ states 'Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios', but the class does nothing to allow or validate them — it simply stores int(offset), and Cursor.from_string happily parses negative offsets from client input. The comment describes intent that is implemented (dangerously) elsewhere; as written it misleads readers into thinking Cursor itself supports/sanitizes negative offsets. Either remove the comment or implement actual validation (e.g., reject negative offsets at parse time for non-advanced cursors).

The PR adds a new paginator class, modifies shared BasePaginator.get_result slicing behavior (affecting Paginator and DateTimePaginator used across the entire API), and adds a new endpoint branch — but includes no tests. The BasePaginator change alters behavior for every cursor-paginated endpoint in the codebase (negative offsets now clamp to 0 for non-prev cursors instead of raising), and the new paginator's negative-offset path, prev-cursor trimming, and datetime-key handling are all untested. Given the critical slicing bug, at minimum tests must cover: negative offset rejection/clamping, prev-cursor round trips, and the audit logs endpoint with optimized_pagination=true for admin and non-admin users.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the coarse lock from BuildIndex introduces a race: two concurrent builds for the same key can both create indexes and leak one, and GetIndex can return a partially-constructed index

The PR removes the function-wide b.cacheMu.Lock() from BuildIndex (previously lines 88-89) and replaces it with a short lock only around the cache insertion at lines 137-139. This means two concurrent callers of BuildIndex for the same NamespacedResource key (which happens: searchSupport.init spawns concurrent builds via errgroup, and getOrCreateIndex can also trigger builds from concurrent Search/handleEvent calls) will both execute bleve.New/bleve.NewMemOnly, both run the builder writing documents, and both insert into b.cache — the second insertion silently overwrites the first. The overwritten bleve.Index is never closed, leaking file handles/disk state (for file-based indexes, the on-disk directory is left behind and will be reopened by a subsequent build, potentially corrupting or duplicating data). Additionally, between the builder writing documents (line 126) and the cache insertion (line 138), another goroutine calling GetIndex will not find the index and will start its own duplicate build. The original coarse lock prevented duplicate builds for the same key; the fix requires per-key locking (e.g., a sync.Map of in-flight builds keyed by NamespacedResource, or a keyed mutex) so that concurrent builds for the same key are deduplicated, while builds for different keys proceed in parallel.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same race condition in BuildIndex caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from covering the whole function to only covering the final cache assignment, leading to concurrent duplicate builds for the same key.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates b.cache without holding cacheMu — data race with concurrent BuildIndex insertions

TotalDocs (line 144) ranges over b.cache with no lock. BuildIndex now writes to b.cache under b.cacheMu.Lock() at lines 137-139, and GetIndex reads under RLock. Since BuildIndex can run concurrently (the whole point of the PR's finer-grained locking), TotalDocs racing with a cache insertion is a concurrent map read/write — a fatal runtime error in Go (concurrent map iteration and map write). TotalDocs is called from searchSupport.init at line 216 (s.search.TotalDocs()) after group.Wait(), but also potentially from metrics or other paths concurrently with getOrCreateIndex-triggered builds. Fix: acquire b.cacheMu.RLock() around the iteration.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same concurrency bug: `TotalDocs` iterates over `b.cache` without synchronization/locking, which causes a concurrent map read/write data race with `BuildIndex` writes, specifically noting the call `s.search.TotalDocs()` in `init`.

false_positives.candidate:
NewResourceServer calls s.Init(ctx) with a context that is never cancelled on construction failure, leaking the watcher goroutine and resources

NewResourceServer creates a cancelable context (ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(...)) at line 229 and stores it on the server struct (s.ctx, s.cancel). It then calls s.Init(ctx) at line 258, which starts the watcher (initWatcher) and, via searchSupport.init, spawns a goroutine reading from the storage event channel. If Init fails (e.g., search index build error or WatchWriteEvents error), NewResourceServer returns nil, err at line 261 — but it never calls s.cancel(). The server object is discarded, so the cancel function is unreachable, and the background goroutines started by initWatcher (the broadcaster goroutine piping events from s.backend.WatchWriteEvents(s.ctx)) keep running forever with a context that will never be cancelled. This is a goroutine/resource leak on every failed startup, and in HA or repeated-restart scenarios it will accumulate pollers holding DB connections. Fix: call s.cancel() (or defer it) before returning the error when Init fails.

Init is now only called from the constructor, but remains exported and uses sync.Once with a shared initErr that Stop() overwrites, creating a data race and broken re-init semantics

The PR removes all lazy s.Init(ctx) calls from the gRPC handlers (Create, Update, Delete, Read, List, Watch, Search, History, Origin, IsHealthy, PutBlob, GetBlob) and instead calls s.Init(ctx) once in NewResourceServer. However, Init (line 293) is still an exported method on the server type, still guarded by s.once, and still writes to the shared s.initErr field. Meanwhile Stop() (line 320) unconditionally writes s.initErr = fmt.Errorf("service is stopping") without any synchronization. If any external caller (or future code) invokes Init concurrently with Stop, or calls Init after Stop, there is an unsynchronized read/write race on s.initErr. More importantly, the once.Do means that if Init is called again after Stop (e.g., a caller retries Init on the same server instance), it will return the stale initErr from the first run — but Stop has since overwritten initErr with "service is stopping"/"service is stopped", so the semantics are now muddled: a second Init returns whatever Stop last wrote. Since Init is now effectively an internal startup step, it should be unexported (init) or the initErr handling should be made race-free and Stop should not clobber the field that Init's once.Do closure reads.

totalBatchesIndexed is incremented inside concurrent errgroup goroutines without synchronization — data race and incorrect metric

In searchSupport.init, totalBatchesIndexed is declared as a plain int at line 177 and incremented at line 189 inside group.Go(func() error { ... totalBatchesIndexed++ ... }) for each namespace. The errgroup runs up to s.initWorkers concurrent goroutines (group.SetLimit(s.initWorkers) at line 179), so multiple goroutines increment the same variable concurrently with no mutex or atomic. This is a data race (undefined behavior under the Go memory model) and will also produce an incorrect count in the span event at line 199 (attribute.Int("namespaced_indexed", totalBatchesIndexed)). Fix: use atomic.Int64, or compute the count as len(stats) after group.Wait() since every stat entry spawns exactly one goroutine.

searchSupport.init starts a second, unbounded event-watching goroutine that duplicates the server's broadcaster watcher and never terminates

searchSupport.init (line 172) calls s.storage.WatchWriteEvents(watchctx) at line 203 with watchctx := context.Background() (line 202) and spawns a goroutine at line 207 that loops forever reading from the events channel and calling s.handleEvent. This is separate from the server's own initWatcher (server.go line 752) which also calls s.backend.WatchWriteEvents(s.ctx) and feeds a broadcaster. The searchSupport goroutine uses context.Background(), which is never cancelled — not by server.Stop() (which only calls s.cancel() on the server's own ctx), and not by any lifecycle hook. When the server shuts down, this goroutine keeps running, keeps consuming events from the storage backend's poller, and keeps mutating the search index. Additionally, both the server's broadcaster and this searchSupport goroutine independently call WatchWriteEvents on the same SQL backend, which spawns two poller goroutines (backend.go line 566) polling the same resource_history table — doubling DB load and potentially racing on index writes. The searchSupport watcher should use the server's cancellable context (s.ctx) and be tied to the server lifecycle, or the event handling should be unified with the existing broadcaster.

Event watcher goroutine does not check channel closure — blocks forever on closed channel and never exits

The goroutine at line 207 does `for { v := <-events; s.handleEvent(watchctx, v) }`. The events channel returned by WatchWriteEvents is closed by the SQL backend's poller when it exits (backend.go line 572: defer close(stream)). Receiving from a closed channel returns nil immediately and forever, so once the channel is closed this goroutine will spin in a tight infinite loop calling s.handleEvent(watchctx, nil) — which will panic on nil pointer dereference at line 226 (evt.Type) or at minimum burn CPU. The loop should be `for v := range events` or check `v, ok := <-events; if !ok { return }`.

bleveIndex.Write/Delete/Flush mutate shared batch state with no synchronization — unsafe for concurrent watch-event handling

bleveIndex.Write (line 172) checks b.batch != nil, calls b.batch.Index(...), and may call b.index.Batch(b.batch) and b.batch.Reset(). Delete (line 190) errors if batch != nil. Flush (line 198) calls b.index.Batch(b.batch), b.batch.Reset(), and sets b.batch = nil. These fields are documented as "only valid in single thread" (line 166) but after the PR's change, handleEvent in search.go can be invoked concurrently: the searchSupport.init goroutine (line 207) calls handleEvent in a single goroutine, but getOrCreateIndex (line 287) can trigger build() concurrently with handleEvent for the same key, and once the index is in the cache, multiple watch events for the same namespace could be processed... actually the searchSupport event loop is single-goroutine, but the index returned by BuildIndex is placed in the cache before Flush is called by searchSupport.build (line 372: index.Flush() after BuildIndex returns). Between BuildIndex returning (line 140) and searchSupport.build calling Flush (search.go line 372), the index is in the cache with b.batch still non-nil; a concurrent Search on that index is fine, but a concurrent handleEvent Write would see batch != nil and try to batch.Index into a batch that build() is about to Flush and nil out — a race on b.batch. More critically, after Flush sets b.batch = nil, concurrent Write calls go directly to b.index.Index which is safe, but the transition itself (Flush setting batch=nil while Write reads batch) is unsynchronized. The bleveIndex needs a mutex protecting batch, or the batch must be fully flushed and nilled inside BuildIndex before the index is published to the cache.

Stop() overwrites initErr with a generic error, losing the original initialization error and breaking error reporting for callers that check Init after Stop

Stop() unconditionally sets s.initErr = fmt.Errorf("service is stopping") at line 321 and later s.initErr = fmt.Errorf("service is stopped") at line 339, overwriting whatever initErr was set during Init. Since Init uses sync.Once and returns s.initErr, any caller that calls Init after Stop (or concurrently) will get "service is stopped" instead of the real initialization error. More importantly, the lifecycle is now: NewResourceServer calls Init synchronously; if it fails, the constructor returns an error and the server is never used — so Stop is never called on a failed-init server. But for a successfully initialized server that is later stopped, if any code path still calls Init (it's exported), it gets the once-cached value... which Stop has clobbered. The initErr field is being used for two purposes (init result and stop status) without synchronization. Separate the concerns: keep initErr immutable after once.Do, and use a separate atomic/bool for stopped state.

IndexMetrics.IndexedKinds is incremented/decremented without nil check in handleEvent, unlike other IndexMetrics usages in the same file

In handleEvent, IndexMetrics.IndexedKinds.WithLabelValues(evt.Key.Resource).Inc() (line 263) and .Dec() (line 271) are called without checking if IndexMetrics is nil. Every other use of IndexMetrics in this file (lines 217, 282, 367) guards with `if IndexMetrics != nil`. If IndexMetrics is nil (which can happen if metrics registration failed or in tests), handleEvent will panic with a nil pointer dereference when processing ADDED or DELETED watch events. This is inconsistent and a latent crash. Fix: add the same nil guard, or better, initialize IndexMetrics to a no-op default so nil checks are unnecessary.

Moving Init from lazy per-request to constructor changes the failure contract: NewResourceServer now blocks on full index build and can fail startup, but callers may not expect constructor to do heavy I/O

Previously, Init was called lazily on the first gRPC request (Create/Update/Read/List/Watch/Search/etc.), so NewResourceServer returned quickly and the server could start serving requests (returning init errors per-request) even if index building was slow or failed. Now NewResourceServer calls s.Init(ctx) synchronously at line 258, which calls searchSupport.init — this builds the entire search index (potentially minutes for large datasets) and starts watchers before the constructor returns. Consequences: (1) The gRPC server registration/startup path now blocks on index build; if the caller has a startup timeout, the process may be killed before the server is ready. (2) If index build fails, NewResourceServer returns an error and the entire ResourceServer fails to construct — previously the server would start and only Search requests would fail. (3) The ctx passed to Init is the server's internal background-derived context (line 229), not a startup timeout context — so a hung index build hangs the constructor forever with no cancellation. Callers of NewResourceServer need to be audited to ensure they can tolerate a long-blocking, failure-prone constructor; ideally Init should be called with a startup deadline context, or the constructor should return the server immediately and Init be called separately by the module lifecycle with proper timeout handling.

More importantly, an empty string group key and `None` group key produce different fingerprints (`"123:"` vs `"123"`), but `build_dedupe_value_key` and `build_counter_value_key` (lines 324-332) treat both `None` and `""` identically by converting `None` to `""`. false_positives.candidate:
Python's built-in hash() is randomized per process, breaking consistent group-to-queue assignment across restarts and workers

FixedQueuePool.get_queue_for_group uses `hash(group_key) % self.num_queues`. In Python 3, `hash()` of strings is salted per process (PYTHONHASHSEED randomization), so the same group key maps to different queue indices in different processes and across restarts. This breaks the core ordering guarantee: two messages for the same subscription can be processed concurrently by different workers (if the consumer runs with multiple processes via --processes, each process has its own pool and different hash seeds), and after a restart a group can move to a different queue, allowing out-of-order processing of the same subscription. The docstring claims 'Each group is consistently assigned to the same queue' but this is only true within a single process. Use a stable hash (e.g., md5/sha1 of the key, or zlib.crc32) instead.

get_committable_offsets iterates a range from min to max offset per partition on every commit cycle

OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets computes `for offset in range(start, max_offset + 1)` and checks set membership for every integer in that span. Kafka offsets are monotonically increasing and can be far apart (e.g., after a long-running consumer, offsets in the millions with sparse in-flight items), so each 1-second commit-loop iteration can iterate over millions of integers per partition, holding the per-partition lock the entire time. This blocks add_offset/complete_offset calls from worker threads (stalling processing) and burns CPU. The algorithm should instead sort the completed offsets and walk only the actual tracked offsets (e.g., iterate over sorted(all_offsets) and stop at the first outstanding one), which is O(k log k) in the number of tracked offsets rather than O(max_offset).

OffsetTracker.partition_locks dict is read and written without synchronization, allowing duplicate locks for the same partition

_get_partition_lock does `self.partition_locks.get(partition)` followed by `self.partition_locks.setdefault(partition, threading.Lock())` with no lock protecting the dict itself. Multiple worker threads can race on first access to a partition: thread A's get() returns None, thread B's get() returns None, and both create separate Lock objects — one wins in the dict, the other thread uses its own orphaned lock. All subsequent synchronization for that partition is then split across two locks, so add_offset/complete_offset/get_committable_offsets/mark_committed are not mutually exclusive, which can corrupt the offset sets (e.g., mark_committed pruning all_offsets while get_committable_offsets iterates it) and produce incorrect commit decisions — potentially committing offsets for messages still being processed (data loss on crash). Guard creation with a single global lock (e.g., `with self._locks_guard: return self.partition_locks.setdefault(partition, threading.Lock())`).

Worker exceptions are swallowed and the offset is still marked complete, causing silent message loss

In OrderedQueueWorker.run, when result_processor raises, the exception is only logged ('Unexpected error in queue worker') and the finally block unconditionally calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)`. The offset is therefore treated as successfully processed and becomes committable, so the failed message is never retried and is silently dropped once the offset is committed. Note that ResultProcessor.__call__ in result_consumer.py also swallows exceptions internally, so most processing failures never even reach this handler — either way the message is lost. This is a data-integrity bug for a Kafka consumer whose contract is at-least-once delivery. On exception the offset should remain outstanding (or the item should be retried / sent to a DLQ), not completed.

submit() exception handler marks the offset complete, committing messages that were never processed

In SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit, the except block logs 'Error submitting message to queue' and then calls add_offset + complete_offset for the message. If the decoder or grouping_fn raised, the message was never enqueued or processed, yet its offset is immediately marked complete and will be committed — permanently skipping that message. The same pattern is used for the `result is None` path (lines 301-304), which is arguably intentional for undecodable messages, but applying it to unexpected exceptions in submit converts a transient failure into silent data loss. The offset should be left outstanding (blocking commits for that partition, surfacing the problem) or the message routed to a DLQ, not completed.

close() can commit offsets for items still queued, and shutdown discards in-flight work without committing or requeuing

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets shutdown_event, joins the commit thread (which stops committing), then calls queue_pool.shutdown(). FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown = True and calls q.shutdown(immediate=False) — with Python's queue.ShutDown semantics, workers finish the item they are currently processing but any items still sitting in the queues are abandoned, and their offsets remain outstanding (never committed, which is safe) — but worse, close() joins the commit thread BEFORE draining the queues, so offsets for items that complete during pool shutdown are never committed even though they were processed. On the next start those messages are reprocessed (at-least-once, acceptable), but the ordering of operations is wrong: the pool should be drained (wait_until_empty) and a final commit performed before the commit thread is stopped. Also, terminate() shuts down the pool without waiting for in-flight items at all. For a consumer whose purpose is exactly-once-ish ordered processing, shutdown should drain queues and flush final offsets.

join() ignores its timeout argument and delegates to close(), which is not a graceful join

ProcessingStrategy.join(timeout) is expected to wait up to `timeout` for the strategy to finish processing outstanding work. Here join() discards the timeout and calls close(), which (per the close() issues above) stops the commit thread and shuts down workers with a hard 5s join each, abandoning queued items. Arroyo's StreamProcessor uses join during shutdown to allow in-flight work to complete; this implementation makes join equivalent to an abrupt terminate and ignores the caller's timeout, so shutdown behavior does not match the ProcessingStrategy contract.

FixedQueuePool is created once per factory but create_with_partitions can be called multiple times, sharing one pool across strategies

ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ creates a single FixedQueuePool (with its worker threads and OffsetTracker) when mode == 'thread-queue-parallel'. create_with_partitions then returns a new SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy wrapping that same pool each time it is called. Arroyo calls create_with_partitions per partition-assignment epoch (e.g., on rebalance), so multiple strategy instances can share one pool and one OffsetTracker. Each SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy also spawns its own commit thread calling commit_function with its own `commit` closure — two commit threads can commit interleaved offset maps from the shared tracker, and shutdown() on the factory sets self.queue_pool = None while previously created strategies still reference the pool, leading to double shutdown and commits from stale strategies. The pool should be created per create_with_partitions call (or the factory should guard against reuse), not per factory instance.

ResultProcessor.__call__ swallows all exceptions, so failed results are treated as processed and their offsets committed

ResultProcessor.__call__ wraps handle_result in a try/except that only logs ('Failed to process message result'). Since OrderedQueueWorker treats the return of result_processor as success and completes the offset, any exception in handle_result (DB errors, assertion failures, etc.) results in the message being acknowledged and committed — silent data loss with no retry and no DLQ routing. This is the queue-mode equivalent of a poison message being dropped. Failures should propagate (so the offset stays outstanding and the partition stalls, surfacing the issue) or be routed to the DLQ policy that the StreamProcessor already supports.

Sentry transaction name hardcodes 'monitors.' prefix for a generic remote-subscriptions component

OrderedQueueWorker.run creates a transaction named f"monitors.{self.identifier}.worker_{self.worker_id}". This module lives in sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers and is generic infrastructure (also used by uptime via ResultsStrategyFactory), but the metric/transaction namespace is hardcoded to 'monitors.', so uptime results processed through this path will be tagged as monitors.* in Sentry/metrics, polluting dashboards and making the identifier misleading. The prefix should be derived from the identifier or made configurable.

wait_until_empty only checks queue size, not outstanding (in-flight) items

FixedQueuePool.wait_until_empty returns True when get_stats()['total_items'] == 0, i.e., all queues are empty. But an item that has been popped by a worker and is currently being processed is no longer counted in qsize(), so wait_until_empty can return True while work is still in flight. Callers using this to assert 'all work done' (as the tests do implicitly via stats checks) can race with in-flight processing. It should also check that the OffsetTracker has no outstanding offsets (or expose outstanding counts in get_stats).

test_different_groups_distributed can pass even if all groups hash to one queue (weak assertion on hash distribution)

The test asserts len(queue_indices) == 3 after hashing 20 group keys with num_queues=3. With Python's randomized string hash this usually passes, but it is probabilistic and, more importantly, it validates distribution rather than the actual requirement — consistent assignment per key (covered by the other test) and correct modulo behavior. If hash() were replaced with a broken function returning a constant, this test would catch it, but as written it is flaky-by-construction (a fixed hash seed could theoretically map all 20 keys to fewer than 3 buckets) and does not test the property that matters for correctness (stability across processes), which is untestable in-process. Consider asserting on a deterministic hash function instead once the implementation is fixed.

New thread-queue-parallel tests poll with fixed iteration counts and no failure message on timeout

The new tests (test_thread_queue_parallel, test_thread_queue_parallel_preserves_order, test_thread_queue_parallel_concurrent_subscriptions, test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_commit, test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling, test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps) use `for _ in range(max_wait): ... time.sleep(0.1)` loops and then assert on results without first asserting the loop actually observed the expected condition. If processing is merely slow (CI under load), the loop exits after max_wait iterations (5 seconds) and the subsequent assert produces a confusing failure, or worse, in test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling the loop breaks only when the condition holds but the final asserts tolerate `len(committed_offsets) == 0` — meaning the test can pass without ever verifying that commits are correctly withheld. The loops should assert the wait condition succeeded (e.g., `assert stats['total_items'] == 0 and ... , 'timed out waiting'`) before proceeding, so slow runs fail loudly at the wait rather than at a downstream assert, and the error-handling test should deterministically verify the no-commit behavior.
