The request should carry a shared secret (e.g. `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`) and the response should be validated (schema + user binding) before being persisted. Also, the returned `Response` is passed to callers that call `.json()`/`.data` on it without checking `response.ok`, so a 4xx/5xx from the sync endpoint yields `undefined` tokens that are then written into credentials (see googlecalendar: `token.access_token` would throw, but hubspot/zoho write `tokenInfo.data` which would be an error body).

`const tokenInfo = await refreshOAuthTokens(async () => await axios.post(...), ...)` then `if (!tokenInfo.data.error)`. In the normal path `tokenInfo` is an axios response (`.data` is the body — ok), but axios throws on non-2xx by default so the `else` branch logging `tokenInfo.data` is only reachable for 2xx responses containing an `error` field. `const resp = await refreshOAuthTokens(async () => await fetch(...), "lark-calendar", credential.userId)` then `const data = await handleLarkError<RefreshTokenResp>(resp, this.log)`. In the normal path `resp` is the `fetch` `Response` (same as before the change — ok). In the sync path `resp` is also a `Response` — ok by luck. But `handleLarkError` presumably throws on non-OK Lark responses; in sync mode a non-200 from the sync endpoint (e.g. 404 for unknown user) will be interpreted as a Lark API error and its body parsed as `RefreshTokenResp`, yielding `data.data.refresh_token === undefined`, which is then written into the credential (lines 91-96), wiping the user's Lark tokens. The sync response must be validated (ok status + expected shape) before its fields are persisted.

`const responseBody = await handleWebexResponse(response, credential.id);` — `handleWebexResponse` (line 270) expects a fetch `Response` and returns `responseClone.json()`. In the normal path `response` is a `Response` (ok). In the sync path it is also a `Response` (ok), but the sync endpoint returns only `{ access_token, expiry_date }` (per the PR contract), which does not match `webexRefreshedTokenSchema` (requires `scope`, `token_type`, `refresh_token`, `refresh_token_expires_in`). `parsedToken.success` will therefore be false and the adapter rejects with "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned" — meaning Webex token refresh is permanently broken whenever credential syncing is enabled. The sync response must be mapped onto the webex token shape (preserving the existing refresh token and computing expiry) instead of being validated against the provider schema.

`const parsedToken = parseRefreshTokenResponse(responseBody, zoomRefreshedTokenSchema);` — when credential syncing is enabled, `parseRefreshTokenResponse` uses `minimumTokenResponseSchema` (only requires `access_token`), so `parsedToken.data` will contain only the fields the sync endpoint returned (e.g. `access_token` and an expiry). But lines 119-122 then unconditionally read `newTokens.refresh_token` and `newTokens.expires_in` — both `undefined` for a sync response — so `key.refresh_token` is set to `undefined` (wiping the stored refresh token) and `key.expiry_date` becomes `NaN`, permanently breaking the Zoom credential. The code must preserve the existing `refresh_token` and derive `expiry_date` from the sync payload's absolute expiry when present.

handleZoomResponse is called on the refreshOAuthTokens result, which in sync mode is a Response but in normal mode is also a Response; however the sync body lacks Zoom's error field so invalid_grant handling is bypassed

`const responseBody = await handleZoomResponse(response, credential.id);` — `handleZoomResponse` throws on non-OK responses and returns the parsed JSON. In sync mode, if the sync endpoint returns 200 with an error payload or a non-JSON body, `responseClone.json()` may throw or return an unexpected shape; the subsequent `if (responseBody.error)` check (line 98) assumes the Zoom error shape. A sync endpoint that returns `{ "error": "user_not_found" }` with 200 would be treated as a Zoom `invalid_grant` only if the string matches; otherwise it falls through to schema validation and rejects with a generic error, and the credential is never invalidated even though the user's tokens are gone. The sync path needs explicit status/shape validation.

`export const APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED = process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY;` — this evaluates to `string | undefined`, not `boolean`. It is used in boolean contexts (`if (!APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED)`), which works, but the exported name and type imply a boolean and the value can be the empty string `""` (falsy, ok) or the secret string itself (truthy). More subtly, the flag does not include `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`, so `refreshOAuthTokens`/`parseRefreshTokenResponse` check `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` — meaning the webhook endpoint is enabled whenever the secret+key are set even if no sync endpoint is configured, which is presumably intended, but the flag should be an explicit boolean (`!!(...)`) and the webhook handler should additionally verify that the encryption key is non-empty before decrypting (see the app-credential.ts finding about the `|| ""` fallback).

The webhook always creates/updates a credential with `userId: reqBody.userId` and never sets `teamId`. Self-hosters syncing credentials for users who belong to teams will have the credential attached to the user rather than the team, so team event types that resolve credentials by `teamId` will not see the synced credential. Conversely, a webhook caller can attach a credential to any user id (the endpoint trusts `userId` after only checking the user exists), which is by design for this feature but means the endpoint is a full credential-write primitive for arbitrary users — combined with the weak secret check, this is a significant privilege. The POST body is `new URLSearchParams({ calcomUserId, appSlug })` but no `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded` header is set (fetch sets it automatically for URLSearchParams bodies in modern runtimes, so this is mostly fine), and — more importantly — no authentication or shared secret is sent, so the sync endpoint cannot verify the caller is really this Cal.com instance (see the security finding). The diff changes `const redirectUri = WEBAPP_URL + `/api/integrations/${appConfig.slug}/callback`` to the literal ``WEBAPP_URL + `/api/integrations/zoho-bigin/callback` ``. If `appConfig.slug` is not exactly `"zoho-bigin"` this changes the OAuth redirect URI and breaks the Zoho Bigin install flow (the redirect URI must match the one registered in the Zoho console). The signature is `(response: any, schema: z.ZodTypeAny)`. In sync mode the `schema` argument is completely ignored (only `minimumTokenResponseSchema` is used), so callers pass provider-specific schemas that are silently discarded — meaning a sync endpoint returning extra/malformed fields is accepted as long as `access_token` is a string. The `any` type also disables type checking at every call site. The function should type the response as `unknown` and, in sync mode, still validate the minimal shape strictly (and ideally require an expiry field, since the whole point of the sync contract is to return token + expiry).

`const appMetadata = appStoreMetadata[app.slug as keyof typeof appStoreMetadata];` then the credential is created/updated with `appId: appMetadata.slug`. More importantly, the web app's build env list (`@calcom/web#build` `env` array, lines 27-38) was NOT updated to include these variables, so production builds may not have them available at runtime in some deployment setups that rely on the turbo env allowlist. In the `updatedBookings.forEach(...)` loop, `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId)` and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId)` are invoked without `await` (and the enclosing `forEach` callback is not async). Consequences: (1) the handler can return before the `cancelled: true` DB update (or the Twilio cancel / row delete for SMS) has completed, so a crash or early response can leave reminders un-cancelled; (2) unhandled promise rejections are possible if the internal try/catch is bypassed; (3) for SMS reminders, `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` now deletes the DB row immediately, so a non-awaited call racing with the later `prismaPromises`/`apiDeletes` `Promise.all` creates unclear ordering. The loop should be `for...of` with `await`, or the promises should be collected and awaited.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
immediateDelete path uses the wrong SendGrid endpoint and never deletes the DB row

`deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminderId, referenceId, immediateDelete = true)` sends `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends` with `{ batch_id: referenceId, status: "cancel" }` in the body. As noted in the PR description, the correct SendGrid cancellation API is `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends/{batch_id}` with `{ status: "cancel" }` — the batch id belongs in the URL path. With the batch_id in the body, SendGrid will not cancel the scheduled send. Furthermore, when `immediateDelete` is true the function `return`s immediately after the API call and never deletes or marks the `workflowReminder` row, so the row stays in the DB with `scheduled: true` and the stale `referenceId`; the CRON cleanup at the top of `scheduleEmailReminders.ts` will eventually delete it only when `scheduledDate` passes, but the SendGrid send itself was never cancelled. This path is used when a workflow or a workflow step is deleted (workflows.tsx lines 214 and 521), meaning deleting a workflow can leave its scheduled emails active. Fix the URL to `/v3/user/scheduled_sends/${referenceId}` and delete/mark the DB row after a successful cancellation.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: in `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` when `immediateDelete` is true, the function returns after the SendGrid API call without deleting or updating the `workflowReminder` record in the database.

true_positives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New cancelled column is nullable with no default, so existing and new rows have NULL instead of false

The migration adds `"cancelled" BOOLEAN` (nullable, no default) and the Prisma schema declares `cancelled Boolean?`. Every existing row gets NULL, and new reminders created in `scheduleEmailReminder`/`scheduleSMSReminder` (emailReminderManager.ts lines 169-193, smsReminderManager.ts lines 148-172) do not set `cancelled`, so they are also NULL. The CRON query uses `cancelled: true`, which correctly excludes NULL rows in Prisma, but any code doing truthiness checks or `cancelled === false` comparisons will misbehave, and the column wastes storage on NULLs. Prefer `BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT false` in the migration and `cancelled Boolean @default(false)` in the schema so the flag has a well-defined value for all rows.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same issue: the new 'cancelled' field/column is nullable and lacks a default value of 'false', resulting in existing (and new) records having NULL values, which can cause incorrect behavior when checking the cancellation status.

false_positives.candidate:
CRON cancellation uses wrong SendGrid endpoint and can cancel the wrong batch

The new cancellation loop calls `client.request({ url: "/v3/user/scheduled_sends", method: "POST", body: { batch_id: reminder.referenceId, status: "cancel" } })`. Per the PR description, the previously used `DELETE /v3/user/scheduled_sends/${referenceId}` was wrong because it removes the cancel status; the correct SendGrid API to cancel a scheduled send is `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends/{batch_id}` with body `{ status: "cancel" }` — i.e. the batch_id must be in the URL path, not in the request body. As written, the request posts to the collection endpoint with a `batch_id` field in the body, which SendGrid will not interpret as a cancellation of that batch. Additionally, `reminder.referenceId` is typed `string | null` and is passed directly as `batch_id`; if it is null the request is malformed. Consequence: cancelled/rescheduled booking emails are still sent, which is exactly the bug this PR claims to fix. The same wrong-endpoint pattern is used in `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` with `immediateDelete: true` (emailReminderManager.ts lines 213-223), which is called from workflows.tsx when a workflow or step is deleted.

Cancellation query does not filter by method, so SMS reminders are treated as SendGrid email batches

`remindersToCancel` is queried with only `cancelled: true` and a `scheduledDate` filter — there is no `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL` filter. The `cancelled` flag is only ever set by `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` (email path), but the query then uses `reminder.referenceId` as a SendGrid `batch_id` for every matching row. For SMS reminders the `referenceId` is a Twilio message SID, not a SendGrid batch id, so the CRON job would send a bogus cancellation request to SendGrid using a Twilio SID. More importantly, the subsequent `prisma.workflowReminder.delete` removes the row regardless of method, and the missing method filter means the intent (only cancel scheduled emails) is not enforced at the data layer. Add `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL` to the `where` clause.

Reminder rows are deleted even if the SendGrid cancellation fails, and a single failure aborts the whole loop

Inside the `for` loop, `await client.request(...)` is awaited before the delete promise is created. If the SendGrid request throws (network error, 4xx/5xx), the exception propagates to the outer `try/catch`, which logs and swallows it — but any reminders already queued in `workflowRemindersToDelete` are still deleted via `Promise.all`, and all remaining reminders in `remindersToCancel` are never processed. So a transient SendGrid failure causes: (1) rows whose emails were NOT actually cancelled to be deleted from the DB (the email will still be sent by SendGrid and the row is gone so it can never be retried), and (2) all subsequent cancelled reminders in the batch to be skipped entirely. The delete should only be enqueued after a successful cancellation response, and per-reminder errors should be caught individually so one failure doesn't abort the rest.

Past-due reminder cleanup deletes cancelled rows before they are processed, and deletes unscheduled rows that were never sent

The first statement `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany({ where: { method: EMAIL, scheduledDate: { lte: now } } })` runs BEFORE the cancellation block. Any reminder whose `scheduledDate` has already passed is deleted here without ever being checked against `cancelled` or being sent/cancelled at SendGrid. Two problems: (1) a reminder marked `cancelled: true` whose scheduled date just passed will be deleted by this statement and never reach the cancellation loop, so the SendGrid scheduled send is never cancelled and the email still goes out; (2) an unscheduled reminder (`scheduled: false`) whose date has passed is silently deleted without the email ever being sent (the later `unscheduledReminders` query only picks up dates within 72h in the future, so past-due unscheduled reminders are lost). The cleanup should exclude `cancelled: true` rows (or run after cancellation), and should not delete unscheduled past-due rows without attempting to send them.

Reschedule reminder cancellation is not awaited and uses immediateDelete for email only

When rescheduling, `originalRescheduledBooking.workflowReminders.forEach((reminder) => { ... deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true); ... deleteScheduledSMSReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId); })` is not awaited (the callback is not async and the calls are not collected). The surrounding `try/catch` therefore cannot actually catch async failures — it only catches synchronous throws. Additionally, the email path uses `immediateDelete: true`, which performs the (incorrect, see other finding) SendGrid cancel synchronously, while the SMS path deletes the DB row immediately. Because nothing is awaited, the new booking's `scheduleWorkflowReminders` (line 1269) can run concurrently with the old reminders' cancellation, and a failure leaves stale scheduled emails active for the old booking. Await each cancellation (e.g. `await Promise.all(originalRescheduledBooking.workflowReminders.map(...))`).

deleteScheduledEmailReminder deletes the row when referenceId is null, losing reminders that were never scheduled at SendGrid

When `referenceId` is null the function deletes the `workflowReminder` row outright. A null `referenceId` occurs for reminders created with `scheduled: false` (scheduled more than 72h out, handled later by the CRON job — see the `else if (scheduledDate.isAfter(currentDate.add(72, "hour")))` branch at line 182-193 which creates the row without a referenceId). Deleting such a row on booking cancellation is correct in intent, but the function conflates two cases: a reminder that was never scheduled (safe to delete) and a reminder that WAS scheduled at SendGrid but whose referenceId was lost/not stored. There is no `scheduled` check, so if a row has `scheduled: true` but a null referenceId (data inconsistency), the SendGrid send cannot be cancelled and the row is silently deleted, leaving an orphaned scheduled email. At minimum, guard with `scheduled: false` before deleting, and log when a scheduled reminder has no referenceId.

deleteScheduledSMSReminder deletes the DB row even when the Twilio cancellation fails

`deleteScheduledSMSReminder` calls `await twilio.cancelSMS(referenceId)` and then unconditionally `await prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` inside the same `try`. If `cancelSMS` throws, the catch block logs the error and the function returns — but because the delete is in the `try` after the cancel, a cancel failure skips the delete (row remains, which is arguably safe). However, the callers in `handleCancelBooking.ts` and `bookings.tsx` no longer delete reminder rows themselves (that logic was removed in this PR), so the ONLY thing standing between a cancelled booking and an SMS being sent is this function's `cancelSMS` call. If Twilio is down or the SID is invalid, the error is swallowed by the `catch` and the reminder row remains `scheduled: true` with a live Twilio SID — the SMS will still be delivered. There is no `cancelled` flag mechanism for SMS (unlike email), so a failed cancellation is unrecoverable and silent. At minimum, the function should rethrow or the callers should be notified, and ideally SMS reminders should also get the `cancelled` flag + CRON-based retry treatment that emails now have.

Reminder cancellation in workflow update is not awaited and rows are no longer deleted

In the `update` mutation, `remindersToDelete.flat().forEach((reminder) => { deleteScheduledEmailReminder(...); deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...); })` is fire-and-forget (no await, non-async callback). The previous code explicitly deleted the reminder rows via `ctx.prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany` and awaited `Promise.all(deleteReminderPromise)`; that deletion was removed in this PR. Now: (1) for email reminders with a referenceId, only `cancelled: true` is set and the row persists until the CRON job deletes it — but the CRON job only processes rows with `scheduledDate` within the next hour, so rows for bookings further out stay in the DB indefinitely with `cancelled: true` (they will never be sent because the unscheduled-reminders query filters `scheduled: false`, but they accumulate); (2) for email reminders WITHOUT a referenceId, `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` deletes the row, but since the call is not awaited, the subsequent `workflowsOnEventTypes.deleteMany` and step updates can run before the delete completes; (3) for SMS reminders the row is deleted inside `deleteScheduledSMSReminder`, again un-awaited. All of these should be collected into a promise array and awaited before proceeding.

userWorkflow.steps.map(async ...) is not awaited — step deletions and reminder cancellations race with the rest of the update

The block `userWorkflow.steps.map(async (oldStep) => { ... })` (line 505) uses `Array.map` with an async callback and is never awaited. Inside it: reminder cancellations (`deleteScheduledEmailReminder`/`deleteScheduledSMSReminder`, themselves async and un-awaited), `ctx.prisma.workflowStep.delete`, `ctx.prisma.workflowStep.update`, and `ctx.prisma.booking.findMany` + `scheduleEmailReminder`/`scheduleSMSReminder` calls. Because the outer `map` promise is discarded, the mutation can return (and the final `workflow.update` / `workflow.findFirst` at lines 814-842 can execute) before any of these complete. Consequences: the response can report a workflow state that doesn't yet reflect step deletions; reminder cancellations for deleted/edited steps may not have run before new reminders are scheduled (duplicate emails); and unhandled rejections from the async callbacks are uncaught. This should be `await Promise.all(userWorkflow.steps.map(async ...))` or a `for...of` loop with awaits.

Cancelled email reminders for far-future bookings accumulate forever

When a workflow is updated and event types are removed, email reminders are now marked `cancelled: true` instead of deleted (line 378). The CRON job `scheduleEmailReminders.ts` only selects cancelled reminders with `scheduledDate <= now + 1 hour` (line 44-51) and deletes them after cancelling at SendGrid. A reminder for a booking that is, say, 30 days out will therefore sit in the DB with `cancelled: true` for 30 days, and — more importantly — the `unscheduledReminders` query (line 80-98) filters `scheduled: false`, so a cancelled-but-still-`scheduled: true` row is never picked up for sending (good), but it is also never cleaned up until its date is within an hour. This is a slow leak of dead rows and means the `cancelled` flag must be checked in every future query that touches workflow reminders. Consider deleting the row immediately when the booking is far in the future and the SendGrid send can be cancelled right away, or adding a cleanup for old cancelled rows.

Unscheduled-reminders query can pick up cancelled reminders and send them

The `unscheduledReminders` query filters `method: EMAIL, scheduled: false, scheduledDate <= now + 72h` but does NOT filter `cancelled: false` (or `cancelled: null`). A reminder that was created with `scheduled: false` (booking more than 72h out) and later cancelled via `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` (which sets `cancelled: true` but leaves `scheduled: false` and keeps the row) will match this query once its `scheduledDate` falls within the 72-hour window. The CRON job will then schedule and send the email via SendGrid even though the booking was cancelled — reintroducing the exact bug this PR is meant to fix, for the >72h cancellation case. The query must add `cancelled: false` (or `NOT: { cancelled: true }`) to the where clause. Note the cancellation block only handles reminders within the next hour, so a reminder cancelled while still >1h out but <72h out is never cancelled at SendGrid and would be sent by this query.

Email reminders cancelled via flag but SMS reminders deleted immediately — inconsistent lifecycle and lost audit trail

For a cancelled booking, email reminders are now marked `cancelled: true` and left in the DB (deletion deferred to the CRON job), while SMS reminders are deleted immediately by `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` (smsReminderManager.ts line 182). This asymmetry means: (1) the `workflowReminders` relation on the booking behaves differently per method, which can surprise any code inspecting reminders of a cancelled booking; (2) if the Twilio cancel fails, the row is still deleted (the delete is in the same try block after the cancel — actually it is skipped on throw, but the caller doesn't await or check, so the outcome is nondeterministic from the caller's perspective); (3) there is no record that an SMS reminder existed for a cancelled booking. For consistency and recoverability, SMS reminders should follow the same pattern: mark `cancelled: true` and let a CRON job perform the Twilio cancellation (the `scheduleSMSReminders` CRON would need a matching block), or at minimum the delete should only happen after a confirmed successful Twilio cancellation and the call should be awaited.

requestReschedule reminder cancellation is not awaited

In the `requestReschedule` mutation, `bookingToReschedule.workflowReminders.forEach((reminder) => { deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId); deleteScheduledSMSReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId); })` is fire-and-forget. The previous implementation collected `PrismaPromise`s and awaited `Promise.all(remindersToDelete)`. Now nothing is awaited, so the mutation can complete (and the reschedule email at line 567 can be sent) before the old reminders are actually cancelled/marked. If the process crashes or the DB update fails silently (both delete functions swallow errors internally), the old booking's reminders remain active and the attendee receives reminders for a booking that has been marked `rescheduled: true` / `CANCELLED`. Collect the promises and `await Promise.all(...)`.

Marking a reminder cancelled does not clear scheduled/referenceId, leaving stale SendGrid state

When a reminder is cancelled via the flag (`prisma.workflowReminder.update({ data: { cancelled: true } })`), the row keeps `scheduled: true` and its `referenceId` (the SendGrid batch id). The CRON job later cancels the SendGrid send and deletes the row, which is fine, but between cancellation and CRON execution the row still claims `scheduled: true`. Any other code that queries scheduled reminders (e.g. to display or count them) will see a cancelled reminder as still scheduled. Consider also setting `scheduled: false` when marking `cancelled: true`, so the row's state is unambiguous, and ensure the CRON cancellation block keys off `cancelled` rather than `scheduled`.

Cancellation loop performs a sequential await per reminder inside a for-loop

The cancellation loop `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel) { await client.request(...); ... }` serializes all SendGrid cancellation API calls. With many cancelled reminders due within the hour (the exact scenario this PR is fixing — previously cancellations failed after 100 pending), the CRON job (running every 15 minutes) could take a long time and risk overlapping runs or timing out. The deletes are already batched via `Promise.all(workflowRemindersToDelete)`, but the API calls are not. Consider batching the SendGrid requests with limited concurrency (e.g. `Promise.all` over chunks, or a concurrency-limited mapper) so the job completes quickly and predictably.

true_positives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blacklist comparison is case-sensitive while blacklist entries are lowercased

`blacklistedGuestEmails` entries are lowercased (line 71), but the guest emails from user input are compared without lowercasing (`blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)` on line 77). A blacklisted address such as `blocked@example.com` can be bypassed by submitting `Blocked@Example.com` (emails are case-insensitive in the local part per common practice and Prisma stores what is given). The guest filter should lowercase `guest` before comparing, e.g. `!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest.toLowerCase())`. The same case-sensitivity issue applies to the duplicate-attendee check on line 76 (`guest === attendee.email`), allowing the same person to be added twice with different casing.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: `blacklistedGuestEmails` is lowercased, while the input `guest` is not lowercased before calling `blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)`, allowing a bypass via uppercase characters.

true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Authorization check uses AND instead of OR for team admin/owner, and allows any attendee to add guests

The permission check computes `isTeamAdminOrOwner = (await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...))`, which is only true when the user is BOTH a team admin and a team owner — a condition that is essentially never true (a user has one role per team). Combined with the `isAttendee` check on line 52, this means the effective authorization is: the booking organizer OR ANY existing attendee of the booking. Any attendee (a guest invited to the meeting) can therefore call `viewer.bookings.addGuests` and add arbitrary email addresses to the booking, triggering calendar updates and emails to those addresses. This is a privilege-escalation/authorization flaw: guests should not be able to modify the attendee list. The `&&` should be `||` (matching the intended 'admin or owner' semantics), and the `isAttendee` branch should almost certainly be removed or restricted (e.g., only the organizer or team admin/owner may add guests).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: the permission check uses AND (&&) instead of OR (||) when checking `isTeamAdmin` and `isTeamOwner`. While it also includes an additional observation about `isAttendee`, the core issue from the golden comment is clearly and accurately captured.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sendAddGuestsEmails ignores eventTypeMetadata email-disable settings and sends scheduled email to new guests without their context

Unlike every other send* function in this file (e.g., `sendScheduledEmails`, `sendRescheduledEmails`, `sendLocationChangeEmails`), `sendAddGuestsEmails` (line 525) accepts no `eventTypeMetadata` parameter and therefore never checks `eventTypeDisableHostEmail`/`eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail`. Event types configured with `disableStandardEmails` (metadata) will still receive organizer/attendee emails when guests are added, violating the organizer's email preferences. The handler has `booking.eventType` available and should pass `booking.eventType.metadata` through. Additionally, new guests receive `AttendeeScheduledEmail` (line 542) — a full 'booking confirmed' email — which may be misleading since no new booking was created for them; a dedicated 'you were added as a guest' template would be more accurate, but at minimum the metadata-based suppression must be honored.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue directly identifies the exact same bug described in the golden comment: `sendAddGuestsEmails` does not accept or check `eventTypeMetadata` for the `disableStandardEmails` flags, causing emails to be sent to hosts and attendees even when disabled.

false_positives.candidate:
Attendee creation is not atomic with the duplicate/blacklist filtering — race condition can create duplicate attendees

The handler first reads the booking's attendees (line 26), filters out emails already present (line 74-78), and then performs a separate `prisma.booking.update` with `createMany` (lines 92-106). There is no transaction and no unique constraint enforcement shown between the read and the write. Two concurrent `addGuests` calls (or a concurrent booking flow adding the same attendee) can both pass the duplicate check and both insert the same email, producing duplicate Attendee rows for one booking. This corrupts attendee lists, calendar events, and emails. The read-filter-write sequence should be wrapped in an interactive transaction (`prisma.$transaction`) with the duplicate check re-evaluated inside it, or rely on a DB unique constraint on (bookingId, email) with `skipDuplicates`/error handling.

Calendar update failure aborts the mutation after attendees were already persisted, leaving DB and calendar out of sync

`eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` (line 165) is awaited outside any try/catch and outside the DB transaction. If the calendar update throws (network error, invalid credentials, provider failure), the new Attendee rows created at line 92 remain committed in the database, but the mutation returns an error to the client. The booking now has guests in the DB who never received a calendar invite update, and a retry would hit the duplicate filter and report 'emails_must_be_unique_valid'. Either wrap the DB write and calendar update in a transaction with compensating logic, or catch the calendar error and report partial success; as written, failures leave inconsistent state with no rollback.

Email sending failure is silently swallowed with only a console.log

The `try { await sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests); } catch (err) { console.log("Error sending AddGuestsEmails"); }` block (lines 167-171) swallows all email errors and still returns `{ message: "Guests added" }` as success. New guests are added to the booking and the calendar is updated, but if the email dispatch fails (SMTP down, template render error), neither the new guests nor the organizer is notified, and the organizer sees a success toast. The error is only written to server logs with no structured logging (the codebase uses `logger` from `@calcom/lib/logger` elsewhere). At minimum this should use the structured logger and ideally surface a degraded-success indication to the caller.

No validation that the booking is in a state that permits adding guests (cancelled/past bookings can be modified)

The handler fetches the booking by id and only checks existence and caller permission. It never checks `booking.status` (e.g., CANCELLED or REJECTED) or whether the booking is in the past. Adding guests to a cancelled booking resurrects attendee rows, sends 'guests added' emails and calendar REQUEST updates for an event that was cancelled, and mutates historical/past bookings. Other handlers in this router (e.g., editLocation) enforce status constraints. A guard such as rejecting when `booking.status === BookingStatus.CANCELLED` (and arguably when the booking end time is in the past) is needed.

Calendar update uses the requesting user's credentials instead of the booking organizer's credentials

`getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` (line 158) loads the credentials of whoever is calling the mutation, and the `EventManager` is constructed with `...user` (the caller). If the caller is a team admin/owner or (per the flawed check) an attendee rather than the booking organizer, the calendar update for the organizer's event is attempted with the wrong user's credentials — the update may fail, be written to the wrong calendar, or be attributed to the wrong account. Calendar mutations for a booking should use the booking organizer's credentials (the booking already includes `user.credentials` and `user.destinationCalendar` in the query at lines 35-40, which are loaded but never used). The loaded organizer credentials should be passed to the EventManager instead of `ctx.user`'s.

Organizer email subject uses attendees[0].name which may be a newly added guest with an empty name

The subject interpolates `name: this.calEvent.attendees[0].name` (line 28). In the handler, newly created guests are inserted with `name: ""` (addGuests.handler.ts line 85), and attendee ordering after `createMany` is not guaranteed to put the original booker first. If a newly added guest (empty name) ends up at index 0, the organizer email subject renders as 'Guests Added: <eventType> with  at <date>' with a blank name. The subject should use the original booker (the attendee that existed before the addition) or fall back to the organizer/team name as the attendee template does (`this.calEvent.team?.name || this.calEvent.organizer.name`).

Client-side validation accepts an array containing a single empty string as valid input path is blocked, but empty-string entries in multi-row input are not rejected before submit when combined with valid emails

The zod schema `z.array(z.string().email())` (line 26) rejects empty strings, so `handleAdd` correctly blocks submission when any row is empty — but only after the user clicks Add, and the error message shown ('emails_must_be_unique_valid') does not distinguish 'invalid/empty email' from 'duplicate email'. More importantly, `isInvalidEmail` is never reset to `false` when the user subsequently edits the emails to valid values (it is only reset on cancel or success), so after one failed attempt the red error banner stays visible even when the input becomes valid. The error state should be cleared on value change (e.g., in `setMultiEmailValue` wrapper) or recomputed on each submit attempt.

MultiEmail mutates/reassigns the `value` prop and uses array index as React key, and removal of the last email hides the input entirely

Line 14 reassigns the `value` prop (`value = value || []`), which is a React anti-pattern (props should not be reassigned) though functionally harmless here. More concretely: (1) `key={index}` on line 26 for a list of editable text inputs causes React to reuse DOM/component state incorrectly when a middle row is removed — typing in row 2 after deleting row 1 can show stale values; a stable key (or the field content) should be used. (2) When the user removes the last remaining email via the remove button (lines 39-43), `value` becomes `[]`, and the component renders only the 'add emails' button (lines 77-91) — the label disappears and the UI affordance changes shape, which is disorienting inside the AddGuestsDialog where the dialog starts with `[""]` (one empty row) and the label 'Add Emails' is shown above the input.

'Add guests' action is offered for bookings where it cannot work (recurring series tab removes edit menu, but action also appears for past/cancelled/rejected bookings and non-organizers)

The `add_members` action is unconditionally added to `editBookingActions` (lines 194-200), which is only rendered under `bookedActions` → shown when `isConfirmed` (line 549) for upcoming bookings, or for past bookings (line 554). It is therefore offered for past bookings (where the server handler does not reject past bookings — see handler finding) and for cancelled bookings in some render paths. Additionally, the menu is shown to any viewer of the booking list; given the server-side authorization flaw (attendees can add guests), the UI gives no indication of who may use it. At minimum the action should be hidden for past bookings (`isBookingInPast`) and cancelled bookings, consistent with how `cancel` is filtered (lines 249-251).

Used backup codes are nulled instead of removed, breaking exhaustion detection and leaving null entries in stored JSON

`backupCodes[index] = null` replaces the used code with `null` rather than removing it from the array. Consequences: (1) the stored JSON array accumulates nulls, so `backupCodes.length` no longer reflects remaining codes; (2) when all 10 codes are used, the array is `[null × 10]`, `user.backupCodes` remains a non-null encrypted string, so the `!user.backupCodes` check that should produce `MissingBackupCodes` never triggers — users see 'incorrect backup code' forever instead of being told to generate new codes; (3) the null entries are indistinguishable from data corruption. Backup codes have only 40 bits of entropy (5 bytes hex), too low for single-use account-recovery codes

`crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex")` produces 10 hex characters = 40 bits of entropy. With 10 codes, the total keyspace is 2^40 ≈ 1.1×10^12. Rate limiting exists (`checkRateLimitAndThrowError` keyed on email in the login path), but the disable-2FA endpoint (`disable.ts`) has no per-user rate limit on backup-code attempts beyond the global limiter, and 40 bits is brute-forceable if rate limits are misconfigured or bypassed (e.g., distributed attempts). Industry guidance for backup/recovery codes is at least 80–128 bits (e.g., 16–32 hex chars). Increasing to `crypto.randomBytes(8)` (64 bits, 16 hex chars) or more would align with OWASP recommendations and the existing 10-char display format can be extended (e.g., two groups).

When such a user switches to the backup code screen, they still need to provide their password (first factor) plus the backup code (second factor). The schema requires password, which is correct. However, the schema does not validate the `backupCode` field at all — it's passed through via `.passthrough()`. This means an empty backup code can be submitted, and the server will return `MissingBackupCodes` or `IncorrectBackupCode`. The client could validate that `backupCode` is non-empty when in backup mode, but this is a UX nit. The actual issue: when `totpEmail` is set (Google/SAML), the password field is hidden (line 193: `{ hidden: twoFactorRequired }`), and the schema forces password to `""`. But the server-side credentials provider for Google/SAML users expects no password (they authenticated via OAuth). The check `if (!user.password && user.identityProvider === IdentityProvider.CAL)` returns UserMissingPassword, but the subsequent password verification at line 40-45 is gated on `user.password && user.identityProvider === IdentityProvider.CAL` — for Google/SAML users with 2FA, no password is required to disable 2FA, only a TOTP or backup code

This means a Google/SAML user with 2FA enabled can disable 2FA by providing only a valid TOTP code or backup code — no password re-authentication. This is a security weakness: if an attacker gains access to a user's Google account (e.g., stolen session), they can disable 2FA with just a TOTP code (which they might phish) or a backup code, without needing the Cal.com password (which the user may not even have). The disable endpoint should require password re-authentication for CAL users (it does) AND require a recent authentication or additional confirmation for all users. Currently, for non-CAL users, the only barrier is the second factor itself — disabling 2FA with a second factor is circular (you need 2FA to disable 2FA). This is actually a common pattern, but it means an attacker with a stolen session + one valid TOTP/backup code can permanently disable 2FA. The finding: the endpoint does not require step-up authentication (e.g., password or recent login) beyond the second factor for non-CAL users, making 2FA disable too easy if the second factor is compromised.

The regex `/"\//.test(callbackUrl)` to strip leading quotes/slashes is fragile and does not match the comment's intent

Line 86: `if (/"\//.test(callbackUrl)) callbackUrl = callbackUrl.substring(1);` — the regex `/"\//` matches a double-quote followed by a forward slash (`"/`). This is intended to strip a leading `"/` from callback URLs that may be quoted. However, the regex is not anchored (`^`), so it matches `"/` anywhere in the string, and `substring(1)` removes only the first character regardless of what it is. If `callbackUrl` is `https://example.com/"/path`, the regex matches `"/` in the middle, and `substring(1)` removes the `h`, corrupting the URL. This is a pre-existing bug (not introduced by this PR), but it's in a changed file and worth noting. The fix is to anchor the regex: `/^"\//` or better, use a proper URL parser.

The setup endpoint returns plaintext backup codes in the response — if the response is logged or cached, codes are exposed

CRITICAL: Backup codes have only 40 bits of entropy — brute-forceable without strict rate limiting, especially in the disable endpoint which has no rate limiting

An attacker with a valid session and password can brute-force the disable endpoint at network speed. Even with rate limiting, 40 bits is considered too low for account recovery codes by modern standards (OWASP recommends at least 80 bits). Increasing to `crypto.randomBytes(8)` (64 bits, 16 hex chars) or `crypto.randomBytes(10)` (80 bits, 20 hex chars) would significantly improve security. The step has already changed to EnterTotpCode, so the user sees the TOTP input with an error message 'Code is incorrect. Please try again.' even though they haven't entered anything. This is a broken UX and a bug. The fix: the button should be `type="button"` and only call `setStep`.

CRITICAL: The 'Lost access' / 'Go back' toggle button lacks type="button" and will submit the form, triggering an unintended 2FA disable API call

The toggle button (line 113-121) is inside `<Form handleSubmit={handleDisable}>` (line 91). It has `onClick` but no `type="button"`. In HTML, a `<button>` without `type` inside a form defaults to `type="submit"`. Clicking 'Lost access' or 'Go back' will: (1) execute the `onClick` handler (toggling state), AND (2) submit the form, calling `handleDisable` with the current form values. If the user has entered their password and clicks 'Lost access' to switch to backup code input, the form submits with the password and an empty `totpCode`/`backupCode`, causing `TwoFactorAuthAPI.disable` to be called. The server will return `SecondFactorRequired` (no code provided), and the error message '2FA required' will appear — but the user just wanted to switch input modes. This is a critical UX bug that will frustrate users and cause unnecessary API calls. The fix: add `type="button"` to the toggle button and the Cancel button (line 122).

The Cancel button lacks type="button" and will submit the form, calling handleEnable with stale totpCode

The Cancel button (line 222-230) is inside `<Form handleSubmit={handleEnable}>`. It has `onClick={() => { onCancel(); resetState(); }}` but no `type="button"`. Clicking it will submit the form, calling `handleEnable` with the current `totpCode` value (which may be a partial or stale code from a previous attempt). This triggers an API call to `TwoFactorAuthAPI.enable(totpCode)` even though the user is cancelling. The `onCancel()` and `resetState()` run, but the form submission also happens, causing a race: the modal may close while the API call is in flight, and the response may set an error message on an unmounted component. The fix: add `type="button"` to the Cancel button.

CRITICAL: Google/SAML users with 2FA cannot use backup codes — the 'Lost access' button is hidden in the totpEmail flow, locking users out if they lose their authenticator

When a Google/SAML user with 2FA logs in, the `signIn` callback redirects to `/auth/login?totp=...`, setting `totpEmail`. The login page renders `ExternalTotpFooter` (line 135-143) which contains ONLY a Cancel button. The 'Lost access' button that switches to the backup code input is part of `TwoFactorFooter` (line 103-133), which is only rendered when `!totpEmail` (line 180-182: `twoFactorRequired ? !totpEmail ? TwoFactorFooter : ExternalTotpFooter : ...`). This means Google/SAML users with 2FA enabled have NO way to use a backup code if they lose their authenticator — they are permanently locked out. The server-side credentials provider supports backup codes (the backup code branch in next-auth-options.ts works for any user with `twoFactorEnabled` and `backupCodes`), but the UI never offers the input. This is a critical feature gap: the PR claims to 'enable their use during 2fa login flow' but only for CAL (password) users, not for Google/SAML users who also have 2FA. The fix: show the 'Lost access' button in the `ExternalTotpFooter` as well, or merge the footers to always offer backup code login when 2FA is required.

Clearing the TOTP input does not clear the form value — stale codes can be submitted after deletion

Line 20-23: `useEffect(() => { if (value) methods.setValue("totpCode", value); }, [value]);` — the `if (value)` guard means that when the user deletes all digits (value becomes `""`), `setValue` is NOT called. The form's `totpCode` retains the last non-empty value. If the user types a 6-digit code, then deletes all digits, and submits the form (e.g., by pressing Enter), the form submits the OLD 6-digit code, not an empty string. This could cause an unintended login attempt with a stale code, or a confusing error message. The fix: remove the `if (value)` guard so `setValue` is always called: `methods.setValue("totpCode", value)`. This is a pre-existing bug but affects the 2FA flow modified by this PR.

`useState([])` infers `never[]` type — TypeScript errors when setting string[] and when mapping

Line 64: `const [backupCodes, setBackupCodes] = useState([]);` — TypeScript infers the type as `never[]`. When `setBackupCodes(body.backupCodes)` is called (line 92), `body.backupCodes` is `any` (from `response.json()`), so no compile error. But when `backupCodes.map((code) => ...)` is called (line 203), `code` is typed as `never`, and `formatBackupCode(code)` expects `string`, causing a TypeScript error: `Argument of type 'never' is not assignable to parameter of type 'string'`. Actually, `never` is assignable to `string`, so no error. But `backupCodes` being `never[]` means any operation that expects `string[]` will fail. The fix: `useState<string[]>([])`.

Setup endpoint can be called repeatedly to rotate TOTP secret and backup codes, enabling account takeover by an attacker with the password

The endpoint checks `user.twoFactorEnabled` (line 42) but NOT whether `user.twoFactorSecret` is already set (setup in progress). It unconditionally generates a new secret and backup codes and overwrites the existing ones (lines 63-72). An attacker who has the user's password (e.g., via credential stuffing, phishing, or a data breach) can call this endpoint repeatedly to: (1) generate a new TOTP secret and configure their own authenticator app, (2) obtain fresh backup codes, (3) invalidate the user's existing authenticator (DoS). The attacker can then complete the setup (enable 2FA with their own TOTP) and lock the user out. There is no 'setup in progress' guard, no idempotency, and no re-authentication requirement beyond the password (which the attacker has). The fix: if `user.twoFactorSecret` is already set and 2FA is not enabled, either return the existing secret/codes (idempotent) or require a fresh session / additional confirmation before rotating.

Setup response lacks Cache-Control: no-store — plaintext TOTP secret and backup codes may be cached

The response (line 78) contains `secret` (TOTP secret), `keyUri`, and `backupCodes` (plaintext). Next.js API routes may set default caching headers, and browsers or intermediaries (proxies, browser extensions) could cache this response. An attacker with access to the browser cache or a shared computer could retrieve the TOTP secret and backup codes, compromising the account. The endpoint should set `res.setHeader("Cache-Control", "no-store")` to prevent any caching.

No error handling around symmetricDecrypt + JSON.parse of backupCodes — corrupted data causes unhandled 500 on login

Line 139-141: `const backupCodes = JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, process.env.CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY));` — if `user.backupCodes` is corrupted (wrong encryption key, DB tampering, partial write), `symmetricDecrypt` may return garbage or throw, and `JSON.parse` will throw. This exception is not caught in `authorize()`, so NextAuth returns a generic 500 error. The user cannot log in, and the error is not logged with context. The same issue exists in `disable.ts` line 58. Fix: wrap in try-catch, log the error, and throw `ErrorCode.InternalServerError` or `MissingBackupCodes`.

No error handling around symmetricDecrypt + JSON.parse of backupCodes — corrupted data causes unhandled 500 on 2FA disable

Same as next-auth-options.ts: line 58 `const backupCodes = JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, process.env.CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY));` — corrupted data causes an unhandled exception and a 500 response. The user cannot disable 2FA and may not be able to log in either. Fix: wrap in try-catch with appropriate error handling.

The PR adds backup code generation, display, login, and disable functionality, but the e2e tests only verify the display screen (download, copy, close buttons). There are NO tests for: (1) logging in with a backup code via the 'Lost access' flow, (2) verifying a used backup code cannot be reused (single-use enforcement), (3) disabling 2FA using a backup code, (4) the exhaustion scenario (all codes used → MissingBackupCodes), (5) incorrect backup code error handling. The TODO at line 12 acknowledges this. The PR checklist admits 'I haven't added tests that prove my fix is effective or that my feature works'. For a security feature like backup codes, this is a significant gap — regressions in single-use enforcement or code consumption would not be caught.

Line 19: `label=""` — passing an empty string as the label prop likely renders an empty `<label>` element in the `TextField` component. This is redundant (there's already a `<Label>` above at line 13) and an accessibility anti-pattern (empty labels confuse screen readers). The `label` prop should be omitted entirely.

Non-CAL users (Google/SAML) can disable 2FA with only a TOTP or backup code — no password re-authentication required

For Google/SAML users (no password), the endpoint proceeds directly to 2FA verification (TOTP or backup code). This means an attacker with a stolen Google session (or stolen backup code) can disable 2FA without any additional authentication beyond the second factor itself. Disabling 2FA with a second factor is circular: you need 2FA to disable 2FA. If the attacker has one valid TOTP code (phished) or one backup code, they can permanently disable 2FA and then log in with just the Google account. The endpoint should require step-up authentication (e.g., recent login timestamp check, or password for CAL users, or email confirmation) for ALL users, not just CAL users.

`body.backupCodes` is not validated — if undefined, `.map` at line 95 throws TypeError

Line 92: `setBackupCodes(body.backupCodes);` then line 95: `body.backupCodes.map(formatBackupCode)`. If the API returns 200 but `backupCodes` is missing (server bug, API version mismatch), `body.backupCodes` is `undefined`, and `.map` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'map')`. `formatBackupCode` assumes exactly 10 characters — shorter codes produce malformed output

Line 163: `const formatBackupCode = (code: string) => `${code.slice(0, 5)}-${code.slice(5, 10)}`;` — if `code` is shorter than 10 chars, `slice(5, 10)` returns a partial or empty string, producing `XXXXX-` or `XXXXX-YY`. `Array.from(Array(10), ...)` creates a sparse array — use `Array.from({ length: 10 }, ...)` instead

Line 61: `Array.from(Array(10), () => crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex"))` — `Array(10)` creates a sparse array of length 10 with no elements. `Array.from` then iterates and maps. A cleaner approach is `Array.from({ length: 10 }, () => ...)` which avoids the sparse array. Micro-optimization, low severity.

The `backupCodes` column stores encrypted JSON. There is no DB constraint to validate the JSON structure or limit size. If the data is corrupted (wrong key, tampering), `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` throws in the login/disable paths (no try-catch). The application should handle parse errors gracefully (see related findings). The schema itself is fine, but the lack of application-level error handling is the issue.

Unanchored regex `/"\//` for callbackUrl stripping can match mid-string and corrupt URLs

Line 86: `if (/"\//.test(callbackUrl)) callbackUrl = callbackUrl.substring(1);` — the regex matches `"/` anywhere in the string, not just at the start. This means for collective events, when EventManager iterates destination calendars and calls createEvent with host B's credential, the Lark/Office365/Caldav services will still create the event on the FIRST destination calendar (host A's) rather than the calendar matching the credentialId passed. The interface change is not honored by these implementations, so multi-host support silently degrades to "create N duplicate events on host A's calendar" for non-Google providers. Each implementation must use the credentialId to select the matching destination calendar entry (as GoogleCalendarService now does).

The code does `let calendar = mainHostDestinationCalendar ? mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration.split("_") : "calendar";` then `if (Array.isArray(calendar)) { const calendarCap = calendar.map(...); calendar = calendarCap[0] + " " + calendarCap[1]; }`. If mainHostDestinationCalendar is undefined, calendar stays the string "calendar" and the Array.isArray branch is skipped — OK. But the undefined-second-element case produces broken user-facing text. Should guard `calendarCap[1] ?? ""` or use a proper display name.

In BaseCalendarService.createEvent, `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = event.destinationCalendar ?? For a collective event with multiple hosts each having their own CalDAV/Apple calendar credential, EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents calls createEvent once per destination entry with a different credential — but each BaseCalendarService instance is constructed with ONE credential (the host's), and `this.listCalendars(event)` returns that host's calendars. The filter then picks only the calendar matching the FIRST destination calendar's externalId, which belongs to a different host/credential. So for host B's credential, the event is either created on no calendar (if externalIds don't match) or on host A's calendar URL using host B's credentials (auth failure). The filter should match by the credential's own calendars (i.e. create on the primary calendar of THIS credential) rather than by the first destination calendar's externalId. referencesToCreate externalCalendarId/credentialId now come from result, but for non-calendar results they are undefined, and for calendar results the externalId is the passed-in destination.externalId which may be undefined

In the else branch (line 380) and the no-destinationCalendar fallback (line 391) and the other_calendar branch (line 403), createEvent is called WITHOUT externalId, so result.externalId is undefined. The booking reference then stores externalCalendarId = undefined, meaning on update/delete the calendar service cannot locate the specific calendar and falls back to primary — which may be wrong for users with multiple calendars. Previously the code used `evt.destinationCalendar?.externalId` which had the same issue but at least was consistent. The reference should store the actual external calendar id returned by the calendar service (creationResult) or the destination.externalId in all branches.

In handlePaymentSuccess, the evt is built with `destinationCalendar: booking.destinationCalendar ? [booking.destinationCalendar] : user.destinationCalendar ? For collective team bookings paid via PayPal, only the organizer's destination calendar is included; other hosts' calendars are not, so calendar events are only created for the organizer. This is the same multi-host gap as handleNewBooking but in the payment-confirmation path — collective paid bookings confirmed via PayPal webhook will miss host calendar events.

Stripe webhook evt.destinationCalendar only includes booking/user calendar, missing team hosts for collective paid bookings

Both getBooking (line 101-119) and handlePaymentSuccess (line 207-229) build evt.destinationCalendar from only `booking.destinationCalendar || user.destinationCalendar`. For collective team bookings where the organizer is not the only host, the other hosts' destination calendars are not included, so when `eventManager.create(evt)` runs (lines 242, 331), only the organizer's calendar receives the event. confirmHandler evt.destinationCalendar only includes booking/user calendar, missing other hosts for collective bookings

The evt built in confirmHandler sets `destinationCalendar: booking?.destinationCalendar ? [booking.destinationCalendar] : user.destinationCalendar ? [user.destinationCalendar] : []`. For collective team bookings requiring confirmation, when the organizer confirms, handleConfirmation → EventManager.create runs with only the organizer's destination calendar. Other hosts' calendars are not included, so their calendar events are not created upon confirmation. The booking query (lines 38-91) doesn't fetch eventType hosts or users with their destination calendars. This breaks the multi-host support for collective events that require confirmation.

bookingReminder evt.destinationCalendar only includes booking/user calendar, not team hosts

The reminder cron builds `selectedDestinationCalendar = booking.destinationCalendar || user.destinationCalendar` and wraps it in an array. For collective team bookings, only one calendar is included. The reminder email itself (sendOrganizerRequestReminderEmail) may not create calendar events, so impact is limited to email content/links, but if any downstream consumer uses evt.destinationCalendar to schedule or display calendar info, hosts are missing. Low impact but inconsistent with the multi-host goal.

Office365CalendarService.createEvent uses `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = event.destinationCalendar ?? [];` and builds the URL from `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.externalId`. When EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents calls createEvent once per destination calendar entry (each with a different credentialId), the Office365 service ignores the credentialId parameter (the interface now requires it but this implementation's signature is still `createEvent(event: CalendarEvent)` — it doesn't even declare the second parameter). So for host B's credential, the service still uses the FIRST destination calendar's externalId (host A's calendar) with host B's access token — either failing auth or creating the event on the wrong calendar. The service must use the credentialId to find the matching destination calendar entry, like GoogleCalendarService does.

Office365CalendarService.updateEvent (line 94-109) always uses `/me/calendar/events/${uid}` and deleteEvent (line 111-123) always uses `/me/calendar/events/${uid}`, ignoring both the `externalCalendarId` parameter and `event.destinationCalendar`. The class declares `destinationCalendar?: DestinationCalendar[] | null;` using the Prisma model type. Error message substring extraction can produce confusing output when start/end indices overlap or exceed string lengths

In the error reporting code (lines 101-111), the start and end indices are computed to strip common prefix/suffix, then `value.substring(start, value.length() - end)` and `sanitized.substring(start, sanitized.length() - end)` are used. If `start + end > value.length()` (which can happen if the strings are very different), `value.length() - end` could be less than `start`, causing a `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException`. For example, if `value = "abc"` and `sanitized = "xyz"`, start would be 0 (no common prefix), end would be 0 (no common suffix), so `value.substring(0, 3)` is fine. But if `value = "a"` and `sanitized = "b"`, start=0, end=0, fine. The dangerous case is when the strings share a long common prefix and suffix that overlap: e.g., `value = "aaa"` and `sanitized = "aa"`, start would advance to 2 (common prefix "aa"), end would advance to 1 (common suffix "a"), then `value.substring(2, 3-1=2)` → `substring(2,2)` → empty string, and `sanitized.substring(2, 2-1=1)` → `substring(2,1)` → `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException` because start > end. This would crash the verifier with an unhelpful exception instead of reporting the illegal HTML. The code should guard against `start + end > length` by clamping or using `Math.min`.

Grant type read from client session context is not the grant type that created the token

getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext() reads the grant type from `clientSessionContext.getAttribute(Constants.GRANT_TYPE)`. However, this attribute is set on the client session context at token-creation time (e.g. in OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse, ResourceOwnerPasswordCredentialsGrantType, StandardTokenExchangeProvider) and, critically, in TokenManager.refreshToken() the attribute is overwritten with `OAuth2Constants.REFRESH_TOKEN` before creating the new access token. More importantly, the attribute persists on the client session across multiple token issuances: a client session created by an authorization-code grant keeps GRANT_TYPE=authorization_code, so a later access token issued via the refresh-token grant on the same client session would be encoded with the stale original grant type unless every issuance path overwrites it. Any token-creation path that does not set this attribute (e.g. service-account/client-credentials flows that build the ClientSessionContext differently, admin-initiated impersonation, or token creation via TokenManager.createClientAccessToken from other callers) will silently encode the wrong grant type or 'na'. The encoded grant type therefore cannot be trusted as 'the grant type used to create this token' without auditing every caller of createClientAccessToken/initToken.

getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext() determines TokenType via `AbstractOIDCProtocolMapper.getShouldUseLightweightToken(session)`, which reads `session.getAttribute(Constants.USE_LIGHTWEIGHT_ACCESS_TOKEN_ENABLED)` and the client attribute. The session attribute is set by token-exchange code paths (e.g. lightweight token exchange) and may be set or cleared at arbitrary points during request processing. If the session attribute is set after initToken() runs, or if a token is created in a context where the session attribute reflects a different decision than the one actually applied to the token (TokenManager decides lightweight-ness in formatTokenType/applyMapper based on the same helper, but the two calls are not atomic), the encoded token-type shortcut can disagree with the actual token type. The PR's stated goal — 'recognize more reliably if access-token is lightweight or not' — is undermined if the encoded value can be wrong; consumers using the prefix to decide whether to trust in-token roles would make incorrect authorization decisions.

Decoding a token id containing a colon in the raw id mis-parses the context

getTokenContextFromTokenId() uses `encodedTokenId.indexOf(':')` to split prefix from raw id. If the raw id itself contains a ':' (KeycloakModelUtils.generateId() produces UUIDs today, but the SPI contract allows custom encoders/providers and the raw id is opaque), the first colon is found correctly only if the prefix contains no colon — which holds for the default encoder. However, the bigger issue: any legacy or foreign token id that happens to contain a colon (e.g. `foo:bar`) is treated as an encoded id; `encodedContext.length() != 6` then throws IllegalArgumentException. Throwing on arbitrary token ids means any code path that decodes a token id (introspection, userInfo, admin API) will throw an unhandled exception for malformed/legacy ids that contain a colon but are not 6-char-prefixed, instead of degrading to UNKNOWN as the no-colon branch does. This is an inconsistent and fragile contract: ids without ':' are tolerated, ids with ':' but wrong prefix length crash the request.

Duplicate-shortcut validation compares map sizes, which does not detect collisions

postInit() validates uniqueness of grant shortcuts by checking `grantsByShortcuts.size() != grantsToShortcuts.size()`. This is incorrect: if two different grant types share the same shortcut, `grantsByShortcuts.put(shortcut, grantName)` overwrites one entry (size stays smaller) while `grantsToShortcuts` gains two entries — sizes differ, so it is caught. But if two different grant types share the same ID (impossible via getId contract) or, more realistically, if a shortcut collides AND a grant name collides in a compensating way, sizes can be equal while mappings are wrong. More importantly, the check cannot detect the case where one grant's shortcut equals another grant's shortcut AND the overwritten entry coincidentally keeps sizes equal (e.g. duplicate shortcut plus duplicate id). The robust check is to detect size shrinkage during insertion (compare size before/after each put) or explicitly check `grantsByShortcuts.containsKey(shortcut)` before putting. As written, the safety net the comment claims ('Validation if there are not duplicated shortcuts') is unreliable.

Lazy refresh of grant maps is not atomic and can permanently cache a wrong mapping

getShortcutByGrantType() and getGrantTypeByShortcut() lazily populate the ConcurrentHashMaps when a grant type deployed after startup is encountered. The check-then-act sequence (`get` returning null, then lookup in sessionFactory, then `put`) is not atomic: two threads can both miss and both put, which is benign for identical values. However, if a custom OAuth2GrantTypeFactory is deployed whose shortcut collides with an existing one, the lazy path silently overwrites the existing mapping (grantsByShortcuts.put(shortcut, grantType)), permanently corrupting the shortcut→grant resolution for previously valid tokens — a token id encoded with the old mapping will now decode to the wrong grant type. The startup validation in postInit() is bypassed entirely by this lazy path.

Removal of the Context copy constructor is a breaking API change for custom OAuth2GrantType implementations

The PR deletes the public copy constructor `Context(Context context)` from OAuth2GrantType.Context. This is a public class in server-spi-private, and third-party/custom grant type providers (the SPI is designed for extension — the PR itself advertises 'provider adds ability for someone to introduce his own provider') may use this copy constructor to wrap/delegate contexts (a common pattern for decorating grant processing). Removing a public constructor without deprecation is a binary- and source-incompatible break for any external implementation. If the copy constructor is no longer needed internally, it should be deprecated first, not removed in the same change.

grantType captured in constructor can be stale when formParams are replaced via setFormParams

The constructor now eagerly captures `this.grantType = formParams.getFirst(OAuth2Constants.GRANT_TYPE)`, but the class still exposes `setFormParams(MultivaluedHashMap)` which replaces the formParams reference. Any caller that constructs the Context and then calls setFormParams() with different parameters (e.g. a wrapper that normalizes or replaces form params) will leave `grantType` holding the old value while `getFormParams()` returns the new ones — an inconsistent state. Either derive grantType lazily in getGrantType() from the current formParams, or update grantType inside setFormParams().

New abstract method getShortcut() on OAuth2GrantTypeFactory breaks all existing third-party grant type factories

The PR adds `String getShortcut();` as a non-default method to the public SPI interface OAuth2GrantTypeFactory. Every existing custom implementation of this SPI (external extensions, downstream products) will fail to compile and, if already compiled, will throw AbstractMethodError at runtime when DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit() iterates all OAuth2GrantType factories and calls getShortcut(). This is a hard backward-incompatibility in a public SPI. The method should be declared `default` (e.g. returning null or a derived value) with a documented requirement to override, so existing factories keep working and unknown shortcuts degrade to the 'na'/UNKNOWN path.

Encoded token id is generated in initToken but other token-creation paths may bypass it

The encoding is applied only in TokenManager.initToken(). Any other code path that creates an AccessToken and sets its id directly (e.g. `token.id(KeycloakModelUtils.generateId())` elsewhere in TokenManager or in other services such as TokenExchangeProvider variants, service-account flows, admin impersonation, or the OIDC 'token' endpoint response building for ID-token-as-access-token in StandardTokenExchangeProvider where an IDToken is reused) will produce access tokens whose jti has no context prefix. Consumers relying on the prefix (the stated purpose: introspection/userInfo optimization, session-type lookup) will see a mix of prefixed and unprefixed ids and must handle both — the PR description claims the encoding is 'used only for access-tokens', but in practice only for access tokens created through initToken. If full coverage is intended, all AccessToken.id() assignments for access tokens must go through the encoder; if not, the fallback behavior for unprefixed ids must be documented and handled by consumers.

Refresh grant overwrites the client session GRANT_TYPE attribute, mutating session state visible to other flows

In refreshToken(), `clientSessionCtx.setAttribute(Constants.GRANT_TYPE, OAuth2Constants.REFRESH_TOKEN)` overwrites the grant type stored on the (persistent) client session context. The original grant type that created the session (e.g. authorization_code) is lost from the session context. Any other consumer reading this attribute later (current or future) will see 'refresh_token' as the session's grant type, which misrepresents the session's origin. If the attribute is meant to record 'the grant type of the most recent token issuance', that should be documented; if it is meant to record the session's originating grant, overwriting it is a data-integrity bug.

UNKNOWN constant value 'na' collides conceptually with the 'unknown' session/token shortcuts 'un' but is a grant-only sentinel mixed into the same namespace

The grant-type sentinel UNKNOWN = "na" is registered in the same shortcut maps as real grant shortcuts (grantsByShortcuts/grantsToShortcuts in the factory). A custom grant type factory could legitimately choose the shortcut "na", which would then be indistinguishable from 'unknown grant type' when decoding. The factory's duplicate-detection would not catch this because "na" is pre-registered after the loop, silently overwriting (or being overwritten by) a real grant. Reserving the sentinel namespace (e.g. validating that no grant shortcut equals "na" at startup) would prevent this ambiguity.

Unit test bypasses factory.postInit and hand-builds internal maps, so it does not test the real wiring

The test's @Before constructs DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory, calls init(null), then directly assigns the package-private fields grantsByShortcuts/grantsToShortcuts with a hand-built HashMap, bypassing postInit() entirely. This means the test never exercises the real population logic (iteration over OAuth2GrantType factories, duplicate-shortcut validation, UNKNOWN registration) and would not catch regressions in postInit(). It also means the test depends on package-private field access, making it brittle. A test that drives the factory through postInit with a real/mock KeycloakSessionFactory would cover the actual production path.

Session type detection calls getUserSession() which can be null for client-credentials/service-account sessions

getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext() unconditionally calls `clientSessionContext.getClientSession().getUserSession()` and then dereferences the result (`userSession.getPersistenceState()`). For client-credentials grants and service-account flows there is no user session (the client session is not attached to a user session), so getUserSession() can return null, causing an NPE during access-token creation for client-credentials — one of the most common grant types. The PR's own example (`trltcc:...` for a transient lightweight client-credentials token) implies client-credentials tokens are expected to be encoded, so this path must handle a null user session (e.g. defaulting to TRANSIENT).

GRANT_TYPE attribute set on a DefaultClientSessionContext wrapper may not propagate to the persisted client session

In PreAuthorizedCodeGrantType.process(), the grant type is set via `sessionContext.setAttribute(Constants.GRANT_TYPE, ...)` where sessionContext is a `DefaultClientSessionContext` created by `DefaultClientSessionContext.fromClientSessionAndScopeParameter(...)`. Whether this attribute is visible later when TokenManager.initToken() reads it via the ClientSessionContext passed to createClientAccessToken depends on DefaultClientSessionContext.setAttribute delegating to the underlying AuthenticatedClientSessionModel notes. If DefaultClientSessionContext.setAttribute only writes to an in-memory map that is not the same instance passed to createClientAccessToken (a different wrapper is created inside TokenManager), the grant type will be lost and the token encoded with 'na'. This path should be verified with an integration test; the unit test does not cover it.

Grant maps are package-private mutable fields, exposing internal state

grantsByShortcuts and grantsToShortcuts are declared without an access modifier (package-private) and are non-final mutable fields on the factory. The unit test relies on this to inject state directly. Exposing mutable internal maps package-wide invites accidental external mutation and makes the class harder to reason about; they should be private with the test using the real postInit() path (or a package-private test hook that is clearly intended for tests).

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Optional.get() without isPresent() check will throw NoSuchElementException when no recovery credential exists

The constructor calls RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) and immediately invokes credentialModelOpt.get() without checking isPresent(). Previously the code used getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream(...).findFirst().get() which had the same latent issue, but now that getCredential() explicitly returns an Optional that can legitimately be empty (federated lookup first, then local), any code path that renders the recovery-code input page for a user without a recovery credential (e.g., a race where the credential was removed, a misconfigured flow, or a user whose credential exists only in a storage provider that doesn't implement getCredentials) will throw NoSuchElementException and produce a 500 error instead of a graceful challenge. The bean should handle the empty case (e.g., throw a meaningful error, disable the input, or fall back), and ideally the template should not render the code-number prompt when no credential exists.
