Although it does not discuss raw List deserialization, it directly matches the concrete bug described in the golden comment.

false_positives.candidate:
Recovery codes stored in user storage are saved as raw (unhashed) codes

In createRecoveryCodesCredential, the generatedCodes list is serialized directly into a UserCredentialModel and passed to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(recoveryCodesCredential). Unlike the local-storage path, where recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(realm, user, credentialModel) hashes each code (RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues hashes the raw codes), the user-storage path stores the raw codes verbatim in the federated credential's challengeResponse/credentialData. Any user-storage provider that persists this value (LDAP attribute, external database, etc.) will hold plaintext recovery codes, which are equivalent to passwords for account recovery. The consequence is that a compromise of the user-storage backend (or its backups/logs) directly yields usable recovery codes, defeating the purpose of hashing them in the local Keycloak DB. The fix is to hash the codes (e.g., via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode) before building the UserCredentialModel, matching what the local credential provider does.

Test user-storage provider validates recovery codes by comparing raw input against stored values without hashing

In isValid(), the recovery-codes branch deserializes the stored credential data and checks generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse())). Because CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential now sends the raw (unhashed) codes to user storage (see the related finding), this comparison only works because both sides are raw. If the production code is fixed to hash codes before storing them in user storage, this test provider will break; conversely, as written, this provider demonstrates and endorses storing plaintext recovery codes in federated storage. The validation should hash the input (RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode / verifyRecoveryCodeInput) and compare against the stored hashed values, consistent with the local Keycloak credential provider.

Recovery codes credential stored in user storage loses userLabel and used-code state

In updateCredential(), the recovery-codes branch builds a CredentialModel with only id, type, credentialData (the raw JSON list), and createdDate. It never sets userLabel, and it stores the list of codes as-is, so there is no per-code 'used' flag persisted. getCredentials() later reconstructs the model via RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(codes, createdDate, userLabel), which marks all codes as unused. This means a code that was already consumed during login remains valid in user storage: the federated isValid() will keep accepting a used recovery code, allowing unlimited reuse of a single recovery code. The provider must persist and honor the used/unused state (e.g., store the full RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel JSON including per-code used flags, and update it when a code is consumed), otherwise the one-time-use guarantee of recovery codes is broken for federated users.

disableCredentialType does not support removing recovery codes from user storage

disableCredentialType() only handles OTP types (setting myUser.otp = null) and logs 'Unsupported to disable credential of type' for everything else, including RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE. Since supportsCredentialType() now advertises recovery-codes support and isConfiguredFor() reports it, the account console/admin REST will list recovery codes as a disableable credential for federated users, but attempting to disable/remove it will silently do nothing (the credential remains in storage and the user can still log in with it). The method should handle RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE by setting myUser.recoveryCodes = null, and getDisableableCredentialTypesStream() should include the recovery-codes type when present.

Used recovery code is removed by credential ID even when the credential lives in federated user storage

After a successful recovery-code login, the code calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId()) when all codes are used. RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential() now returns the federated credential first, and for a federated credential the ID is the one assigned by the user-storage provider (or a dummy id). removeStoredCredentialById only removes credentials from the local Keycloak DB; for a federated credential this either throws, silently no-ops, or removes nothing, so the consumed-codes state in user storage is never updated. The consequence is that once all codes are used, the federated credential is never invalidated/removed and the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action logic (which keys off allCodesUsed() on the federated model) may repeatedly trigger or, worse, the storage-side credential keeps accepting codes. The removal path must go through the credential manager's federated-aware removal (e.g., updateCredential with the consumed state, or removeStoredCredentialById only for local credentials), not blindly call removeStoredCredentialById with a federated ID.

getCredential prefers federated credential but ignores local credential when both exist

getCredential() returns the first federated recovery-codes credential if present, and only falls back to the local stored credential when no federated one exists. If a user has recovery codes in both the local Keycloak DB (e.g., created before the user was federated, or created by a code path that bypassed the storage check) and in user storage, the local credential is silently ignored: login validation via credentialManager().isValid() may still check both, but the post-login bookkeeping in RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator (allCodesUsed check and removal) and the code-number display in RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean operate only on the federated one. This can lead to inconsistent state where a stale local credential remains valid forever and is never cleaned up, or where the displayed 'next code number' does not match the credential actually being validated. The method should either return all matching credentials or document/enforce a single source of truth, and callers should handle the both-exist case (e.g., prefer local, or remove the stale one).

Recovery-codes federation test does not verify one-time use of codes or removal/invalidation after all codes are consumed

testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only logs in once with recovery code index 0 and asserts success. It never attempts to reuse the same code (which must fail), never consumes all 12 codes to verify the credential is invalidated/removed and the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action is re-triggered, and never verifies that the used-code state is persisted in the user storage. Given that the production change is specifically about creating and validating recovery codes in user storage, the absence of these assertions leaves the core security property (codes are single-use and the credential lifecycle works for federated users) untested. The test should reuse a consumed code and assert failure, and ideally drive the flow until all codes are used.

true_positives.golden_comment: Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Exit code change from 4 to 3 for recreate upgrade breaks documented contract and existing automation

The constant RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE is changed from 4 to 3 in this PR. The accompanying documentation in docs/guides/server/update-compatibility.adoc (lines 128-130) is updated to say exit code 3 means 'Rolling Upgrade is not possible. The deployment must be shut down before applying the new configuration.' and exit code 4 means the feature is disabled. However, this is a breaking change to the exit-code contract of the `update-compatibility check` command: any existing CI/CD pipeline or script written against the previous release (where 4 meant 'recreate upgrade required') will now misinterpret exit code 3 as an unexpected error (picocli software error is 1, usage error is 2, and scripts commonly treat any non-0/3/4 code as failure) and, worse, will treat exit code 4 as a distinct 'feature disabled' case only if they were updated. Since the tool is explicitly documented as 'fully scriptable' and 'GitOps friendly' with consumers relying on exit codes, silently renumbering an existing exit code (rather than only adding the new code 4) breaks backward compatibility for anyone already using the command. The renumbering should be avoided (keep RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE = 4 and use a new code such as 5 for FEATURE_DISABLED), or at minimum the change must be called out as a breaking change in release notes; as written, the docs present the new numbering as if it were always the contract.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same concern: the exit-code change affects existing automation and needs to be documented as a breaking change in release notes. Although it also proposes preserving the old numbering, its release-note recommendation and explanation of migration impact align with the golden comment.

false_positives.candidate:
Feature check runs before configuration validation, so --features=rolling-updates is never actually parsed for the check itself

In UpdateCompatibilityCheck.run() (and identically in UpdateCompatibilityMetadata.run()), the guard `if (!Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ROLLING_UPDATES))` is evaluated at the very start of run(), before `validateConfig()` is called. Profile.isFeatureEnabled reads the statically initialized Profile (Profile.getInstance()), which is only configured from CLI options/environment during the normal Keycloak configuration/validation phase. The `--features` option is a standard Keycloak CLI option processed by the configuration machinery; whether it has been applied to the Profile singleton at the point run() executes depends on command initialization order in the Quarkus CLI framework. The distribution test UpdateCommandDistTest passes `--features=rolling-updates` as a CLI argument and expects the command to proceed, which suggests the option is honored, but the ordering is fragile: if Profile is initialized lazily or the feature option is applied after run() begins (e.g., when running via `kc.sh update-compatibility ... --features=rolling-updates` in a non-optimized or build-affected mode), the check would incorrectly report the feature as disabled and exit 4 even though the user explicitly enabled it. The feature check should be performed after validateConfig() (which triggers full option processing) or the enabled-features state should be read from the parsed command options rather than the global Profile singleton, to make the gating deterministic.

No test asserts the exit code for the feature-disabled path (exit code 4)

The new testFeatureNotEnabled test only asserts that the error message 'Unable to use this command. The preview feature 'rolling-updates' is not enabled.' appears in the CLI output; it never asserts the process exit code. The whole point of introducing CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED = 4 (and documenting it in docs/guides/server/update-compatibility.adoc lines 132-134 as the contract for scripts) is that automation can branch on exit code 4. Without an assertion such as `assertEquals(4, cliResult.exitCode())` (or the equivalent CLIResult API), a regression that exits with 0, 1, or 2 instead of 4 would not be caught, and the documented scripting contract would silently break. The test should assert the exit code equals CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED.

Test parameterization silently skips enabling the rolling-updates feature when updateStrategy is null

In createInitialDeployment(UpdateStrategy updateStrategy), when updateStrategy is null the method returns early at line 105-107 (`if (updateStrategy == null) { return kc; }`) before the code at lines 112-115 that sets the FeatureSpec with Profile.Feature.ROLLING_UPDATES.getKey(). The parameterized test upgradeStrategy() supplies both null and UpdateStrategy.RECREATE, so the null case (testImageChange-null and testCacheMaxCount-null) runs without the rolling-updates feature enabled in the Keycloak CR. Given that the operator documentation added in this PR (docs/guides/operator/advanced-configuration.adoc lines 446-450) states that 'the feature rolling-updates must be enabled. Otherwise, the Keycloak Operator will fail', the null-strategy test case is exercising a deployment configuration that the operator is documented to reject, and the test's expectations (e.g., eventuallyRollingUpgradeStatus for testCacheMaxCount-null) may be passing for the wrong reason or masking a validation failure. Either the null case should also enable the feature (so both parameters test the strategy behavior with the feature on), or the test should explicitly assert the operator's behavior when the feature is missing. As written, the test coverage for the default (no update strategy) path does not match the documented requirement.

Exit code table formatting is broken: rows 0-3 are missing the leading pipe, producing a malformed AsciiDoc table

In the exit-code table (lines 116-135), the first four rows begin with `m|0`, `m|1`, `m|2`, `m|3` while the newly added row begins with `m|4` — all are missing the leading `|` cell delimiter that AsciiDoc tables require (a cell must start with `|`). Only the header row `|===` / `|Exit Code |Description` and the final row use the correct `|` prefix. As a result the rendered table will be malformed: the `m|N` rows will not be parsed as table rows at all (the `m` is an unintended literal prefix), so exit codes 0 through 3 will render as plain paragraph text outside the table, and only the header and the new exit-code-4 row will appear as a table. The rows should be `m|0` corrected to `|0` (i.e., `|m|0` style consistent with the last row: a leading `|` followed by the `m` cell marker). This makes the documented exit-code contract — which scripts depend on — visually broken in the published guide.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

registerListener now gates V1 cleanup behavior behind ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ, breaking permission cleanup when only V2 is enabled

The diff wraps the entire event-handling body in 'if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ))'. Previously the listener unconditionally disabled permissions on role/client/group removal. ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is a separate feature flag from ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (the V2 evaluator is selected when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, see AdminPermissions.evaluator). With V2 enabled but V1 disabled, RoleRemovedEvent, ClientRemovedEvent, and GroupRemovedEvent will no longer trigger setPermissionsEnabled(..., false), leaving stale fine-grained permissions referencing deleted roles/clients/groups. This is a data-integrity regression: orphaned permissions remain active and may grant access based on policies referencing non-existent entities. The guard should either be removed (the cleanup is harmless when permissions are disabled) or check for either feature flag.

This is a speculative but concrete risk given that multiple other inherited methods throw UnsupportedOperationException.

In UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission (lines 94-133), `resourceStore.findByName(server, user.getId())` looks up a resource by name (the user id). The issue is that the fallback does not consider per-user deny policies when falling back: if a user has a per-user resource with a deny policy, findByName would find it and the fallback would not be used — correct. true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
concatenatedRSToASN1DER produces invalid DER for r or s with high bit set

In concatenatedRSToASN1DER, the raw r and s halves of the signature are copied into a byte array of size len+1 with a leading zero byte (System.arraycopy(signature, 0, r, 1, len)) and then converted via new BigInteger(r). This always yields a positive BigInteger whose toByteArray() includes the leading zero byte, so the encoded INTEGER is always len+1 bytes long. That is correct only when the original value had its high bit set (requiring a sign-padding zero). When the high bit is clear, DER requires the minimal encoding without the leading zero; the extra 0x00 makes the INTEGER non-minimal and therefore invalid DER. Strict verifiers (and RFC 6979/JWS interop with other implementations) will reject signatures produced by this method whenever r or s has a clear high bit, which happens with probability ~1/2 per component. The correct approach is new BigInteger(1, Arrays.copyOfRange(signature, 0, len)) (signum 1, magnitude only), letting BigInteger.toByteArray() add the sign byte only when needed. Note the two throwaway ASN1Encoder.create().write(...) calls on lines 114-115 are dead code and should be removed.
true_positives.reasoning: Although the candidate focuses on a separate DER encoding concern, it explicitly identifies the two throwaway ASN1Encoder.create().write(...) calls as dead code that should be removed, matching the golden issue of discarded encoder results and redundant operations.

true_positives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

readLength() returns -1 for the indefinite-length form (0x80, line 133-135), but readSequence() (line 49) treats the returned length as a plain int and loops while (length > 0), decrementing by the size of each element. With length == -1 the loop condition is true and length only grows more negative as elements are consumed, so the loop never terminates on well-formed input and will keep calling readNext() until it throws EOFException from an exhausted stream — i.e. indefinite-length SEQUENCE encodings (valid BER, produced by some libraries) are rejected with a confusing EOF error rather than parsed or cleanly rejected. Additionally, readSequence never checks that the declared length matches the bytes actually consumed, and readNext() computes element size as content length plus the bytes consumed for tag+length via mark/reset, which double-counts nothing but also does not validate against the remaining sequence length, so a sequence whose declared length disagrees with its contents is silently accepted. For a signature-verification path, accepting structurally inconsistent DER is undesirable; at minimum the indefinite-length case must be rejected explicitly with a clear IOException.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying issue: indefinite-length encoding produces length = -1, which readSequence mishandles when controlling iteration and subtracting element sizes. Its claim that -1 > 0 is true is incorrect, but the core concern matches the golden comment.

false_positives.candidate:
integerToBytes truncates the most significant bytes when the value is larger than the target length

integerToBytes(BigInteger s, int qLength) handles the case qLength < bytes.length by copying the LAST qLength bytes (System.arraycopy(bytes, bytes.length - tmp.length, tmp, 0, tmp.length)). For an ECDSA r or s value, the magnitude can legitimately be up to qLength+1 bytes because BigInteger.toByteArray() prepends a 0x00 sign byte when the high bit is set; in that case dropping the leading zero is correct. But if the value is genuinely larger than qLength (e.g. a malformed/forged DER signature where r or s >= curve order, which is exactly the input an attacker controls when verifying a JWT), this silently truncates the most significant bytes and returns a wrong-length, wrong-value r/s instead of rejecting the signature. asn1derToConcatenatedRS is used on the verification path, so a crafted DER signature with oversized integers would be silently mangled rather than rejected, and the resulting concatenated value fed to the JCA verifier. The method should throw (e.g. IOException) when bytes.length > qLength + 1, or when the value does not fit in qLength bytes, instead of truncating.

Out-of-bounds length check uses the total input size instead of the remaining bytes

In readLength(), the sanity check for long-form lengths is `if (length >= limit)` where limit is the total length of the whole input byte array (set in the constructor), not the number of bytes remaining at the current read position. A nested element deep inside a larger structure can therefore declare a length up to the full input size even though far fewer bytes remain, and the check passes; the subsequent read(length) then fails only later with a generic EOF IOException. This weakens the early corruption detection the check is meant to provide (the comment says 'out of bounds length found'). The check should compare against the bytes remaining (limit minus bytes already consumed), e.g. track position and compare length > remaining.

CryptoProvider.order() is documented as 'The higher number has preference over the lower number', and the PR description says the Keycloak testsuite keeps using DefaultCryptoProvider via ordering. But detectProvider() sorts with Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order).reversed() and then picks foundProviders.get(0). Comparator.reversed() sorts descending, so get(0) is the provider with the LOWEST order value — the opposite of the documented contract. Concretely: AuthzClientCryptoProvider.order() == 100 and DefaultCryptoProvider.order() == 200, so when both are on the classpath (exactly the scenario this PR creates for the authz-client module, which depends on keycloak-core and is used in the testsuite where DefaultCryptoProvider is present), the authz client provider (100) wins over DefaultCryptoProvider (200), contradicting both the javadoc and the stated intent that the testsuite keeps using DefaultCryptoProvider. Either remove .reversed() or fix the javadoc; as written the code and documentation disagree and the wrong provider is selected.

The other public factory methods create() (line 60) and create(InputStream) (line 72) delegate to create(Configuration) so they are covered, but any code path that constructs AuthzClient without going through these factories, or any other entry point in the authz-client that uses CryptoIntegration.getProvider() (e.g. ECDSA signature verification of tokens via the crypto provider), will hit 'Illegal state. The test constructor generates the key pair with KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair(), which on a standard JDK produces a 256-bit (secp256r1) key. It then signs with Signature.getInstance(JavaAlgorithm.getJavaAlgorithm(algorithm.name())) — for ES384 that is SHA384withECDSA and for ES512 SHA512withECDSA — but the signature length is still determined by the 256-bit curve, so algorithm.getSignatureLength() (96/132 bytes for ES384/ES512) does not match the actual r||s size (64 bytes). asn1derToConcatenatedRS then splits the DER into halves of signLength/2 = 48/66 bytes, which does not correspond to the real r and s, and concatenatedRSToASN1DER re-encodes with the wrong lengths. The test only asserts that asn1derToConcatenatedRS(concatenatedRSToASN1DER(x)) == x. false_positives.candidate:
max_processes=0 silently disables all flusher processes

`self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` treats a falsy `max_processes` (0) the same as `None`, falling back to one process per shard. More importantly, the CLI option `--flusher-processes` in `src/sentry/consumers/__init__.py` (line 433) has `default=1` and no validation that it is >= 1, so an operator passing `--flusher-processes 0` (or a negative value) gets `num_processes = min(0, len(shards)) = 0`, an empty `process_to_shards_map`, zero spawned processes, and a flusher that never flushes anything — segments accumulate in Redis until the hard backpressure path rejects all messages. There is no guard rejecting non-positive values, and no test covers this case.

Shard-to-process assignment is not stable across rebalances, causing duplicate/missing flush ownership

`process_index = i % self.num_processes` assigns shards to processes by their position in `buffer.assigned_shards` (the iteration order of the `partitions` mapping passed to `create_with_partitions`). When the consumer rebalances and the set/order of assigned partitions changes, the same Redis shard can be mapped to a different process index, and — critically — the *old* SpanFlusher instance's processes are never terminated on rebalance: `close()` (line 322) explicitly does not shut down the flusher, and `create_with_partitions` creates a brand-new SpanFlusher with new processes while the old ones keep running (they are daemon processes, so they survive until the whole consumer exits). Two processes can then flush the same shard concurrently, racing on `flush_segments`/`done_flush_segments` in Redis and potentially producing duplicate segments to the buffered-segments topic or corrupting segment state. The old code had a single process per SpanFlusher instance with the same close() behavior, but with one process per shard the blast radius of a leaked flusher is much larger (N leaked processes per rebalance, each holding a Kafka producer).

Per-shard SpansBuffer instances in the parent process are never used for flushing and create a second set of Redis connections

In `_create_process_for_shards`, a new `SpansBuffer(shards)` is created in the parent process and stored in `self.buffers[process_index]` (line 125). This parent-side buffer is only used in `submit()` for `record_stored_segments()` (line 270) and `get_memory_info()` (line 301). However, the actual flushing is done by a *separately pickled* `shard_buffer` inside the child process (line 97-104), which maintains its own Redis client pool and its own internal segment bookkeeping. This means: (1) the parent's `record_stored_segments()` updates statistics on a buffer whose Redis state is not the one being flushed, so backpressure decisions based on `any_shard_at_limit` in the child (line 172) and memory info from the parent (line 301) may be inconsistent; (2) the parent now holds N extra SpansBuffer objects each with Redis connection pools, doubling Redis connection usage; (3) `record_stored_segments` on the parent buffer tracks segments that the child buffer flushes, so the parent's view of stored segments drifts from reality. The original design had a single shared buffer; the multiprocessed version needs the bookkeeping to live in exactly one place.

Thread-based test processes are never killable, and kill() is skipped for them in production restart path

In `_ensure_processes_alive`, the restart path calls `process.kill()` only `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` (line 254). When `produce_to_pipe` is set, processes are `threading.Thread` instances (line 108), which have no `kill()` — so a hung thread-based flusher is never stopped before `_create_process_for_shards` spawns a replacement (line 259), leaking the old thread. In production this branch is not hit (real processes are used), but the asymmetry means the health-check/restart logic is only half-implemented for the thread mode that tests rely on, and any future use of thread mode in production would leak hung threads indefinitely. Additionally, `threading.Thread` has no `exitcode` attribute, so `getattr(process, "exitcode", "unknown")` at line 229 always yields "unknown" for threads, degrading the `no_process_unknown` metric cause.

Dead code: _create_process_for_shard is never called

`_create_process_for_shard(self, shard: int)` (lines 127-132) is defined but never referenced anywhere in the file — `_ensure_processes_alive` restarts via `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` directly. It appears to be leftover from an earlier per-shard restart design. Dead code in a concurrency-critical class invites confusion about which restart path is authoritative.

Shard assignment uses modulo on list position, not on shard id — shard ownership changes when partition set changes

The mapping `process_index = i % self.num_processes` where `i` is the enumeration index of `buffer.assigned_shards` means shard ownership is a function of *which other shards are assigned*, not of the shard id itself. If the consumer is assigned partitions {0,1,2,3} with num_processes=2, shard 0→proc0, 1→proc1, 2→proc0, 3→proc1. After a rebalance to {1,2,3}, shard 1→proc0, 2→proc1, 3→proc0 — shard 1 moved from proc1 to proc0. Since each process has its own SpansBuffer with its own Redis segment state and its own Kafka producer, a shard changing owner means the new owner starts with an empty in-memory view of that shard's segments while the old owner may still hold unflushed state. Combined with the fact that old processes are not stopped on rebalance (see close() finding), this can cause the same shard's segments to be flushed by two different buffers concurrently, producing duplicate or interleaved segments in the buffered-segments topic. A stable hash of the shard id (e.g., `shard % num_processes`) would keep ownership stable across rebalances as long as num_processes is unchanged.

join() terminates processes without joining them, risking lost in-flight Kafka produces

In `join()` (lines 328-348), after waiting for each process to exit (or the deadline to expire), the code calls `process.terminate()` (line 347) if it is still alive. `terminate()` sends SIGTERM, which kills the child immediately — any spans already produced to the Kafka producer's internal buffer but not yet acked (the `producer_futures` at line 200 are only awaited inside the main loop) are lost, and any segments already popped from Redis by `flush_segments` but not yet `done_flush_segments`-ed (line 205) are lost from Redis without being written to Kafka. The original single-process code had the same terminate() call, but with N processes the window for losing in-flight data is N times larger. A graceful shutdown would close the producer (flushing pending futures) before terminating, or at least join with a short grace period before SIGTERM.

New multiprocessed flusher test only checks process count, not that shards are actually flushed by the right process

`test_flusher_processes_limit` asserts `len(flusher.processes) == 2` and that 4 shards are distributed across the map, but never submits any spans, never advances the drift, and never asserts that any message is produced. It would pass even if the flusher processes crashed immediately on startup (they are daemon threads in test mode). There is no test that verifies: (1) each shard's segments are flushed exactly once when multiple shards share a process; (2) the per-process backpressure/health values are independent; (3) restart logic works per-process; (4) the `max_processes` default (None → one process per shard) behaves correctly. The existing `test_basic` only covers a single shard, so the multi-shard sharing path — the core new behavior of this PR — is effectively untested for correctness.

The new lines 60-62 add `step.poll()` followed by a hardcoded `time.sleep(0.1)` to 'give flusher threads time to process after drift change'. The flusher thread loop sleeps 1 second between iterations when there is nothing to flush (line 182 of flusher.py, though monkeypatched to no-op in the test), but the thread scheduling is still non-deterministic — under CI load, 0.1s may not be enough for the thread to wake, flush, and append to `messages` before `step.join()` and the `(msg,) = messages` unpacking at line 66. A polling loop (e.g., wait up to N seconds for `len(messages) == 1`) would be robust. This is a classic source of flaky tests in multiprocessed/threaded code.

Main consumer buffer and flusher shard buffers can diverge: process_spans writes to one buffer, flusher reads from another

`create_with_partitions` creates `buffer = SpansBuffer(assigned_shards=[p.index for p in partitions])` (line 67) which is passed to `process_batch` (line 79/90) — this is the buffer that `process_spans` writes segments into. Separately, `SpanFlusher.__init__` creates its own per-process `SpansBuffer(shards)` instances (flusher.py line 93) that the child processes use to call `flush_segments`. These are different Python objects with different Redis client pools, but they point at the same Redis keys. The critical question is whether `SpansBuffer` keeps any in-memory state that must be shared between the writer (process_batch) and the flusher (child process). Looking at the original single-process design, the same `buffer` object was shared between `process_batch` and the flusher thread, so any in-memory segment index maintained by SpansBuffer was consistent. Now the flusher uses a fresh SpansBuffer that never saw the `process_spans` calls — if SpansBuffer maintains an in-memory registry of stored segments (e.g., for `record_stored_segments` or segment size tracking), the flusher's buffer will have no knowledge of segments written by the main buffer, potentially causing segments to never be flushed or to be flushed with incorrect metadata. This needs verification against SpansBuffer's implementation; if SpansBuffer is purely Redis-backed this is fine, but the parent-side `self.buffers` used for `record_stored_segments` (flusher.py line 270) suggests there is in-memory state that is now split across three sets of objects.

--flusher-processes CLI option lacks validation for non-positive values

The `--flusher-processes` click option (lines 432-437) accepts any integer with no `click.IntRange(min=1)` or callback validation. Passing 0 results in `num_processes = 0` (see flusher.py line 60: `min(0, len(shards))`), which creates zero flusher processes and silently stops all flushing — segments accumulate in Redis until backpressure rejects all incoming messages, effectively halting span ingestion with no error surfaced until the Redis memory limit is hit. A `click.IntRange(min=1)` would fail fast at startup with a clear error message.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The BrowserReportingCollectorEndpoint returns HttpResponse objects but the endpoint inherits from Endpoint which expects rest_framework.response.Response objects.

Validation logic incorrectly uses .get('timestamp'), which treats a timestamp of 0 as absent. It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator passes negative offsets to Django queryset slicing, which raises AssertionError

In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0, the code executes `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start_offset (line 880-882). Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ explicitly asserts that slice indices are non-negative ('Negative indexing is not supported.'), so any request with a negative cursor offset will raise an unhandled AssertionError and produce a 500 error. The comment claiming 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is factually wrong. This code path is reachable from the audit logs endpoint whenever an admin passes a cursor with a negative offset (cursors are client-supplied strings parsed in Cursor.from_string, which accepts negative integers).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: OptimizedCursorPaginator uses negative slice offsets on Django querysets, which do not support negative slicing and raise an AssertionError.

true_positives.golden_comment: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Admin-gated pagination feature relies on client-controlled query param and exposes a broken/dangerous code path

The optimized paginator is enabled purely by the client-supplied query parameter `optimized_pagination=true` combined with an admin check (`request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`). The feature is undocumented, untested, and — per the paginator bugs — actively dangerous: it enables negative-offset slicing on querysets. Gating a dangerous code path on a query string flag rather than a server-side configuration or feature flag means any superuser (a broad population in Sentry's model) can trigger the broken negative-slicing path, and the flag provides no audit trail. Additionally, `organization_context.member` may be None for users without a membership, causing an AttributeError on `.has_global_access` — the expression is not null-safe.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the same null-safety bug: organization_context.member can be None, and accessing .has_global_access when optimized pagination is enabled raises AttributeError. Although it adds unrelated concerns and does not specify API-key or org-token authentication, it matches the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key assumes numeric key; audit logs order by datetime, causing TypeError

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does `int(math.floor(value) ...)` on `getattr(item, self.key)`. The audit logs endpoint uses this paginator with `order_by="-datetime"`, so self.key is 'datetime' and the value is a datetime object. math.floor() on a datetime raises TypeError ('unsupported operand type(s) for -: datetime.datetime'... actually math.floor(datetime) raises TypeError: must be real number, not datetime). The class is a copy of Paginator (integer keys), not DateTimePaginator, so using it with a datetime ordering — exactly what the endpoint does — will crash during build_cursor when computing cursor keys. The endpoint should either use DateTimePaginator semantics or the paginator must handle datetime keys.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: get_item_key applies numeric math.floor/ceil operations to a datetime key when the audit logs endpoint uses order_by="-datetime", causing a TypeError.

false_positives.candidate:
BasePaginator.get_result change breaks prev-cursor pagination by clamping negative offsets to 0

The modification to BasePaginator.get_result changed `results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` to `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset; results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])`. For a prev cursor (is_prev=True) with a negative offset — which OffsetPaginator-style prev cursors legitimately produce (e.g. `Cursor(limit, page - 1, True, page > 0)` yields offset -1 on the first page) — the old code sliced with the negative offset, while the new code passes the raw negative offset only when is_prev is True... actually the new code preserves the negative offset for is_prev, but for non-prev cursors it clamps negative offsets to 0, silently returning the first page instead of erroring or handling the value. More importantly, the change alters behavior for all existing paginator subclasses (Paginator, DateTimePaginator) that share BasePaginator.get_result: previously a negative offset would hit Django's 'Negative indexing is not supported' assertion; now non-prev negative offsets silently clamp to 0, returning incorrect data (the first page) instead of failing. This is a silent data-correctness change to a shared, widely-used code path with no test coverage shown.

OptimizedCursorPaginator prev-cursor trimming logic uses unclamped offset, producing wrong page sizes

In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, the prev-cursor trimming branch checks `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra:` (line 891) using the raw `offset = cursor.offset`, but the actual slice was performed with `start_offset` which may differ from `offset` (when offset is negative and advanced features are enabled, or when offset is negative and is_prev is False where start_offset = max(0, offset)). When start_offset != offset, the length comparison `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` is computed against the wrong expected length, so the extra fetched row is not trimmed (or a legitimate row is trimmed), corrupting page contents and cursor boundaries. The same mismatch exists in the inherited BasePaginator code at line 192, where the slice now uses start_offset but the trim check still uses `offset`.

paginate() called with unknown keyword argument enable_advanced_features

The endpoint calls self.paginate(..., paginator_cls=OptimizedCursorPaginator, ..., enable_advanced_features=True). The paginate helper on the API endpoint base class does not accept an `enable_advanced_features` parameter — it forwards only known kwargs (queryset, paginator_cls, order_by, on_results, etc.) to the paginator constructor. Passing an unrecognized keyword will raise a TypeError at runtime ('unexpected keyword argument'), making the optimized path completely broken — every admin request with optimized_pagination=true will 500. Even if paginate forwarded **kwargs, the OptimizedCursorPaginator constructor signature is `__init__(self, *args, enable_advanced_features=False, **kwargs)`, so it would work only if forwarding exists, which it does not in the standard endpoint paginate implementation.

OptimizedCursorPaginator is a verbatim copy of BasePaginator.get_result with no actual optimization

OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates BasePaginator.get_result almost line-for-line; the only behavioral differences are the negative-offset branch (which is broken, see other findings) and accepting an enable_advanced_features flag. There is no query optimization (no keyset/seek pagination, no deferred fields, no index hints, no count_hits avoidance). The claimed 'optimized query path for large datasets' in the docstring is false — the class performs the same OFFSET-based slicing as the base paginator, which is precisely the slow pattern for high-volume tables. Shipping this as a 'performance enhancement' is misleading and adds a maintenance burden and a dangerous code path for zero measured benefit.

Pre-existing typo queryset.order_b introduced in untouched code path (context for review)

Line 105 contains `queryset.query.order_b = tuple(new_order_by)` — a pre-existing typo (should be `order_by`) in BasePaginator.build_queryset. It is not introduced by this diff, but it means the branch that un-reverses an explicitly descending order_by silently does nothing, which interacts with the new paginator subclass that relies on build_queryset. Worth fixing while touching this file, but not caused by this PR.

Undocumented query parameter optimized_pagination added to an EXPERIMENTAL public API endpoint

The endpoint's publish_status is EXPERIMENTAL and it is a public API surface. The PR adds an undocumented, admin-only query parameter (`optimized_pagination`) that switches paginator implementations and changes response cursor semantics. API consumers cannot discover this parameter, and because cursor formats differ between DateTimePaginator and OptimizedCursorPaginator (datetime-millis vs raw value), a client that flips the flag mid-pagination will receive cursors it cannot use with the other paginator, causing incorrect/empty pages. The parameter should be documented, or the feature should be server-side only.

Comment claims negative offsets are allowed, but no validation or handling exists in Cursor

The added comment in Cursor.__init__ states 'Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios', but the class does nothing to allow or validate them — it simply stores int(offset), and Cursor.from_string happily parses negative offsets from client input. The comment describes intent that is implemented (dangerously) elsewhere; as written it misleads readers into thinking Cursor itself supports/sanitizes negative offsets. Either remove the comment or implement actual validation (e.g., reject negative offsets at parse time for non-advanced cursors).

No tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator, the BasePaginator offset change, or the endpoint's new branch

The PR adds a new paginator class, modifies shared BasePaginator.get_result slicing behavior (affecting Paginator and DateTimePaginator used across the entire API), and adds a new endpoint branch — but includes no tests. The BasePaginator change alters behavior for every cursor-paginated endpoint in the codebase (negative offsets now clamp to 0 for non-prev cursors instead of raising), and the new paginator's negative-offset path, prev-cursor trimming, and datetime-key handling are all untested. Given the critical slicing bug, at minimum tests must cover: negative offset rejection/clamping, prev-cursor round trips, and the audit logs endpoint with optimized_pagination=true for admin and non-admin users.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the coarse lock from BuildIndex introduces a race: two concurrent builds for the same key can both create indexes and leak one, and GetIndex can return a partially-constructed index

The PR removes the function-wide b.cacheMu.Lock() from BuildIndex (previously lines 88-89) and replaces it with a short lock only around the cache insertion at lines 137-139. This means two concurrent callers of BuildIndex for the same NamespacedResource key (which happens: searchSupport.init spawns concurrent builds via errgroup, and getOrCreateIndex can also trigger builds from concurrent Search/handleEvent calls) will both execute bleve.New/bleve.NewMemOnly, both run the builder writing documents, and both insert into b.cache — the second insertion silently overwrites the first. The overwritten bleve.Index is never closed, leaking file handles/disk state (for file-based indexes, the on-disk directory is left behind and will be reopened by a subsequent build, potentially corrupting or duplicating data). Additionally, between the builder writing documents (line 126) and the cache insertion (line 138), another goroutine calling GetIndex will not find the index and will start its own duplicate build. The original coarse lock prevented duplicate builds for the same key; the fix requires per-key locking (e.g., a sync.Map of in-flight builds keyed by NamespacedResource, or a keyed mutex) so that concurrent builds for the same key are deduplicated, while builds for different keys proceed in parallel.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying race: narrowing b.cacheMu locking to the final cache insertion allows concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same key to duplicate expensive index construction. Its additional claims do not change this core match.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates b.cache without holding cacheMu — data race with concurrent BuildIndex insertions

TotalDocs (line 144) ranges over b.cache with no lock. BuildIndex now writes to b.cache under b.cacheMu.Lock() at lines 137-139, and GetIndex reads under RLock. Since BuildIndex can run concurrently (the whole point of the PR's finer-grained locking), TotalDocs racing with a cache insertion is a concurrent map read/write — a fatal runtime error in Go (concurrent map iteration and map write). TotalDocs is called from searchSupport.init at line 216 (s.search.TotalDocs()) after group.Wait(), but also potentially from metrics or other paths concurrently with getOrCreateIndex-triggered builds. Fix: acquire b.cacheMu.RLock() around the iteration.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same unsynchronized iteration over b.cache in TotalDocs racing with concurrent BuildIndex writes, potentially causing a Go concurrent map iteration/write panic. The candidate also identifies the same s.search.TotalDocs() call site, though it describes additional possible concurrency paths.

false_positives.candidate:
NewResourceServer calls s.Init(ctx) with a context that is never cancelled on construction failure, leaking the watcher goroutine and resources

NewResourceServer creates a cancelable context (ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(...)) at line 229 and stores it on the server struct (s.ctx, s.cancel). It then calls s.Init(ctx) at line 258, which starts the watcher (initWatcher) and, via searchSupport.init, spawns a goroutine reading from the storage event channel. If Init fails (e.g., search index build error or WatchWriteEvents error), NewResourceServer returns nil, err at line 261 — but it never calls s.cancel(). The server object is discarded, so the cancel function is unreachable, and the background goroutines started by initWatcher (the broadcaster goroutine piping events from s.backend.WatchWriteEvents(s.ctx)) keep running forever with a context that will never be cancelled. This is a goroutine/resource leak on every failed startup, and in HA or repeated-restart scenarios it will accumulate pollers holding DB connections. Fix: call s.cancel() (or defer it) before returning the error when Init fails.

Init is now only called from the constructor, but remains exported and uses sync.Once with a shared initErr that Stop() overwrites, creating a data race and broken re-init semantics

The PR removes all lazy s.Init(ctx) calls from the gRPC handlers (Create, Update, Delete, Read, List, Watch, Search, History, Origin, IsHealthy, PutBlob, GetBlob) and instead calls s.Init(ctx) once in NewResourceServer. However, Init (line 293) is still an exported method on the server type, still guarded by s.once, and still writes to the shared s.initErr field. Meanwhile Stop() (line 320) unconditionally writes s.initErr = fmt.Errorf("service is stopping") without any synchronization. If any external caller (or future code) invokes Init concurrently with Stop, or calls Init after Stop, there is an unsynchronized read/write race on s.initErr. More importantly, the once.Do means that if Init is called again after Stop (e.g., a caller retries Init on the same server instance), it will return the stale initErr from the first run — but Stop has since overwritten initErr with "service is stopping"/"service is stopped", so the semantics are now muddled: a second Init returns whatever Stop last wrote. Since Init is now effectively an internal startup step, it should be unexported (init) or the initErr handling should be made race-free and Stop should not clobber the field that Init's once.Do closure reads.

totalBatchesIndexed is incremented inside concurrent errgroup goroutines without synchronization — data race and incorrect metric

In searchSupport.init, totalBatchesIndexed is declared as a plain int at line 177 and incremented at line 189 inside group.Go(func() error { ... totalBatchesIndexed++ ... }) for each namespace. The errgroup runs up to s.initWorkers concurrent goroutines (group.SetLimit(s.initWorkers) at line 179), so multiple goroutines increment the same variable concurrently with no mutex or atomic. This is a data race (undefined behavior under the Go memory model) and will also produce an incorrect count in the span event at line 199 (attribute.Int("namespaced_indexed", totalBatchesIndexed)). Fix: use atomic.Int64, or compute the count as len(stats) after group.Wait() since every stat entry spawns exactly one goroutine.

searchSupport.init starts a second, unbounded event-watching goroutine that duplicates the server's broadcaster watcher and never terminates

searchSupport.init (line 172) calls s.storage.WatchWriteEvents(watchctx) at line 203 with watchctx := context.Background() (line 202) and spawns a goroutine at line 207 that loops forever reading from the events channel and calling s.handleEvent. This is separate from the server's own initWatcher (server.go line 752) which also calls s.backend.WatchWriteEvents(s.ctx) and feeds a broadcaster. The searchSupport goroutine uses context.Background(), which is never cancelled — not by server.Stop() (which only calls s.cancel() on the server's own ctx), and not by any lifecycle hook. When the server shuts down, this goroutine keeps running, keeps consuming events from the storage backend's poller, and keeps mutating the search index. Additionally, both the server's broadcaster and this searchSupport goroutine independently call WatchWriteEvents on the same SQL backend, which spawns two poller goroutines (backend.go line 566) polling the same resource_history table — doubling DB load and potentially racing on index writes. The searchSupport watcher should use the server's cancellable context (s.ctx) and be tied to the server lifecycle, or the event handling should be unified with the existing broadcaster.

Event watcher goroutine does not check channel closure — blocks forever on closed channel and never exits

The goroutine at line 207 does `for { v := <-events; s.handleEvent(watchctx, v) }`. The events channel returned by WatchWriteEvents is closed by the SQL backend's poller when it exits (backend.go line 572: defer close(stream)). Receiving from a closed channel returns nil immediately and forever, so once the channel is closed this goroutine will spin in a tight infinite loop calling s.handleEvent(watchctx, nil) — which will panic on nil pointer dereference at line 226 (evt.Type) or at minimum burn CPU. The loop should be `for v := range events` or check `v, ok := <-events; if !ok { return }`.

bleveIndex.Write/Delete/Flush mutate shared batch state with no synchronization — unsafe for concurrent watch-event handling

bleveIndex.Write (line 172) checks b.batch != nil, calls b.batch.Index(...), and may call b.index.Batch(b.batch) and b.batch.Reset(). Delete (line 190) errors if batch != nil. Flush (line 198) calls b.index.Batch(b.batch), b.batch.Reset(), and sets b.batch = nil. These fields are documented as "only valid in single thread" (line 166) but after the PR's change, handleEvent in search.go can be invoked concurrently: the searchSupport.init goroutine (line 207) calls handleEvent in a single goroutine, but getOrCreateIndex (line 287) can trigger build() concurrently with handleEvent for the same key, and once the index is in the cache, multiple watch events for the same namespace could be processed... actually the searchSupport event loop is single-goroutine, but the index returned by BuildIndex is placed in the cache before Flush is called by searchSupport.build (line 372: index.Flush() after BuildIndex returns). Between BuildIndex returning (line 140) and searchSupport.build calling Flush (search.go line 372), the index is in the cache with b.batch still non-nil; a concurrent Search on that index is fine, but a concurrent handleEvent Write would see batch != nil and try to batch.Index into a batch that build() is about to Flush and nil out — a race on b.batch. More critically, after Flush sets b.batch = nil, concurrent Write calls go directly to b.index.Index which is safe, but the transition itself (Flush setting batch=nil while Write reads batch) is unsynchronized. The bleveIndex needs a mutex protecting batch, or the batch must be fully flushed and nilled inside BuildIndex before the index is published to the cache.

Stop() overwrites initErr with a generic error, losing the original initialization error and breaking error reporting for callers that check Init after Stop

Stop() unconditionally sets s.initErr = fmt.Errorf("service is stopping") at line 321 and later s.initErr = fmt.Errorf("service is stopped") at line 339, overwriting whatever initErr was set during Init. Since Init uses sync.Once and returns s.initErr, any caller that calls Init after Stop (or concurrently) will get "service is stopped" instead of the real initialization error. More importantly, the lifecycle is now: NewResourceServer calls Init synchronously; if it fails, the constructor returns an error and the server is never used — so Stop is never called on a failed-init server. But for a successfully initialized server that is later stopped, if any code path still calls Init (it's exported), it gets the once-cached value... which Stop has clobbered. The initErr field is being used for two purposes (init result and stop status) without synchronization. Separate the concerns: keep initErr immutable after once.Do, and use a separate atomic/bool for stopped state.

IndexMetrics.IndexedKinds is incremented/decremented without nil check in handleEvent, unlike other IndexMetrics usages in the same file

In handleEvent, IndexMetrics.IndexedKinds.WithLabelValues(evt.Key.Resource).Inc() (line 263) and .Dec() (line 271) are called without checking if IndexMetrics is nil. Every other use of IndexMetrics in this file (lines 217, 282, 367) guards with `if IndexMetrics != nil`. If IndexMetrics is nil (which can happen if metrics registration failed or in tests), handleEvent will panic with a nil pointer dereference when processing ADDED or DELETED watch events. This is inconsistent and a latent crash. Fix: add the same nil guard, or better, initialize IndexMetrics to a no-op default so nil checks are unnecessary.

Moving Init from lazy per-request to constructor changes the failure contract: NewResourceServer now blocks on full index build and can fail startup, but callers may not expect constructor to do heavy I/O

Previously, Init was called lazily on the first gRPC request (Create/Update/Read/List/Watch/Search/etc.), so NewResourceServer returned quickly and the server could start serving requests (returning init errors per-request) even if index building was slow or failed. Now NewResourceServer calls s.Init(ctx) synchronously at line 258, which calls searchSupport.init — this builds the entire search index (potentially minutes for large datasets) and starts watchers before the constructor returns. Consequences: (1) The gRPC server registration/startup path now blocks on index build; if the caller has a startup timeout, the process may be killed before the server is ready. (2) If index build fails, NewResourceServer returns an error and the entire ResourceServer fails to construct — previously the server would start and only Search requests would fail. (3) The ctx passed to Init is the server's internal background-derived context (line 229), not a startup timeout context — so a hung index build hangs the constructor forever with no cancellation. Callers of NewResourceServer need to be audited to ensure they can tolerate a long-blocking, failure-prone constructor; ideally Init should be called with a startup deadline context, or the constructor should return the server immediately and Init be called separately by the module lifecycle with proper timeout handling.

Dedupe update is enqueued before condition group validation, causing state corruption when condition group is missing

`build_fingerprint` at line 172-176 builds the fingerprint as `f"{self.detector.id}{':' + group_key if group_key is not None else ''}"`. This is inconsistent with the `None` case which produces `"123"`. More importantly, an empty string group key and `None` group key produce different fingerprints (`"123:"` vs `"123"`), but `build_dedupe_value_key` and `build_counter_value_key` (lines 324-332) treat both `None` and `""` identically by converting `None` to `""`. The expression `int(dv) if dv else 0` handles `None` correctly (returns 0), but if Redis returns `b'0'` (the string "0"), `int(b'0')` returns `0`, which is fine. However, the real issue is that `pipeline.execute()` may return results in a different order than the keys were added if the pipeline was not properly reset or if commands were added conditionally. More critically, the code at line 194 calls `pipeline.reset()` after the first `pipeline.execute()`, but then reuses the same pipeline object for counter keys at lines 202-203. However, the issue is that `DetectorStateData.counter_updates` is typed as `dict[str, int | None]`, and the values from Redis are correctly converted. But looking more carefully at line 222, `counter_updates[gk]` is passed directly to `DetectorStateData`. If `self.counter_names` is empty, `counter_updates` remains `{}` (initialized at line 195), and `counter_updates[gk]` at line 222 would raise a `KeyError` because `gk` is not in the empty dict. This is a bug: when `counter_names` is empty, `get_state_data` will crash with `KeyError` at line 222 because `counter_updates` is an empty dict but the code tries to access `counter_updates[gk]`.

KeyError when counter_names is empty in get_state_data

In `get_state_data` (lines 178-224), `counter_updates` is initialized as an empty dict at line 195. It is only populated inside the `if self.counter_names:` block at line 196. In `process_detectors` (lines 47-70), for each detector, `handler.evaluate(data_packet)` is called, then for each result with a non-None `result`, `create_issue_occurrence_from_result(result)` is called (line 62), which produces to Kafka. On retry, the same data packet will be re-evaluated, and since the dedupe value wasn't persisted, the detector will produce duplicate occurrences to Kafka. false_positives.candidate:
Python's built-in hash() is randomized per process, breaking consistent group-to-queue assignment across restarts and workers

FixedQueuePool.get_queue_for_group uses `hash(group_key) % self.num_queues`. In Python 3, `hash()` of strings is salted per process (PYTHONHASHSEED randomization), so the same group key maps to different queue indices in different processes and across restarts. This breaks the core ordering guarantee: two messages for the same subscription can be processed concurrently by different workers (if the consumer runs with multiple processes via --processes, each process has its own pool and different hash seeds), and after a restart a group can move to a different queue, allowing out-of-order processing of the same subscription. The docstring claims 'Each group is consistently assigned to the same queue' but this is only true within a single process. Use a stable hash (e.g., md5/sha1 of the key, or zlib.crc32) instead.

get_committable_offsets iterates a range from min to max offset per partition on every commit cycle

OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets computes `for offset in range(start, max_offset + 1)` and checks set membership for every integer in that span. Kafka offsets are monotonically increasing and can be far apart (e.g., after a long-running consumer, offsets in the millions with sparse in-flight items), so each 1-second commit-loop iteration can iterate over millions of integers per partition, holding the per-partition lock the entire time. This blocks add_offset/complete_offset calls from worker threads (stalling processing) and burns CPU. The algorithm should instead sort the completed offsets and walk only the actual tracked offsets (e.g., iterate over sorted(all_offsets) and stop at the first outstanding one), which is O(k log k) in the number of tracked offsets rather than O(max_offset).

OffsetTracker.partition_locks dict is read and written without synchronization, allowing duplicate locks for the same partition

_get_partition_lock does `self.partition_locks.get(partition)` followed by `self.partition_locks.setdefault(partition, threading.Lock())` with no lock protecting the dict itself. Multiple worker threads can race on first access to a partition: thread A's get() returns None, thread B's get() returns None, and both create separate Lock objects — one wins in the dict, the other thread uses its own orphaned lock. All subsequent synchronization for that partition is then split across two locks, so add_offset/complete_offset/get_committable_offsets/mark_committed are not mutually exclusive, which can corrupt the offset sets (e.g., mark_committed pruning all_offsets while get_committable_offsets iterates it) and produce incorrect commit decisions — potentially committing offsets for messages still being processed (data loss on crash). Guard creation with a single global lock (e.g., `with self._locks_guard: return self.partition_locks.setdefault(partition, threading.Lock())`).

Worker exceptions are swallowed and the offset is still marked complete, causing silent message loss

In OrderedQueueWorker.run, when result_processor raises, the exception is only logged ('Unexpected error in queue worker') and the finally block unconditionally calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)`. The offset is therefore treated as successfully processed and becomes committable, so the failed message is never retried and is silently dropped once the offset is committed. Note that ResultProcessor.__call__ in result_consumer.py also swallows exceptions internally, so most processing failures never even reach this handler — either way the message is lost. This is a data-integrity bug for a Kafka consumer whose contract is at-least-once delivery. On exception the offset should remain outstanding (or the item should be retried / sent to a DLQ), not completed.

submit() exception handler marks the offset complete, committing messages that were never processed

In SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit, the except block logs 'Error submitting message to queue' and then calls add_offset + complete_offset for the message. If the decoder or grouping_fn raised, the message was never enqueued or processed, yet its offset is immediately marked complete and will be committed — permanently skipping that message. The same pattern is used for the `result is None` path (lines 301-304), which is arguably intentional for undecodable messages, but applying it to unexpected exceptions in submit converts a transient failure into silent data loss. The offset should be left outstanding (blocking commits for that partition, surfacing the problem) or the message routed to a DLQ, not completed.

close() can commit offsets for items still queued, and shutdown discards in-flight work without committing or requeuing

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets shutdown_event, joins the commit thread (which stops committing), then calls queue_pool.shutdown(). FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown = True and calls q.shutdown(immediate=False) — with Python's queue.ShutDown semantics, workers finish the item they are currently processing but any items still sitting in the queues are abandoned, and their offsets remain outstanding (never committed, which is safe) — but worse, close() joins the commit thread BEFORE draining the queues, so offsets for items that complete during pool shutdown are never committed even though they were processed. On the next start those messages are reprocessed (at-least-once, acceptable), but the ordering of operations is wrong: the pool should be drained (wait_until_empty) and a final commit performed before the commit thread is stopped. Also, terminate() shuts down the pool without waiting for in-flight items at all. For a consumer whose purpose is exactly-once-ish ordered processing, shutdown should drain queues and flush final offsets.

join() ignores its timeout argument and delegates to close(), which is not a graceful join

ProcessingStrategy.join(timeout) is expected to wait up to `timeout` for the strategy to finish processing outstanding work. Here join() discards the timeout and calls close(), which (per the close() issues above) stops the commit thread and shuts down workers with a hard 5s join each, abandoning queued items. Arroyo's StreamProcessor uses join during shutdown to allow in-flight work to complete; this implementation makes join equivalent to an abrupt terminate and ignores the caller's timeout, so shutdown behavior does not match the ProcessingStrategy contract.

FixedQueuePool is created once per factory but create_with_partitions can be called multiple times, sharing one pool across strategies

ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ creates a single FixedQueuePool (with its worker threads and OffsetTracker) when mode == 'thread-queue-parallel'. create_with_partitions then returns a new SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy wrapping that same pool each time it is called. Arroyo calls create_with_partitions per partition-assignment epoch (e.g., on rebalance), so multiple strategy instances can share one pool and one OffsetTracker. Each SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy also spawns its own commit thread calling commit_function with its own `commit` closure — two commit threads can commit interleaved offset maps from the shared tracker, and shutdown() on the factory sets self.queue_pool = None while previously created strategies still reference the pool, leading to double shutdown and commits from stale strategies. The pool should be created per create_with_partitions call (or the factory should guard against reuse), not per factory instance.

ResultProcessor.__call__ swallows all exceptions, so failed results are treated as processed and their offsets committed

ResultProcessor.__call__ wraps handle_result in a try/except that only logs ('Failed to process message result'). Since OrderedQueueWorker treats the return of result_processor as success and completes the offset, any exception in handle_result (DB errors, assertion failures, etc.) results in the message being acknowledged and committed — silent data loss with no retry and no DLQ routing. This is the queue-mode equivalent of a poison message being dropped. Failures should propagate (so the offset stays outstanding and the partition stalls, surfacing the issue) or be routed to the DLQ policy that the StreamProcessor already supports.

Sentry transaction name hardcodes 'monitors.' prefix for a generic remote-subscriptions component

OrderedQueueWorker.run creates a transaction named f"monitors.{self.identifier}.worker_{self.worker_id}". This module lives in sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers and is generic infrastructure (also used by uptime via ResultsStrategyFactory), but the metric/transaction namespace is hardcoded to 'monitors.', so uptime results processed through this path will be tagged as monitors.* in Sentry/metrics, polluting dashboards and making the identifier misleading. The prefix should be derived from the identifier or made configurable.

wait_until_empty only checks queue size, not outstanding (in-flight) items

FixedQueuePool.wait_until_empty returns True when get_stats()['total_items'] == 0, i.e., all queues are empty. But an item that has been popped by a worker and is currently being processed is no longer counted in qsize(), so wait_until_empty can return True while work is still in flight. Callers using this to assert 'all work done' (as the tests do implicitly via stats checks) can race with in-flight processing. It should also check that the OffsetTracker has no outstanding offsets (or expose outstanding counts in get_stats).

test_different_groups_distributed can pass even if all groups hash to one queue (weak assertion on hash distribution)

The test asserts len(queue_indices) == 3 after hashing 20 group keys with num_queues=3. With Python's randomized string hash this usually passes, but it is probabilistic and, more importantly, it validates distribution rather than the actual requirement — consistent assignment per key (covered by the other test) and correct modulo behavior. If hash() were replaced with a broken function returning a constant, this test would catch it, but as written it is flaky-by-construction (a fixed hash seed could theoretically map all 20 keys to fewer than 3 buckets) and does not test the property that matters for correctness (stability across processes), which is untestable in-process. Consider asserting on a deterministic hash function instead once the implementation is fixed.

New thread-queue-parallel tests poll with fixed iteration counts and no failure message on timeout

The new tests (test_thread_queue_parallel, test_thread_queue_parallel_preserves_order, test_thread_queue_parallel_concurrent_subscriptions, test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_commit, test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling, test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps) use `for _ in range(max_wait): ... time.sleep(0.1)` loops and then assert on results without first asserting the loop actually observed the expected condition. If processing is merely slow (CI under load), the loop exits after max_wait iterations (5 seconds) and the subsequent assert produces a confusing failure, or worse, in test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling the loop breaks only when the condition holds but the final asserts tolerate `len(committed_offsets) == 0` — meaning the test can pass without ever verifying that commits are correctly withheld. The loops should assert the wait condition succeeded (e.g., `assert stats['total_items'] == 0 and ... , 'timed out waiting'`) before proceeding, so slow runs fail loudly at the wait rather than at a downstream assert, and the error-handling test should deterministically verify the no-commit behavior.

If it did not raise (e.g. on a list-backed source), a negative offset would index from the end of the result set, returning rows from arbitrary positions outside the paginated window, and combined with the `is_prev` handling below (which compares `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` with a negative offset) the cursor math produces inconsistent next/prev cursors. The claim 'This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level' does not hold: the queryset is filtered by organization, but the offset manipulation lets a client jump to any position in that organization's dataset, and the resulting cursors can be replayed to enumerate rows outside the intended page window. false_positives.candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator prev-page trimming uses negative offset in length comparison, corrupting results

In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, the prev-page trimming logic `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra: results = results[:-1]` uses the raw `offset` (which may be negative when enable_advanced_features allowed it through). With a negative offset, `offset + limit + extra` can be less than the actual fetched length, so the extra sentinel row is never trimmed, and the sentinel row (which exists only to detect 'has more previous results') is included in the returned page. Conversely when the comparison accidentally matches, a legitimate data row is dropped. This produces duplicated or missing rows at page boundaries for prev cursors under the advanced-features path. The same expression in BasePaginator (line 192) is only reached with non-negative offsets in the original code path, so the new negative-offset branch introduces a new way to hit this logic with invalid values.

Undocumented query parameter switches the paginator implementation, changing the response contract

`use_optimized = request.GET.get('optimized_pagination') == 'true'` silently swaps the paginator class for privileged users. The two paginators produce different cursor semantics (OptimizedCursorPaginator emits integer keys via math.floor on the sort value, DateTimePaginator emits millisecond timestamps), so the `cursor` values in the response `Link` header are not interchangeable between the two modes. A client that starts paginating with the default paginator and then adds `optimized_pagination=true` (or vice versa) will feed a cursor of one format into the other paginator, producing wrong pages or errors. There is no API versioning, no documentation of the parameter, and no validation that the cursor format matches the selected paginator. This is a contract break hidden behind an undocumented flag.
