However, the controller actions use `params.require(:group_id)`, expecting the parameter to be named `group_id`. With Rails member routes, the id parameter is named `id`, not `group_id`. This means `params.require(:group_id)` will raise `ActionController::ParameterMissing` at runtime, breaking both endpoints. The controller should use `params.require(:id)` to match the route definition, or the routes should be defined with an explicit `:group_id` segment.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same route/controller parameter mismatch: group member routes provide params[:id], while the actions require params[:group_id], causing runtime failures and broken group membership functionality.

false_positives.candidate:
SQL injection via ILIKE search parameter

The `index` action interpolates the raw `params[:search]` value directly into a SQL string: `groups.where("name ILIKE ?", "%#{search}%")`. While the `?` placeholder protects against classic injection of the search term itself, the `%` and `_` wildcard characters in the user-supplied search string are not escaped, allowing wildcard injection (e.g. searching `%` matches all groups, `_` matches any single character). More importantly, this pattern is fragile and the change from `ilike` to `ILIKE` suggests a hand-rolled query. The search term should be sanitized (e.g. `search.gsub(/[%_]/, '\\\0')`) or use a proper query builder to prevent wildcard abuse and any future refactoring from introducing true injection.

add_members silently ignores usernames with surrounding whitespace

In `add_members`, `usernames.split(",")` does not strip whitespace from each username. If the client sends `"user1, user2"` (with a space after the comma, which is common when users type comma-separated lists), `User.find_by_username(" user2")` will return nil and the user will be silently skipped. The member is not added but the response is still `success_json`, so the admin UI shows no error. Each username should be stripped: `usernames.split(",").map(&:strip).each do |username|`.

remove_member does not verify the user is actually a member before deleting

In `remove_member`, `group.users.delete(user_id)` is called without checking whether the user is actually a member of the group. While `delete` on a non-member is a no-op at the database level, the action still returns `success_json` and calls `group.save`, which triggers unnecessary validations and callbacks. More importantly, if `user_id` refers to a non-existent user, the delete silently succeeds. The controller should verify the user exists and is a member, returning a 404 or 422 if not, so the admin UI can show an appropriate error.

totalPages calculation is off-by-one for exact multiples of limit

The `totalPages` computed property uses `Math.floor(this.get("user_count") / this.get("limit")) + 1`. For a group with exactly 100 users and limit 50, this returns `Math.floor(100/50) + 1 = 3`, but there are only 2 pages (offsets 0 and 50). The correct formula is `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)`. This causes the pagination UI to show an extra page, and clicking "next" on the last real page navigates to an empty page. The `currentPage` computed has a similar issue with its base calculation.

Error handler assumes e.responseText is valid JSON without checking

In the `save` action's error callback: `var message = $.parseJSON(e.responseText).errors;`. If the server returns a non-JSON response (e.g., a 500 HTML error page, or a network error where `responseText` is undefined), `$.parseJSON` will throw a SyntaxError, masking the original error and leaving `disableSave` potentially stuck (though `finally` handles that). The code should check that `e.responseText` exists and handle parse failures gracefully, falling back to a generic error message.

Stray closing div tag inside table row Line 19 contains `` inside the `{{#each}}` loop within a `` structure. A `` inside a `` (without a matching opening `
`) is invalid HTML. Browsers will typically ignore it or hoist it out of the table, potentially breaking the table layout. This should be removed.

Template iterates over 'members' but controller sets 'model'

The template was changed from `{{#each m in model}}` to `{{#each m in members}}`, and the route `group-members.js.es6` now sets `controller.set("model", model)` where `model` is the Group object. The Group model's `findMembers()` sets a `members` property on the group object (line 35 of group.js: `members: result.members.map(...)`). Since the controller is likely an ObjectController or the template context is the group model, `members` should resolve to `model.members`. However, if the controller is not proxying to the model, `members` will be undefined. The template should either use `{{#each m in model.members}}` to be explicit, or the controller should explicitly set `controller.set('members', model.get('members'))` after `findMembers()` resolves. The current code relies on implicit property proxying which may not work depending on the controller type.

removeMember action in item view template won't bubble to controller correctly

The template `group_member.hbs` uses `{{action "removeMember" member}}` inside an `{{#each member in members itemView="group-member"}}` loop. The `itemView` is `Discourse.View` (from `group-member.js.es6`), not a controller. In Ember, actions in item views bubble to the view's controller, but since this is a plain View (not an ItemView with a specific controller), the action will bubble to the parent controller (the admin-group controller). However, the `removeMember` action expects `member` as a parameter, and in the `{{action}}` helper within an `{{#each}}` with `itemView`, the context may not correctly pass the `member` object. The action should be tested to ensure `member` is correctly passed; alternatively, use `{{action "removeMember" this}}` from within the view's context or use `targetObject` explicitly.

members action performs two count queries instead of one

The `members` action calls `group.users.count` (line 25) and then `group.users.order(:username_lower).limit(limit).offset(offset)` (line 26). The `count` query and the subsequent `members` query are separate database queries. While this is acceptable for pagination metadata, the `count` could be optimized by using `group.users.count` only when needed, or by using a single query with `COUNT(*) OVER()` window function (PostgreSQL) to get both total and page in one query. For groups with many members, this is two full queries instead of one. This is a minor performance concern but worth noting for large groups.

offset parameter is not validated, allowing negative offsets

The `members` action does `offset = params[:offset].to_i` without validating that it's non-negative. A negative offset (e.g., `?offset=-50`) will be passed to ActiveRecord's `.offset()`, which in PostgreSQL treats negative offsets as 0, but this behavior is database-dependent and could cause unexpected results. The offset should be clamped: `offset = [params[:offset].to_i, 0].max`. Similarly, `limit` is not validated to be within a reasonable range (e.g., max 100 or 200), allowing a client to request `?limit=1000000` and potentially cause performance issues.

Test for add_members on automatic group uses group_id: 1 which may not be automatic

The test `"cannot add members to automatic groups"` uses `group_id: 1`, assuming group with id 1 is automatic. However, group IDs are not guaranteed—the test database may have groups with different IDs, or group 1 may not exist or may not be automatic. The test should explicitly create an automatic group: `group = Fabricate(:group, automatic: true)` and use `group_id: group.id`. Relying on a hardcoded ID of 1 is fragile and may cause the test to pass or fail for the wrong reasons depending on test ordering and database state.

Test for remove_member on automatic group uses hardcoded group_id: 1

Same issue as the add_members test: the test `"cannot remove members from automatic groups"` uses `group_id: 1` assuming it's an automatic group. This is fragile—the test should create an explicit automatic group with `Fabricate(:group, automatic: true)` and use its ID. Additionally, as noted in the other finding, this test uses `xhr :put` instead of `xhr :delete`, so it's not actually testing the remove_member endpoint.

addMembers action has TODO comment indicating incomplete functionality

The `addMembers` action contains `// TODO: should clear the input` and does not clear the `usernames` property after successfully adding members. This means after clicking "Add", the user-selector input still contains the previously entered usernames. If the admin clicks "Add" again without changing the input, the same members will be re-added (though the server should handle duplicates gracefully). The `usernames` property should be cleared after a successful add: `self.set('usernames', null)` or `self.set('usernames', '')` in the success callback of `addMembers`.

create action does not set alias_level, defaulting to 0 (nobody)

The `create` action sets `name` and `visible` but does not set `alias_level`. The Group model likely has a default `alias_level` of 0 (which maps to "nobody" in the UI). This means newly created groups are invisible to everyone by default, which may not be the intended behavior. The admin UI sends `alias_level` in the `save` action (via `asJSON()`), but the `create` action ignores it. The `create` action should also accept and set `alias_level`: `group.alias_level = params[:alias_level].to_i if params[:alias_level].present?`.

update action always sets visible even when param is absent

The `update` action does `group.visible = params[:visible] == "true"` unconditionally. If the client sends a PUT request without a `visible` parameter (e.g., only updating `alias_level`), `params[:visible]` is nil, and `nil == "true"` is false, so `visible` is set to false. This means any update that doesn't explicitly include `visible=true` will make the group invisible. The update should only modify `visible` if the parameter is present: `group.visible = params[:visible] == "true" if params.key?(:visible)`.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
should_block? performs a write during validation, and its return value is wrong when no record exists

BlockedEmail.should_block? is called from EmailValidator.validate_each (lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13), i.e. during User validation, yet it mutates the database (increments match_count, sets last_match_at, saves). This means a mere validation attempt — including failed validations, GET-triggered checks, or User.new(...).valid? in a console — permanently writes to blocked_emails. Also, when no record exists, `record` is nil and the method returns nil (falsy) — fine — but when a record exists with action_type :do_nothing, it still performs the write even though the email will not be blocked, inflating match_count for emails that are explicitly allowed. The statistics write should be moved out of the validation path (e.g. into the controller after a failed signup, or done atomically and only when actually blocking).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying issue: a blocking-check method unexpectedly writes statistics to the database during a read/validation operation. Although it adds concerns about return values and allowed emails, the core side-effect issue matches the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Domain whitelist/blacklist regex is injectable and matches substrings

email_in_restriction_setting? builds a Regexp directly from the SiteSetting value: `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)` after only escaping dots. The setting is admin-controlled so the injection risk is limited to admins, but the bigger correctness/security bug is that the pattern is unanchored: '@(example\.com)' matches 'user@sub.example.com' AND 'user@notexample.com' (substring match, no boundary). A blacklist entry for 'example.com' will also block 'myexample.com', and a whitelist entry for 'example.com' will wrongly admit 'user@evilexample.com'. The domain list should be split on commas/whitespace and each domain anchored: Regexp.new("@#{Regexp.escape(domain)}$", true) per domain, matching any of them. This is a real bypass/false-positive issue for the email restriction feature that this PR relocates into the validator.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same underlying issue: email_in_restriction_setting? uses an insufficiently anchored domain regex, allowing unintended domain matches and email whitelist bypasses. The candidate's additional injection concern and inaccurate example matches do not change the shared core finding.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Email matching is case-sensitive; blocked emails can be bypassed with case variation

should_block? does `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` with no downcasing or normalization. The users table stores email as given (User validates uniqueness on the raw email string), and the signup form sends whatever the user typed. An attacker who adds a BlockedEmail entry for 'spam@example.com' can trivially bypass it by registering 'SPAM@example.com' or 'Spam@Example.com'. The lookup must normalize: `BlockedEmail.where(email: Email.downcase(email)).first` (the codebase already has Email.downcase used in users_controller.rb:269), and ideally the email column should be stored downcased on create (before_validation). Without this the entire blocklist feature is ineffective.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same case-sensitive lookup in BlockedEmail.should_block?, which allows a blocked email address to bypass the blocklist by changing its capitalization.

false_positives.candidate:
Blocked-email check is skipped when the email is blank or nil

validate_each receives `value` which is the raw attribute. If value is nil (email not yet assigned) or an empty string, `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` is still called with nil/'' — for nil, `where(email: nil).first` returns nil so it is harmless, but the guard `record.errors[attribute].blank?` means the blocked check only runs when no other error exists. More importantly, the validator never checks that value is a syntactically valid email before doing the domain regex match: `value =~ regexp` on line 21 will raise NoMethodError (undefined method =~ for nil) if value is nil when a whitelist/blacklist setting is present, crashing validation with a 500 instead of a validation error. Add `return if value.blank?` at the top of validate_each.

Changing email validation from separate presence/uniqueness validators to combined `validates` alters error messages and hash shape returned to the client

The old code used `validates_presence_of :email` and `validates_uniqueness_of :email`, which add errors like 'Email can't be blank' and 'Email has already been taken'. The new `validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true` produces the same default messages, so that part is equivalent — but the PR also adds `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice(...)` to the create failure response in users_controller.rb. The client (create_account_controller.js:274) checks `result.errors && result.errors.email` — with to_hash, errors.email is an array of message strings, which works — but the change from the previous response shape (message only) is an API contract change for any other API consumer, and `user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")` echoes back the submitted email verbatim, including any HTML/script content, into a JSON response that the client pushes into rejectedEmails and re-renders; ensure the client treats it as text (it does, via Ember binding) but note the response now includes raw user input. The bigger issue: uniqueness validation on email is not case-insensitive — 'User@Example.com' and 'user@example.com' are treated as different by `validates :uniqueness_of`, yet the DB unique index on users.email is also case-sensitive, so this is consistent, but the BlockedEmail lookup (see separate finding) is what must be case-insensitive.

Error response now includes raw submitted attributes (name, username, email) without sanitization

The create failure path now returns `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")`. These are the raw, un-sanitized params the user submitted (set via User.new_from_params). The values are echoed back in the JSON response and the JS client pushes result.values.email into rejectedEmails and compares it against the email input. While Ember escapes on render, returning raw user input in an API response is an unnecessary reflection vector; at minimum the email should be the normalized/downcased form. Consider returning only what is needed (the email) and normalizing it.

rejectedEmails comparison is case-sensitive, so a rejected email can be re-submitted with different casing

The client-side check `this.get('rejectedEmails').contains(email)` compares the exact string. If the server rejected 'Spam@Example.com', the user can immediately retype 'spam@example.com' (or any case variation) and the client-side check passes; the form will be re-submitted and only fail again server-side. The comparison should be case-insensitive (compare downcased values), matching the server-side normalization the BlockedEmail lookup should have (see related finding). Also note the server returns the email in result.values.email — if the server normalizes differently than the client, the client-side rejection will never trigger.

blocked_emails.email has no length limit and no normalization; unique index is case-sensitive

t.string :email with no limit defaults to 255 in most adapters, but there is no downcasing on store and the unique index on email is case-sensitive (default PostgreSQL behavior). Combined with the case-sensitive lookup in BlockedEmail.should_block?, entries 'Spam@x.com' and 'spam@x.com' are treated as distinct rows, defeating the blocklist. The migration should either add a functional unique index on lower(email) or enforce downcasing in the model's before_validation, and the model should normalize on lookup.

No test for case-insensitive matching of blocked emails

The spec suite for BlockedEmail covers default action_type, statistics updates, and both action types, but never tests that should_block? matches an email regardless of case (e.g. record 'block@spam.org' vs query 'BLOCK@SPAM.ORG'). Given that email case-insensitivity is a real-world requirement (and the current implementation is case-sensitive, which is a bug), this is exactly the scenario that needs a regression test. Add a test asserting BlockedEmail.should_block?('BLOCK@SPAMFROMHOME.ORG') returns true when the stored record is lowercase.

EmailValidator spec does not test the whitelist/blacklist domain logic that was moved into it

The spec only stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? and checks the blocked path. The validator also contains the relocated email_domains_whitelist / email_domains_blacklist logic (lines 4-12), which is security-relevant (it is the only thing preventing signups from blacklisted domains). There are no tests covering: whitelist present and email not in whitelist → error; whitelist present and email in whitelist → no error; blacklist present and email in blacklist → error; blacklist present and email not in blacklist → no error. Since this PR moves that logic from User into EmailValidator, the existing User model specs (if any) may no longer exercise it. Add specs for the domain restriction branches.

Blocked-email validation only runs when email_changed?, so existing users changing other attributes bypass the blocklist, and email changes are not checked against BlockedEmail

`validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` means the custom EmailValidator (which includes the BlockedEmail.should_block? check) only runs when the email attribute has changed. This is intentional for the signup path, but it means: (1) any code path that creates or saves a User with an email that matches a BlockedEmail entry but where email_changed? is false (e.g. an admin editing a user, or a user whose email was set before the blocklist entry was added and who re-saves) will not be blocked; (2) more critically, the change_email flow in UsersController (users_controller.rb:265-286) creates an EmailToken for a new email but never validates the new email against BlockedEmail — a blocked user can change their email to another blocked address via the preferences flow, because EmailToken creation does not run User email validation. The blocklist must also be enforced in the change_email path (and ideally in EmailToken creation), not only on User save with email_changed?.

Missing newline at end of file

true_positives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.

Login/signup buttons and icons still use float:left inside flex container, causing layout breakage

The `.contents` element is now a flex container (line 17: `@include flexbox()`), but its children `.login-button, button.sign-up-button` (lines 42-47) and `.icons` (lines 53-61) still use `float: left`. The `float: left` declarations on these elements are now dead code and the visual layout will differ from the pre-flexbox version. It does not mention the additional non-Ember/noscript panel right-alignment regression, but matches the float/flex issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order mixin uses -moz-box-ordinal-group which is incompatible with flexbox order semantics

The `order()` mixin (lines 125-131) emits `-moz-box-ordinal-group: $val` (line 127). The old Firefox flexbox implementation (`-moz-box`) uses `-moz-box-ordinal-group` with 1-based integer values, while the standard `order` property (and `-webkit-order`, `-ms-flex-order`) uses 0-based integers. Passing the same `$val` (e.g., `3` from header.scss line 39, `2` from topic.scss line 30) to both properties means Firefox's old flexbox will interpret the value differently (off-by-one), causing `.panel` and `.extra-info-wrapper` to appear in the wrong visual order in old Firefox versions. The mixin should either not emit `-moz-box-ordinal-group` at all (since `-moz-box` is ancient and rarely targeted), or adjust the value for that property (e.g., `$val + 1`).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying issue: legacy box-ordinal-group requires 1-based values, but the mixin passes the standard order value unchanged. Although it focuses on the Mozilla property and different examples, its proposed $val + 1 correction addresses the golden comment's bug.

false_positives.candidate:
inline-flex mixin emits invalid -moz-inline-box and missing standard fallback ordering

The `inline-flex()` mixin outputs `display: -moz-inline-box` (line 111), which is not a valid value for the `display` property in Firefox's old flexbox implementation (Firefox only supported `-moz-box`, never `-moz-inline-box`), so that declaration is dropped. More importantly, the mixin places the prefixed values before the standard `inline-flex` (line 113), which is correct, but it omits `display: -webkit-inline-flex` ordering issues aside, the real problem is that `-moz-inline-box` is invalid CSS that will be ignored, and older Firefox versions that only support `-moz-box` will fall back to `display: block`-like behavior for `.badge-wrapper.bullet` elements, breaking the intended inline-flex layout in those browsers. The invalid `-moz-inline-box` declaration should be removed or replaced with `-moz-inline-flex` (which Firefox never supported either, so the mixin should just use `-webkit-inline-box`, `-ms-inline-flexbox`, and `inline-flex`).

Header layout breaks because .panel uses margin-left:auto with order(3) but .title was removed without replacement flex item

The diff removes the `.title { float: left; }` rule entirely (lines 16-18 of the diff) and adds `@include flexbox()` + `@include align-items(center)` to `.contents`, but there is no remaining flex item to push `.panel` to the right via `margin-left: auto`. However, the `.title` selector was deleted from the SCSS, meaning the HTML element with class `title` (the site title/logo area) is no longer styled as a flex item and, more critically, the `margin-left: auto` on `.panel` only works if there are other flex items taking up space. Without the `.title` being a flex item (or any other left-side content), the header layout will collapse or misalign: the logo/title area will not be pushed left, and `.panel` will not be pushed right as intended. The `.title` rule removal appears to be an accidental deletion rather than intentional—the original code had `.title { float: left; }` to position the title, and the flexbox conversion should have kept equivalent styling (e.g., making `.title` a flex item with appropriate flex properties) rather than deleting it entirely.

The `.small-action` element is now a flex container (lines 264-265: `@include flexbox()` + `@include align-items(center)`), but its children `.topic-avatar` (line 270: `float: left`), `.small-action-desc .avatar` (line 298: `float: left`), and `button` (line 309: `float: right`) all use `float`. The flex conversion needs to use `margin-left: auto` on the button or `order` properties instead of relying on floats.

order(2) applied to .extra-info-wrapper without a flex container parent

The `.extra-info-wrapper` element has `@include order(2)` (line 30), but the `order` property only has an effect on flex items (children of a flex container). Looking at the surrounding code, `.extra-info-wrapper` appears to be a sibling of `#topic-title` (which contains `.title-wrapper` with `float: left`), and there is no parent element with `display: flex` that contains `.extra-info-wrapper` as a direct child. The `flexbox()` mixin (lines 100-106) emits `display: -moz-box` (line 102) for old Firefox, but Firefox's old flexbox implementation also supported `display: -moz-flex` as an intermediate unprefixed-ish value before the standard `flex`.
