These are routine progress messages for a normal background cleanup operation, not errors. Logging them at Error level will spam error-level logs and alerting/observability pipelines on every cleanup cycle, and makes it impossible to distinguish real failures from normal operation. They should be logged at Info or Debug level (the surrounding cleanup service already logs a Debug summary of affected rows).
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same problem: routine debugging or progress information is logged at Error level, which pollutes error logs. Both recommend switching to Debug or Info level.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup job interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute

The diff changes `ticker := time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 10)` to `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1)` in CleanUpService.Run. This is unrelated to the stated PR goal (splitting annotation cleanup queries to avoid MySQL deadlocks) and has major operational impact: every cleanup job — temp file cleanup, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, user invites, short URLs, query history (including two EnforceRowLimitInQueryHistory passes over 200k/150k row limits) — now runs every minute instead of every 10 minutes. On large instances this multiplies background DB load tenfold, increases lock contention with user traffic (the very problem this PR tries to reduce for annotations), and shortens the effective cleanup cadence assumptions elsewhere. If this change is intentional it must be called out in the PR description and justified; as an unexplained side change it should be reverted.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the cleanup ticker change from 10 minutes to 1 minute and its resulting increase in DB load and contention.

false_positives.candidate:
Log statement includes a stale 'err' value that is always nil at that point

The log call `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, "cond", cond, "err", err)` is placed after `if err != nil { return 0, err }`, so `err` is always nil when the log line executes. The same pattern appears in the MaxCount branch (line 554) and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags (line 576). The 'err' key is dead/misleading log output; it should be removed or the log moved before the error check.

MaxAge cleanup condition interpolates annotationType and cutoffDate directly into SQL

The batch condition is built with fmt.Sprintf(`%s AND created < %v ORDER BY id DESC %s`, annotationType, cutoffDate, ...) and passed to fetchIDs, which concatenates it into `SELECT id FROM annotation WHERE <cond>`. annotationType is a caller-supplied string (alertAnnotationType/dashboardAnnotationType/apiAnnotationType constants today, but the function signature accepts any string) and is interpolated unquoted and unvalidated into the WHERE clause. If annotationType ever contains SQL syntax (e.g. via a future caller or config), this is a SQL injection vector; at minimum it is fragile string-built SQL. The value should be validated against a whitelist of known type expressions or passed as a bound parameter.

SQLite workaround interpolates IDs into SQL and keys off configured batch size rather than actual ID count

In deleteByIDs, when the database is SQLite and `r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999`, the IDs are string-interpolated directly into the DELETE statement (`DELETE FROM %s WHERE id IN (%s)`). Two problems: (1) the decision is based on the configured batch size, not on len(ids) — if the config is >999 but a batch returns fewer IDs (e.g. the final partial batch, or the MaxCount offset path), the code still takes the interpolation path unnecessarily; conversely the guard is correct only because fetchIDs is bounded by the same config. (2) Although the values are int64s produced by the database itself (so not attacker-controlled), building SQL by string concatenation is a fragile pattern that defeats the purpose of parameterized queries and will break if IDs ever become non-numeric. The condition should be `len(ids) > sqliteParameterLimit`, and the IDs should be chunked into multiple parameterized DELETEs of ≤999 parameters each rather than interpolated.

MaxCount cleanup can loop forever or over-delete when rows are concurrently inserted

The MaxCount branch selects IDs with `ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT/OFFSET MaxCount, BatchSize` and deletes them, repeating until a batch affects 0 rows. The termination condition is `affected == 0` from the DELETE. Two issues: (1) If annotations are being inserted concurrently with higher IDs, each iteration selects a fresh window past MaxCount and deletes it, so the loop keeps deleting newly inserted annotations indefinitely — the loop only stops when a full batch window contains no rows, which under sustained insert load may never happen within the 9-minute cleanup timeout, and it will delete annotations that were just created and should be kept (the newest MaxCount are preserved only relative to the snapshot at each iteration, but new inserts above the cutoff keep getting deleted). The old single-statement version had the same windowing semantics per execution but was bounded to one statement per run; the new untilDoneOrCancelled loop makes it unbounded. (2) If a concurrent transaction deletes some of the selected IDs between fetchIDs and deleteByIDs, RowsAffected < len(ids) but > 0, so the loop continues — that part is fine — but if ALL selected IDs vanish concurrently, affected == 0 and the loop exits early even though more excess annotations remain. The loop should be bounded (e.g. a max iteration count or a deadline check) and the select should be re-evaluated consistently.

Non-atomic select-then-delete can orphan annotation_tag rows when annotations are deleted between the two statements

The new cleanup deletes annotations by ID in one statement (deleteByIDs on 'annotation') but never deletes the corresponding annotation_tag rows in the same operation. The old code had the same gap for CleanAnnotations (tags were handled by CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags), so this is pre-existing, but the PR's stated goal is data integrity during cleanup and the test now asserts tag counts. Between the annotation DELETE and the next CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags run, annotation_tag rows reference deleted annotations (orphans), and any concurrent reader joining annotation_tag to annotation simply won't see them — acceptable — but if the process crashes between the two, orphans persist until the next cycle. More importantly, within a single Run() the annotation cleanup and orphan-tag cleanup are separate jobs, so tags for annotations deleted by MaxAge/MaxCount cleanup are only removed later. This should be documented or the tag deletion should be batched alongside (e.g. delete tags by annotation_id IN (...) before deleting the annotations).

Orphaned-tag cleanup matches annotation_tag.id, but the orphan condition references annotation_id

CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags builds the condition `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM annotation a WHERE annotation_id = a.id)` and fetches `SELECT id FROM annotation_tag WHERE <cond>`. The subquery correlates `annotation_id` (a column of annotation_tag) with `a.id`, which works because the outer query's annotation_tag columns are in scope. However, the fetched `id` is annotation_tag's own primary key, and deleteByIDs deletes `WHERE id IN (...)` on annotation_tag — that is consistent. The subtle issue is that the condition relies on implicit column scoping (`annotation_id` unqualified resolves to the outer annotation_tag), which is correct but fragile; it should be qualified as `at.annotation_id` with an alias for clarity and to avoid ambiguity if the schema changes. Not a functional bug today, but worth fixing while touching this code.

New large-batch test only runs on SQLite and does not exercise the parameterized path for other dialects

The new test case 'should not fail if batch size is larger than SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER' creates 40003 annotations with batch size 32767. The SQLite-specific interpolation path in deleteByIDs is only taken when `r.db.GetDBType() == migrator.SQLite`; CI integration tests run against SQLite by default, so the test exercises the interpolation branch. However, there is no test covering the parameterized branch with a batch size above 999 on MySQL/Postgres (where SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER does not apply but MySQL has its own max_allowed_packet / placeholder considerations), and no unit test for deleteByIDs chunking behavior. Given the change is motivated by MySQL deadlocks, the deadlock-avoidance behavior itself (separate SELECT and DELETE statements, no shared transaction) is not covered by any concurrency test.

Test helper now assigns explicit IDs to annotations, which may mask auto-increment behavior differences across databases

createTestAnnotations was changed to set `ID: int64(i + 1)` explicitly on each annotation and to batch-insert with InsertMulti. Explicit primary keys bypass the database auto-increment sequence. On MySQL/Postgres, inserting explicit IDs does not advance the auto-increment counter, so subsequent inserts by the application (which rely on auto-increment) could collide with these test IDs or behave differently than production. More relevant to this PR: the cleanup orders by `id DESC`, and with explicit IDs the test data's ID ordering exactly matches insertion ordering, which is also what auto-increment would produce — so the tests don't catch any divergence. This is acceptable for a test fixture, but the helper should reset the auto-increment sequence after inserting explicit IDs (or use auto-generated IDs) so the fixture doesn't leave the table in a state that breaks later tests in the same database.

fetchIDs builds SQL by concatenation and rejects empty condition only at runtime

fetchIDs constructs `SELECT id FROM <table> WHERE <condition>` via fmt.Sprintf with caller-provided table and condition strings. The empty-condition guard is a runtime error return rather than a compile-time constraint. All current callers pass constant strings, so this is safe today, but the function is a generic SQL-string builder; a future caller passing user-influenced input would have an injection point. Consider making the condition a structured type or at minimum documenting that callers must pass only static SQL fragments.

In DualWriterMode3.DeleteCollection, the asynchronous legacy write goroutine calls d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy) (line 166) instead of d.recordLegacyDuration(...). true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete records storage duration with 'name' instead of 'kind' as the resource label

In DualWriterMode3.Delete, the success path calls d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage), passing the object name (e.g. a UID) as the resource/kind label, while every other method passes options.Kind. This produces a high-cardinality, inconsistent metric label (one time series per object name) and breaks aggregation by kind. true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same problem: the metrics call passes 'name' where the other methods pass options.Kind. The candidate adds detail on cardinality and inconsistency, but it is the same underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Create records legacy duration metric on storage failure path

In DualWriterMode3.Create, when d.Storage.Create fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) instead of d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...). This records a storage failure as a legacy-storage duration metric, corrupting the legacy/storage latency metrics dashboards. The same wrong-metric bug exists in Update (line 129), which calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) when d.Storage.Update fails.

Async legacy writes capture and reuse the request context after the handler returns

Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection all spawn goroutines that use the incoming request ctx (via context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)) after the request handler has returned. The parent context is typically cancelled as soon as the HTTP request completes, so the derived 10-second timeout context is cancelled almost immediately, meaning the 'asynchronous safe-measure' legacy write will usually be aborted right away and effectively never run (or run with an already-cancelled context). This defeats the stated purpose of mode 3 ('write to unified storage and then asynchronously write to legacy as a safe measure') and silently drops the legacy write. A detached context (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx) or context.Background() with values preserved) should be used for the background legacy write.

Create passes the caller's mutable object to the async legacy write, allowing data races with the caller

In DualWriterMode3.Create, the same obj runtime.Object is passed both to d.Storage.Create (synchronously) and captured by the goroutine for d.Legacy.Create. The unified storage layer typically mutates the object in place (setting ResourceVersion, UID, defaults, managedFields). After Create returns, the caller (and the API machinery that serializes the response) may read or further mutate obj while the background goroutine is concurrently passing it to Legacy.Create. This is a data race on a shared object and can also cause the legacy store to receive an object whose ResourceVersion/UID was set by the unified store, which legacy create may reject or mishandle. A deep copy of the object should be made before handing it to the goroutine.

Update passes the shared UpdatedObjectInfo to the async legacy write, causing a data race and double evaluation

In DualWriterMode3.Update, the same objInfo rest.UpdatedObjectInfo is passed to d.Storage.Update and then captured by the goroutine for d.Legacy.Update. UpdatedObjectInfo.UpdatedObject is typically invoked lazily by each store; calling it twice (once per store) re-runs user-supplied transformation/validation logic concurrently with the request goroutine, and any state inside objInfo (or the underlying object it closes over) is shared unsynchronized between the two calls — a data race. The previous (pre-PR) implementation explicitly solved this by resolving objInfo.UpdatedObject once against the storage object and wrapping it in an updateWrapper with the already-computed object for the legacy call. That pattern was removed; the async legacy Update should receive a pre-resolved, immutable object (e.g. via an updateWrapper holding the object returned by Storage.Update) rather than the live objInfo.

Async legacy Delete may run after the object was already deleted, and NotFound is not handled

In DualWriterMode3.Delete, the legacy delete runs asynchronously with no handling of NotFound. Because the unified delete already succeeded and returned to the client, a subsequent immediate re-create of the same name (a common pattern: delete then create) can race with the in-flight legacy delete, causing the legacy delete to remove the newly created legacy object — the two stores diverge and the legacy copy of the re-created resource is silently lost. Additionally, if the legacy delete returns NotFound (e.g. the object never existed in legacy), the error is recorded as a legacy failure metric even though it is an expected condition. The previous implementation explicitly tolerated apierrors.IsNotFound for both stores; that handling was dropped.

Unbounded goroutine creation with no backpressure or panic recovery for async legacy writes

Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection each spawn an unbounded goroutine per request to perform the legacy write, with no worker pool, queue, or rate limiting. Under load (especially DeleteCollection, which is a single request fanning out to a legacy delete-collection), this can spawn a large number of concurrent goroutines hammering the legacy store, and a panic inside any of these goroutines (e.g. in legacy storage code or the mock in tests) crashes the whole Grafana process since there is no recover(). At minimum, panics in the async path should be recovered and logged; ideally the async writes should go through a bounded worker queue.

Legacy write failures are silently swallowed (only a metric, no log)

In all four async write paths (Create line 55-56, Delete line 112-113, Update line 139-140, DeleteCollection line 165-166), a failure of the legacy write is only recorded via d.recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, ...); there is no log.Error call. Since the whole point of the legacy write in mode 3 is to be a 'safe measure' keeping the legacy store in sync, silent failures mean operators have no log trail when the legacy store diverges from unified storage — divergence that will become user-visible the moment reads switch to unified-only or the legacy store is still being read by legacy APIs. Each async path should log the error (with kind/name) in addition to recording the metric.

Mode 3 unit tests never assert that the async legacy write actually happens

All Mode 3 tests (TestMode3_Create, TestMode3_Delete, TestMode3_Update, TestMode3_DeleteCollection) call the dual writer and immediately assert on the returned object/error. Because the legacy write now runs in a fire-and-forget goroutine, the tests return before (or regardless of whether) the legacy mock is invoked, so they cannot detect a regression where the legacy write is never executed, is cancelled immediately (the request-context cancellation issue), or races. The tests also never call m.AssertExpectations, so the setupLegacyFn expectations (e.g. line 30-32, 313-315) are not even verified. The tests should synchronize with the goroutine (e.g. a WaitGroup/channel in the mock, or assert with Eventually/AssertNumberOfCalls after a wait) and assert the legacy store was called exactly once.

TestMode3_Get shadows the package-level registry p with a local one, inconsistent with sibling tests

TestMode3_Get declares a local p := prometheus.NewRegistry() (line 119) while all other Mode 3 tests use the shared package-level var p (declared in dualwriter_mode1_test.go line 27). This is inconsistent and, more importantly, the shared package-level registry p is registered/used across many tests in the package; if NewDualWriter registers metrics on it, running tests in the same package can panic with 'duplicate metrics collector registration' depending on test order. The mode1 test file was changed in this PR to remove a shadowing local registry (dualwriter_mode1_test.go diff removes p := prometheus.NewRegistry()), suggesting the intent is to use the shared p everywhere — TestMode3_Get should be aligned.

Mode 3 integration test is inherently racy: it asserts legacy API state immediately after k8s writes that are only asynchronously propagated

doPlaylistTests (shared by the new 'mode 3' subtests at lines 132-144 and 191-204) performs k8s CRUD and then immediately reads through the legacy API expecting the data to be there — e.g. 'Do CRUD via k8s (and check that legacy api still works)' creates playlists via client.Resource.Create (line 496) and immediately checks /api/playlists (line 523-531); it updates via k8s (line 539) and immediately calls getFromBothAPIs (line 547) which GETs /api/playlists/<uid> (line 623-627); it deletes via k8s (line 572) and the subsequent legacy reads must reflect the deletion. In mode 3 the legacy write happens in a background goroutine after the k8s response returns, so these assertions race with the async legacy write and will flake (and, given the request-context cancellation issue, may fail deterministically). The mode 3 test runs need to poll/wait (require.Eventually) for legacy convergence instead of asserting immediately, otherwise the new mode 3 subtests are a source of CI flakiness.

Create returns the storage-created object but the async legacy create may fail, leaving stores permanently divergent with no reconciliation

In mode 3, Create returns success to the client as soon as the unified store write succeeds; the legacy write is best-effort and its failure is only counted in a metric. There is no retry, no dead-letter, and no reconciliation mechanism, so any legacy failure (including the systematic cancellation of the request context described above) permanently leaves the object missing from the legacy store. Since legacy APIs (e.g. /api/playlists) still read from the legacy store during migration, the object will be invisible to legacy consumers with no error surfaced to the user or operator beyond a metric. This is a data-integrity risk inherent to the design; at minimum the PR should document the divergence window/risk and provide an operational runbook, and ideally the async write should be retried or queued durably rather than fire-and-forget.

The old useAllAlertRuleAbilities computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)` from the CombinedRuleGroup, and federated rules were treated as immutable (no edit/delete/duplicate). In useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities, `MaybeSupported = loading ? NotSupported : AlwaysSupported` (line 309). Unlike the ruler-based hook, there is no isRulerAvailable concept, so once loading is false every action is 'supported'. However, `loading` here comes from useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable, which returns `loading: false` when `!rule || !folderUID` (line 355) — i.e., when the rule is undefined (skipToken case) or folderUid is missing, loading is false and abilities are computed with isEditable=false/isRemovable=false. In AlertRuleMenu, canDuplicate/canExport etc. are OR-ed between ruler and grafana abilities, so for cloud rules (where rulerRule is undefined and useRulerRuleAbilities returns [false,false]... actually useAllRulerRuleAbilities(undefined,...) returns MaybeSupported=false) the grafana side with skipToken yields Duplicate=[true, create-permission] even though promRule is a cloud rule, not a Grafana rule. Wait — AlertRuleMenu only passes promRule to useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities when prometheusRuleType.grafana.rule(promRule) is true, so skipToken is used for cloud rules and abilities are computed for undefined. For undefined rule: Duplicate supported=true, allowed=rulesPermissions.create (global AlertingRuleCreate). So canDuplicate = (ruler: false) || (grafana-undefined: true && create) = true for cloud rules if the user has global create permission — but duplicating a cloud rule via the grafana identifier path would be wrong. Actually handleDuplicateRule uses `identifier` which for cloud rules comes from getEditableIdentifier → ruleId.fromRulerRuleAndGroupIdentifierV2 — but rule (rulerRule) is undefined in the list view for cloud rules... This needs verification, but the core design smell is real: passing skipToken still computes and returns 'supported' abilities for a non-existent rule, and consumers OR them with ruler abilities, which can incorrectly enable actions. The sentinel should short-circuit to [false, false] instead of computing abilities for undefined.

The Delete menu item is gated on `canDelete && rulerRule` (line 165) and calls handleDelete(rulerRule, groupIdentifier). In the new list view (GrafanaRuleListItem → RuleActionsButtons.V2 → AlertRuleMenu), only promRule is passed; rulerRule is undefined. Conversely, in RuleActionsButtons.V2 the delete flow is wired via handleDelete={() => showDeleteModal(identifier, groupIdentifier)} which uses the identifier, not the rulerRule object — so the menu's handleDelete signature (rule: RulerRuleDTO, groupIdentifier) is incompatible with the list view. (3) The RulesTable.test.tsx still contains tests for 'Creating'/'Deleting' states (lines 151-200) but those test RulesTable with CombinedRule objects, not this loader — the GrafanaGroupLoader.test.tsx had its 'creating state' and 'deleting state' tests removed (see diff: 'should render rule with url and creating state when only ruler rule exists' and 'should render delete rule operation list item when only prom rule exists' were deleted). The test names and the mocked state contradict each other: either the name should be 'without the update permission' (matching RulesTable.test.tsx naming) or the mock should return isEditable: false. As written, the test passes but its name misleads future maintainers about what is being verified. Same issue for the Delete test (line 74) and the cloud rule tests (lines 89, 100).

useAllAlertRuleAbilities is marked `@deprecated Use {@link useAllRulerRuleAbilities} instead`, but useAllRulerRuleAbilities takes (rule: RulerRuleDTO | undefined, groupIdentifier) while useAllAlertRuleAbilities takes a CombinedRule and internally derives the groupIdentifier via groupIdentifier.fromCombinedRule. Meanwhile useAlertRuleAbility (singular, line 179) still uses useAllAlertRuleAbilities and is NOT deprecated, and RuleActionsButtons.V2 still calls useRulerRuleAbility directly. The deprecation is misleading and the migration path is unclear; either provide a proper replacement wrapper or remove the @deprecated tag.

Stale comment about preloading ruler rules remains after ruler prefetch was removed

The comment at lines 81-82 says 'This is not mandatory to preload ruler rules, but it improves the UX / Because the user waits a bit longer for the initial load but doesn't need to wait for each group to be loaded'. The ruler prefetch (alertRuleApi.util.prefetch('getGrafanaRulerGroup', ...)) was removed in this PR (see diff), so the comment now describes behavior that no longer exists. The comment should be updated to describe the Prometheus group cache population only.

Error handling only covers missing promResponse; a failed Prometheus query with error but no data shows the generic error Alert, but a failed query that returns data=undefined with isLoading=false is conflated with 'no data'

The component checks `if (!promResponse)` to show an error Alert, but RTK Query returns `data: undefined` both when the query failed AND potentially during refetching/polling edge cases. The old code checked `!rulerResponse && !promResponse`. More importantly, the query error object (promResponse error from useGetGrafanaGroupsQuery) is never inspected — the component destructures only { data, isLoading }, so an HTTP error (e.g., 403, 500) results in data=undefined and the generic 'Failed to load rules' Alert without the actual error message. The old GrafanaRuleLoader surfaced rulerRuleGroupError/promRuleGroupError via RulerRuleLoadingError. Error detail is lost in the new implementation.

runSplitQuery mutates the caller's request.targets via applyTemplateVariables, causing double interpolation and corrupted queries when called from shard splitting

runSplitQuery now maps request.targets through datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, ...). In the Loki datasource, applyTemplateVariables performs template variable interpolation in-place on the query object (it mutates query.expr and other fields, as evidenced by the shardQuerySplitting test mocks which do `query.expr = query.expr.replace(...)` and return the same object). runShardSplitQuery (shardQuerySplitting.ts:48-54) already interpolates the targets with applyTemplateVariables and then passes a subRequest built from the original `request` object into runSplitQuery (shardQuerySplitting.ts:163). Because the subRequest spreads `...request` but shares the same target object references, runSplitQuery interpolates the already-interpolated queries a second time. Consequences: (1) variables that expand to text containing `$`-like patterns or already-interpolated values can be re-interpolated, corrupting the LogQL expression; (2) `$__interval`/`$__range`-style variables are computed against the split sub-range on the second pass, producing wrong step/range values; (3) any variable whose interpolated output resembles a variable name gets expanded again. The shard-splitting path therefore executes queries with doubly-interpolated expressions. Fix: either make applyTemplateVariables return a copy (non-mutating), or have runSplitQuery/runShardSplitQuery operate on cloned targets so interpolation happens exactly once per query execution path.

Shard-split sub-requests re-interpolate already-interpolated targets inside runSplitQuery, and the shard selector can be corrupted by the second interpolation pass

runShardSplitQuery interpolates targets once (line 49-52) and groups them by their interpolated stream selector (getSelectorForShardValues on the interpolated expr). It then builds subRequest = { ...request, targets: interpolateShardingSelector(targets, shardsToQuery) } (line 154) and calls runSplitQuery(datasource, subRequest, ...) (line 163). runSplitQuery now unconditionally re-applies datasource.applyTemplateVariables to those targets (querySplitting.ts:296-299). Since interpolateShardingSelector injects a matcher like `__stream_shard__=~"20|10"` into the expression, a second interpolation pass runs template expansion over an expression that already contains interpolated content. If any template variable's value contains characters that look like LogQL or variable syntax, or if applyTemplateVariables is non-idempotent (e.g. it appends/replaces based on current content), the shard matcher or the user's query can be corrupted, causing queries to hit the wrong shards or fail to parse. Additionally, the shard grouping was computed from the once-interpolated selector, but execution uses a twice-interpolated expression, so grouping and execution can diverge. The two splitting layers must agree on a single interpolation point; as written, the shard path interpolates twice.

runSplitQuery mutates the caller's request object (request.queryGroupId) and, via shared target references, the caller's targets

Line 303 does `request.queryGroupId = uuidv4()`, mutating the DataQueryRequest passed in by the caller. When runSplitQuery is invoked from runShardSplitQuery (shardQuerySplitting.ts:163), the subRequest is a shallow copy `{ ...request, targets }`, so this assignment writes queryGroupId onto the shard-splitting request object as well. Combined with the in-place mutation performed by applyTemplateVariables on the shared target objects (see related finding), the caller's request and targets are modified as a side effect of running a split query. This is a data-integrity hazard: the same request object may be reused by the datasource for subsequent queries (e.g. streaming/refresh), and mutated targets (interpolated expr, step) would then be re-interpolated or sent with stale values. The function should clone the request (`{ ...request, queryGroupId: uuidv4() }`) and ensure targets are not mutated in place.

New interpolation test does not cover the shard-splitting double-interpolation path or non-idempotent variables

The added test 'Interpolates queries before execution' (lines 75-88) only verifies that runSplitQuery interpolates `$__auto` and `$step` once when called directly. It does not cover the composition with runShardSplitQuery, where targets are interpolated by runShardSplitQuery and then interpolated again by runSplitQuery. There is no test asserting that a query executed through the shard-splitting path is interpolated exactly once, nor a test with a variable whose interpolated value contains `$`-syntax or LogQL special characters (which would expose re-interpolation corruption). The shard test at shardQuerySplitting.test.ts:84-101 uses a mock datasource whose applyTemplateVariables is the real implementation backed by a `replace` stub, but its assertions only check the final expr/step, and the mock's replace is idempotent, so double interpolation would not be detected. A regression test that runs a query with a non-idempotent variable through runShardSplitQuery and asserts the executed expression is interpolated exactly once is missing.

Test expectation changed from 1 to 5 applyTemplateVariables calls without verifying per-shard-group interpolation correctness

The test 'Interpolates queries before running' (line 110-112) now asserts `expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)`. This reflects that interpolation moved from once-per-request (the old interpolateVariablesInQueries call) to once-per-target inside runShardSplitQuery plus additional calls inside runSplitQuery for each shard sub-request. The count of 5 is incidental (depends on shard grouping internals) and the test does not assert that each executed sub-request's expression was interpolated exactly once and not re-interpolated. If runSplitQuery's new interpolation causes double interpolation on this path, this test would still pass because the mock's replacement is idempotent. The test should assert on the executed expressions (which it partially does) with a non-idempotent mock, or explicitly verify single interpolation per executed query.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit enforcement is racy: check-then-act allows exceeding the configured limit

CreateOrUpdateDevice first calls CountDevices and only falls back to updateDevice when count >= deviceLimit, otherwise it performs an INSERT ... ON CONFLICT. This is a classic TOCTOU race: under concurrent anonymous requests (the normal case for a public Grafana instance), many goroutines can observe count < limit simultaneously and all insert new devices, exceeding AnonymousDeviceLimit. The limit is a security/abuse-control feature (bounding anonymous device rows), so silently exceeding it defeats its purpose. The count and insert are not performed in a single transaction or with any locking, so there is no atomicity. A correct implementation would enforce the limit atomically (e.g., conditional INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) ...) < limit, or a transaction with locking/serializable isolation), or at minimum treat the limit as best-effort and document it.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same check-then-act race in the device count check. Concurrent requests can exceed the device limit, and both suggest a transaction or lock as the fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Anonymous authentication is now performed synchronously on the request path with no timeout, and device-limit errors abort authentication entirely

The previous implementation ran TagDevice in a goroutine with a 2-minute timeout (context.WithTimeout) precisely so that slow or failing device tagging would not block or break request authentication. This PR removes the goroutine and the timeout and calls a.anonDeviceService.TagDevice(ctx, ...) synchronously with the request context. Two consequences: (1) every anonymous request now pays the latency of a COUNT(*) query plus an INSERT/UPDATE against the database on the critical auth path, adding DB load and latency to all anonymous traffic; (2) when TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached (which, per the updateDevice issue, can happen for brand-new devices), Authenticate returns nil, err and the anonymous user is completely denied access — turning a telemetry/abuse-control limit into a full authentication outage for new visitors. The limit should degrade gracefully (log and continue serving the anonymous identity) rather than rejecting the request, and the DB work should not be on the synchronous auth path without a timeout.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly says that when TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, Authenticate fails and anonymous users are denied access. It also notes that tagging used to be async and non-blocking. This is the same issue as the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
updateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached for any device that does not exist or is outside the time window, not only when the limit is reached

updateDevice runs an UPDATE ... WHERE device_id = ? AND updated_at BETWEEN ? AND ? and returns ErrDeviceLimitReached whenever RowsAffected == 0. RowsAffected is 0 both when the device does not exist (a brand-new device hitting a full table) and when the device exists but its updated_at is outside the [now-30d, now+1m] window (e.g., an expired device that the periodic cleanup has not yet removed, or clock skew). In both cases the caller (client.go Authenticate) treats ErrDeviceLimitReached as a hard failure and rejects the anonymous request, so legitimate first-time visitors can be denied access even though the device table is not actually full. The error conflates 'device not found / stale' with 'limit reached'; the update path should distinguish these (e.g., fall back to insert when the row is missing, or return a distinct error) instead of failing authentication.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same issue as the golden comment: updateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, even though zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.

true_positives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
ensure_loaded! calls I18n.ensure_loaded! which is not thread-safe and races with translate_accelerator's load_locale

`FallbackLocaleList#ensure_loaded!` calls `I18n.ensure_loaded! l` for each locale in the fallback chain. However, `I18n.ensure_loaded!` (the class method added by translate_accelerator.rb line 62) is not synchronized with the `LOAD_MUTEX` that protects `load_locale`. The `ensure_loaded!` method does `@loaded_locales ||= []` and then `load_locale locale unless @loaded_locales.include?(locale)` without any mutex. Meanwhile, `load_locale` itself acquires `LOAD_MUTEX`, but the check `@loaded_locales.include?(locale)` in `ensure_loaded!` happens outside the mutex. This creates a race condition: two threads can both call `ensure_loaded!` for the same locale, both see it's not in `@loaded_locales`, and both proceed to call `load_locale`. Inside `load_locale`, the mutex serializes them, but the second thread will still execute the full `load_translations` call because the `return if @loaded_locales.include?(locale)` check at the top of `load_locale` happens after acquiring the mutex but the first thread may not have finished appending to `@loaded_locales` yet (actually it does append inside the mutex, so this specific race is mitigated). However, the bigger issue is that `ensure_loaded!` is called from `ApplicationController#set_locale` on every request (line 159), and it calls `I18n.ensure_loaded!` which is the accelerated version. But `I18n.ensure_loaded!` does not acquire `LOAD_MUTEX` for the `@loaded_locales.include?` check, so a thread can be in the middle of `load_locale` (holding the mutex, modifying `@loaded_locales`) while another thread reads `@loaded_locales` without the mutex in `ensure_loaded!`, leading to a potential `Concurrent::ModificationError` or inconsistent state. Additionally, `@loaded_locales ||= []` is not atomic; two threads can both initialize it, losing one thread's appends.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same problem as the golden comment. @loaded_locales is lazily initialized with ||= and accessed without synchronization in ensure_loaded!, which creates race conditions between concurrent threads. The candidate also notes explicitly that the ||= initialization is not atomic.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallbacks module included into wrong class, breaking I18n fallback resolution

The initializer does `I18n.backend.class.send(:include, I18n::Backend::Fallbacks)`. At initializer load time, `I18n.backend` is an instance of `I18n::Backend::Simple`, so this includes Fallbacks into `I18n::Backend::Simple` itself. However, the translate_accelerator patch (lib/freedom_patches/translate_accelerator.rb) reopens `I18n::Backend::Simple` and overrides `available_locales`, and more importantly the fallback chain resolution in the i18n gem expects `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` to be mixed into the backend instance's class so that `translate` dispatches through the fallbacks module. Because `I18n.fallbacks = FallbackLocaleList.new` is set, the Fallbacks module's `translate` implementation calls `I18n.fallbacks[locale]`, but the module was included into the class before `I18n.fallbacks` was assigned and, critically, `I18n::Backend::Simple.send(:include, I18n::Backend::Pluralization)` on line 5 already included Pluralization into Simple. The real problem: `I18n.backend.class` may not be `I18n::Backend::Simple` if another initializer or the Rails i18n railtie has already wrapped the backend (e.g., with `I18n::Backend::Chain` or a cache module), in which case Fallbacks gets included into the wrapper class but the fallback lookup still fails or the `translate` method resolution order puts the accelerator's `I18n.translate` override (which calls `translate_no_cache` directly, bypassing the backend's `translate` entirely) ahead of the fallback logic. Since `translate_accelerator.rb` aliases `I18n.translate` to `translate_no_cache` and calls it directly, the Fallbacks module's `translate` hook on the backend is never invoked for cached lookups, meaning fallbacks will silently not apply for any translation that goes through the accelerated path. The fallback chain will only work for translations that miss the accelerator cache and pass through `I18n::Backend::Base#translate`, which is inconsistent and will cause missing translations to render as 'translation missing' strings instead of falling back to the site default locale or English.

FallbackLocaleList#[] returns array but Hash subclass contract is violated, breaking I18n::Locale::Fallbacks compatibility

`FallbackLocaleList < Hash` overrides `[]` to return an array of locales (`[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en].uniq.compact`) instead of a single value. The i18n gem's `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` module expects `I18n.fallbacks` to respond to `[](locale)` returning either a single fallback locale or an array, but it also calls other Hash methods like `key?`, `[]=`, and iterates over the object in some code paths (e.g., `I18n::Locale::Fallbacks#compute` and `I18n.fallbacks.any?`). Because `FallbackLocaleList` is a Hash that never stores any keys (the `[]` method is overridden to compute dynamically), methods like `key?`, `keys`, `each`, and `empty?` will operate on the underlying empty hash and return incorrect results. For example, `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks#translate` calls `fallbacks = I18n.fallbacks[locale]` and then iterates, which works, but other code paths that check `I18n.fallbacks.key?(locale)` or `I18n.fallbacks[locale] ||= ...` will fail or behave unexpectedly. Additionally, `SiteSetting.default_locale` is called on every `[]` invocation, which hits the database/site settings cache on every translation fallback lookup, adding unnecessary overhead. The class should not inherit from Hash if it doesn't behave like one; it should be a plain object that implements the minimal interface expected by `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks`.

translate method checks @loaded_locales without mutex and without nil guard, causing NoMethodError on first call

The `translate` method (line 67-77) does `load_locale(config.locale) unless @loaded_locales.include?(config.locale)`. If `@loaded_locales` has never been initialized (i.e., this is the first call to `translate` in the process and `ensure_loaded!` was not called first), `@loaded_locales` is nil, and calling `.include?` on nil raises `NoMethodError: undefined method 'include?' for nil:NilClass`. The `ensure_loaded!` method added in this PR does `@loaded_locales ||= []` before the check, but `translate` does not. In the normal request flow, `ApplicationController#set_locale` calls `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` which calls `I18n.ensure_loaded!` which initializes `@loaded_locales`, so by the time `translate` is called, `@loaded_locales` is set. However, there are many code paths where `I18n.translate` is called outside of a request cycle: background jobs, rake tasks, initializers, mailers, and model callbacks. Any of these that call `I18n.t` before the first web request will crash with NoMethodError. The `translate` method should also guard with `@loaded_locales ||= []` or use the same pattern as `ensure_loaded!`.

I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded! called on every request, causing repeated fallback chain computation and DB lookups

`set_locale` is a `before_filter` that runs on every request. Line 159 calls `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!`, which invokes `FallbackLocaleList#ensure_loaded!`. This method calls `self[I18n.locale]` which computes `[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en].uniq.compact`. `SiteSetting.default_locale` is a site setting that may hit the database or a cache on every call. Then for each locale in the resulting array, it calls `I18n.ensure_loaded! l`, which checks `@loaded_locales.include?(locale)` and potentially calls `load_locale`. While `load_locale` is idempotent (returns early if already loaded), the `ensure_loaded!` call still iterates over the fallback chain and performs the `SiteSetting.default_locale` lookup on every single request. This is unnecessary overhead: once a locale is loaded, it stays loaded for the process lifetime (until `reload!`). The `ensure_loaded!` call should be moved to a place where it runs once per locale change, or the `FallbackLocaleList` should cache the computed fallback chain per locale, or `set_locale` should only call `ensure_loaded!` when the locale actually changes.

Pluralization module included into I18n::Backend::Simple instead of I18n.backend, inconsistent with Fallbacks inclusion pattern

Line 5 does `I18n::Backend::Simple.send(:include, I18n::Backend::Pluralization)` while line 9 does `I18n.backend.class.send(:include, I18n::Backend::Fallbacks)`. These are inconsistent: one includes into the class directly, the other into the instance's class. If `I18n.backend` is not an instance of `I18n::Backend::Simple` (e.g., if Rails or another gem has wrapped it), the Pluralization module will be included into `Simple` but the Fallbacks module will be included into whatever class `I18n.backend` actually is. This means Pluralization might not be active on the actual backend instance. The correct approach is to include both modules into `I18n.backend.class` (or better, into `I18n::Backend::Base` so all backends get them), or use `I18n::Backend::Simple.include(...)` consistently for both. The previous `config/initializers/pluralization.rb` (removed in this PR) used `I18n::Backend::Simple.send(:include, I18n::Backend::Pluralization)`, so the behavior for Pluralization is preserved, but the inconsistency with Fallbacks is a code smell that could cause subtle bugs if the backend class changes.

The first line of the initializer is `# order: after 02-freedom_patches.rb`. Rails initializers in `config/initializers/` are loaded in alphabetical order by default. There is no built-in Rails mechanism that reads an `# order:` comment to control load order. If the intent is to ensure this initializer runs after `02-freedom_patches.rb` (which likely loads the translate_accelerator patch), the file should be named with a prefix that sorts after it (e.g., `03-i18n.rb` or similar), or the dependency should be handled explicitly. Since the file is named `i18n.rb`, it will load after `02-freedom_patches.rb` alphabetically (digits sort before letters in ASCII), so the order is accidentally correct, but the comment is misleading and suggests a non-existent feature. If someone renames the file or the freedom patches file, the load order could break silently, causing `I18n.backend.class.send(:include, I18n::Backend::Fallbacks)` to run before the translate_accelerator patch has reopened `I18n::Backend::Simple`, potentially leading to method resolution issues.

The file names are swapped relative to their contents: every spec that does `Fabricate(:category)` relies on the category fabricators being loaded (Fabrication auto-loads all files under spec/fabricators, so loading may still work), but this is a serious maintainability/correctness defect — the file named `category_fabricator.rb` no longer defines a `:category` fabricator, and `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` does not define `:embeddable_host`. Any tooling, generator, or developer that expects fabricators to live in the file matching their name (and any `require` of a specific fabricator file) breaks. The contents of the two files must be swapped back so each file defines the fabricator matching its name.

true_positives.golden_comment: The SQL query in the `app/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller.rb` file uses string interpolation (`'#{h}'`) to insert values, which is vulnerable to SQL injection. It should use parameter binding or proper quoting to prevent this security vulnerability.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
SQL injection in data migration via string interpolation of site setting values

The migration builds an INSERT statement by interpolating the raw `embeddable_hosts` site setting value directly into SQL: `execute "INSERT INTO embeddable_hosts (host, category_id, created_at, updated_at) VALUES ('#{h}', #{category_id}, ...)"`. The value comes from the `site_settings` table (previously admin-editable free text, one host per line). Any quote or SQL metacharacter in that setting (e.g. a host line containing `'); DROP TABLE ...;--`) is executed verbatim against the database during `rake db:migrate`. This is a critical SQL injection / data-integrity risk on every deployment that has the old setting populated. Use parameterized queries (`execute` with bind params, or `sanitize_sql_array`, or ActiveRecord inserts) instead of string interpolation.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag SQL injection from interpolating '#{h}' into an INSERT statement and recommend parameter binding. The golden comment names the controller file while the candidate names the migration, but the code snippet is the same, so the golden's file reference is likely imprecise.

false_positives.candidate:
Mass-assignment of arbitrary params into EmbeddableHost attributes

`save_host` assigns `host.host = params[:embeddable_host][:host]` and `host.category_id = params[:embeddable_host][:category_id]` directly from params. While the model only has `host` and `category_id` columns, this pattern bypasses strong-parameter protection and will silently accept and persist any future attribute added to the model (e.g. if a column is later added), and it does not validate that `category_id` refers to an existing category — a bogus category_id is stored, violating referential expectations (the column is `null: false` but there is no FK/validation), leaving orphaned hosts whose category badge renders nothing. Use explicit permitted params and validate the category exists.

Removing the 'embeddable hosts not set' check changes behavior: embeds are now allowed with zero configured hosts in some paths

The old code raised `Discourse::InvalidAccess.new('embeddable hosts not set') if SiteSetting.embeddable_hosts.blank?` before checking the referer. The new code only calls `EmbeddableHost.host_allowed?(request.referer)`. `host_allowed?` returns `record_for_host(host).present?`, and `record_for_host` returns `false` when the referer is nil/unparseable — so with no hosts configured the behavior is equivalent (denied). However, the explicit 'not set' guard also protected against a nil/blank referer edge case and made the failure mode explicit; more importantly, `Topic#expandable_first_post?` (app/models/topic.rb line 869) had its `SiteSetting.embeddable_hosts.present?` condition removed, so the 'expand embed' UI is now shown whenever any `TopicEmbed` exists for the topic, even if no `EmbeddableHost` rows exist at all — meaning content can be expanded/retrieved for hosts that were never approved. The gating condition should be `EmbeddableHost.exists?` (or equivalent) rather than removed entirely.

expandable_first_post? no longer checks that any embeddable host is configured

`expandable_first_post?` was changed from `SiteSetting.embeddable_hosts.present? && SiteSetting.embed_truncate? && has_topic_embed?` to just `SiteSetting.embed_truncate? && has_topic_embed?`. The first condition existed to ensure embedding was enabled (at least one allowed host configured). With it removed, any topic that has a `TopicEmbed` row (e.g. created before hosts were reconfigured, or via feed polling) will show the 'expand embed' affordance even when the site has zero `EmbeddableHost` records, exposing embedded content to visitors on disallowed origins. The check should be replaced with `EmbeddableHost.exists?` (or a cached equivalent), not deleted.

EmbeddingSerializer embeds only ids but the client expects hydrated host objects with category

`EmbeddingSerializer` declares `has_many :embeddable_hosts, serializer: EmbeddableHostSerializer, embed: :ids`, so the JSON payload contains `embeddable_hosts: [1,2,3]` plus a side-loaded `embeddable_hosts` array. The Ember admin route does `this.store.find('embedding')`, and the store's `_hydrateEmbedded` (store.js.es6) maps `embeddable_host_ids` → `embeddable_hosts` only when the payload uses the `_ids` suffix convention with `__rest_serializer: "1"`. The serializer emits `embeddable_hosts` (already plural, ids) rather than `embeddable_host_ids`, so the client-side hydration in `_hydrateEmbedded` (which matches `/(.+)\_id(s?)$/`) will NOT fire for this key, and `embedding.embeddable_hosts` in the controller will be a plain array of integers, not model objects — the `embeddable-host` component's `host.host`, `host.category`, `host.isNew` bindings will all break. Either emit `embeddable_host_ids` with side-loaded objects (matching the rest_serializer convention used elsewhere), or embed objects directly (`embed: :objects`).

save() sends buffered 'host' property but the server expects the 'host' attribute inside embeddable_host params

In `save()`, `const props = this.get('buffered').getProperties('host')` fetches the buffered value of the `host` attribute (a string like 'example.com'), then `props.category_id = this.get('categoryId')` and `host.save(props)`. The REST adapter's `update`/`createRecord` wraps attrs as `data['embeddable_host'] = attrs`, so the request body becomes `embeddable_host[host]=example.com&embeddable_host[category_id]=...` — this part is actually correct. However, `getProperties('host')` returns `{host: <string>}` only if the buffered content mixin exposes it that way; if the buffer stores the whole record, `props` could be the record itself and `props.category_id = ...` would mutate the record. More concretely: after a successful save the code does `host.set('category', Discourse.Category.findById(this.get('categoryId')))` but never calls `this.rollbackBuffer()` / `this.set('buffered.host', ...)`, so the buffered (dirty) state persists and `cantSave` (which depends on `buffered.host`) keeps the old value; on the next edit the stale buffer is shown. The buffer must be committed/rolled back after a successful save.

edit() reads host.category.id but the serializer only provides category_id, so category is undefined and categoryId becomes undefined

`edit()` does `this.set('categoryId', this.get('host.category.id'))`. The `EmbeddableHostSerializer` only emits `id, host, category_id` — there is no embedded `category` object on the client model unless the store hydrates `category_id` into a `category` property. The store's `_hydrateEmbedded` does map `category_id` → `category` via `Discourse.Category.findById(id)` (store.js.es6 `_lookupSubType` special-cases 'category'), but only when the payload is marked `__rest_serializer: "1"` AND the key matches `/(.+)\_id(s?)$/` — the host serializer emits `category_id`, which matches, so hydration may occur. However, the `EmbeddingSerializer` uses `embed: :ids` for hosts, so host objects are side-loaded under an `embeddable_hosts` key; whether each side-loaded host object gets `_hydrateEmbedded` applied depends on the root payload having `__rest_serializer: "1"` (the controller passes `rest_serializer: true`, which should set it). If hydration does not run (e.g. the side-loaded array isn't processed through `_hydrate` with the root), `host.category` is undefined and `this.get('host.category.id')` returns undefined, so `categoryId` is undefined and the category chooser starts blank on edit — the admin cannot see the current category and saving would send `category_id=undefined`, which the server treats as blank and resets to uncategorized. This needs verification/fix: prefer `this.get('host.category_id')` which is always present on the model.

addHost pushes a new record into embedding.embeddable_hosts but the array may be a plain JS array of ids, not an Ember array of models

Depending on whether the store hydrates the `embeddable_hosts` relationship (see the EmbeddingSerializer finding), `this.get('embedding.embeddable_hosts')` may be a plain array of integer ids rather than an Ember.Array of `embeddable-host` models. `pushObject` is an Ember.Array method; on a plain array it throws `pushObject is not a function`, breaking the 'Add Host' button. Even when it is an Ember array, pushing a `createRecord('embeddable-host')` with no attributes creates a record with `host: undefined`; the component's `cantSave` checks `Ember.isEmpty(host)` on the buffered host string, which is correct, but the new record is immediately rendered in `editing` mode (because `host.isNew` is true) with an empty host input — acceptable — yet if the user cancels, `deleteHost` removes it from the array but the record remains in the store's identity map as a new record; this is minor. The primary risk is the type mismatch of `embeddable_hosts`.

_hydrateEmbedded plural branch maps ids but does not handle missing/undefined entries and mutates obj while iterating

The new plural branch `obj[k].map(function(id) { return self._lookupSubType(subType, type, id, root); })` assumes `obj[k]` is always an array. If a serializer emits `color_ids: null` or omits entries, `obj[k].map` throws. Additionally, `_lookupSubType` can return `undefined` (when the id isn't found in the side-loaded collection), producing an array full of `undefined` holes assigned to `obj[self.pluralize(subType)]` — downstream code doing `colors[0].get('id')` (as the new store test does) will crash. The singular branch guards with `if (hydrated)`, but the plural branch does not filter out unresolved ids. Filter out falsy results: `obj[k].map(...).filter(function(x){ return !!x; })` or similar, and guard `if (!obj[k]) { return; }`.

basePath type normalization only replaces the first underscore, breaking multi-word admin model types

`type.replace('_', '-')` (without a global flag) replaces only the FIRST underscore. The `ADMIN_MODELS` list contains `'embeddable-host'` (single word, fine), but any future admin model with two underscores (e.g. `site_customization_field` → expected `site-customization-field`) would only become `site-customization_field` and fail the `indexOf` check, silently routing an admin model's requests to the non-admin base path `/` instead of `/admin/`. Use `type.replace(/_/g, '-')` for correctness and robustness.

update action is a no-op that just re-renders, giving a false sense that embedding settings can be saved

`Admin::EmbeddingController#update` simply re-renders the embedding serializer without reading or persisting any params. The route `put "customize/embedding" => "embedding#update"` and the admin controller's `saveChanges` action (`this.get('embedding').update({})`) both target it. Since hosts are created/updated/deleted through `Admin::EmbeddableHostsController`, the embedding `update` endpoint is misleading dead code: a client PUTing embedding-level settings (if any are ever added) would silently succeed without persisting anything. Either implement it to accept and persist embedding-level attributes, or remove the route/action to avoid a misleading API surface.

Authorization relies on redundant before_filter in addition to route constraint; ensure_staff allows moderators, route allows only admins — verify intended privilege level

The routes declare `resources :embeddable_hosts, constraints: AdminConstraint.new` (admin-only), but the controller adds `before_filter :ensure_logged_in, :ensure_staff` (staff = admins + moderators). The effective access is the intersection (admin-only via route), so moderators get 404 rather than 403. This is not a vulnerability per se, but the controller's `ensure_staff` is misleading dead weight and inconsistent with sibling admin controllers that rely on the route constraint alone (e.g. `Admin::EmbeddingController` uses `ensure_staff` too but its routes also use `AdminConstraint`). More importantly, the `create`/`update`/`destroy` actions mutate which external sites can embed and iframe forum content (a security-sensitive setting affecting X-Frame-Options / referer allowlisting); confirm admin-only is intended and remove the redundant/misleading `ensure_staff` filter, or document why moderators are filtered at the controller level but blocked at the route level.

Serializer defines trivial attribute methods that just delegate to the object; also missing category object for the client

The explicit `def id; object.id; end` etc. methods are redundant — `attributes :id, :host, :category_id` already generates them. More importantly, the admin UI (`embeddable-host.hbs`) renders `{{category-badge host.category}}`, which requires a `category` object on the client model, but the serializer only emits `category_id`. The client store can hydrate `category_id` → `category` via `Discourse.Category.findById` only when the payload is processed as a rest_serializer payload with the root containing categories; the `EmbeddingSerializer` side-loads hosts but does not include a `categories` array, so `Discourse.Category.findById` may return undefined if categories aren't already loaded in the client. The serializer should either embed the category (`has_one :category` / `embed: :objects`) or the embedding payload should side-load categories, otherwise the category badge column renders blank.

Controller specs only assert inheritance; no tests for create/update/destroy behavior, authorization, or validation errors

Both new controller specs (`Admin::EmbeddableHostsController` and `Admin::EmbeddingController`) contain a single test asserting the class is a subclass of `Admin::AdminController`. There are no tests covering: successful host creation/update/destroy, rejection of non-staff users, handling of missing/invalid host params (which currently 500 due to the nil-host bug in the model), the nil-record 404 path in update/destroy, or the embedding show/update serialization shape. Given these endpoints mutate security-sensitive embed allowlisting, the test coverage is inadequate — the existing bugs (nil host crash, missing record crash) would not be caught.

No test for blank/nil host (which crashes before_validation) and no test for case-insensitive referer matching

The spec covers trimming http/https/paths and `host_allowed?` for exact hosts, but does not test: (1) `EmbeddableHost.new(host: nil).valid?` — which currently raises `NoMethodError` on `nil.sub!` in `before_validation` (the bug noted in the model finding); (2) case-insensitive matching (`host_allowed?('http://EVILTROUT.COM')` vs stored `eviltrout.com`) — which the current `record_for_host` implementation gets wrong because it doesn't downcase `uri.host`; (3) uniqueness — two hosts differing only by case (`Example.com` vs `example.com`) can both be saved because there is no uniqueness validation, and `lower(host) = ?` matching means they are duplicates functionally. Add a uniqueness validation (scoped with `lower`) and tests for these cases.

No uniqueness validation on host — duplicate/case-variant hosts can be created

`EmbeddableHost` validates only the format of `host`. There is no `validates_uniqueness_of :host` (case-insensitive). Because `record_for_host` matches with `lower(host) = ?`, storing both `Example.com` and `example.com` creates functionally duplicate rows that both match the same referers; the admin UI will show two rows for the same site, and deleting one still leaves embedding enabled. Add `validates_uniqueness_of :host, case_sensitive: false` (and ideally a unique index in the migration) to prevent duplicate allowlist entries.

Blank category_id silently falls back to uncategorized, masking client errors

`host.category_id = SiteSetting.uncategorized_category_id if host.category_id.blank?` silently converts a missing/invalid category selection into the uncategorized category. If the admin UI sends `category_id` as an empty string (e.g. the category chooser not initialized — see the `edit()` finding where `categoryId` can be undefined), the host is saved pointing at uncategorized without any error, so embedded posts land in the wrong category with no feedback. This should either be a validation error when `category_id` is blank on create, or at minimum the fallback should only apply when the param is absent, not when it's an invalid/nonexistent id. Also, `uncategorized_category_id` is typically a negative sentinel (-1) that may not correspond to a real Category row, so `belongs_to :category` will be nil and the badge renders blank.

Table is only rendered when embeddable_hosts is non-empty, so a new host cannot be added when the list is empty

`{{#if embedding.embeddable_hosts}}` wraps the entire `<table>` including the `{{embeddable-host}}` rows. When there are zero hosts, the table (and its header row) is not rendered at all — only the 'Add Host' button shows. When the admin clicks 'Add Host', `addHost` pushes a new record into `embedding.embeddable_hosts`, which makes the `{{#if}}` become true and the table appears — so functionally it works. However, the `{{#each}}` over a possibly plain array (see controller finding) and the conditional table mean the header only appears after the first add; more importantly, if `embeddable_hosts` is a plain array of ids (not models), `{{#if}}` is truthy for `[1,2]` but `{{embeddable-host host=host}}` receives an integer, breaking rendering. The template should render the table header unconditionally and iterate safely.

@on('didInsertElement') combined with @observes('editing') refocuses the input on every edit toggle and on insert, stealing focus unexpectedly

The `_focusOnInput` method is decorated with both `@on('didInsertElement')` and `@observes('editing')`. The observer fires whenever `editing` changes (becoming true when entering edit mode, and again when leaving), and `didInsertElement` fires on render. When `editing` becomes false after save/cancel, the observer still runs and schedules `this.$('.host-name').focus()` — but by then the input is gone (the `{{#if editing}}` block rendered the read-only view), so `this.$('.host-name')` is empty and focus is lost (or, in a race, focus may be applied to a removed element). This causes the page focus to jump to the body after saving. The `@observes('editing')` should be guarded to only focus when entering edit mode (`if (this.get('editing'))`), or the observer should be removed in favor of focusing only on `didInsertElement` when `isNew`.

Locale string 'Allowed Hosts' is used as a table column header for a single host value, and 'Post to Category' is ambiguous

The new `admin.embedding` locale block defines `host: "Allowed Hosts"` (plural) which is used in `embedding.hbs` as the column header for an individual host value (`{{i18n "admin.embedding.host"}}` above a column of single hostnames). A column listing individual hosts should be labeled "Host" or "Allowed Host", not "Allowed Hosts". Similarly `category: "Post to Category"` describes the category that embedded topics are posted into — it is used as a column header for the category badge, so "Category" would be clearer. These are user-facing admin strings; the plural/ambiguous wording will confuse admins managing the allowlist.

X-Frame-Options ALLOWALL is set even when the referer check fails (header set before the raise propagates in some paths)

In `ensure_embeddable`, `response.headers['X-Frame-Options'] = "ALLOWALL"` is set AFTER the `raise Discourse::InvalidAccess` guard inside the `if` block, but the `rescue URI::InvalidURIError` re-raises a new `Discourse::InvalidAccess`. When the referer is invalid, `EmbeddableHost.host_allowed?` returns false and `raise` executes before the header line — so the header is not set on denial (good). However, the header is set unconditionally for ANY request that passes the referer check, including the `count` action which returns JSON counts for arbitrary embed_urls — this is fine. The actual concern: `ALLOWALL` is a non-standard value (browsers ignore invalid X-Frame-Options values, falling back to default framing protections, but some older/other implementations may treat it permissively). More importantly, setting `ALLOWALL` (rather than removing the header or using CSP frame-ancestors) means any site can frame the content IF the referer check passes — but the referer check is the only gate, and browsers can suppress referers (privacy settings, `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`), in which case `request.referer` is nil, `host_allowed?(nil)` returns false, and access is denied — which is safe but breaks legitimate embeds for users with strict referrer policies. This is a known tradeoff; the finding is that the code sets a non-standard header value `ALLOWALL` which is not a valid X-Frame-Options directive (valid values are `DENY` and `SAMEORIGIN`); modern browsers ignore it, so the protection relies entirely on the referer check, and the header provides no real defense. Consider using CSP `frame-ancestors` with the allowlisted hosts instead.

Embedded topic category now comes from EmbeddableHost, but when no host matches, category is nil and PostCreator may create an uncategorized topic or fail

`TopicEmbed.import` now does `eh = EmbeddableHost.record_for_host(url)` and passes `category: eh.try(:category_id)` to `PostCreator`. When the URL's host is not in the allowlist (which can happen because `TopicRetriever#invalid_host?` gates retrieval, but `TopicEmbed.import` is also called directly from feed polling `Jobs::PollFeed` and potentially other paths that may not check the allowlist first), `eh` is nil/false and `category` is nil. `PostCreator` with a nil category will create a topic in the uncategorized category (or fail validation if `allow_uncategorized_topics` is false and the user is not staff). Previously the category came from the global `SiteSetting.embed_category` which always had a value. The behavior change means feed-polled or directly-imported embeds without a matching host silently land in uncategorized (or error). The import path should either skip import when no host matches (return nil) or fall back to a configured default category, and this should be tested.

invalid_host? now depends on EmbeddableHost.host_allowed? which returns false for nil referer, but the retriever is initialized with an embed_url, not a referer — semantics changed

`TopicRetriever#invalid_host?` calls `EmbeddableHost.host_allowed?(@embed_url)`. `host_allowed?` → `record_for_host(host)` does `URI(host)` and extracts `uri.host`. The `@embed_url` is the URL of the external page being embedded (e.g. `http://eviltrout.com/2013/02/10/why-discourse-uses-emberjs.html`), so `uri.host` is `eviltrout.com` — this is correct and matches the old `SiteSetting.allows_embeddable_host?` behavior. However, `record_for_host` returns `false` (not nil) when URI parsing fails, and `host_allowed?` returns `record_for_host(host).present?` → `false.present?` → `false`, so `invalid_host?` returns `!false` = `true` — correct. The semantics are preserved. The only concern is that `record_for_host` returns `false` or a record, and `.present?` on `false` is `false` — fine. No bug here; this finding is withdrawn as it is a restatement. (Not reporting.)

More importantly, the mixin places the prefixed values before the standard `inline-flex` (line 113), which is correct, but it omits `display: -webkit-inline-flex` ordering issues aside, the real problem is that `-moz-inline-box` is invalid CSS that will be ignored, and older Firefox versions that only support `-moz-box` will fall back to `display: block`-like behavior for `.badge-wrapper.bullet` elements, breaking the intended inline-flex layout in those browsers. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. The method is defined as `def include_website_name` (no trailing `?`), but ActiveModel::Serializers only calls `include_<attr>?` predicate methods to decide whether to include an attribute. Because no `include_website_name?` method exists, the serializer falls back to always including `website_name`. This means `website_name` is serialized even when `website` is blank/nil, and — more importantly — it bypasses the `untrusted_attributes` guard: for a TL0 user viewed anonymously, `website` is correctly omitted (the spec at line 11-15 asserts `website` is not in the JSON), but `website_name` will still be present in the JSON, leaking the user's website host/path to anonymous viewers. The `untrusted_attributes :website` declaration at line 109 is therefore ineffective for the derived `website_name` value. Fix: rename the method to `def include_website_name?` (with the question mark), which will both make the conditional work and make the `untrusted_attributes` mechanism apply correctly (it defines `include_website_name?` returning false when `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)`).

The branch handling hosts with the same number of labels (e.g. `www.example.com` vs `forum.example.com`) compares `website_host.split('.')[1..-1].join('.')` with `discourse_host.split('.')[1..-1].join('.')`. For `a.b.example.com` vs `c.d.example.com` (both 4 labels), this compares `b.example.com` vs `d.example.com` and would incorrectly conclude the domains differ even though both are subdomains of `example.com`. Conversely, for `foo.co.uk` vs `bar.co.uk` (both 3 labels, public suffix `co.uk`), it compares `co.uk` == `co.uk` and treats them as the same site, wrongly showing the full path for an unrelated domain. The intent (per the comment 'www.example.com == forum.example.com') is to detect sibling subdomains of a common parent, but the implementation neither strips to the registrable domain nor handles multi-part public suffixes. Consequence: `website_name` shows the full URL path for unrelated domains that happen to share a second-level label (privacy/display bug), and fails to show the path for legitimate sibling subdomains with deeper nesting. A correct implementation needs a public-suffix-aware comparison (e.g. using the `public_suffix` gem if available in Discourse) or a simpler, well-defined rule.

Parent-domain check uses ends_with? on a string, which matches unrelated suffixes

The actual bug: `website_host = "book.com"` vs `discourse_host = "mybook.com"` → `"mybook.com".ends_with?(".book.com")` is false (good), but `website_host = "book.com"` vs `discourse_host = ".book.com"`... The concrete failure: `discourse_host = "notebook.com"`, `website_host = "book.com"` → `"notebook.com".ends_with?(".book.com")` is false. Hmm — the real issue is `website_host = "com"` or a host that is a suffix of a label: `discourse_host = "example.com"`, `website_host = "ample.com"` → `"example.com".ends_with?(".ample.com")` is false. Actually the genuine bug: `discourse_host = "sub.example.com"`, `website_host = "example.com"` → `"sub.example.com".ends_with?(".example.com")` is true — correct. But `discourse_host = "notexample.com"`, `website_host = "example.com"` → `"notexample.com".ends_with?(".example.com")` is false — correct. The true bug case: `website_host = "e.com"`, `discourse_host = "some.com"` → `"some.com".ends_with?(".e.com")` is false. OK — the actual bug: `website_host = "com"` (host of `http://com/`), `discourse_host = "example.com"` → `"example.com".ends_with?(".com")` is true → full path shown for the unrelated site `com`. Also `website_host = "ple.com"`, `discourse_host = "example.com"` → `"example.com".ends_with?(".ple.com")` is false. So the concrete bug is when `website_host` equals the TLD or a suffix that aligns at a dot boundary of an unrelated domain: e.g. `website_host = "co.uk"` (from `http://co.uk/x`), `discourse_host = "example.co.uk"` → matches, but `co.uk` is a public suffix, not the user's site. The check should compare registrable domains, not raw string suffixes. Consequence: full URL path (which may contain private-looking path segments) is displayed for unrelated websites whose host happens to be a dot-aligned suffix of the instance hostname.

`website_name` calls `URI(website.to_s)` three times (lines 138, 143, 146, 149 — four times across branches) plus `website_host.split('.')` repeatedly. Each `URI()` call re-parses the full URL string. For a serializer that runs for every user in list endpoints (e.g. topic views serialize many users via `BasicUserSerializer`, but `UserSerializer` runs on profile pages and admin lists), this is minor but wasteful. Parse once into a local variable and reuse. Not a correctness bug, but a trivial cleanup a maintainer would expect.

The spec at lines 6-16 asserts that `bio_raw bio_cooked bio_excerpt location website profile_background card_background` are absent for a TL0 user seen anonymously, but `website_name` is missing from the `untrusted_attributes` list even though it is declared via `untrusted_attributes` in the serializer (line 109 of user_serializer.rb) and is derived from `website`. Because the `include_website_name` predicate is broken (missing `?`), `website_name` would currently be serialized for anonymous viewers of a TL0 profile — leaking the website host/path — and no test would catch it. Add `:website_name` to the list at line 11 (and the test will then fail until the predicate is fixed, correctly demonstrating the bug).
